China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:14:51 UTC
02:14:51 KST

China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Artificial intelligence is becoming a defining force in economic development, international competition, and national security. While striving to develop more powerful AI systems, China also seeks to determine how they should be governed, shared, and secured in a rapidly changing world.
A technology shaping China – and the world
By June 2026, the number of users of AI products in China had exceeded 500 million, underscoring the technology’s growing reach in one of the world’s largest digital economies. Together with the US, China is a key engine of AI development and innovation. Its domestic choices and international initiatives have consequences well beyond its borders.
At the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping advanced proposals for more inclusive AI cooperation, industrial development, and technological exchange. At the same time, State Security Minister Chen Yixin set out a national security perspective that places AI at the center of strategic competition and calls for stronger safeguards.
China’s AI policy combines the pursuit of international openness with domestic security governance. Understanding how Beijing seeks to reconcile these objectives is essential to understanding its ambitions for AI – and the emerging global order around it.
Xi’s BRICS vision: AI as a shared opportunity
Xi’s proposals at the New Delhi summit place AI cooperation within a broader effort to connect technological development with economic growth and international inclusion. The emphasis is on widening access to the capabilities, skills, and industrial networks that make AI economically useful.
China has proposed taking a pioneering role in establishing a BRICS AI open-source community, supporting cooperation on the development and application of large language models, and organizing specialized seminars and training courses. The stated objective is to build an open ecosystem in which countries can exchange knowledge and expand their capacity to develop and use AI.
This approach is particularly relevant for emerging economies. Access to AI requires not only the availability of software, but also computing infrastructure, technical expertise, investment, and the ability to adapt technologies to local needs. Open-source collaboration and skills development can help accessibility, although they cannot by themselves eliminate disparities in resources or technological capabilities.
Xi’s digital industry cooperation initiative extends the same idea into the infrastructure and skills underpinning the digital economy. China has proposed a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, alongside digital skills training, technological exchange, and industrial alignment.
A third proposal focuses on AI-enabled new industrialization. Here, the objective is to deepen cooperation in research and development, practical applications, and industrial and supply chains.
Taken together, these initiatives present AI as a means of expanding productive capacity. For BRICS members, the proposals raise practical questions about how to share expertise, develop compatible infrastructure, and translate technological cooperation into tangible industrial outcomes.
Chen Yixin’s warning
Xi’s international cooperation agenda coincides with a more security-focused assessment from Chen Yixin, China’s minister of state security. In an article published during the summit, Chen described AI as a central arena of global scientific and technological competition and a new front in strategic rivalry among major powers.
Chen’s argument begins with a dual imperative: innovation must be the primary driving force, while security must remain a bottom-line requirement. In this framing, AI is simultaneously an engine of economic and social transformation and a technology capable of changing the conditions of national security.
His assessment identifies several interconnected risks. AI-generated content, including deepfakes and automated online activity, could affect political security by enabling the rapid production and dissemination of misleading information. Chen also warns that AI may transform cyber operations, making it easier to identify vulnerabilities, develop malicious software, and automate elements of complex attacks.
Another concern is the potential for AI-assisted data collection and analysis to amplify espionage and information-security risks. Chen points to the possibility of sensitive government data, commercial secrets, and personal information being gathered or exposed through intelligent crawling, data mining, and profiling.
He also identifies structural challenges: concentration of technological capabilities could deepen inequalities between countries, while AI-driven decision-making could strain existing systems of social governance. In the military sphere, he argues that AI is helping move warfare toward an increasingly intelligent era, with implications for sensing, decision-making, and targeting.
These concerns are not confined to China. Cybersecurity, data protection, misinformation, military applications, and the concentration of technological power are subjects of international debate. What distinguishes Chen’s article is the way it brings them together under a comprehensive national security framework.
From principles to institutions
Chen calls for AI security to be integrated into other key areas of national security, supported by stronger cross-sector cooperation and improved capacity to identify and anticipate emerging risks. He also calls for an AI safety supervision platform, expanded risk assessment and monitoring, and greater investment in fundamental research and core technologies, including computing chips, development frameworks, and application software. His article advocates strengthening AI infrastructure while reducing vulnerabilities associated with dependence on critical technologies.
Chen advocates the implementation of China’s Cybersecurity Law and Counter-Espionage Law, alongside further development of rules addressing AI research, applications, data protection, algorithmic security, and accountability. He also emphasizes public communication and national security awareness.
These measures reflect Beijing’s view that AI governance cannot be separated from overarching questions of technological self-reliance, data control, and national security, and that when it comes to AI, innovation has to be inseparable from oversight.
A global governance agenda
China’s domestic security priorities sit alongside an international agenda that predates the New Delhi summit. Its 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative calls for people-centered development, international cooperation, respect for national sovereignty, and broader access to AI technologies. It also advocates risk-based governance, privacy and data protection, human oversight, and greater representation for developing countries.
The initiative supports discussions within the United Nations framework on establishing an international institution for AI governance. Chen’s article echoes several of these themes, describing AI as an international public good and calling for cooperation that helps Global South countries strengthen their technological capabilities and bridge the global intelligence gap.
China recently released its AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, following earlier versions issued in 2024 and 2025. The updated framework revises risk classifications and adjusts technical and governance measures in response to emerging challenges.
Making openness and security compatible
China’s international and domestic AI agendas may seem to be contradictory, but a country can support international technology exchange while seeking to protect sensitive data, strengthen infrastructure, and manage risks. The challenge is determining where legitimate safeguards end and restrictions on cooperation begin.
For China, the task is to demonstrate that its security framework can support innovation and international engagement without unnecessarily constraining them. For its partners, the task is to assess how cooperation will work in practice: what technologies will be accessible, how data will be protected, and how shared initiatives will be governed.
BRICS member countries have different development priorities, regulatory systems, and strategic interests. A common AI ecosystem will require practical arrangements that accommodate those differences while delivering measurable benefits.
A defining question for the AI era
Xi Jinping’s BRICS proposals and Chen Yixin’s national security assessment capture two dimensions of China’s AI strategy: expanding the technology’s reach internationally while strengthening its governance at home.
AI cooperation could widen access to technological capabilities and support industrial development. Security governance could help address genuine risks involving cyber operations, sensitive data, and increasingly autonomous systems. Yet both agendas also raise questions about implementation, institutional accountability, and the balance between openness and control.
China’s approach will be judged by the practical outcomes it delivers: whether cooperation is genuinely inclusive, whether safeguards are effective and proportionate, and whether international partners can participate on mutually understood terms.
The underlying proposition is that artificial intelligence need not be treated as a domain of zero-sum competition. When innovation is prioritized and security requirements are treated as non-negotiable, the technology can be steered toward benefit for all.

Burnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures – but his promises will take time to come good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:13:39 UTC
02:13:39 KST

Hope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again.
Just forget about the last two years, after the party won a historic majority but where the mood never matched the achievement. Now, as conference delegates and MPs filed out of the hall after Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister, it was close to euphoria. Where the hell have you been all our lives? What have we been doing – when you were right there all along?
That feeling rarely lasts: Burnham himself warned he would make choices that would be a harsh comedown from this Labour high. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country.
In his sights are some of the most untouchable topics in British politics: social care, the triple lock, Brexit, public control of water and council homes and changing the voting system.
Burnham wrote the speech almost entirely alone, working on it until the very last minute. Cabinet ministers have been full of tales of how often meetings overrun with the new prime minister, clearing their diaries for the extra half an hour, because of his desire to chew the fat, to understand, to argue, to persuade.
Close friends saw the speech just the night before, as Burnham reworked it. But strategists in No 10 were very clear that the new prime minister did need to introduce himself, his story, to the country that barely knows him.
Each judicious choice of an anecdote from his past drew on his personal history to explain his desire to make fundamental change. The home in Old Roan in Merseyside bought by his grandmother Kitty, which gave his family security that the younger generation cannot now experience: sold, he explained, to pay for Kitty’s care, which he will promise future generations will never happen under a new national care service. The care of his dad, Roy, who died two weeks ago, and his promise to his care workers that he would elevate their profession.
Burnham was overcome with emotion at the moment he spoke about his father, pausing for so long it caused one member of the audience to cry out: “You can do it Andy.” They want to back him, they want to believe.
Unusually for a conference speech, Burnham did not use the speech to attack his opponents. There were no reference to either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage. But one of the loudest cheers came from the crowd as Burnham drew the dividing line with the right in the starkest terms on public ownership.
“The British right talk about ‘taking back control’. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said, the reddest of red meat to a jubilant Labour crowd.
So, was it Burnham – and Labour – unleashed? No, because the prime minister is still constrained by his own party manifesto and the state of the public finances. “I would love to go quicker,” he said. “But I have to be honest about what the country can afford.”
His most radical promises are promises deferred. The party will overhaul the triple lock by 2030, the national care service can only be paid for if the party ditches its tax pledges, it can only explore a customs union, the single market, even rejoining, outside the manifesto’s “red lines”.
Even at this most united Labour conference the party has seen in two decades, there remains a proud Labour tradition – pessimism. And there are causes for concern, which creep in when cabinet minsters are at their most candid. The first is the impatience of the country for change – and that being told to wait will not be enough.
People, they say, are suffering now. The budget will need to show that any sparse funds that remain must be delivered to giving people relief from everyday costs.
“People need to start feeling actual benefits next year. We have got less time than we might think,” one cabinet minister said.
The second is a fear that Labour is not speaking to a broad enough base, no matter the elevation in Liverpool. Though there has been a discernible “Burnham bounce”, the polls are volatile. A YouGov poll on the eve of Burnham’s speech put Reform UK back in first place by a tiny margin.
Labour is reuniting a progressive coalition with a divided right, which is an advantage but which is unlikely to put them in majority territory. There are few cabinet ministers who are so frustrated with the constraints of their own legacy manifesto that they want to swap that for the constraints of a Lib Dem manifesto. There is no sign of revival yet in Wales or Scotland, so crucial to a Labour majority government.
When the dust clears and Labour strategists pick over the bodies of the sacred cows that Burnham promised to slay in his speech, many will probably wonder why he didn’t choose an easier life.
But perhaps now Burnham has waited this long to be prime minister – and watched so many others squander the office – he knows he has no choice but to tool up for the fight.

Staff at the hospitals facing closure disagree. They have recorded two appeals to Vladimir Putin.
Medical workers at Maternity Hospital No. 4, which is slated for closure, complained that management suggested they look for jobs in other cities or retrain for a new profession and threatened to put those who objected on “blacklists.” “If you fall out of favor with a chief doctor, and then with the Health Ministry, you won’t be able to find another job in medicine,” staff members said.
Workers at Maternity Hospital No. 6 said the chief doctor has been urging them in meetings since August to resign or change specialties because the hospital was not financially viable. All 133 staff members opposed the closure.

Barclays has watered down its return-to-office plans after a major staff backlash, with the bank allowing some employees to wait until next year before having to be in at least three days a week.
The bank this summer announced the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October, with more senior employees expected to come in for at least four days. That compares with current rules requiring staff to come in for two days.
Now Barclays has offered a reprieve after thousands of bank staff signed an open letter drafted by the Unite union, calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work.
The bank will allow staff to delay complying with the order until 2027. However, they will need to ask and receive permission to do so from their line manager by the end of this week.
In a memo emailed to staff, Barclays’ executive committee announced: “We are extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition … We are also reviewing our flexible working policy.”
The extension, first reported by the Financial Times, could give unions more time to request further concessions. Barclays and Unite said they would continue discussions on the issue, which has become a flashpoint across the banking sector.
Banks ranging from JP Morgan to Revolut have clamped down on remote working after the Covid pandemic, arguing it harms the training of younger staff.
Unite have said that while they recognise face-to-face working can support collaboration, team development and relationship building: “We do not accept that this requires a blanket, one-size-fits-all increase in mandatory office attendance.”
The union has requested a series of concessions, including:
- 
  Automatic exemptions of in-office attendance rules during school holidays and Christmas.
- 
  Capping in-office requirements at one day a week for any carers or people with disabilities.
- 
  Flexible start and finish times to allow for cheaper off-peak travel costs and to accommodate school pickup and drop-offs.
- 
  Subsidised onsite meal costs.
- 
  A single, consolidated payment made to all staff to make up for the costs of coming into the office, before March 2027.
A spokesperson said: “Unite is continuing to engage with Barclays on its proposals relating to colleagues’ working arrangements.”
In an emailed statement, a Barclays spokesperson said: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned.
“We have continued to listen to colleague feedback to ensure colleagues have the right support while enabling us to deliver the benefits of working together in person. This includes transitional measures for those whose personal circumstances currently prevent them from meeting the new arrangements.”

Kyiv • UNN
“Milan” scouts missed Shevchenko’s hat-trick against “Barcelona” and ordered a VHS recording from Mediaset. The video helped finalize the transfer in 1999.
Andriy Shevchenko’s transfer to "Milan" took place thanks to a VHS tape from the Mediaset newsroom. Scouts from the Italian club were not present at the famous match against "Barcelona", in which the Ukrainian striker scored a hat-trick, so the sporting director had to order a video recording of the game from journalists, after which the Italian club completed the transfer. Sportmediaset writes, as reported by UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Shevchenko made it to "Milan" not only because of his hat-trick against "Barcelona" in the Champions League, but also because of the publication’s newsroom.
"Ariedo Braida, who was the sporting director of "Milan" at the time, wrote down in his notebook the name of that exceptionally fast striker from Kyiv's "Dynamo". And on November 5, 1997, Shevchenko did something phenomenal at Camp Nou: a sensational hat-trick against Louis van Gaal’s "Barcelona", which they thrashed 4–0," the publication notes.
However, it later emerged that there were no "Milan" scouts in Catalonia during the match, and Braida then contacted the newsroom.
"Braida contacted the Mediaset newsroom, which at that time held the rights to broadcast the Champions League, and ordered a VHS tape recording of this extraordinary game. Shevchenko was subsequently watched live, and Braida convinced President Berlusconi to invest 45 billion lire ($24 million) to bring him to Milan in the summer of 1999. It seemed like a huge sum, but in fact it was not," the publication adds.
Additional information
In the 1997/1998 season, "Dynamo" were drawn in the same Champions League group as "PSV", "Newcastle", and "Barcelona".
In the matches against "Barça", most fans backed the Spanish team, but a Kyiv supporter did not lose hope. When asked, "But it is still "Barcelona", isn’t it?" he replied: "And we are "Dynamo" Kyiv—so what?".
And indeed, in the two-leg tie, "Dynamo" left "Barcelona" in tatters, defeating the Catalans by an aggregate score of 7–0. It was in the second match that Andriy Shevchenko, who is celebrating his 50th birthday today, produced his breakthrough. It was "Sheva" who scored a hat-trick against "Barça" in the second match, while the team featured such world football stars as Víctor Baía, Luís Figo, and Rivaldo, and Serhii Rebrov delivered the final blow to the Catalans.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday unveiled what he described as the first municipal strategy of its kind in the United States to combat antisemitism, announcing investments in hate-crime prevention, security coordination and Jewish cultural institutions.
The announcement comes nearly nine months after Mamdani took office and revoked several executive orders issued by his predecessor, Eric Adams, including measures concerning antisemitism and boycotts of Israel.
"Over the last year, I've met with Jewish New Yorkers across the five boroughs," Mamdani said. "Time and again, I've heard the same thing: antisemitism is real, and it is growing."
According to figures cited by the mayor, Jewish residents account for approximately 12% of the city's population, while antisemitic incidents represent more than half of its confirmed hate crimes. Police recorded 229 antisemitic incidents between January and August, an 8% increase over the corresponding period last year.
Mamdani increases NYC hate crime prevention budget by $26 million
Mamdani said his administration had increased hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, or more than 800%, compared with last year. The strategy includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate-motivated violence.
The city will also revive an interagency security working group disbanded in 2024, bringing together agencies including the NYPD and Department of Transportation to identify threats before attacks occur.
Cultural investments include $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture.
"Jewish New Yorkers should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America," Mamdani said.
On his first day in office, Mamdani revoked an Adams executive order adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism. The definition includes examples addressing certain forms of anti-Zionist rhetoric, including denial of Jewish self-determination.
He also rescinded an order restricting city agencies from participating in boycotts or divestment targeting Israel, along with a directive requiring police to examine regulations governing protests outside houses of worship. Mamdani retained the Mayor's Office to Combat Antisemitism.
Seven major New York-area Jewish organizations criticized the reversal of the IHRA and boycott orders. Mamdani defended the decision, arguing that some Jewish organizations had concerns about the definition and pledging to fight antisemitism through prevention and community engagement.
The newly announced strategy does not adopt a replacement definition of antisemitism. The administration maintains that existing hate-crime and anti-discrimination laws provide a basis for enforcement without a single codified definition.
Mamdani concluded his announcement by appealing to New Yorkers to protect their Jewish neighbors.
"Our safety is bound up together," he said. "That is the work we are undertaking at City Hall, and I am asking every New Yorker to join us."

He added that his memory is "kinda fuzzy," and that he and another man felt bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand."
Jane Doe responded in a similar fashion, CBS wrote, saying that her memory was "super clouded too," and that they had all been intoxicated.
She added that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal," and that she reportedly enjoyed being with him and another man. Later, CBS said, she suggested the three of them smoke together again, "but like leave out the extra 5 billion men and ketamine."
'Not one guy was arrested' defense team claims
According to CBS, Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, confirmed that messages were exchanged between Doe and the defendant, but could not confirm whether they were the texts sent at the time.
Giuffra argued Doe was "in denial and traumatized shortly after the alleged assaults," and that "she was intoxicated to the point of incapacity that night and was trying to find out what happened." Giuffra also said Doe felt unable to take an aggressive tone with the defendant.
CBS News New York also managed to acquire a video of the fraternity's group Snapchat conversation from the night the alleged rape took place. At 1:42 a.m. on the date of the alleged rape, CBS reported, a message was sent "suggesting that a woman was available for sex."
Later, one fraternity brother asked if the "shop was still open" and received a positive reply.
"Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact," Giuffra told CBS News New York last week.
Lawsuit reopened after alleged victim files civil lawsuit
New York state prosecutors reopened the investigation into the alleged 2024 gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house on Monday, after a civil lawsuit filed this month by the alleged victim sparked renewed outrage.
In a lengthy statement, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten confirmed that his office would present the case against seven alleged perpetrators to a grand jury for a possible indictment.
He also sought to explain why prosecutors did not pursue criminal charges two years ago, saying that the lawsuit's allegations differed from the alleged victim's original account in 2024. The woman, who prosecutors have not named, gave a statement to campus police at the time, according to Van Houten, that "described her drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual."
Giuffra did not immediately respond to a request for comment. He told CNN in a statement that the police report was "not materially different" from the civil lawsuit's claims and criticized the district attorney's office for not pursuing a more thorough investigation sooner, the network reported.
The lawsuit, filed against the seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell University and several other defendants, asserted that the woman, then a 20-year-old student at Cornell, was "plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication" by fraternity members, leaving her unable to consent before she was sexually assaulted.
Members of the fraternity used a Snapchat group chat to encourage others to join in, according to the lawsuit, which included a photo of some messages as well as details about the alleged assault itself.
In a statement, a Cornell spokesperson said the school supports Van Houten's decision and noted that the Chi Phi chapter involved in the case has remained barred from campus since 2024. Cornell previously investigated the allegations, resulting in "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell."
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," said the spokesperson, Kyle Kimball.
It was not immediately clear if all of the fraternity members named in the lawsuit have legal representation. Jeremy Saland, a defense lawyer who represents one of the members, said in a statement that his client had done nothing more than respond to the chat with an immature comment and that his client "welcomes any further investigation by the district attorney."
In the US, fraternities are college-based clubs for male students, often sharing a house together. The national Chi Phi fraternity, which was founded more than two centuries ago, did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.

Lindsay Clancy returns to court for hearing after murder case mistrial ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:10:31 UTC
02:10:31 KST

Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday, as her lawyers sought to head off a retrial by having a judge find the Massachusetts woman not guilty of murder for the killing of her three young children in 2023.
Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, took up the issue after declaring a mistrial on September 4, which occurred after a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous verdict on whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz's office has in the weeks since been silent on whether it plans to retry Clancy, 36, on first-degree murder charges, which carry a life sentence.
No one at Clancy's trial disputed that she strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
Defense lawyer Kevin Reddington during her first trial sought to convince jurors that she did not understand what she was doing was wrong and that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.
Total, complete lack of evidence
During Tuesday's hearing, Reddington told Sullivan that there was a "total and complete lack of evidence" at the trial to prove she killed the children and knew what she was doing was wrong.
He said non-lawyers had trouble understanding the idea that someone could admit culpability while maintaining a lack of criminal responsibility. That was leading many members of the public to call Clancy a "demon" and call for her execution, he said.
"This is coming from politicians, from President Trump all the way down," Reddington said.
Several jurors have in televised interviews stated that but for the one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find her not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
If found not guilty on those grounds, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her commitment would then be subject to regular review by the court.
Prosecutors have several options before them, including trying to reach a plea deal or retrying Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a jury trial and proceed before a judge.
Clancy's lawyers file series of motions to head off retrial possibility
Clancy's lawyers have filed a series of motions seeking to head off the possibility of a retrial by urging Sullivan to declare her not guilty and bar a retrial on the grounds that there was no reason to declare a mistrial and that it would as a result violate her right to avoid being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy.
They say jurors had been clear in notes delivered to the judge that the holdout had been refusing to apply the court's instructions on how to determine if prosecutors proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the juror should have been dismissed rather than allowing the case to be retried.
Her attorneys have also asked Sullivan to allow them to review normally confidential records about the jury and the holdout and question him about his truthfulness during the jury selection process and his cellphone use.
Sullivan said he would take up that issue and several other motions during a November 2 hearing. The holdout's lawyer, Edward Paltzik, told Fox News in an interview that aired on Monday that his client, Michael Desronvil, "had zero doubt" and "rigidly applied the reasonable doubt standard."

EC under fire

Russian daily casualties highest since war began
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:04:48 BST
02:04:48 KST

The Ukrainian General Staff recorded 2,090 Russian casualties, killed and wounded, in the twenty-four hours to 28 September, the highest daily total it has reported since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, according to British Defence Intelligence.
In its daily update on the war, the Ministry of Defence organisation set the figure against the rest of the record. Three previous daily totals above 2,000 were recorded during 2024, and the fourth-highest, of 1,960, came earlier this month on 16 September.
British Defence Intelligence stated: “The casualty rate has remained high since the summer, highly likely as Russia maintains its intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly in the vicinity of the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia.”
The fortress belt is the line of fortified towns in Donetsk oblast running through Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka, built up since 2014 and the principal obstacle to any Russian advance across the remainder of the region. Dobropillia sits to the west of that line, north of Pokrovsk, and became a focus of fighting after Russian forces pushed a narrow salient towards it, which Ukrainian units then worked to cut off.
Casualty figures in this war have to be handled with care whichever direction they come from. The Ukrainian daily total counts killed and wounded together without separating them, covers the whole front rather than any one sector, and is compiled by one of the belligerents. Western estimates of total Russian losses have generally been produced separately and with wide margins, and the British assessment has for some time been that Russia continues to accept losses at a rate it can sustain in manpower terms while taking ground at a pace measured in fields rather than towns.
What the figure does indicate, if the trend holds, is the cost of the tempo Russia has chosen to maintain through the autumn rather than pausing to reconstitute, with the highest and fourth-highest daily totals of the entire war now both falling within the past fortnight.
British Defence Intelligence has published updates on the war since shortly after the invasion began, releasing them through the Ministry of Defence account most days, and the format has settled into a short set of observations drawing on open sources alongside its own material. The updates carry the probability language deliberately so that readers can distinguish between what the organisation knows, what it assesses and how confident it is in the assessment.

Netanyahu is embracing Israel’s isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations General Assembly last week sounded more like a speech marking the end of an era than one opening a new chapter. Perhaps behind it was an awareness that this could be the last time he stands on that podium as Israel’s Prime Minister.
With the approach of Israel’s elections, set for October 27, Netanyahu’s political future has become inseparable from the way he addresses Israelis and the world. Yet his speech appeared directed primarily at his electoral audience at home, with little regard for the international community.
Netanyahu did not come to New York to offer a new political vision, propose a way out of the war, or present a vision for the region’s future. He came above all to defend his standing in Israel and his conduct of the war, while recasting Israel from a state facing growing international criticism into a purported victim confronting a hostile world. The question was thus turned on its head: instead of asking what Israel was doing to Palestinians and to the region, the focus became what the world was doing to Israel.
The sight of dozens of delegations walking out of the hall as he entered provided a striking image of the very predicament Netanyahu sought to deny. Rather than treating it as a sign of growing political isolation, however, he incorporated it into a narrative of “heroism”. The more others walked out, the more steadfast he appeared in his own telling. And the louder the criticism became, the more determined he was to present himself as the leader who stands alone but refuses to bend.
Israelis united against the world
When political options narrow, military force and confrontational rhetoric can serve as substitutes for a political way forward. The aim was less to convince the world that Netanyahu had a plan to end the conflict than to demonstrate that he could still defy the world and reject its demands — and ultimately settle the conflict by force.
At the same time, the speech was clearly directed at Israelis. Netanyahu spoke of unity, resilience, and courage, of Israel standing against its enemies, invoking the image of a leader who protects his people and knows how to confront the world. This is what led some analysts to describe it as an electoral speech rather than a diplomatic one.
Netanyahu was not trying to convince the world that Israel had changed; he was trying to convince Israelis that Israel did not need to change. The speech sought to move the narrative from accusation to victimhood, from isolation to heroism, and from accountability to persecution.
But the image of a united Israel he presented sits uneasily with the country’s internal reality. Israel’s divisions did not begin on October 7. The war was preceded by a profound crisis over the nature of the state, democracy, the judiciary, religion, society, and identity. These divisions have deepened around Netanyahu’s project and that of his allies. Presenting himself as the leader who unites Israelis against the world, therefore, overlooks the fact that his own policies have been part of the internal struggle that has divided Israeli society.
This is the deeper political meaning of the false heroism in the speech: an attempt to turn isolation into evidence of strength, the absence of a political solution into proof of steadfastness, and the world’s rejection of Israeli policies into evidence that those policies are justified.
What should Palestinians take from this?
Simply, that force may impose new realities, but it cannot by itself turn them into lasting legitimacy. Palestinians should not compete with Israel over power, but consolidate their existence and national rights as a political and legal reality grounded in self-determination, freedom, and equality. That requires moving beyond reaction, strengthening unified national institutions and resilience, and speaking to Israelis and the world in a language aimed at ending the conflict rather than denying the other side.
Between the end of Netanyahu and a new image of Israel
Perhaps the absence of a meeting between Netanyahu and Donald Trump during this visit was more than a matter of protocol. The meeting was not on the U.S. president’s schedule at a time when Netanyahu is fighting an electoral battle and facing growing international isolation. It would be an exaggeration to turn that absence alone into a judgment about his political future. But the question remains legitimate: did it reinforce Netanyahu’s sense that his political era is approaching its end, and that Israel itself is paying the price for conflating the state with his government and its policies?
Netanyahu has increasingly blurred, in both his rhetoric and political practice, the distinction between the Israel he claims to represent and himself as the person who represents it. At this moment, the new Israel exposed by war and international isolation appears more starkly before the world: a state attempting to protect its old image through force, even as the gap widens between that image and what the world sees in its policies — occupation, settlement expansion, genocidal war, ethnic cleansing, and the denial of Palestinian rights. The construction of ever more “iron walls” may not be enough to conceal this image forever.
If this was indeed Netanyahu’s final address to the General Assembly as prime minister, he wanted to leave the podium with the image he had chosen for himself: a leader standing alone but refusing to bend, confronting the world while insisting that his people stand united behind him.
Yet his speech revealed another image: a leader trying to turn isolation into heroism, force into a substitute for politics, and the denial of the Palestinian people’s rights into a reality imposed through brute power. Perhaps this is the clearest irony of all: he sought to present himself as the leader whom the world could not isolate, yet, unwillingly, he may have contributed to deepening Israel’s isolation.

The United States and the United Kingdom sank a decommissioned American frigate off the coast of Scotland — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
American and British forces attacked the decommissioned USS Klakring with missiles and a torpedo off Scotland. The ship sank at a depth of 1.8 km.
The U.S. and British navies sank the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring during the joint Atlantic Thunder 2026 exercise near the Hebrides, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
The ship was attacked from the sea, air, and underwater: the American destroyer USS Paul Ignatius launched the anti-ship version of the SM-6 missile, the British HMS Portland fired a Naval Strike missile, and a Wildcat helicopter used a Sea Venom missile against a surface target for the first time.
The final strike was delivered by the American nuclear-powered submarine USS Massachusetts with a heavy Mk 48 torpedo. The former warship then sank approximately 150 nautical miles from the northwest coast of Scotland and came to rest on the seabed at a depth of about 1.8 kilometers.
USS Klakring served in the U.S. Navy from 1983 to 2013. Uncrewed underwater vehicles will now survey the wreckage so that experts can assess the impact of different types of weaponry.
Before the sinking, potentially environmentally hazardous materials were removed from the frigate. As the specialist publication Navy Lookout notes, the use of an American ship was explained, among other things, by the division of costs: the United States paid for preparing and transporting the frigate across the Atlantic, while the United Kingdom paid for use of the range.

He added: “Cybersecurity is becoming more and more of a risk. We are working [at] everything we can to protect our infrastructure, to work with industry.”

EU court rejects Poland’s request to suspend implementation of Mercosur trade deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:57:50 UTC
01:57:50 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

The Court of Justice of the European Union has rejected a request from Poland to suspend the implementation of the EU’s recently launched free trade agreement with the Mercosur bloc of South American countries.
The CJEU found that the Polish government had failed to prove its claims that the trade deal would cause serious harm to European farmers, consumers or the environment.
#ECJ: Order in Case C-460/26 R Poland v Council: should the implementation of the Council’s decision authorising the provisional application of the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement be suspended pending the Court’s ruling?#CJEU #Mercosur pic.twitter.com/ocb4I4PsE8
— EU Court of Justice (@EUCourtPress) September 29, 2026
Poland has long been critical of the agreement, in particular over the potential negative impact that imports of agricultural products from Mercosur, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, could have on Polish farmers, who have repeatedly protested against the deal.
In January, Poland failed in a bid to block the agreement at the European Council, where 21 of the EU’s 27 member states voted in favour of the deal.
Although the agreement has not yet received final ratification – still requiring approval from the European Parliament and national parliaments – it nevertheless went into provisional force on 1 May. Shortly afterwards, Poland submitted a complaint to the CJEU, calling for implementation of the agreement to be suspended.
It argued, first of all, that the process through which the deal had been provisionally implemented violated the EU’s treaties.
Second, it claimed that liberalising trade in agricultural products without imposing the same production standards in both the EU and Mercosur created a risk of harm to human and animal health, the environment, the income of farmers, and the functioning of the market in the EU.
Poland has filed a complaint to the European Court of Justice against the EU's free-trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc that recently went into provisional force.
It wants the agreement to be suspended until the court issues a ruling https://t.co/wE7DIbDazU
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026
However, on Tuesday, the CJEU announced that it had dismissed the application to suspend the agreement, finding that “Poland has not provided any concrete evidence to establish the likelihood and imminence of serious and irreparable damage”.
The court pointed out that agricultural products from Mercosur could already be imported to the EU before the free-trade deal, and that they were and continue to be subject to food safety and health regulations similar to those for products manufactured in the EU.
It also noted that the new trade deal includes tools allowing the EU to bar products that do not meet standards, including emergency measures in the case of a serious threat to human, animal or plant life.
Finally, the CJEU said that Poland’s “general and abstract claims” regarding potential harm to farmers and markets did not include “any evidence capable of establishing, with a sufficient degree of probability, that the implementation [of the agreement]…will cause disruption”.
In response to the court’s decision, the Polish government’s spokesman, Adam Szłapka, immediately blamed the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) administration, which was in power in Poland from 2015 to 2023.
Szłapka said that the details of the Mercosur deal had been agreed during that period and that PiS had “failed to secure Polish interests in any way”. He argued that it was the current government which secured the addition of last-minute safeguards intended to protect farmers.
The spokesman also noted that Polish agricultural exports to the Mercosur bloc have actually increased under the new agreement while imports from there have fallen, showing that “Polish farmers are profiting from this”.

However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the foreign policy office of President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the CJEU’s decision showed the impotence of the current pro-EU government.
“The government and Prime Minister Tusk first said that the EU-Mercosur agreement would be ‘safe for Polish farmers’. Then they failed to build a blocking coalition in the European Council,” wrote Przydacz.
“In the end, under pressure from public opinion in Poland, they filed a complaint with the ECJ. [It was] so weak that they lost the request for interim relief,” he added. “Ineffective policy and ineffective government.”

California recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:56:56 UTC
01:56:56 KST

Breadcrumb
California formally recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
California has formally recognised the Islamic Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha festivals as state holidays, making it the second state of the United States to do so.
Authored by Assembly member Matt Haney, Assembly Bill 2017 (AB 2017) now allows state and school employees to observe both Eids by using existing personal holiday credits or available leave.
The legislation also permits K-12 schools and community colleges to close for Eid, provided such closures are established through locally negotiated arrangements.
Many states, cities and school districts recognise Eid locally, but not as statewide holidays. Washington state was the first one to officially recognise the two festivals as state holidays in 2025.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the holy fasting month of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha honours Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) willingness to obey God by sacrificing his son.
Eid al-Adha, the most important event in the Muslim calendar, coincides with and marks the culmination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest mosque and site, the Kaaba.
The California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-CA) welcomed Governor Gavin Newsom’s signing of AB 2017, saying it addresses a longstanding challenge for the state’s more than one million Muslim residents who are often forced to choose between practicing their faith and showing up to school or work.
"For far too long, Muslim students and employees in California have had to make the difficult choice between participating in observances essential to their faith or falling behind on their academic or professional obligations. AB 2017 removes these structural barriers and aligns state policy with the values of inclusion, equity, and respect for cultural diversity that define our state," it said in a statement shared on its website.
CAIR, the United States' largest Muslim organisation, said the passage comes at a time of increased Islamophobia in the country, saying it recently documented a 183% increase in incidents targeting mosques and Islamic centres from May to July compared to the same three-month period last year.
"Officially recognising these holidays sends the necessary and powerful message that California values and protects its Muslim community in the face of growing hostility".
In May, a shooting at the Islamic Centre of San Diego by two gunmen killed a security guard and two community members outside the mosque.

Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
- Published
The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement.
It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff.
They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month.
BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.
At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated".
Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".
The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident.
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."
The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations.
SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented.
"The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said.
BAPS apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused" earlier this month, adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation.
BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.

Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:52:37 UTC
01:52:37 KST

Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.
Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen.
But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.
The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.
A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice-president.
It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.
Following the Houthis’ push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, their forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.
“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city, trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front.
“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”
The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile after the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.
The former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provided some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.
The STC has urged the Giant Brigades to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.
“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.
“The UN-recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is, so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”
The White House has been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done in the past in Yemen, sometimes to brutal effect.
Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.
Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.
The World Health Organization said 838 people had been killed and 3,643 others injured due to the escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.
The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday they published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.
The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.
April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war was existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis were not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”

Police officers and emergency services are working at the sites, documenting the consequences of the attack.
As Ukrinform previously reported, on Tuesday the Russian army struck a school in Sumy with guided aerial bombs while children were inside the shelter.
Photo: National Police

A change in prison culture is vital – as is more money to reduce overcrowding | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

Pia Sinha’s significant expertise inside and out of the prison system makes her a voice to trust on why our jails are struggling badly (The truth about UK prisons and organised crime: ‘They’re your good lads. Respectful. Keep their noses clean’, 22 September). I lead a charity, Spark Inside, that uses life coaching to support rehabilitation and culture change across our prisons.
We work with staff who go into the service because they want to make a difference. But the challenges of the environment can stifle that spirit. This is why since 2020 we have coached more than 150 prison staff, supporting them in problem-solving, resilience and confidence.
The 2022 prisons white paper said staff hold the greatest potential to make prisons safe, decent places that help prisoners change. Investing in staff wellbeing is an essential part of making prisons more rehabilitative and preventing future victims.
The next step is to change prison culture. We’ve started training prison staff with coaching skills so they can have more transformative interactions with people in their care. We started with gym staff because, as Sinha highlighted, exercise is often the only activity available to those inside.
We bring together staff and people in prison to build trust, empathy and understanding – breaking down the “us and them” culture.
People who live and work in prisons may not agree on everything, but usually they share a desire to improve the environment they are in. When we support people to tap into their strengths and potential, and bring them together with a shared purpose, change can happen.
Vicki Cardwell
CEO, Spark Inside
At the time that Pia Sinha was working at HMP Wandsworth, I was working for the then Department for Education and Skills in the prisoners’ learning and skills unit.
Its aim was to increase the qualifications offered to prisoners and to improve the outcomes, particularly in literacy and numeracy, and in NVQs, often to match the work that prisoners were already doing in prison workshops and kitchens. Such programmes provided structure, achievement and better job prospects on release.
But every year the prison population increased while the funding declined. In overcrowded prisons, more prisoners stay locked up, with little access to education or training. And in some ways, that kind of intervention in prison is too late; a crime has been committed and a victim has suffered.
Intervention and support for families or children at risk would reduce the prison population in time. Whichever way it’s done, it costs money, with results only visible in a few years’ time, when another government may claim the success. Hard choice, but if put to the electorate, it might get votes.
Phil Hind
Edinburgh
In Zoe Williams’ excellent piece on Pia Sinha, the last paragraph was the most telling. The relentless focus on punishment produces diminishing returns for society but, sadly, too often seems an easy and popular fix. Victims deserve better than being the justification for ever longer or harsher punishment. Victims should have support to manage and minimise the physical and mental impact of the crime.
Yes, punishment has its place, as does protection of the victims and others. But once we properly support victims in managing their trauma, wider society can focus more on future protection through rehabilitation. It would probably also cost less in the long run.
Stephen Evans
Horsforth, West Yorkshire

Labour has its own role in this climate of hate and racism | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:57 UTC
01:48:57 KST

In her article, Polly Toynbee mentions the rise of racism globally, citing Donald Trump and the usual suspects (There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham, 22 September). She fails to mention that the Labour party has also indulged in overt and dog-whistle racist rhetoric.
Keir Starmer spoke about Britain becoming “an island of strangers”. He later retracted it, but the message was out there. Wes Streeting, when health secretary, agreed with Katie Lam on the problem of foreign doctors (rather than the real problem of disastrous NHS restructures, poor management and underfunding). More recently, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said that a video clip where Zack Polanski says a few sentences in Urdu makes him “uncomfortable”.
In refusing to call out Labour’s role in creating a climate of hate, Toynbee fails to address the seriousness of the problem. Labour politicians indulging in or endorsing racist rhetoric does far more to normalise racism than when it comes from Trump and his supporters. And if we choose not to identify the real problem, we have no hope of making it better.
Name and address supplied
History clearly confirms Polly Toynbee’s main point that the rise of divisive scapegoating politics in a time of economic pressures ultimately represents a genuine threat to everyone’s basic rights. Immigration policy issues cannot be separated from turning this tide, since they are central to the lure of today’s far-right populism.
A sizeable minority of Reform UK voters cannot be persuaded to change their allegiance as they now feel part of a wider “community of grievance”. Its myths and symbols seemingly explain current predicaments, revive old prejudices and suggest simple solutions. But many others have simply not heard these anti-immigrant notions being challenged. Too many mainstream politicians have echoed them instead, giving the far right control of the agenda and greater legitimacy.
The majority of Britain’s voters share a traditional milder patriotism and can understand the need for immigration to grow our economy, in a country with an ageing population and labour shortages, and the need to avoid splitting communities. That case has to be made, before the poison spreads.
John Chowcat
Bridge, Kent
The rising tide of grievance that is powering Reform and rightwing sentiment is threatening the whole idea of democratic politics here and abroad. It must be confronted. It appals me that so-called responsible commentators argue that it is “understandable” because politics doesn’t deliver what people want.
When what people want is defined by those with the most money and influence and involves selfish, discriminatory, reactionary and violent attitudes and behaviour it is the antithesis of democratic politics because that has to be founded on the principles of equity and justice. Without that, we are lost. Responsible politicians must lead the fight against that or the very ground on which they stand will be taken from under their feet. That slide into chaos already has far too much momentum.
Neil Blackshaw
Alnwick, Northumberland
 Polly Toynbee’s powerful plea to defeat anti-migration fascism reminded me of the words of the nurse Edith Cavell before she was executed by the Germans in the first world war. “Patriotism is not enough. I must have no hatred or bitterness towards anyone.”
E Douglas Lawson
Cheltenham, Gloucestershire

Xi’s narrative of WWII obscures the ROC’s role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:45 UTC
01:48:45 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) discussed US-China cooperation during World War II (WWII) at a White House state dinner on Thursday last week, he left out a name central to that history: the Republic of China (ROC).
“Over 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in a fight against Japanese militarist aggressors,” Xi said at the dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump.
China did fight alongside the US, but its government at the time was the ROC, now based in Taiwan. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) was founded in 1949, four years after the war ended.
Photo: Yang Mien-chieh, Taipei Times
Leaving the ROC unnamed was likely aimed at helping Beijing portray the wartime alliance as part of the PRC’s own history, Taiwanese academics said yesterday at a forum in Taipei on the summit.
Wang Hsin-hsien (王信賢), director of National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations, said Xi stood to gain if the alliance came to be remembered simply as one between “China” and the US.
Repeated use of such language by Washington could make “the erasure of the Republic of China ... very apparent,” Wang said.
The White House’s own fact sheet, issued on Friday, also referred simply to “China.”
“The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” it said, without identifying the ROC.
The US’ de facto embassy in Taiwan was more specific when in a post in September last year commemorating the war’s end, American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene referenced the First American Volunteer Group, nicknamed the “Flying Tigers,” who fought alongside the ROC Air Force.
The Mainland Affairs Council on Friday protested Xi’s remarks, saying they did not reflect that it was the ROC that fought alongside the US.
Institute for National Policy Research vice president Kuo Yu-jen (郭育仁) on Saturday said that Xi’s comments had two goals.
One of them was to “suggest that the Republic of China has completely disappeared and been replaced by the People’s Republic of China,” he said.
The other was for Xi to highlight Japanese wartime militarism through his reference to fighting “Japanese militarist aggressors” amid strained China-Japan relations.
He linked it to Tokyo’s campaign for a permanent UN Security Council seat and its call to remove the UN Charter’s “enemy state” clauses, which refer to countries that fought against the charter’s signatories during WWII.
Days before Xi’s remarks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for those clauses to be remove in a UN General Assembly address that also urged Security Council reform.
Tzeng Wei-feng (曾偉?), an associate research fellow at the National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations, said that despite the WWII remarks, he saw no clear sign that the visit had immediately changed Washington’s Taiwan policy.
However, he said he was concerned how language used in prominent diplomatic settings could spread and endure.
He pointed to the 1972 Shanghai Communique, in which the US “acknowledged” that people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait maintained there was one China and that Taiwan was part of China.
Beijing’s later portrayal of that wording as US “recognition” of its position showed how an interpretation of diplomatic language could spread and endure, Tseng said.
“Xi isn’t saying this just for Trump to hear,” he said. “He’s saying it for the whole world to hear.”

Rate of crashes killing older people increases slightly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:42 UTC
01:48:42 KST

In the first seven months of this year, 1,569 people died from motor vehicle crashes within 30 days of a crash, including 697 older people, up 5 percent from the same period last year, data from the Ministry of Transportation and Communications showed.
Crash-related deaths were down by 220, or 12.3 percent, compared with the same period in 2023 and down 18 deaths, or 1.1 percent, from the same period last year, the data showed.
The overall trend remains positive as the number of crash-related deaths, including those from drunk-driving incidents and those involving motorcycles, older people, children and adolescents or pedestrians, all declined compared with the same period of 2023, the minstry said.
Deaths of children and adolescents and among people involved in alcohol-related crashes both fell by more than 54 percent, it added.
However, the number of fatal crashes involving older people increased compared with the same period last year, Department of Railways, Highways and Road Safety Director-General Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌) said.
The increase was concentrated in Taoyuan, Taichung and Hualien County, where 50 percent of fatal crashes involving older people were related to motorcycle crashes and 20 percent were due to collisions involving pedestrians, Wu said.
Crashes commonly occurred when motorcycles were turning left at intersections or pedestrians were crossing the road, he said.
The fourth quarter of the year is historically the peak period for fatal crashes involving older people, the ministry said, with shorter daylight hours and larger day-night temperature differences.
It advised older people to wear bright clothing or reflective accessories when going out in the early morning or late at night.
Drug-driving incidents occurred often so far this year, with 23 people killed in the first six months of the year and seven in July alone, ministry data showed.
Beginning in July, the method for counting drug-driving incidents was changed, National Police Agency Traffic Division section chief Chen Chi-feng (陳其鋒) said.
Statistics were expanded to include not only instances in which the first party involved in the crash was under the influence of drugs, but also when a crash involved a second party who was drug-driving and committed a traffic violation, to more accurately count drug-driving crashes, he said.
The news system recorded 105 drug-driving crashes in July, falling to 89 last month, Chen said.

It’s not the price of your toothbrush but how you use it | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:37 UTC
01:48:37 KST

Emine Saner offers a fascinating survey of the expensive toothbrush tech on offer (The rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market?, 22 September). As a dental hygienist, however, I remind patients at every appointment that this simple fact remains: the best way to maintain oral hygiene is to brush for two minutes at least twice daily and to floss daily. No toothbrush offers a short-cut solution to this, no matter how expensive. A premium toothbrush risks becoming like a gym membership: reassuring to have, perhaps, but something that makes no difference unless it is used.

'White House oppressing both Iranians and Americans'

'White House oppressing both Iranians and Americans'
IRGC letter to American people urges break from US war policies
TEHRAN — The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a 26-page open letter to the American people this week, urging them to break with the foreign policy of their government and to reconsider what they have been told about U.S. wars in West Asia.
The letter is addressed to scholars, students and media workers. It says the American public is not the target of Iran's resistance. Rather, the target is a political class that turns war into a business and uses the country's power against people in the region and at home.
"The men enthroned at the White House oppress both Iranians and Americans," the letter states.
The letter is signed by the IRGC's public relations office and circulated in English and Persian. Its central message is that Americans have been misled about Iran and about their own government's role in the region.
Much of the document calls on Americans to separate themselves from the "U.S. war machine." It asks university communities to refuse research and media work that helps plan or justify attacks that kill civilians. It says silence in the face of such policies makes Americans complicit in decisions taken in their name. "This is not a call for hostility toward Americans, but for them to hold their own leaders accountable," the letter reads.
The letter then lists historical grievances that it says explain the hostile nature of Iran-U.S. ties. It begins with the U.S.-orchestrated 1953 coup in Iran, which installed a dictator and created the roots of decades of hostility. It points to the Iran-Iraq War, which it explains was an American-backed effort to destroy Iran's new government through Saddam Hussein. It also cites the 1988 downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the USS Vincennes, calling it a crime that was rewarded instead of punished.
The letter adds that these policies continue through sanctions, covert operations and support for armed groups opposed to Iran. It asks Americans to "test that record against what they have been told about Iran by their own media and politicians."
On its designation as a "terrorist" organization by the U.S. government, the IRGC rejects the label as a political tool used by Washington to isolate and silence its opponents. It says the American people should see the IRGC "not as a threat but as the main line of defense against Western and Zionist domination." Iran's resistance is regional and defensive, the letter says, while U.S. power is expansionist and driven by interests outside the region.
The document is written from the position of an Iran that, it says, has survived a major military aggression launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, 2026. The letter devotes several pages to that aggression. It says the war failed to break Iran's will or change its course, and that the "outcome has exposed the limits of American military power in the region."
From that experience, the IRGC draws a larger conclusion: the United States is a declining power, and Iran's doctrine and worldview have already won a moral and strategic victory.
"It is perfectly clear which of the two leaders God supports," the letter says, contrasting Iran's leadership with a "self-enriching" elite in Washington.
The IRGC also accuses American politicians of treating foreign wars as financial opportunities. It notes that some trade stocks based on the outcomes of conflicts. It says the same leaders who speak of democracy and human rights have little concern for the Americans who bear the costs of war. That charge, the letter says, should unite Americans and Iranians rather than divide them.
The closing section is a warning. "America's crimes have turned the world into a powder keg that is ready to explode," the letter states. It says the American public has the power and the responsibility to stop a course that is unsustainable and dangerous for West Asia and for the United States itself.
The letter ends by invoking the Golden Rule, found in the Talmud and the Gospels, and calls on Americans to demand immediate change before more conflict spreads.
