French students and police clash as school blockades turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:19:30 UTC
00:19:30 KST

French teenagers blockading their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher shortages and long timetables have clashed with police, as politicians traded verbal blows over how to respond.
Demonstrations that began in Paris last week have escalated and spread across France, with the authorities reporting the arrests of 164 people on Monday.
On Tuesday, high school pupils in Lille, northern France, set fire to dustbins and threw bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at police, who responded with teargas after protesters vandalised bus shelters and advertising hoardings.
There were confrontations between children and police in Bordeaux, Rennes and Nantes in western France, and Marseille in the south. At the Lamartine lycée, in the north of Paris, students waved placards complaining they had exhausting timetables. One read: “8am-6pm. More hours of lessons than sleep.”
On Monday, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said protests had broken out at 180 schools, and 12 officers, 12 students and three school staff had been injured.
By midday on Tuesday, the education ministry was reporting protests at 300 high schools, a further 40 arrests and that 10 students and staff had been injured.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said earlier that escalating the demonstrations would be “irresponsible”. He posted on X: “Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students staff or police.”
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), responded to ministers’ instructions to police, posting on X on Monday: “The high school students protesting are harmless. The Lecornu government has ordered a crackdown. This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone. Hands off our youth. Elected officials and France Unbowed activists, step in wherever you can.”
Lecornu, responding on X, called Mélenchon’s intervention an “irresponsible escalation”. “The duty of an elected official of the republic is to protect young people and call for calm. Exploiting their anger for partisan purposes is wrong,” he wrote.
He added that Mélenchon’s accusation of racism was “an insult”.
The protests came as French unions went on strike over the government’s budget plans, which include €54m in public spending cuts. Many public sector workers stopped work on Tuesday, including an estimated 40% of primary school teachers.
Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéene (the high school students’ union) had called for a total blockade of France’s high schools as a parallel action but urged protesters to “remain peaceful”. He said the union was protesting about a “general lack of resources, overcrowded classrooms of sometimes 32-35 students and the shortage of teachers and staff”.
He said a circular sent by the interior and the education ministries to the police, telling them to maintain public order outside high schools “with a proportionate use of force”, was a “absolute scandal”.
“We’re talking about pupils of 15-18 years old and the government’s only response is automatic and institutionalised repression. It’s unacceptable. High school pupils are taking action to demand fairer and more equitable conditions and they’re being met with the BAC [anti-criminal brigade] and the CRS [riot police],” Rani said.
He added that some teachers and school staff had stood in front of students to protect them from police. “Those are the images you should be showing,” Rani told BFM TV.
Caroline Chevé, secretary general of the main teachers’ union the Fédération Syndicale Unitaire (FSU – Unitary Trade Union Federation), who joined protesters at a march in central Paris on Tuesday, said she understood pupils’ frustration. “They’re facing the same challenges as we are. They’re in overcrowded classrooms. Sometimes they don’t have enough teachers because of staffing shortages. They see the same reality as we do, and they’re angry,” Chevé said.

British PM Andy Burnham to revamp pensions, vows greater control of services in economic overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

British PM Andy Burnham to revamp pensions, vows greater control of services in economic overhaul
- British PM Andy Burnham plans to overhaul state pensions, making elderly care free and delinking pension rises from wage growth to fund a national care service.
- He vows to bring water, energy, and housing under greater public control, repealing the ban on public ownership of water companies and enhancing regional powers.
- Burnham commits to fiscal discipline, promising fully funded policies without increasing borrowing, aiming to address long-term UK challenges and political instability.
AI generated
LONDON – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised “a new economy and new politics”, saying he would overhaul state pensions in a plan to make care for the elderly free at the point of use.
“This is the deal: a state pension that rises every year, no care charges, and a high-quality national care service to give peace of mind in later life,” he said, explaining that his government would de-link the rise in pension increases from the rise in average earnings.
“This change will generate significant savings, which we will use to build up our national care service,” Burnham said, vowing that the policy – which he plans to introduce after the next election if Labour is returned to power – would be fully funded and not increase borrowing.
The triple lock has been in place since 2011, and guarantees that the state pension rises annually by the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%. It is helped to reduce pensioner poverty, but many economists warn the policy is increasingly unaffordable given other pressures on the public purse.
Burnham also pledged in his speech to the governing Labour Party to bring water, energy and housing under greater public control.
He told Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool that he would “break the mould” and tackle issues his predecessors had failed to address. To that end he pledged to overturn the ban on public ownership of water companies instituted in the 1980s.
“We rely on them, we pay for them, and once again we will have power over them,” he said.
Burnham said he would introduce a Bill that would bring about “the repeal of Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”. He added that regional mayors would have new powers to hold water companies to account, that loopholes used to pay bosses “excessive bonuses” would be closed, and that there would be “tougher consequences” for firms which “repeatedly fail”.
“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules, to get our borrowing and debt down,” he said, a day after his Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey vowed fiscal discipline.
Burnham is seeking to move away from the cheaper, feel-good policies that have characterised his first two months in office and flesh out his longer-term vision for tackling some of the biggest challenges facing the UK, in a bid to turn the page on the country’s political instability.
“It is always in my mind that I am the seventh prime minister in 10 years,” Burnham said. “It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.”
He said in his speech that he would not shy away from “the things politicians usually avoid”. Ahead of the address, he promised he would outline plans to reform social care and to take greater public control of industries such as water and energy.
Burnham’s senior ministers, including Healey, have used their conference appearances this week to roll the pitch for more difficult decisions to come, including plans to cut spending on benefits. BLOOMBERG

Migrant shipwreck off Tunisia leaves at least two dead, six reported missing
ROME, Sept 29 - German charity group Sea-Watch said on Tuesday it had rescued 28 migrants and recovered two bodies, including that of a child, following a shipwreck off the coast of Tunisia.
The group's ship Aurora found five survivors and the dead bodies in a deflated rubber dinghy in the early hours of Tuesday, the charity said.
It rescued another 23 survivors, including a toddler, from an offshore oil and gas platform where they had taken refuge after the shipwreck.
Those rescued reported that at least six people, including three children, were missing, Sea-Watch said on social media, adding the Aurora was now heading to the Italian island of Lampedusa.
"Governments celebrate falling arrival numbers as a success. We see what that ‘success’ means: at least two dead and six missing, including three children," said Sea-Watch spokesperson Julia Winkler, calling for a state-run European search-and-rescue programme.
Over 22,000 sea migrants have arrived in Italy so far in 2026, interior ministry data showed, compared to more than 50,000 reported in the same period of 2025.
In the same period, more than 1,970 people have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean in a bid to reach Europe, Sea-Watch said. REUTERS

National Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:16:39 UTC
00:16:39 KST

Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member.
Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that the report by the investigative website Mediapart was false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election.
“We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him.
Journalists at Mediapart said they had independently authenticated the comments allegedly written between 2013 and 2015, including in email groups and on messaging services. Bardella was aged 17 to 18 at the time and was a member of the party that was then called the Front National.
The alleged comments included “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. He is also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”.
Mediapart’s investigation has shaken Le Pen’s presidential campaign. Since Le Pen took over the party leadership in 2011, she has sought to detoxify the party image and move it away from its antisemitic past in order to increase its electoral reach.
When Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, co-founded the party in 1972, its ranks included former members of a Waffen SS military unit under Nazi command during the second world war.
Pierre Bousquet, a former member of the Waffen SS Charlemagne division, was the party’s treasurer for its first nine years. Another early member had been in the paramilitary militia under Philippe Pétain, the leader of the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis and ensured the deportation of one-quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps, about 76,000 people.
In 1987, Jean-Marie Le Pen described the Holocaust as a “mere detail” of the second world war. In the decades that followed he was convicted more than 15 times for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity as he repeated negationist comments, including saying the Nazi occupation was “not particularly inhumane”.
Marine Le Pen, who expelled her father from the party in 2015 after he repeated antisemitic comments, has in recent years directly appealed to French Jewish voters. She said her party would protect them, describing the RN as “the best shield for our fellow French citizens of Jewish faith”.
Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in an attempt to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. In 2023, Bardella told a TV interviewer he did not think Jean-Marie Le Pen was antisemitic, before backtracking on his comments after criticism.
The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, responding to the Mediapart investigation, wrote on social media: “To all those with a short memory: antisemitism isn’t an accident in the RN, it’s that party’s history. That’s the real face of the far right.”
Aurore Bergé, the minister for equality and against discrimination, said the “antisemitic and conspiracy theory” content of the alleged messages “reminds those who might have forgotten the nature of the far right”.
Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the Socialist presidential primary, wrote on social media that no public relations exercise would fundamentally change the RN. “Let us never forget that they all joined a party founded by antisemitic fanatics and out-and-out racists,” he said.
Yonathan Arfi, of the CRIF, the umbrella group of French Jewish organisations, told France Culture radio he was “stupefied by the virulence of the antisemitic comments” allegedly made by Bardella. He said that if true, the comments undermined the RN’s claims to have detoxified its image.
He asked: “How could a political party leader, having made such sickening comments, reach such a high position in a party that claims to have changed and now fights against the hatred of Jews?”
The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, said Bardella, an MEP, should resign from all his political positions. She said: “The man who presents himself today as the biggest defender of Jews … is in reality an obsessional antisemite.”

US-Iran talks in New York: What’s the latest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:09:53 UTC
00:09:53 KST

US-Iran talks in New York: What’s the latest?
Both sides remain interested in a diplomatic settlement but differ on how to achieve one.
Indirect talks between the United States and Iran aimed at ending the seven-month-long war continue – most recently via Qatar as mediator on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York – but the two sides still disagree about the agenda.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi left New York on Tuesday after telling state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) that he expects an official response to Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by the end of the day. The proposal, which Iran said would see the strait reopened within seven days, was first passed to the US via Qatari mediators last week.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
- list 2 of 3US-Iran talks continue, but ‘deal unlikely’ before midterm elections
- list 3 of 3Hormuz and Yemen: Iran offers de-escalation at a price others will pay
United States President Donald Trump was reported to have rejected that offer, under which Tehran would reopen the strait in return for Washington lifting its naval blockade, waiving sanctions, releasing an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and enforcing a wider regional ceasefire that includes Lebanon.
Under Iran’s proposal, wider peace talks, including discussions of its nuclear programme, would begin only then
Despite Trump’s public rejection, Araghchi says he has not yet received a formal response from Washington. Meanwhile, US media reports that Trump may well be willing to relax sanctions and unfreeze Iranian assets have been strongly denied by the US president.
Instead, US officials say, the US wants a deal that resolves all outstanding issues, particularly Tehran’s nuclear programme, in one go, rather than pursuing a gradual, step-by-step approach.
Here’s what we know about the talks:
What happened in the Qatar-mediated talks?
Qatari mediators met Araghchi in New York on Monday to discuss how to advance Tehran’s proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and then progressing to wider peace talks.
In a post on Telegram, Araghchi insisted that the talks focused solely on the Strait of Hormuz. He denied that the US had formally rejected the Iranian proposal.
“Despite what the US president said, I said that we were waiting for the official US response through the mediators … They [Qatar] had ideas, and we discussed them. They are going to raise this issue with the American side again, and then the final response from the American side will be conveyed to us through the Qatari mediator,” Araghchi said late on Monday.
Araghchi also said negotiations had become more “serious”, but cautioned that Tehran’s position has not changed.
“I state firmly that there has been no change in Iran’s position. Our conditions for opening the strait are clear. Our position on other issues is also clear. At present, there has been no discussion at all about flexibility,” he added.
Tehran’s proposal includes elements of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU), which was signed by both the US and Iran on June 17.
Is Trump willing to accept some Iranian demands?
A US official told The Associated Press news agency last week that Trump is not willing to make a final peace deal with Iran until the issue of its nuclear programme is addressed. According to the official, who has not been named, the US president would be willing, however, to grant Iran sanctions relief and release some frozen funds if progress is made on the nuclear file.
Then, on Monday, US-based news outlet Axios also reported that Trump had offered Iran sanctions relief in return for concessions on its nuclear programme. The report also cited US officials, one of whom told Axios that the indirect talks had been “positive and constructive”, adding that Tehran had indicated it was “flexible” on nuclear issues.
Trump, however, angrily denounced the story as a “hoax” in a post on Truth Social, the social media platform he owns. He said the story was “not true” and demanded Axios remove the article.
Iran has been heavily sanctioned for decades. The restrictions have severely affected Iranians’ quality of life, including their access to essential medicines and healthcare.
In August, the US announced yet more sweeping economic sanctions on Iran and countries that trade with it as it sought to apply more economic pressure to isolate the country from the global economy during the diplomatic deadlock in their war.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the campaign as the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.
It is difficult to quantify exactly how many Iranians have been killed by what Tehran views as “economic warfare”. However, a study published last year by the highly regarded medical journal The Lancet Global Health concluded that more than 564,250 people worldwide die annually as a result of US sanctions.
What does the US want?
In late February, just before the US launched its first strikes on Iran, the two sides were already holding talks hosted by Oman, which included the issue of Iran’s nuclear programme.
But before those talks could conclude, the US and Israel launched strikes, triggering the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas is shipped in peacetime, by Iran. The closure of the strait has since become the primary point of contention between the two sides, when it had not been an issue before the war began. The strait is currently subject to blockades by both sides.
Throughout the war, Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to strike a deal with Tehran. However, serious differences between the two sides will need to be resolved first, including the order in which issues are addressed for the purpose of peace talks.
Iran wants to establish its control of the Strait of Hormuz, have sanctions lifted and assets unfrozen, as well as ensure an end to US-Israeli strikes before it will go back to negotiating other issues, such as its nuclear programme. This was the order of events laid out in the MoU agreed between Iran and the US in June, but which quickly fell apart.
The US, however, wants everything to be on the table at the same time – it does not want to agree to anything relating to these Iranian demands before it addresses the other issues.
Scott Lucas, professor of US politics and international relations at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that Washington effectively wants Iran to surrender.
“The Strait of Hormuz has become a fundamental issue. The question here is, will both sides give? The memorandum of understanding clearly gave Iran a role in the management of the strait,” Lucas said.
“When the Trump administration pulled away from negotiating on the basis of the memorandum, they effectively went back to the idea of Iran having to completely allow passage through the Strait of Hormuz with no guarantees over it, in terms of not only what it means for Iran financially, but [also] in terms of Iranian security. The Iranian government is not going to agree to that, so we’re stuck in this limbo right now,” he added.
“Are the Trump folks going to come back to the talks on the basis of the memorandum of understanding or something that is a revised version of it, or are they going to try and break the government with economic warfare until at least after the US elections in November? That’s where we are right now.”
What does Iran want?
After half a century of bitter enmity with Washington, Iran wants to consolidate what it sees as the strategic gains it has made during a war it did not start. This specifically includes its newly established ability to close the Strait of Hormuz, sending global energy markets into a tailspin and placing additional pressure on the Trump administration.
Since US-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, Hormuz has dominated talks aimed at ending the war and emerged as Tehran’s greatest point of leverage. Prior to the conflict, Iran did not exert control over the waterway and all commercial shipping passed through freely.
For this reason, Iran will not move on to wider peace talks until it has leveraged its control of the strait to get its demands met. “Our discussion is clear. Right now, it is only about the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi said late on Monday.
“The opening of the Strait of Hormuz is also subject to the fulfilment of a series of conditions that we announced to the other side.”
Ali Salehian, director of the Center for Intellectual Diplomacy at the Governance and Policy Think Tank in Iran, told Al Jazeera that Tehran does not believe Washington will honour any future deal as it did not honour what was agreed under the Pakistan-brokered June MoU.
“For Iran, the bottom line of every negotiation with Trump, considering all of his misbehaving and [military] targeting of Iran during negotiations, is the Islamabad MoU,” Salehian said.
“Tehran thinks that if the US doesn’t fulfil its commitments based on the MoU, there is no guarantee that any kind of future deal would be sustainable.”
What is likely to happen next?
It does not look likely that the diplomatic standoff will be eased anytime soon, analysts say.
Both the US and Iran have indicated throughout the war that they would prefer a diplomatic settlement to a continuation of the war. However, Trump has continued to threaten Iran with more strikes if it does not agree to a deal, and Araghchi told US news outlet NBC on Sunday that Tehran is also prepared to resume fighting, even though it has not abandoned diplomacy.
“We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” he said.
Trump said last week that he expects a deal will be reached, but not until after the US midterms on November 3.
“For the moment, the Trump administration is going to try to make the Iranian government capitulate through economic warfare,” Lucas said.
However, a deep sense of distrust remains between the two sides. Senior Iranian officials believe Trump will restart the war after the midterms on a far greater scale and that Israel would also participate.
If that theory proves true, Tehran may well prefer the fighting to resume before November’s elections, as it would allow Iran to impose a greater cost on Trump.
“The reaction of the Iranians to that might be to actually trigger the war themselves, early, right before the midterm elections in order to maximise the pain that [it] will impose on the US president,” Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the US-based Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Al Jazeera earlier this month.

CDC reports two measles deaths in US as cases hit 35-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

CDC reports two measles deaths in US as cases hit 35-year high
US sees record-breaking measles surge amid controversy over anti-vaccine rhetoric and revised death tracking system.
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed two measles-related deaths from the 3,659 confirmed cases this year, the highest number of cases in 35 years.
The CDC did not specify on Tuesday in which states the deaths occurred. However, Pennsylvania has been hardest hit by the outbreak with more than 900 reported cases.
The preventable disease was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 but has made an aggressive comeback in recent years, which some have linked to a rise in vaccine scepticism.
Members of US President Donald Trump’s administration, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. and the president himself, have been criticised for promoting debunked claims linking vaccines to autism, among other misleading statements.
Deficiencies in fatality tracking triggered a public feud between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Kennedy after Pennsylvania reported four measles-related deaths this year, which the CDC did not include in its national tally. Kennedy has maintained that only one of the deaths was caused by measles.
The agency has faced significant staffing and budgetary turmoil after losing nearly 30 percent of its workforce due to sweeping federal employee layoffs following Trump’s January 2025 inauguration and a wave of voluntary retirements and resignations.
In August, Trump signed an executive order aimed at getting states to modify childhood vaccine recommendations by splitting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots and spacing out childhood appointments — a plan public health experts warned increases infection risks by requiring return visits. The order went into effect despite decades of global evidence proving combination vaccines are safe and effective.
A few weeks ago, the CDC shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count, moving away from rapid real-time reporting from state health departments — a move that has sparked intense pushback.
The federal agency has said it is working with state epidemiologists to develop a standard definition of measles-related deaths to ensure consistent reporting across jurisdictions, adding that the number of deaths is subject to change as additional information becomes available and reviews are completed.

Is it a bird? Is it a plane? It's a newly discovered microraptorine dinosaur that sheds light on the evolution of flight gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:04:35 UTC
00:04:35 KST

Most birds fly, but they don't all fly the same way. All but the secondarily wingless use their wings to create aerodynamic lift and thrust, but having done that, they exhibit a range of aviating abilities, from humdrum flapping to gliding and soaring, to hovering – hummingbirds are especially good at that – and diving. There is a range.
Birds are dinosaurs that survived, and we assume they all inherited their flight apparatus from very early birds. Now the burning question of the day is this.
In the Paraves, the group of extant birds and their closest (and extinct) dinosaurian relatives, did flight-related features emerge once starting about 150 million years ago, or multiple times? Did birds and microraptorine dromaeosaurids, their closest cousins, inherit their flight accoutrements from a common ancestor, or did they develop them independently?
Microraptorines in Chinese fossil beds are a good place to quest for answers, because some but not all of them exhibited aerial adaptations. We do not know if they could fly, but they had features that animals that can fly do have.
Now deep analysis of a newly discovered "four-winged" microraptorine (which just means small feathered dinosaur) found in Liaoning, northeastern China, strongly suggests that the flight features emerged more than once, Andrea Cau, Qiang Ji, Xuri Wang, and colleagues reported in Nature Communications on Wednesday. They named the animal Norellraptor barsboldi. They add that analysis of its fossil tissues suggest that its arms, shall we say the upper wings, seem to have developed precocially compared with today's birds.
Norellraptor was found in a fossil formation spanning about 145 million to 100 million years ago, in which several species of microraptorines have been found. That adorable reconstruction image focuses on the wings, less on the fangs in its beak. The ray of sunlight is a nice touch.
The animal is shown aloft, but actually, the paleontologists are not saying it could fly. Yet analysis of its flight-friendly features and comparison of their presence or absence in related animals shore up the hypothesis that flight equipment emerged more than once, the team says, elaborating: "The sequences of flight-related novelties reconstructed along the two lineages [birds and microraptorines] differ consistently."
Norellraptor isn't the first "four-winged" dinosaur to be found. In the case of another one, Anchiornis huxleyi, palaeontologists actually are quite sure based on its molting pattern that it didn't fly. Here also is the Instagram page of "Jian," a microraptorine dromaeosaurid shown mounting an aerial assault on an early bird that didn't get the worm. We don't actually know that it could fly either.
Back to the new paper: Based on close analysis of dozens of sites on the fossil and comparison with its (extinct) peers and birds, the team estimate that only around 30 percent of the flight-related anatomical changes identified in microraptorines also appeared in birds. Moreover, the order in which these shared characteristics appeared in birds and microraptorines wasn't the same, they deduce.
What does that imply? That microraptorines and birds did not inherit flight apparatus from a common ancestor. They underwent distinct developmental processes, Cau and the team suggest. A reasonable corollary is that the microraptorine and bird lineages experienced different selective evolutionary pressures.
Regarding the "four wings," this refers to long feathers on their legs. Note that while birds today generally have scales on their legs, likely retained from their distant reptilian ancestry, some have luxuriously feathered hind limbs, including owls and certain raptors. Long feathers on the feet of the likes of the Silkie chicken are the result of selective pressures by breeders. But the propensity was there.
It died young
What have we? Birds and microraptorines descended from a common ancestor. From that point, the family trees that different palaeontologists draw for these creatures are disputed. But we can probably safely say that today's birds did not arise from a single dinosaur.
Paleontologists have identified a transition from the group of feathered but flightless dinosaurs to aviating ones from at least 150 million years ago. The birds we know and love to eat emerged from theropods, a broad group of bipedal carnivorous dinosaurs, and it seems that as it does, evolution got experimental.
Whether or not Norellraptor could fly is an open question that may be resolved by future fossil discoveries. Maybe it skipped around on its amply feathered limbs, or could glide. The animal was not large by dinosaurian standards, measuring 57 centimeters (22.4 inches) long, about half the size of today's turkeys. Its preservation was exquisite, the paleontologists gush; nary a bone missing. They add that it was discovered by a local farmer who preferred to remain anonymous.
Based on analysis of its bones, it died at about age 3. The natural lifespan of chickens and crows is about five to 10 years, though the margin of error is very wide. Some captive crows pass 30. Our microraptorine apparently died as a young adult and we just add that while there is research into the colors of dinosaurs based on fossil melanosomes, the hues imagined for this lovely animal are just that.

Spain is planning to override standard migration procedures and tighten rules on asylum-seeking for migrants who arrived in its North African enclave of Ceuta in July's mass crossing, a draft decree seen by Reuters showed, prompting outcry from legal experts and NGOs.
The decree, designed to speed up applications and deportations for the over 10,000 migrants who remain in the tiny territory, would mark a major strategic shift for Spain's leftist, pro-immigration government, a staunch advocate of multilateral rules and institutions, as it struggles to contain the political fallout from the border crisis.
Spain's Interior Ministry declined to comment on the draft.
More than 70,000 people illegally crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta via land and sea in late July in an unprecedented rush, rattling European leaders and exposing the limits of a recent overhaul of migration rules intended to tighten borders.
Under the measures in the draft, first leaked to Spanish newspaper El País and not yet confirmed, migrants appealing a rejected asylum application must do so from outside the country if the EU deems it safe, as is the case for Morocco, regardless of their personal circumstances.
New decree applies retroactively
The decree, which would apply retroactively to migrants arriving since the mass crossing of July 30 and 31, also permits the government to skip a standardized review of asylum requests by a commission including representatives from the UN refugee agency.
Migrants' applications would be withdrawn if they were unreachable for five days and anyone deemed to have behaved in a "violent or threatening" manner would have their right to remain immediately revoked.
Asked at a news conference about plans to shorten processing timeframes for migrants, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analyzing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" because of questions of international law.
Spanish lawyers and NGOs decried the draft measures in statements to Reuters and other media, with 13 NGOs, including Spain's Commission for Assistance to Refugees (CEAR) and Oxfam, describing them as a "grave threat" to Spain's commitment to human rights conventions.

Psychological resilience may buffer children’s brains against some effects of abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:00:54 UTC
00:00:54 KST

Among children with lower psychological resilience, those who experienced more abuse showed brain-network patterns linked with depression, physical symptoms and later anxiety, according to a study published in Development and Psychopathology. These associations did not appear in children with average or higher resilience. The findings suggest resilience may protect against some effects of abuse, although it did not appear to provide the same protection against neglect.
Childhood adversity can influence mental health in many ways. Abuse may place children in a state of heightened alertness, making them more sensitive to possible danger and more likely to interpret ordinary experiences as threatening. Stress can also affect how the brain coordinates systems involved in emotions, attention and physical sensations.
Psychological resilience describes the ability to adapt and continue functioning during difficult circumstances. It is not necessarily a fixed personality trait. Researchers increasingly view resilience as a capacity that can change with support, relationships and intervention.
The research team wanted to investigate whether resilience altered the relationship between different forms of adversity and the way brain networks communicate. They were particularly interested in whether abuse and neglect affected the brain in the same way. Although both experiences can harm children, abuse involves threat and fear, while neglect more often involves a lack of emotional, physical or material support.
Led by Yuanyuan Li of Beijing Normal University, the team studied 94 children, 48 boys and 46 girls, between the ages of 10 and 14 who attended elementary schools in rural China. The authors describe the sample as marked by poverty and by the experience of being “left behind,” a term for children in rural China whose parents have migrated to cities for work.
Participants completed questionnaires about childhood adversity, resilience, depression, anxiety and physical symptoms. Abuse was measured as a combination of physical and emotional abuse, and neglect as a combination of physical and emotional neglect. Resilience was assessed with a questionnaire asking how well children cope with challenges, such as whether they feel able to deal with whatever comes their way.
Immediately afterward, the children underwent a resting-state functional MRI scan, which tracks how closely activity in different brain systems rises and falls together while a person lies still without performing a specific task. This synchronization, known as functional connectivity, is often interpreted as a sign of how strongly brain systems communicate. Six months later, the children again reported their depression, anxiety and physical symptoms.
Two children were excluded because they moved excessively during scanning, leaving 92 participants, with an average age of about 11.8 years, for the main analysis. The researchers examined connections within and between seven large-scale brain networks. The key findings involved three of them: the limbic network, which helps process emotions and motivation; the ventral attention network, also known as the salience network, which identifies important or potentially threatening information; and the somatomotor network, which processes movement and bodily sensations.
Across the full sample, neither abuse nor neglect was linked to any of the brain-network measures after the researchers accounted for age, sex, perceived socioeconomic status and the other type of adversity. The associations with abuse emerged only when children’s resilience levels were taken into account.
Among children with lower resilience, greater exposure to abuse was associated with stronger connectivity between the limbic network and the somatomotor network. This pattern helped explain the link between abuse and more physical complaints, such as headaches, stomachaches and tiredness, as well as higher depression scores at the initial assessment.
In these children, greater abuse was also associated with stronger connectivity between the limbic and ventral attention networks. Both brain patterns helped explain higher anxiety levels six months later, even after the researchers accounted for the children’s anxiety at the start of the study. These associations were absent in children with average or higher resilience.
However, the results did not show the same protective effect for neglect. Neglect was not significantly associated with the brain-network measures, regardless of the children’s resilience levels, although children who reported more neglect did tend to report more depressive symptoms, both at the start of the study and six months later. This ran counter to the researchers’ expectation that resilience would protect against both forms of adversity.
The authors suggested that neglect may be more chronic and widespread in the study population, potentially making it harder for resilience alone to offset its effects. They argued that addressing neglect may require easing the underlying deprivation, for example by providing more material resources and supporting more responsive caregiving.
Li and colleagues concluded: “Our findings reveal that psychological resilience specifically shields against the neurotoxic effects of abuse by modulating networks involved in emotion regulation, salience, and sensorimotor processing.”
Some limitations should be noted. For example, the study measured adversity and brain connectivity at the same time, so it cannot establish cause and effect. The children also reported their own past experiences of adversity, which may introduce recall bias, since children may not remember or report past experiences accurately. Sexual abuse was not assessed because of the sensitivity of the topic in Chinese elementary schools. The sample was also relatively small for detecting subtle effects, and the link between brain connectivity and later anxiety was no longer statistically significant when the researchers used a stricter standard for excluding children who moved during scanning.
The study “Psychological resilience moderates the relationship between childhood adversity, brain network connectivity, and wellness” was authored by Yuanyuan Li, Zelin Liu, Bowen Hu, Jiahua Xu, Jiale Xiao, Boxuan Chen, Ting Tian, Ying He, Shaozheng Qin and Danhua Lin.

EU pays extra $113B in energy costs without receiving more gas or oil: Commissioner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

Melike Pala
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The European Union has paid more than €100 billion ($113 billion) in additional energy costs this year without receiving any extra gas or oil, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday.
Speaking ahead of an informal meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin, Jorgensen said the figure highlighted the risks of the bloc's continued dependence on imported energy.
"We have now surpassed €100 billion that we've paid extra for our energy this year without receiving one extra molecule of gas or oil," he said.
Jorgensen said the situation demonstrated how "unsustainable" it was for Europe to remain dependent on energy sources from outside the bloc.
"We used to be dependent on Russia. That, thankfully we are now getting out of, but nonetheless, it is still the case that when prices go up on the global market. It also hurts our citizens. It hurts our industries," he said.
Jorgensen said the EU needed to reduce its reliance on imported fossil fuels and increase the use of domestically produced renewable energy.
He pointed to the bloc's electrification action plan and ongoing negotiations with EU lawmakers on a grids package, saying stronger connections across Europe would help make energy supplies cheaper and faster for consumers and industry.
Asked whether he had received assurances from US Energy Secretary Chris Wright regarding a possible US diesel export ban, Jorgensen said he had sent a clear message to his US counterpart.
"It is not in the interests of anybody, not the US, not us," he said, adding that he was encouraged that Wright had publicly said he did not support such a ban.
He said the EU was not currently facing a security-of-supply crisis and did not expect one, but acknowledged that the coming winter could present challenges.
"We are entering a winter that currently looks so challenging that we want to eliminate any uncertainties that can be eliminated" Jorgensen said, adding that several member states had raised concerns over energy supplies.

The Tempi rail disaster in February 2023 killed 57 people when a passenger train traveling from Athens to Thessaloniki collided head-on with a freight train in central Greece. The crash prompted investigations into railway safety and the handling of the crash site.
Separately, a criminal trial over the disaster is underway in Larissa, with 36 defendants facing charges. They include officials and employees from organizations across Greece's railway sector, Transport Ministry officials, and the stationmaster who was on duty on the night of the crash. ■

Piotr Matys, senior foreign exchange analyst at In Touch Capital Markets, told Anadolu that the US and European bond markets diverged due to differences in country-specific developments and volatility in oil prices, reflecting in the exchange rate.
“With yields spread widening in favor of the dollar, the EUR/USD continues to lean lower despite momentum indicators a bit stretched,” he said. “The euro could be particularly sensitive to a fresh set of US data that will be released throughout this week, culminating with non-farm payrolls on Friday.”
He added that if the US data weakens hawkish expectations, the exchange rate could see a corrective rebound or trade sideways.
Kit Juckes, head of foreign exchange strategy at Societe Generale, told Anadolu that the exchange rate dropped below the low it reached in late June.
“That it held up for so long is testament to the success of President Trump’s verbal campaign to hold down the dollar, but elevated oil prices, a strong economy, high bond yields, and Federal Reserve policy tightening are too powerful a force to be talked away,” he said. “How much further we go in the short term, may depend on this week’s US inflation, employment, and ISM (Institute of Supply Management) data, but as long as energy prices are this elevated, a slow grind lower for EUR/USD seems the path of least resistance.”
Juckes added that a gradual decline in the euro/dollar exchange rate is likely to continue so long as energy prices remain this high.

“Two days ago I was fired from Soho House, the one at Shoreditch,” the unnamed employee claimed on an account named “Soho House Opp”. “I was fired after I complained about people changing labels and selling out-of-date food to customers.”
A Soho House spokesperson said the employee’s contract had been terminated for reasons unrelated to his complaint.
The club chain is popular with celebrities, with Kate Moss, Kendall Jenner and Ellie Goulding among those spotted in its venues. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, met on a blind date in 2016 at its 76 Dean Street house in London, and Meghan has been seen drinking coffee at its Cotswolds location, Soho Farmhouse, since her move to London.
A Hackney council spokesperson said it had received, and was reviewing, a health and safety complaint relating to Shoreditch House, one of the club’s 10 London locations.
The spokesperson said: “We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation.”
The employee claimed he had been “pressured” to change labels to mask out-of-date food. He said he had first made an internal complaint and then, when he did not feel sufficient action was taken, submitted a complaint to the council. He says that shortly after this, he was fired.
It is illegal to sell food past its “use-by” date, but food can be sold after its “best before” date as long as it is of acceptable quality. Restaurants and other commercial kitchens have a strict legal duty to ensure all food served to customers is safe and fit for human consumption.
A Soho House spokesperson apologised for the mislabelling incident, and said it was an isolated occurrence but that they had launched an investigation.
They added: “We’re really sorry that this isolated food labelling incident took place at one of our kitchens. This is not how we expect our Houses to operate and it is not company policy. We have taken immediate action, including our director of health and safety together with an external independent consultant conducting an investigation as a matter of priority.”
The spokesperson said the location takes food hygiene seriously, adding: “Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us. Shoreditch House has consistently achieved the highest food hygiene rating score of 5 from environmental health inspections – including the most recent in March this year – and also performed strongly in an independent and unannounced external audit last week.”
Soho House was founded in 1995 with a single club in the central London area from which it takes its name. It has 10 locations in London, and 48 that are either open or planned around the world, ranging from Paris and Istanbul to Bangkok and Mumbai. It has four clubs in Los Angeles and three in New York.
The club chain has had some financial issues in recent years, with members complaining it is no longer as exclusive as it used to be. The owners have attempted to turn its fortunes around by opening a more “exclusive” location in Mayfair and launching mini two-sip cocktails, as well as IV drips, to attract younger members.

US state recognizes Muslim holidays Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as official holidays
Unknown

Merve Aydogan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The US state of California has officially recognized Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, the two major Islamic holidays, under a new law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Assembly Bill 2017, signed into law Sunday, adds the holidays to the official state holiday calendar.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, the Islamic month of fasting. Eid al-Adha is celebrated during the annual Hajj pilgrimage.
Public schools and community colleges may close for the two holidays through existing local procedures. Eligible state employees may also receive holiday credit for the holidays.
"The designation of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha as state holidays is a civil calendar determination that acknowledges their cultural significance to California communities," according to the law.

Why You Should Make a Reverse Bucket List
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:56:21 UTC
23:56:21 KST

Your bucket list is probably full of big dreams: go sky-diving, learn to speak Italian, finally take that trip to see the northern lights. You might think that all that possibility should give you something to look forward to—but spend enough time staring at everything you haven’t done, and your yet-to-be-checked off aspirations can start to feel like more proof you’re somehow behind.
That’s what bothered Simon Sinek, who hosts the podcast A Bit of Optimism and is the author of books including Start With Why, about the concept of a bucket list. “You’re staring at a list of things you’ve never done, and it’s kind of depressing,” he says. “Even if you make your way through the list and things come off, you die with a list of things you've never done. And that just leads to disappointment and regret.”
About 15 years ago, in a small act of rebellion, Sinek started keeping a reverse bucket list: a log of all the wonderful things he’d already experienced, like the time he saw a complete rainbow instead of just part of one.
Sinek keeps his list on his phone, where he sometimes stumbles across it while searching for something else. Then he gets sidetracked revisiting his own life and remembering experiences he’d forgotten about. “It’s joy scrolling,” he says. “Why shouldn’t I get credit for these things that showed up organically in my life?”
Here’s how to take stock of the big milestones and small moments worth remembering—and give yourself a chance to enjoy them all over again.
How a reverse bucket list can help you feel more fulfilled
A reverse bucket list works because it interrupts one of your brain's most stubborn habits: always looking ahead to what's next instead of pausing to appreciate what's already happened. “So much of daily life is focused on the next goal, the next milestone, or the next thing we haven't done yet,” says Rachel Needle, a psychologist in West Palm Beach, Fla. That translates into rarely stopping long enough to notice “everything we've already experienced, survived, learned, or built.”
Making the list gives you a reason to notice the lovely, surprising, unexpectedly funny things that happen in the middle of an ordinary day, which are easy to miss when you’re already thinking about what’s next. When you start actively seeking out these moments, you may find that you spend more time celebrating what's already part of your life, rather than dwelling on what’s missing.
“Instead of thinking, ‘I'm not there yet,’ you begin noticing, ‘Look how much is already part of my story,’” Needle says. “That shift alone can change how you see your life.”
Keeping track of these experiences can be especially helpful for people who feel perpetually behind or tend to compare themselves with others. “We get lost in what everyone else is doing, so we forget what we’re actually doing,” says Alyssa Kushner, a licensed clinical social worker in New York. Writing down your own personal highlights gives you something to revisit when it feels like everyone else is having a better time. She keeps her old journals for precisely that reason: They remind her of the friends, trips, and fun she might otherwise overlook. Rereading them gives those memories a little more time and attention. “You’re feeling it and you’re savoring it,” she says.
Those reminders may lift your mood and support your self-esteem, too—especially when you recognize your own role in making something good happen. As Kushner puts it: “I did take that risk. I did build that friendship. I did get through that season.” When it’s easier to focus on what’s going wrong, the list offers concrete reminders of what’s gone right.
What to put on your reverse bucket list
Aim to make your entries specific, whether the experience was big or small. For example, you might record a Tuesday dinner with friends: “Everyone stayed at the table chatting for three hours.”
There’s room for big milestones (an awe-inspiring trip or promotion at work) as well as what Kushner describes as “micro moments of joy.” “These are the daily things that happen that we might kind of gloss over, but that are just as important,” she says. “Maybe it was a beautiful morning and you got to soak in the sun, and you had your coffee or your matcha, and you just felt content. It could be a random five-minute exchange with a stranger that was a really nice moment of connection. It could be something you felt proud of yourself for.” Every time she sees flowers, for example, she feels happy.
Include a few details that help you return to the scene, Kushner suggests: what you saw, heard, or felt, and what made it worth remembering. Maybe you caught the scent of flowers on your walk or laughed so hard with a friend that you forgot what started it.
You can also give yourself credit for things that didn’t come with a souvenir or a celebration. Needle suggests including challenges you’ve overcome, relationships you’ve nurtured, and moments when you did something that took courage. “You’re more resilient than maybe you’re giving yourself credit for on a regular basis,” she says. On her own list: finishing her book proposal, reconnecting with friends, and planning a trip to London with her mom.
The point is to choose what mattered to you. As Needle puts it: “You’re not trying to prove anything to yourself or anyone else that you lived an impressive life.”
How to make—and revisit—a reverse bucket list
Keep track of these memories in a journal or notebook, or on your phone—whatever you’re most likely to return to. Treat it as a living document that grows as you have new experiences and remember old ones you’d almost forgotten.
If you like a little structure, Needle suggests a weekly check-in: Add whatever comes to mind, then spend some time rereading old entries.
Or take Sinek’s approach and skip the schedule. He adds things when they happen. “There’s no rules here,” he says.
Whatever your system, make sure you periodically revisit what you’ve written. Linger over an entry long enough to remember what made you laugh, who was there, or how you felt. As Needle puts it, the point is “letting yourself feel good about it again.”

former railway signal box reopens as l’aiguilleuse red-orange kiosk-bar in nantes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:55:44 UTC
23:55:44 KST

former railway signal box reopens as l’aiguilleuse red-orange kiosk-bar in nantes
designed by studio téré, the former railway signal box-turned-kiosk-bar sits within the jardins de l’estuaire new public park.
Studio Téré gives a 1960s railway signal box a new public role
L’Aiguilleuse is a project by Studio Téré that transforms a former 1960s railway signal box into a small kiosk-bar located at the heart of the Jardins de l’Estuaire, a new public park on the Île de Nantes, France. Originally part of the Nantes-État railway infrastructure, the building once controlled train movements entering the station. As the surrounding railway landscape gradually disappeared, the signal box remained as a small but distinctive fragment of the site’s industrial history.
Rather than replacing it, the project gives this existing building a new public use. The former technical building becomes a place for meeting, resting and light catering, extending the life of this railway heritage while preserving its identity. With a floor area of 36 sqm, the interior is dedicated to the operation of the kiosk-bar. Its relationship with visitors therefore takes place largely outside.
Red-orange accents give the converted signal box a new identity
The interventions by Studio Téré are deliberately understated and legible. The ground floor opens widely onto the public space. Three facades open widely with bi-fold windows and folding metal shutters, revealing the counter and turning the building into an open pavilion connected to the surrounding park.
The red-orange color highlights the metalwork, joinery and facade lettering, reinforcing the building’s presence in the landscape. Two large painted lettering compositions contribute to the new identity of the place. The intervention preserves several characteristic elements of the former signal box, including the original clock and railway signalling lights. These elements are integrated into the new identity of the building and maintain a direct connection with its previous use.
A luminous upper level turns L’Aiguilleuse into a signal
At night, the upper level becomes a luminous signal within the park. The program for the new venue was developed through a public consultation process involving local residents and future users. The new name ‘L’Aiguilleuse’ refers to the former railway signal operators, while its feminine form also contributes to a broader effort to the feminisation of names in public space. By transforming this railway signal box into a new public venue, L’Aiguilleuse becomes a new urban landmark within a district undergoing major transformation.
project info:
name: L’Aiguilleuse
 architect: Studio Téré | @studio_tere
location: Nantes, France
floor area: 36 sqm
client: SAMOA – Société d’Aménagement de la Métropole Ouest Atlantique
photographer: Nina Ducleux | @nina_ducleux

'He's Basically a Republican Now': Fetterman Turns to GOP Donors For Campaign Cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:55:06 UTC
23:55:06 KST

Senator John Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat who has spent much of the past two years antagonizing his own party, is now turning to Republicans for campaign cash.
In recent weeks, Fetterman has sent fundraising appeals through email addresses associated with Republican candidates and committees, including one from “info@gopsquad.com.” One of the messages declared, “I’m always going to reject Socialism and the Anti-American way of life,” and urged recipients to help Fetterman “stand with America” and “reject the extremes.” The same address has also been used for messages supporting President Trump’s voting restrictions and urging readers to donate to Republican candidates in the midterms.
The emails, reported earlier by The Intercept and also obtained by TIME, are the latest sign of how dramatically Fetterman’s electoral strategy has changed since arriving in the Senate in 2023. The former progressive backed by Bernie Sanders has increasingly built his political identity around opposition to the left, unwavering support for Israel, and a willingness to embrace conservative voters. His campaign is now reaching into the fundraising infrastructure of the party he insists he has no intention of joining, as his support among Democrats has eroded and his fundraising has sharply declined.
The fundraising appeals appeared under several other Republican-linked domains, including Unshakeable Conservatives and Freedom Faction. It remains unclear who owns the lists or the arrangement Fetterman’s campaign has with the groups behind them. Campaigns routinely rent or otherwise obtain access to donor lists as a way of reaching new potential contributors.
Fetterman’s office did not return a request for comment.
Another fundraising email sent this month from the gopsquad handle came with Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah listed as the sender. It was focused on Fetterman, and began, “I just got an email from John. He's basically a Republican now.”
Fetterman has not said whether he will seek a second term in 2028. Over the weekend, during an on-stage interview at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin, he said he was raising money with a reelection bid “as the possibility” and suggested he would wait until after the November midterms to decide.
Several Pennsylvania Democrats are already considering a challenge to him in 2028, even as Republicans continue to encourage him to leave the party. Rep. Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democrat who has been critical of Fetterman, says that the latest fundraising effort fit a pattern that was already apparent. “More than a year ago, I called John Fetterman ‘Trump’s favorite Democrat,’” Boyle says, “so it should come as no surprise that he’s now using that label to raise money from Republicans.”
Rep. Chris Deluzio, another Pennsylvania Democrat, says that Fetterman has become a “distraction” from the party’s effort to win the midterms and combat the Trump Administration. “That’s my focus. Anyone who stands in the way of that work will have to answer to the voters soon enough,” Deluzio says.
Fetterman’s political transformation appears to have hampered his fundraising. He raised roughly $76 million in the two years before taking office in 2023, an extraordinary sum for a first-time Senate candidate, powered by an enormous small-dollar fundraising operation and the enthusiasm of progressives who saw the hoodie-wearing, working-class populist as a different kind of Democrat. But since then, the political coalition around him has steadily come apart. Fetterman raised about $7.4 million during his first two years in the Senate and less than $2 million since the beginning of 2025, according to federal campaign finance records. His political action committee has raised only a few hundred thousand dollars since 2023.
Fetterman has hardly hidden the shift. His redesigned campaign website boasts that he “thinks for himself” and tells visitors, “You should too.” He has become a regular presence on Fox News and other conservative programs. In July, he attended a retreat hosted by Rupert Murdoch, appearing on a panel with Republican Senator Katie Britt of Alabama. He has formed a joint fundraising operation with Senator Dave McCormick, the Republican who represents Pennsylvania alongside him, allowing their campaigns and political committees to raise money together.
Earlier this month, he appeared by video at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas. Fetterman introduced McCormick in a recorded message, attacked the “extremes of socialism,” and called on Bernie Sanders to “sit a few out” after the Vermont Senator backed left-wing candidates in Democratic primaries. The appearance was jarring for Democrats in part because Sanders had been among the most prominent supporters of Fetterman’s own Senate campaign.
Fetterman, for his part, has repeatedly rejected the suggestion that his political evolution will eventually lead him to joining the GOP. At the Texas Tribune Festival, he argued that Democrats should be a “big-tent” party with room for someone who supports both Israel’s actions in Gaza and holding Iran accountable. “I don’t have a reason to” join the Republican Party, Fetterman said, noting that he still votes with Democrats on most partisan matters. He has also said he has “no path as a Republican.”
Still, Fetterman voted in support of Trump and the Republican Party on 26% of Senate votes during 2025, the highest rate of any Senate Democrat. He has repeatedly sided with Republicans on immigration, government funding, Trump’s nominees and the President’s use of military force. Most recently, he cast the deciding vote against an effort to curb Trump’s use of force in Iran. Pennsylvania Republicans now view Fetterman more favorably than they view McCormick, the actual Republican Senator representing their state, according to a poll conducted last month by The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University. Nearly two-thirds of Pennsylvania Democrats viewed Fetterman unfavorably.
Asked in Texas why he would not become an independent, Fetterman’s answer captured the peculiar place he now occupies in American politics. “I’m not a Republican,” he said.
Later in the evening, an audience member asked again why he hadn’t left the Democratic Party. “Because I’m a lifelong Republican,” Fetterman said. Immediately realizing his mistake, he put his hand to his head and joked that he knew the line would get clipped and go viral.

NATO Chief Says Not All Responses to Russian Hybrid Attacks Will Be Public
NATO has all the tools needed to respond to Russian sabotage and other hostile actions, while allies should remain calm and continue supporting Ukraine, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated on September 29, according to The Guardian.
Russian hybrid operations across Europe have increasingly combined sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incursions, and attacks on critical infrastructure while remaining below the threshold of conventional war, as UNITED24 Media recently detailed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Rutte was asked whether recent sabotage incidents against alliance members should still be described as “hybrid threats.”
The Guardian reported that he agreed the phrase can understate the seriousness of the threat.
“It sounds a bit cuddly,” Rutte stated, referring to the term “hybrid threat.”
He emphasized that NATO “has all the response options we need,” even if some measures are not made public. The Guardian wrote that Rutte urged allies not to overreact while continuing defense investments and support for Ukraine.
“I would urge some calm, because we are investing in our defense [and] Russia is not in a good place,” Rutte stated.
He added that allies should “carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going,” describing continued assistance to Kyiv as the most effective response to Russian actions in the so-called grey zone.
“The best response to any action in this grey zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine,” Rutte stated, according to The Guardian.
Rutte also warned allies against underestimating Russia, while arguing that NATO retains a stronger overall position.
“We should not be naive about Russia,” he stated. “They know we are stronger and we have to make sure by carrying on with our investments that we are also stronger in two, three, five years from now.”
Pressed further on sabotage and other hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledged that they “are having an impact.” The Guardian reported that he again stressed NATO has “all the response options: sometimes visible, sometimes not.”
Rutte also emphasized the importance of publicly attributing hostile incidents to Russia when evidence allows. He praised Estonia for doing so on September 29 after authorities linked an August arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics in Tallinn to Russian special services.
“I applaud it,” Rutte stated.
NATO is acting “in the spirit of staying calm, carrying on,” he added. “We are stronger, and they know it.”
The EU had recently considered a NATO-style emergency protocol to coordinate collective responses to Russian sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, and other hybrid operations. The proposed mechanism was intended to address hostile actions that remain below the threshold for triggering NATO’s Article 5.

Russian Mercenaries Used Live Prisoners to Practice Stabbing People in the Heart in Mali
Russian mercenaries in Mali used live prisoners to practice killing people with knives, including stabbing them in the heart, while other captives were deliberately wounded and mutilated for tactical medicine training, according to a former Wagner fighter now held in Ukrainian captivity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The former mercenary described the alleged practices in an interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Karpenko published in September 2026. He said Russian instructors used at least three captured Africans for training exercises and that none survived.
The fighter said he signed a contract with Wagner in 2023 and traveled to Mali via Syria that September, remaining there until April 2024. According to his account, approximately 120 to 130 Wagner personnel traveled with him, with mercenaries receiving about $3,000 per month.
One prisoner, he said, was drugged before Russian personnel used him to demonstrate how to kill a person by stabbing them in the heart. “They showed us how to kill with a knife to the heart. They picked two people, those who were ready, and said: ‘Here, stab him in the heart,’” the former Wagner fighter said.
He also described Russian instructors deliberately inflicting severe injuries on other prisoners so mercenaries could practice treating battlefield wounds and stopping major bleeding. In one case, he said an explosive charge was attached to a prisoner’s leg and detonated before the group practiced treating the resulting injury.
“We gathered for medical training, and they brought in a captured terrorist. They strapped a TNT charge to his leg. They set it off, everyone moved away, and his leg, of course, was blown off,” he said.
According to the former Wagner fighter, the same prisoner was later deliberately shot near an artery in the armpit so the mercenaries could practice controlling another severe hemorrhage. The prisoner subsequently died, he said.
A third prisoner had his leg cut off with an axe before the mercenaries practiced applying a tourniquet, according to the fighter. “They were practicing bandaging on the third one’s leg, but they simply chopped his leg off. Yes, they tightened a tourniquet… Well, so that everything would be like in extreme situations, so that it would be realistic,” he said.
The former Wagner member said all three prisoners died during the exercises. His account could not be independently verified.
After returning to Russia, the fighter said he signed a contract with the Russian Defense Ministry in August 2025 and joined Russia’s 14th Separate Guards Special Purpose Brigade, a military intelligence special forces formation. He was later captured by Ukrainian forces while fighting against Ukraine.
Wagner personnel have previously faced allegations of serious abuses during Russian operations in Africa. UN experts have documented allegations involving Wagner-linked personnel in the Central African Republic, including violence, intimidation, and other abuses against civilians.
Russia expanded Wagner’s operations across Africa before the death of the group’s founder, Yevgeny Prigozhin, in 2023. Moscow subsequently moved to bring much of the organization’s overseas network under greater state control, while Russian military-linked personnel continued operating in Mali and other African countries.

British premier says 'Brexit has done more harm than good'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:53:58 UTC
23:53:58 KST

Aysu Bicer
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday he will “lay out to the country” different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit “has done more harm than good.”
Speaking at the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Burnham said Britain could not have “the clear path we need into the rest of this century” without deciding on its future relationship with the EU, which he described as “still our largest market.”
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referrendum in which about 52% of voters chose to leave.
The prime minister said he would use the opportunity around the summit to set out the choices available to Britain.
“And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in,” he said.
Burnham also announced that Labour's next manifesto would contain a commitment to change the UK's electoral system.
He said he was creating a “new national commission on electoral reform” and invited all political parties to take part in its work.
“In past years, you have voted twice to support electoral reform. I hear you, I agree with you,” Burnham said.
“We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard,” he added.
‘May pay a political price’
Burnham promised to put Britain "on a new path" and unveiling policies on water, housing, energy and education.
"When we pull as one, there is nothing we can't do," he said. “Today, we draw a line on a decade of division. We stop doom scrolling on posts running Britain down. And we put the country on a new path.”
He acknowledged he "may pay a political price" for his announcements but said “someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”
‘Water is a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain’
Burnham said Environment Secretary Angela Eagle would introduce a "strengthened Water Bill" including the repeal of “Margaret Thatcher's ideological ban on public ownership of water companies.”
"Water is a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain," he said, criticising sewage dumping, high prices and problems with infrastructure.
He, however, did not announce plans to nationalize any individual water companies.
Housing, energy and education
Burnham said the government could introduce legislation making it easier to reclaim homes from negligent landlords.
He also pledged to bring down energy prices and asked the energy secretary to speed up efforts to decouple green energy prices from gas prices.
On education, he promised to “rebuild a system of comprehensive education in this country with parity between academic and technical.”
Burnham criticised the political direction taken since the 1980s, saying: “Homes, water, energy, transport, care, healthcare - broken up and sold off.”
"The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place," he said.
Growth and fiscal rules

Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The European Commission proposed a five-point plan on Tuesday to help the EU prevent and respond to sudden, large-scale irregular arrivals at its external borders.
The proposal follows a surge in arrivals in Ceuta this summer, which the Commission said showed how quickly an emergency could develop despite irregular border crossings being at their lowest since 2021, according to a statement.
The plan calls for stronger cooperation with partner countries, reinforced external borders, improved early warning systems, action against migrant smuggling networks and more effective returns.
Among the proposals is a new European Emergency Response Framework for situations in which mass movements of people are “engineered and weaponised.”
The Commission also plans to propose a stronger mandate for the EU border agency, Frontex, including personnel and equipment that could be deployed immediately and a larger role in returns.
To improve early warning, the Commission wants Frontex to be able to monitor social media in connection with external border management. It also urged member states to report developments affecting the borders promptly through the EU’s surveillance system, EUROSUR.
The plan seeks closer cooperation with online platforms and financial institutions to identify smuggling activity and illicit financial flows. It also urges the Council to adopt a proposed sanctions regime allowing asset freezes and travel bans against migrant smugglers.
On returns, the Commission called for greater cooperation with countries of origin and transit on readmission and wider use of Frontex support.
“We will reinforce our foundation of strong external borders, effective migration diplomacy, the Pact on Migration and Asylum, and credible returns,” said EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner.
The plan will be presented to member states at the Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting Oct. 1-2.

Burnham pledges to scrap pension triple lock from 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:49:38 UTC
23:49:38 KST

LIVERPOOL, England ― U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham Tuesday pledged to scrap the controversial pension triple lock by 2030, replacing it with a new mechanism that he says will fund his national care service.
Under the new system, the state pension would no longer rise by earnings if they are the highest each year, instead rising by a “double lock” of at least an increase in inflation or 2.5% annually.
Burnham told the Labour Party conference that he will ensure that the state pension also holds its value relative to wage growth, the third aspect of the "triple" lock he wants to drop, in the long term.
Advertisement
Any changes would come after the next election, which will need to be held in 2029 at the latest.
“This change will generate significant savings, which we will use to build up our National Care Service,” Burnham said.
“Some may not realise it, but older people with nothing more than the state pension or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today. Under my plan, this will no longer happen.”
The Labour Party estimated in a note following Burnham's speech that the changes would save £15 billion per year by the end of the 2030s, rising to £50 billion a year by 2050.
The triple lock is divisive and has been called “unsustainable” by economists as it costs the Treasury around £16 billion a year and is set to rise further as inflation and earnings increase.
However, Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said that Burnham’s changes won’t fund his social care plans.
“It is great news that Andy Burnham has neutered the worst element of the triple lock,” he said. “Better reforms were available, but this one is a big improvement. It will not, however, be the answer to funding universal social care.”
