Alaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:37:09 UTC
23:37:09 KST

Alaska Airlines is overhauling cabins across Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines to add hundreds of high-end seats and building new airport lounges, banking on customers' continued willingness to pay a premium for travel luxuries to grow its profits into the next decade.
The changes were announced ahead of Alaska's investor day in Seattle on Tuesday, when the carrier's executives will face questions on the new offerings, how the airline is coping with the profit-eating surge in jet fuel this year, and its ability to reach its goal of $1 billion in added profit from end of 2024 to the end of 2027. It said Tuesday that it's two-thirds of the way there.
Investors are also likely to tie the new products to the company's prospects to grow its co-branded credit card and loyalty program, which have generated billions for airlines.
Alaska said it's working to become more reliant on revenue from premium seats, international flights, its loyalty program and cargo, which is higher margin than the main cabin. It forecast on Tuesday that those more lucrative products will reach close to 60% of its total revenue by 2030, up from 53% currently.
Even with the cabin changes, Alaska, which completed its merger with Hawaiian Airlines in September 2024, will continue to operate the two airlines as separate brands.
Here are some of the changes:
- Alaska's Boeing 787 Dreamliners will get 34 lie-flat suites in a new offering it's calling Aurora. It will also have 35 seats in a new premium-economy section, called Premium Reserve, on the 787-9 and 787-10, starting in 2028.
- "At least" 25 of the yet-to-be certified Boeing 737 Max 10s will have 12 lie-flat Aurora suites and premium-economy seats, a bid to compete with other airlines on lucrative cross-country routes.
- Hawaiian Airlines' 24 Airbus A330s will each get 22 all-new first-class suites with sliding doors, starting in 2028, and its first-ever premium-economy section, with 28 seats.
- The carrier will open a new 41,000-square-foot Alaska lounge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, with dedicated space for Aurora suites flyers, similar to the tiered lounge system Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines have.
- Hawaiian is building an almost 13,000-square-foot lounge in Honolulu's Terminal 1, slated to open in early 2028.
U.S. airlines have been spending the past few years revamping their cabins to add more premium seats, often at the expense of coach seats, since first-class fares can go for many times more than an economy-class ticket, and customers keep paying to sit closer to the front. Most of Alaska Airlines' fleet doesn't have lie-flat or other premium options that are common on competitors' jets.
Alaska is far from the first carrier to remodel its cabins, but that might work to its benefit when the fresh product hits the market.
"There is an advantage to being the last mover in that you've seen what your competitors have and if you want to you can try to one-up them," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of Atmosphere Research Group, a travel consulting firm.
Hawaiian Airlines A330 overhaul
The Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330s, used for flights to Hawaii, Asia and Oceania, have "aging interiors," said Shane Jones, Alaska's head of fleet.
The new options will bring the total count down to 254 seats from 278 on those planes. Jones said the new options will give Alaska a range of premium choices, from the honeymoon splurge to repeat Hawaii visitors looking for a step-up from coach.
He told CNBC that the airline spent months looking at fabric samples at the company's headquarters in Seattle under different types of lighting to pick the right one.
Some shades were too bright pink, while others were too drab. He said that the airline wanted to evoke the colors and mood of tropical escapes to Hawaii with a wave pattern sewn into the seat, and that the carrier evaluated how many waves were enough because too many could be dizzying.
Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said more than half of Hawaii's visitors are traveling from the West Coast of the U.S., a customer base that is "valuable to us from an economic perspective, just in terms of their income, their travel budget, their spending patterns, their flying patterns. And so this gives us an opportunity to elevate the experience."
Meanwhile, Alaska has been expanding its international flying from Seattle, including to London, Iceland and Italy, with more destinations slated to begin this fall. International travel demand has held up despite surging fuel prices, airline executives have said.
Debit card debut, frequent flyer program changes
Alaska is also planning to launch early next year a rewards debit card for its Atmos loyalty program, expanding the carrier's co-branded cards it offers with Bank of America. Airlines, including Southwest Airlines and United Airlines, have started offering their own rewards debit cards with Sunrise Bank.
Alaska said the new debit card is aimed at younger and new arrivals in the U.S. and said it "expands the program's reach beyond traditional credit products."
Also, starting on Thursday, Atmos frequent flyer program members will have to choose between earning miles by distance traveled, price of the ticket or segments flown. Airlines have largely moved away from distance-based earnings, instead prioritizing how much travelers spend on the airline or on rewards credit cards.
Correction: This story has been updated to correct the issuer of Southwest and United airline debit cards.

Consumer optimism slides sharply as fears escalate over rising prices and jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:36:47 UTC
23:36:47 KST

Consumer sentiment fell to its lowest level since 2014 in September as an inflation-weary public took a dimmer view on the labor market and the impact higher prices would have on their finances, the Conference Board reported Tuesday.
The board's Consumer Confidence Index tumbled to 81.9, a decline of 6.7 points and a reading well below the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 89.
Respondents cited concerns over inflation and the jobs outlook. For the first time in the four-year history of the survey question, more respondents said their personal finances were bad as opposed to good.
"Consumer appraisals of current business conditions became negative for the first time since September 2024," said Dana Peterson, the Conference Board's chief economist.
"Consumers' write-in responses regarding factors affecting the economy were mostly pessimistic in September," she added. "References to prices, the high cost of goods and services, and oil and gas prices in particular, rose to new heights, reflecting September's surge in fuel costs."
Other readings showed similar deterioration: The board's Present Situation Index fell 7.9 points to 109.3, while the Expectations Index, a six-month outlook window, slipped 5.9 points to 63.6.
On the labor front, the differential between those saying jobs are "plentiful" against "hard to get," a closely watched barometer of labor market health, eroded further, down 2.5 percentage points to just 1.7%.
Those results came against rising inflation expectations, pushed by continued uncertainty over the Iran war, which has been reflected in financial markets by surging Treasury yields and mortgage rates.
Respondents on average expect an inflation rate of 6.1%, an increase of 0.3 percentage point from August. The median expectation also rose 0.3 point to 5.1%.
The Conference Board's reading is in keeping with similar surveys. The University of Michigan's consumer survey showed sentiment fell 7% in September to its second-lowest reading on record.
In other economic news Tuesday, job openings in August edged lower to 7.08 million, down 256,000 for the month amid sharp declines in professional and business services as well as healthcare-related jobs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported. The Wall Street consensus had been for 7.2 million openings.
Hires edged higher for the month while quits were little changed and layoffs fell slightly.

Burnham vows to seek new ‘long-term’ relationship with EU in emotional Labour conference speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:34:26 UTC
23:34:26 KST

Andy Burnham has staked his future on a gamble that the public will back radical progressive policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that his agenda will break the mould of the last 40 years and “allow us to rise again”.
In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto, acknowledging that he may end up paying the price for creating sharp new dividing lines in politics.
“I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”
However, while the prime minister said he would try to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living, he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances.
“These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,” he told Labour activists.
“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down. The approach I am outlining today is the responsible one.”
With global economic storm clouds gathering and Labour dropping behind Reform UK in one poll this week, Burnham was determined to leave his audience in the conference hall in Liverpool, and at home, some hope.
During his hour-long speech, in which he paused several times after being overcome with emotion at mentioning the death of his father, he said he wanted to show the UK was “something worth saving, worth fighting for”.
He said: “I believe the plan I have outlined today will not just hold us together, it will allow us to rise again.”
Burnham promised to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong, saying it was time to admit “Brexit hasn’t given us control” and that it was a handbrake on growth.
In his strongest hint yet that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he said he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship with the bloc at the reset summit this autumn.
Options could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, the customs union or single market, or even reversing Brexit in its entirety.
“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” he said. “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a high level of growth and prosperity for Britain.”
While public attitudes towards leaving the EU have shifted over time, Burnham’s shift away from Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines will still be a big political gamble in seats such as his own, Makerfield, which voted for Brexit.
Burnham confirmed he would end the pensions triple lock should Labour win the next election and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.
He plans to break the link between wage growth and pensions and promised instead a rise based on inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, which he claimed would still leave millions of pensioners better off.
He said pensioners would benefit from the new care system – which would be expected to follow the Scottish system in covering care costs but not accommodation – and a promise to exempt them from income tax.
Burnham suggested that care workers were “invisible to the political class” but he told them: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”
As well as a promise to fix the broken system, the prime minister’s words will be interpreted as a sign he is preparing to carve out migrant care workers from Shabana Mahmood’s immigration measures.
In another commitment to a long-held belief, Burnham also confirmed he would put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto, announcing a cross-party national commission to consider options to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation.
“We can’t succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times,” he said. “It is always in my mind that I’m the seventh prime minister in 10 years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
“We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on 30% of the vote or less.”
Burnham said it was the drive of his government for every person to feel greater control over the basics of life and renew faith that systems could work for them.
He said the common wealth of Britain, its homes, energy, water and care, had been stripped out and sold for profit. “The wealth we had created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few,” he said.
“The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said in remarks that drew a standing ovation.
Burnham promised two new pieces of legislation later this year, including a leasehold reform bill that would put curbs on charges for homes.
“The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” he said. “This is the break we are making with the flawed thinking of the last 40 years. Not seeing housing only as a market with winners and losers, but as an essential everyone needs for a good life.”
He said a water bill would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on state-owned water companies, which was a “symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain”. There will be new curbs on bosses and pay and new powers for mayors over water systems.
He also confirmed the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid, while ministers will speed up the breaking of the link between energy prices and the international gas market.
The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “Burnham wants to take Britain back to the 1970s – a time of more government control, more trade union control and no economic growth. There is a reason our country took a different course after that decade.
“Nothing Burnham announced today will do anything to fix Britain’s long-term problems. He had no plan to fix our stagnant economy. No plan to fund defence. No plan to sort out the spiralling welfare bill beyond more government schemes.”
Reform UK’s Nigel Farage said: “By potentially scrapping the triple lock, Andy Burnham will abdicate his responsibility to British pensioners. Instead of cutting our bloated benefits bill, stopping migrants from accessing benefits, or slashing foreign aid, he’s considering launching an offensive against our elderly.”
Labour MPs responded with relief and enthusiasm to Burnham’s conference address, which the prime minister wrote almost entirely alone, with more than one describing it as the speech of their political lifetimes.
However, there were words of caution from some ministers and Downing Street insiders, who will be more interested in how the speech goes down with the wider public at home than in the room.
“I don’t want to be negative, but we’ve got to be realistic,” one cabinet minister said. “We just don’t know what’s going to happen with the economic headwinds. But if anybody can get us through it, Andy can.”

Who is sabotaging Syria's recovering gas network?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:32:16 UTC
23:32:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is sabotaging Syria's recovering gas network?
A second act of sabotage against Syria's gas network in six weeks has raised questions over who is targeting the country's recovering energy infrastructure as Damascus attempts to restore electricity production after years of war.
A fire broke out on Monday evening on a gas pipeline between al-Shola and Deir al-Zour following an explosion at an isolation valve, according to the Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC), which said the blast was caused by an act of sabotage.
The attack halted the flow of gas from the Jbeissa plant in Hasakah to electricity-generating stations, while emergency crews isolated the affected section of pipeline as pressure in the network fell.
No group has claimed responsibility and Syrian authorities have not identified any suspects.
However, the incident follows another attack on infrastructure connected to Jbeissa on 18 August, when an explosion struck the plant's gas export pipeline.
The SPC said an investigation into that incident found it had been caused by "deliberate sabotage", forcing the company to halt pumping and affecting supplies to several electricity-generating turbines.
The two incidents come as Syria's new authorities attempt to revive an energy sector devastated by more than a decade of war, sanctions and the fragmentation of the country's oil and gas fields between rival armed groups.
Jbeissa has become an important part of those efforts.
In January, the SPC began pumping raw gas from the Jbeissa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs province, with around 1.2 million cubic metres passing through the network each day to support electricity generation.
Damascus has also been working to reconnect other major eastern gas facilities to the national network.
Earlier this month, gas began flowing from the al-Tabiya facility, commonly known as the Conoco gas field, in Deir al-Zour after rehabilitation work on wells and pipelines damaged or left unusable during the war.
The facility is expected to produce around 1.5 million cubic metres of gas per day, with much of it destined for electricity generation.
The rehabilitation drive follows a major shift in control over Syria's energy resources earlier this year, when the government took control of key oil and gas fields previously held by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in the northeast.
That has given Damascus access to resources that could play an important role in restoring electricity supplies and rebuilding an economy battered by years of conflict.
It has also left a sprawling network of wells, processing facilities and pipelines requiring protection across areas that remain vulnerable to armed groups.
Who could be behind the attacks?
There is currently no public evidence linking either act of sabotage to a particular group.
One possibility authorities will have to consider is the Islamic State group, which retains cells in eastern Syria despite the collapse of its territorial "caliphate" in 2019.
Deir al-Zour remains one of the group's principal areas of activity in Syria. ISIS attacks have continued in the province during 2026, particularly against security forces, amid concerns that changing territorial control in the northeast has created new security gaps.
However, ISIS has not claimed either of the attacks on the Jbeissa network, despite regularly publicising its operations.
The complicated security landscape of eastern Syria also leaves other possibilities.
For years, Deir al-Zour was divided between competing forces and contained an extensive presence of Assad regime forces, Iran-backed armed groups, tribal formations, the SDF and ISIS cells.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad and subsequent expansion of the Sharaa government's control have transformed that landscape, but networks established during the conflict have not necessarily disappeared.
Whether remnants of former regime or Iran-aligned networks retain the ability or incentive to target energy infrastructure is therefore one question surrounding the attacks, although there is currently no evidence connecting them to either incident.
Local disputes provide another possible explanation.
Control of oil fields, smuggling routes and energy resources has long been intertwined with tribal, armed and criminal networks in eastern Syria. Clashes between local gunmen over control of oil wells have continued during the post-Assad period, while unidentified armed groups remain active across Deir ez-Zor.
Sabotage therefore does not necessarily point to a centrally directed insurgent campaign.
Why target Syria's gas network?
Whatever the motive, the attacks expose the vulnerability of infrastructure central to Damascus's plans for economic recovery.
Syria has recently reported a substantial increase in electricity generation, while the government is attempting to rehabilitate damaged fields, pipelines and processing plants and attract foreign companies back into the country's energy sector.
Restoring eastern gas production is central to that strategy because additional domestic gas can be fed directly into power generation.
Repeated attacks on pipelines could therefore have consequences far beyond the immediate damage caused by an explosion.
They could interrupt electricity production, increase repair costs and complicate attempts to convince foreign investors that Syria's energy infrastructure can be operated securely.
Two incidents in six weeks are not enough to establish that Syria is facing a coordinated campaign against its gas network.
But with Damascus attempting to bring some of the country's most valuable energy assets back into production, the attacks demonstrate that repairing Syria's pipelines may prove easier than securing them.

The Trump administration's new chatbot aimed at helping Americans navigate official government websites is powered by artificial intelligence from Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia said Tuesday.
"We have great partners behind the scenes," Gebbia told CNBC's "Squawk Box" shortly before the site, America.gov, went live around 10 a.m. ET.
A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to a company blog post published Tuesday morning, which said, "Google is proud to be named a technology partner in this vital initiative, leveraging Gemini to help more than 100 million people access critical public resources with greater speed and ease."
"By supporting the administration's vision for digital modernization, we are committed to making these everyday public services seamless, accessible, and responsive for all Americans," the post read.
Grok developer xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX and renamed SpaceXAI, did not respond to CNBC's request for comment. Gebbia sits on the board of directors of Tesla, which is led by Musk, owns a piece of SpaceXAI and uses Grok in its vehicles.
"Every day, 40 million people interact with a government website trying to get something done. And I think we could all agree that we wish it was better," Gebbia told CNBC.
The AI tool interacts with all of the roughly 29,000 government websites to respond to user questions with up-to-date information, Gebbia said.
"You come to America.gov and you ask for what you need, and in a chat interface, we go off on the back end and scan across all those tens of thousands of websites to pull in any information that is specific to whatever your request is, and give you a personalized response that's only from official sources," he said. "So there's no chance of getting outdated or inaccurate information like you might on third-party websites."
The site is being unveiled at a day-long event in Washington's Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, attended by President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other administration officials and industry leaders.
"It's not just simply a website. It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said in a speech at the event.
The gathering will also include a range of panel discussions on AI and other topics, including, energy, health, space and agriculture.

While he said the four-weekly routes will improve connectivity, Sengstschmid hopes visitors will use Baku as a gateway to explore the country further afield.
“It's really to travel beyond Baku – to travel along the Silk Road, through the side valleys, ancient heritage villages,” he said, while also highlighting the country’s UNESCO World Heritage Sites, settlements, cities on the greater Caucasus Mountains and the Khan’s palace.
Another hidden gem he spoke about was Sim in southern Azerbaijan. Sengstschmid described the village as "a fairy-tale with moss", replete with wooden buildings, waterfalls, and various fauna and flora.
“It feels a bit like you're in the jungle, but in the middle you're basically in Azerbaijan,” he said. “And this describes the diversity you can experience once you really go out of the city – dive into the country and meet the wonderful, lovely people.”
He also pointed to the country's diversity with various climate zones, which offers travellers experiences in semi-desert landscapes to mountain peaks that exceed 4,000 metres high above sea level all in one destination.
In 2025, tourism to the country generated 7 billion Azerbaijani Manat (€3.5 billion), which accounted for 5.4% of the country’s GDP. Azerbaijan has garnered visitors by hosting major events such as Formula 1, and previously Eurovision and COP29.
When asked to sum the country in three words, he replied with “real, warm and uplifting”. For Sengstschmid, Azerbaijan “continues to reveal many new sights and this is what it still does to me, although living there for many, many years and calling it my home”.

EU leaders are set to call on Ukraine to “intensify” reforms - media
Kyiv • UNN
The EU will call on Ukraine to accelerate anti-corruption and tax reforms in order to receive financial support for 2026. So far, €14.9 billion has been allocated.
EU leaders are set to call on Ukraine to accelerate work on domestic reforms, which would unlock billions of euros in financial support earmarked for 2026, according to a preliminary draft of the European Council conclusions for next month. UNN writes about this, citing Rapporteur.
Details
The text contains a call on "all participants, including Ukraine, to intensify efforts to ensure the disbursement" of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan and funding under the Ukraine Facility for 2026.
Only €14.9 billion of the €45 billion loan earmarked for this year has so far been disbursed, partly because Ukraine's parliament has not adopted the anti-corruption and tax reforms demanded by Brussels, the publication writes.
The heads of state and government of the bloc's countries will meet on October 15 and 16 for talks on Ukraine, defense, migration, and the EU's next long-term budget.
The draft document emerged against the backdrop of what the publication describes as "growing frustration in Brussels over Ukraine's failure to carry out reforms linked to the €90 billion EU loan, which is intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's financing needs for 2026 and 2027".
On Monday, Ukraine's Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko, as the publication interprets it, "appeared to reject" Brussels' demand that Kyiv introduce tax reforms linked to the loan, arguing that Ukrainian businesses and citizens are already suffering because of increasingly brutal Russian drone and missile strikes, as well as Moscow's naval blockade of the Black Sea, which is destroying the economy.
"To be honest, I am not sure that now is the right time to introduce additional taxes for Ukrainians," Marchenko said at an event organized by the European Policy Centre, a Brussels-based think tank.
According to an internal briefing document seen by the publication, "Brussels has identified several reforms as being 'at risk' due to the Ukrainian parliament's inability to adopt the reforms."
"These include a law abolishing the tax exemption for imported parcels and a law on taxing income earned through digital platforms," the publication says.
"…it is very important that funding and reforms move forward together so that we can support Ukraine's resilience, as well as Ukraine's path to the EU," a European Commission spokesperson told reporters on Monday.
Marchenko will discuss Ukraine's financing needs at a meeting of the Ukraine Donor Platform, which coordinates international financing for Ukraine, to be held today, September 29, in Brussels and chaired by European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos, the publication writes.
The draft European Council conclusions may be changed.

Faculty's role in campus antisemitism overlooked over last decade, new AMCHA research reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:29:56 UTC
23:29:56 KST

Faculty-led anti-Zionist activism, anchored primarily around public backing for academic boycotts of Israel, has served as a central and long-overlooked driver of campus antisemitism, AMCHA Initiative Director Tammi Rossman-Benjamin argues in a new book chapter.
The chapter, titled "Measuring Faculty Anti-Zionist to Predict and Combat Campus Antisemitism," is featured in the new volume Toward the Last Encampment: Campus Culture and the Jews Before and After October 7, edited by Alvin H. Rosenfeld and published by Wicked Son.
Drawing on six empirical studies spanning more than a decade, the research demonstrates that faculty endorsement of academic boycotts consistently predicts where antisemitism is most likely to emerge, concentrate, and intensify across US campuses.
AMCHA began compiling a national database of faculty publicly endorsing academic boycotts against Israel in 2013. According to the research, faculty support served as an objective measure of anti-Zionism because endorsements are verifiable, academic boycotts demand concrete action within the academy, and their explicit goal is to de-normalize Israel and Zionism in academic life.
Across six studies, the data revealed a consistent pattern linking faculty boycotters to campus hostility. Campuses with higher numbers of faculty academic boycotters experienced increased levels of reported antisemitic activity, with faculty support emerging as a stronger predictor of the targeting of Jewish students for harm than even the presence of an anti-Zionist student group.
Furthermore, academic departments with one or more faculty boycotters were significantly more likely to sponsor events featuring boycott-supporting speakers. Specifically, Ethnic Studies units with a boycotter were roughly 10 times more likely, Gender Studies about 12 times more likely, and Middle East Studies about 5 times more likely to host such events.
Additionally, campuses with five or more academic boycotters were approximately seven times more likely to have a department issue or endorse an anti-Zionist statement. The report defines anti-Zionist statements as those containing rhetoric that denies Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state or demonizes and delegitimizes Israel, Israelis, Zionism or Zionists.
Classroom instruction was similarly affected, as courses taught by instructors who supported academic boycotts had a median of approximately 78 percent of their required readings authored by boycott supporters, compared to a median of 17 percent in courses taught by instructors who did not support boycotts.
Antisemitism escalated after October 7
The chapter also examines how the dynamic escalated following the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attacks, as individual faculty activism transformed into organized networks through chapters of Faculty for Justice in Palestine (FJP). AMCHA's research found that campuses with pre-existing academic boycotters were significantly more likely to establish FJP chapters.
Where FJP groups were present, the likelihood of physical assaults on Jewish students was more than seven times higher, violent threats were about 3.4 times higher, and campus protests and encampments lasted significantly longer compared to comparable institutions.
To help university leaders, trustees, parents, and policymakers evaluate these institutional risks, the research highlights the Anti-Zionist Faculty Barometer, a tool that compiles objective metrics, including the number of faculty boycotters, FJP presence, chapter activity levels, and departmental statements, to rank campuses on a scale from negligible to extreme.
The chapter concludes that faculty boycott activity functions as both a signal and a driver of campus antisemitism, with organized faculty activity amplifying its effects and making visible a faculty dimension that universities have overlooked for years.
Three recommendations to address campus antisemitism
To address these challenges, Rossman-Benjamin outlines specific recommendations for institutional and government leaders.
First, school administrators must establish robust safeguards and enforcement mechanisms to prevent faculty from using academic positions and departmental affiliations to promote politically motivated activism that targets students and colleagues for harm.
Second, state and federal legislators should consider enacting legislation, such as Texas's pioneering 2023 law prohibiting state-funded colleges from implementing academic boycotts, to withhold government funding from schools that permit faculty to engage in such behavior.
Third, in the absence of official action, university stakeholders should actively press leaders to end the politicization of academic units and protect the campus community from the politically motivated misuse of academic positions.
Reflecting on the overarching findings of the research, Rossman-Benjamin notes, "For years, universities have treated campus antisemitism largely as a problem of student activism or isolated incidents, while one of the most consequential forces has received far less scrutiny."
She adds, "October 7 did not create this problem. It exposed a problem that had been building inside our universities for years, with faculty playing a critical and largely overlooked role. Across study after study, faculty support for academic BDS emerges as an extraordinarily important indicator of antisemitism – and the evidence shows that its influence can reach from individual professors into classrooms, departments, organized faculty networks and the broader campus environment."

UK Charity Commission investigates Doctors Without Borders following alleged terror links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:29:31 UTC
23:29:31 KST

The UK Charity Commission has opened a regulatory compliance case into Medecins Sans Frontieres (UK), widely known as Doctors Without Borders, responding to a detailed report filed by UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI). The report focuses on allegations that the international medical charity maintains connections with terrorist organizations active in the Gaza Strip.
A senior case manager within the Charity Commission’s High Risk Compliance division formally notified UKLFI of the decision via email last Wednesday, indicating that the agency had initiated a compliance case to evaluate the situation and review the specific points outlined in the report.
A UKLFI spokesperson commented in a statement: “We welcome the Charity Commission’s confirmation that it has opened a regulatory compliance case concerning Medecins Sans Frontieres UK and will consider the serious concerns raised in our report.”
“We hope that the Charity Commission will examine these matters thoroughly and establish whether MSF UK and its trustees have complied with their legal and regulatory obligations,” the spokesperson added.
MSF's connection with Hamas, other terror groups
The regulatory development follows a submission presented by UKLFI in early September, which drew attention to the charity’s purported connections with Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP). The dossier compiled by UKLFI highlights multiple individuals previously or currently employed by MSF in Gaza who are accused of maintaining active roles within proscribed groups or publicly celebrating terrorist operations.
Prominent among the cited instances is Fadi Jihad Mohammed al-Wadiya, an MSF physiotherapist who was killed during a June 2024 airstrike in Gaza. Although MSF initially rejected Israeli assertions linking him to PIJ operations, the PIJ subsequently released statements and imagery in February 2026 designating al-Wadiya as a commander and deputy head of its manufacturing division. In response, MSF maintained that it lacked prior knowledge of any military affiliation and reiterated its policy against knowingly retaining individuals involved in combat activities.
Additional scrutiny within the report targets other personnel, including a driver flagged by Israeli defense officials as a Hamas sniper and a physician allegedly tied to the PFLP medical apparatus who shared social media content praising terrorist acts. The filing also scrutinizes operational ties between MSF and the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, noting instances where medical stock was shared or transferred.
MSF's financial, governance oversight
Regarding financial and governance oversight, UKLFI has requested that the regulatory body investigate whether MSF UK leadership maintained sufficient supervision over international operational centers receiving charitable capital, and whether safeguards are robust enough to prevent asset diversion to militant factions. Public filings indicate that MSF UK generated upwards of £95 million in total income throughout 2024, which included £2.7 million earmarked specifically for humanitarian initiatives across the Palestinian territories.
While the Charity Commission emphasized that opening a regulatory compliance case does not imply formal findings of culpability or breaches of charity legislation on the part of the trustees, the move ensures a formal examination of the points raised.
A UKLFI spokesperson said in a statement: “MSF is one of the world’s most prominent medical charities, and its humanitarian work depends on the confidence of donors that their contributions are being used exclusively for legitimate charitable purposes.”
The spokesperson added, “Providing medical care to civilians in conflict zones is vital, but humanitarian objectives do not remove the obligation to undertake rigorous due diligence and ensure that charitable funds, facilities, and personnel are not used to support terrorism.”
After the compliance case opened, MSF said in a statement that it “unequivocally rejects the allegations that we knowingly hired people with ‘ties to terrorism.’ MSF would never knowingly employ anyone involved in military activities, which contradicts our core values and ethics. Any employee who engages in military activity would pose a danger to our staff and patients.
“We understand why the Charity Commission is engaging with us in relation to these allegations and we are cooperating fully. We are confident in the integrity of our processes. MSF remains fully committed to transparency, regulatory compliance, and its charitable mission of providing vital medical assistance to people who need it most.”

Zelensky, Jewish community leaders commemorate 85th anniversary of Nazi's Babyn Yar WWII massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:29:24 UTC
23:29:24 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky attended an annual memorial ceremony to commemorate the tens of thousands of Jews massacred by Nazis at Babyn Yar on Tuesday, which happened 85 years ago on September 29 and 30, 1941.
Several Jewish Ukrainian leaders, including those from the Chabad community, were present at the event. The ceremony was organized by Ukraine's Presidential Office, the Babyn Yar memorial complex, and the Federation of Jewish Communities of Ukraine.
"We must remember the terrible things that happened here many years ago, and now they are happening again, this time at the hands of the Russians," Zelensky said.
"Thank you very much for being with us here today, and thank you for praying for Ukraine, for Ukrainians, for all those who have been killed in Ukraine, for the tragic moments we have endured, and for the Jews who were tortured and murdered. Never again!" Zelensky stated.
Representatives from about 50 countries attended, including Israel's Ambassador to Ukraine Roi Rosenblit. Zelensky thanked the ambassadors and the international community for their "help in fighting against the terrible things the Russians are doing to us, to humanity, and to civilization."
Ukrainian security forces deployed special air-defense systems and snipers positioned around the site due to concerns over a possible attack, particularly threats posed by Russian drones.
Zelensky discusses arrangements for remains of Israeli teen killed in Kyiv to be returned to Israel
While attending, Zelensky discussed Daniel Umansky, an Israeli child who was killed by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv last week, with the FJCU, particularly regarding the arrangements to transport his remains to Israel for burial.
One of the attendees, who has been running Jewish community and educational institutions in Kyiv for nearly 30 years, discussed her grandmother, who was murdered in Babyn Yar.
"Grandmother Sonia was murdered in her fifties. We were unable to find a photograph of her, but we recently located a testimony at Yad Vashem containing her details," Rebbetzin Devorah Leah Levenhartz said.
"It turns out that before her murder, she lived not far from where we ourselves lived, and she now gets to be part of the thriving Jewish community we established...It is almost impossible to comprehend," she added.
"The tragedy of Babyn Yar is an absolutely tragic and bloody example, and today we are meeting on the 85th anniversary of the tragedy of Babyn Yar," Zelensky said in his address.
"This tragedy reminds us how painful it is to lose our family and loved ones, and how the value of human life can be diminished," he added.
"I want to thank you for understanding the value of life. That is, of course, felt especially strongly in Ukraine during this shameful, unprovoked war by Russia against Ukraine, against society, against people, and against life itself," he continued.
What happened in the Babyn Yar Massacre?
On September 29-30, 1941, the Nazis gunned down nearly 34,000 Jews in Babyn Yar in what would later be considered the first massacre of the Jews in the Holocaust.
Babyn Yar is located near Kyiv, which the Nazis took control of on September 19, 1941. A few days later, there was a large explosion at the German command post that killed many German soldiers. The Nazis blamed the explosion on the Jews, intensifying their hatred, so when the SS troops entered Kyiv, the city's Jews were immediately marked for destruction.
Between September 29 and 30, nearly 34,000 Jewish men, women, and children were marched to the ravine of Babyn Yar, stripped and machine-gunned into a mass grave, which was immediately covered, burying some of the victims alive.
The grave was filled with thousands more bodies over the next two years. The total is unclear, but at least 100,000 people were murdered at Babyn Yar over two years. The victims were primarily Jewish, but they also included communists, Soviet prisoners of war, and Roma people.
Despite the tragedy that occurred at Babyn Yar, it took the Soviet Union 25 years to acknowledge the massacre. After trying unsuccessfully to build a sports stadium over the mass grave in 1961, the Soviet Union constructed a small obelisk to stand at the site.
In 1974, a 15-meter memorial statue was erected, but still, there was no hint of the fact that Jews had been murdered at Babyn Yar, as the identification of the victims was vague and did not mention the word 'Jew.'
Only in 1991, 50 years after the massacre, when Ukraine declared independence, was the identity of the victims properly recorded on the memorial, recognizing the massacre of Jews at the site.
Ariella Marsden contributed to this report.

Syria calls on EU to pressure Israel to end attacks on its territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:27:12 UTC
23:27:12 KST

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al Shaibani has called on the European Union to move beyond statements of concern and exert effective pressure on Israel to halt its continuing attacks on Syria.
“This systematic aggression against a country that is recovering requires more than statements of concern; it requires effective pressure to stop these attacks,” Shaibani told a joint press conference with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in Damascus on Tuesday.
He called on the EU Foreign Affairs Council to take “a decisive position by calling these attacks by their true name” and demanding the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines held on Dec. 8, 2024.
Shaibani also called for the issue to be explicitly placed on the agenda of the EU’s Political and Security Committee.
He said Europe’s rejection of changing borders by force should apply equally on the other side of the Mediterranean.
Israel has carried out repeated strikes and ground incursions in southern Syria since the fall of the Bashar al Assad regime in December 2024. Syria says Israel must withdraw from territory it occupied after Dec. 8, 2024 and has reaffirmed its commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement.
Shaibani reiterated that the occupied Golan Heights are Syrian territory and said UN Security Council Resolution 497 considers Israel’s annexation of the territory “null and void.”
He welcomed the EU’s rejection of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights and said Damascus remains fully committed to the 1974 disengagement agreement, while seeking active European support for renewing the mandate of the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF).
Last week, Syrian President Ahmed al Sharaa told the UN General Assembly that Israel had carried out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and around 300 arrests and detentions of Syrians, while reiterating Damascus’ demand for an Israeli withdrawal to the Dec. 8, 2024 lines.
New Syria-EU partnership
Shaibani said his talks with Kallas also covered plans for a new Syria-EU partnership agreement to replace the 1977 accord.
He said the two sides aim to prepare a joint scope paper before the end of the first quarter of 2027 and agreed to institutionalise their discussions through technical committees.
Damascus also seeks to elevate cooperation into a strategic commitment by including Syria in the EU’s multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034, Shaibani said.
The Syrian foreign minister said Damascus supports maintaining restrictive measures against figures from the Assad regime but called for sanctions to be lifted from Syrian government institutions and state entities.
The EU lifted its economic sanctions on Syria in May 2025 to support the country’s transition and reconstruction, while maintaining targeted restrictions against individuals and entities linked to the former Assad regime and measures imposed on security grounds.
The EU considers that networks linked to the ousted regime continue to retain influence and pose a risk of undermining the transition process and hampering efforts towards national reconciliation and accountability.
In May 2026, the bloc renewed those targeted measures until June 1, 2027, while removing several Syrian state entities from its sanctions list.
Shaibani said Syria had rejected from the outset becoming a platform for attacks or an arena for settling regional scores amid the latest conflict in the region.
He said Damascus stood in solidarity with Gulf countries and Jordan over Iranian attacks against them while continuing to advocate diplomatic solutions.
The top diplomat also said the conflict had demonstrated the risks of relying on a single corridor for energy and trade, arguing that Syria’s geography provides one of the shortest routes linking East and West.
“Stability in Syria is an integral part of Europe’s own security,” he said.
Kallas’ visit to Damascus comes days after she met Shaibani in New York on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, as part of a series of meetings the Syrian foreign minister held with international officials.
The EU has recently expanded its diplomatic presence in Syria and sent an ambassador to Damascus after a 14-year absence.

Erdoğan meets with economic team amid turmoil in fund market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:26:00 UTC
23:26:00 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan met with his economic team and the heads of relevant institutions on Sept. 29, as Türkiye weighs further measures in response to turmoil in the investment fund market.
Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek, and the heads of Borsa İstanbul, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK) attended the meeting.
The crisis surrounding Turkish investment funds accused of operating Ponzi-style schemes has impacted around 500,000 people, while authorities ordered the liquidation of roughly 130 funds with a combined value of $17 billion earlier this month.
Speaking after the cabinet meeting on Sept. 28, Erdoğan said the state would confront anyone found to have harmed the public or manipulated markets through investment funds, while stressing that the problems were limited and posed no broader risk to Türkiye’s financial system.
“Whoever reaches for the rights, law, property or assets of the nation will find us and the state standing against them,” Erdoğan said.
“The problem that has occurred is limited to a small part of the fund market. There is no risk that has spread to our financial system,” he said.
Erdoğan emphasized that Turkish capital markets remain resilient and have “solid foundations", saying they have sufficient capacity to overcome the current test.
The turmoil in the fund market has brought oversight mechanisms in capital markets to the forefront of discussions in Ankara, with potential new measures aimed at preventing similar problems from recurring now under consideration, daily Milliyet has reported.
Following the turmoil, the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has been evaluating potential measures, including limits on the combined positions held in individual stocks by funds managed by the same portfolio management company, minimum liquidity thresholds linked to stress tests, and the establishment of an early warning system for real-time monitoring of risks.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK), which had already launched a regulatory process before the crisis, has introduced a number of measures aimed at reducing risks, particularly in money market funds and equity hedge funds. These steps include restrictions on unsecured borrowing between related parties and regulations designed to prevent unusual price movements.
One of the proposals under consideration within the AKP is the introduction of limits on the aggregate exposure of funds managed by the same portfolio management company to a single stock. Rather than reviewing each fund’s position separately, regulators could calculate the combined holdings of all funds under the same manager and impose binding caps, particularly for stocks with low free-float levels.
As the judicial investigation into the fund crisis expands, AKP officials are also assessing its political implications alongside its economic and legal dimensions. After parliament reconvenes for the new legislative year on Oct. 1, the party may consider launching a parliamentary enquiry into all aspects of the crisis.

Eiffel Tower chief to step down over removal of women staff during Hindu group's visit
The head of the Eiffel Tower is set to step down in the wake of a controversy sparked by the removal of female workers during a private visit of the Paris landmark by members of the Hindu sect BAPS, which triggered a staff walkout earlier this month and sparked outrage in France.
The operating company that runs the Eiffel Tower said Tuesday its chief would step down at the end of this year in the wake of a controversy over the removal of women staff during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been in charge of the Paris landmark since 2018, would leave his job at the end of the year after an internal probe revealed that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of women staff, the company SETE said in a statement.
Staff at the iconic 330-metre (1,083-foot) tower staged a walkout on September 8 in protests at management's decision days earlier to sideline female workers during a visit by members of the Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha.
The group, known as BAPS, is a worldwide religious and civic organisation within the Swaminarayan sect, a conservative branch of Hinduism, with ties to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. It had been holding celebrations to mark the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple near the French capital.
Read moreEiffel Tower row over Hindu sect BAPS unites French politicians – but divides Indian diaspora
The incident sparked outrage in France, prompting politicians of all stripes to denounce an attack on fundamental liberties, and attracting scrutiny of BAPS's activities.
In a statement after the incident, the Hindu group offered "sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation".
Ariel Weil, chair of SETE, said Tuesday she had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented.

Italy completes withdrawal of armed forces from Iraq after 12 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:21:27 UTC
23:21:27 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Italy has completed the withdrawal of its armed forces from Iraq, ending a 12-year deployment, Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said Tuesday.
The last personnel, who had remained to recover and transfer logistical equipment, have returned, Crosetto said in a statement. The withdrawal was completed ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline agreed with Iraqi authorities.
“From tomorrow, therefore, our military presence in Iraq will end,” Crosetto said. He said the move was part of a new phase agreed with Iraq and partner countries, in which Iraqi security forces would assume full responsibility for the country’s security.
The US-led coalition’s Operation Inherent Resolve and NATO Mission Iraq will continue operating from other countries, he said. The NATO mission will temporarily operate from the alliance’s Joint Force Command in Lago Patria, near Naples.
Crosetto said thousands of Italian troops had served in Iraq over the past 12 years, contributing to the fight against ISIS (Daesh) and training Iraqi armed forces and security forces in the Kurdish region.
Italy plans to continue working with Iraq through training, exchanges of expertise and efforts to develop Iraqi military capabilities, he added.
The Defense Ministry said the Italian withdrawal had been largely completed by March. Two Italian Carabinieri remain in Iraq as part of the separate EU Advisory Mission, EUAM Iraq, which is authorized by the Iraqi government.

Can Trump and Xi turn a trade truce into lasting economic peace?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:21:09 UTC
23:21:09 KST

As wars and crises continue to rage across Eurasia, from Ukraine to the Persian Gulf and Gaza, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met at the White House in Washington on September 24, raising hopes that their talks could bring greater stability to global politics.
The two leaders greeted each other warmly, with Trump highlighting the potential for "harmony, peace and success" in future ties between the two countries, while Xi spoke of "charting the course for the great shift of China-US relations".
Their cordial exchanges offered a striking contrast to the tensions that have defined relations between Washington and Beijing in recent years.
Beyond a two-month truce covering $30 billion in goods, the leaders left without substantive agreements on key disputes, including a timeline for resolving tariff differences, Taiwan, and the war with Iran.
Many of those contentious matters were effectively deferred to another summit.
Despite leaving many issues unresolved, experts say a cordial meeting between the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries is itself significant at a time when the international order faces mounting challenges.
“The international status quo is potentially more perilous than at any time since 1945, as evidenced by a stagnating global economy and highly fractious geopolitics,” Dan Steinbock, an international economist and geopolitical analyst, tells TRT World.
“In such circumstances, a US-China summit, even when serving largely as a diplomatic holding pattern, is vital. It set a stage to manage friction and lock in future exchanges, which could be arenas for more structural discussions,” he adds.
Diplomacy matters
Compared with the former communist superpower Soviet Union, an adversary of the Western world, China’s “ideological system and approach are more sophisticated” and, with its growing economic and technological capabilities, poses “fundamentally different, and in many ways more difficult, challenges” to the US, Walter Russell Mead, an American strategist, wrote in a recent article.
As a result, a cordial meeting with Xi at what the Chinese leader described as a “historic juncture” matters both for US interests and the future direction of global politics, analysts say.
“China and the United States must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other,” Xi said.
“The fact that this meeting took place at all is in itself a good thing. We shouldn't judge these summits by whether they solve problems, because that's not their purpose,” Altay Atli, a senior scholar at Sabanci University’s Istanbul Policy Center, tells TRT World.
Since Trump’s May meeting with Xi in Beijing, US-China relations have faced disruptions on several fronts, from the collapse of the Iran ceasefire and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to new US sanctions on buyers of Russian oil, accusations over AI model theft and tensions over Taiwan.
Despite these disruptions, Xi, who was notably absent from last week’s UN meeting, travelled to Washington, where Trump greeted him at the airport with a red-carpet welcome.
It marked the first time in 11 years that a US president had personally greeted a Chinese leader at the airport. The visit itself was therefore a significant political development, according to Atli.
“That is a strong signal that both sides want to keep moving forward. But of course, the concrete results were modest as the deep disagreements over technology, Taiwan, and Iran remain exactly where they were. So I'd call it a summit of stabilisation rather than radical change,” he says.
Can truce turn into concrete peace?
Despite the conciliatory gestures and praise from both sides, experts doubt that the two-month business truce can create the conditions for lasting economic peace.
“Truces happen during wars, but this is far more than a trade or economic war. As Chinese leaders often say internally, it is primarily a science and technology war, then a systems war, an values/ideology war and then finally a trade war,” Charlie Parton, a senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a British think tank, says.
Unlike the Soviet Communist Party, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has undergone various transformations under different leaders, adopting a semi-capitalist model in response to Western global dominance. According to Parton, Beijing believes the US is “trying to contain and repress its global rise”.
Washington, meanwhile, has a similarly adversarial perception of Beijing, believing that China is “trying to unseat it as the leading global power,” he says.
“Both assessments are correct.”
As a result, increasingly negative perceptions on both sides mean the recent summit is unlikely to offer “a recipe for lasting peace,” says Parton, who previously served as the EU’s First Counsellor on China.
“It would be unwise to speculate on what goes through the mind of either leader. But certainly Xi came to Washington with a clear idea of what he has been seeking for some time and there is no indication or likelihood that he deviated from that,” he tells TRT World.
“Trump admires strong men such as Xi, and Xi almost certainly knows that the best way of handling Trump is to smile and be polite. But that won't alter his actions.”
Other analysts also caution against expecting a permanent settlement, while still seeing potential for a managed relationship in which the two countries develop mechanisms to address their differences.
“Turning the ongoing business truce into a permanent economic peace would require a reset on the US side, which remains unlikely. It is not impossible, but it is improbable at the moment,” Steinbock tells TRT World.
However, if the renewed diplomatic engagement displayed by the two leaders in Washington were coupled with gradual rapprochement on bilateral challenges, it could “pave the way to manage more structural conflicts between the world's two largest economies spanning industrial policy, technology controls, tariffs, and strategic rivalry,” he adds.
What the future holds
Before the end of 2026, Trump and Xi are expected to meet twice more, lending weight to Trump’s assertion that while the two countries have “different systems”, they have “never gotten along better”.
The next scheduled meeting will take place at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, while the year’s final meeting will be in Miami in December for the G20 gathering.
Behind diplomatic civility, Xi has grown more confident with the Trump administration, which is grappling with an unpopular, unresolved war with Iran, high energy prices and midterm elections just weeks away.
Since 2017, Beijing has made significant advances in areas ranging from electric vehicles and clean energy to AI, while strengthening its global standing through international groupings such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO).
Before shaking hands with Trump, Xi had maintained a busy diplomatic schedule, participating in the BRICS summit in New Delhi, making a significant visit to Cairo, an influential player in Middle Eastern affairs, and attending the SCO meeting in Kyrgyzstan, an energy-rich Central Asian state.
“He arrived as a leader who appeared to have the Global South behind him. Whether that backing is as solid as it looks is another question, but in diplomacy appearances matter. Now compare that with Trump, who is dealing with an unpopular war with Iran, high energy prices, and midterm elections in a few weeks,” Atli says.
While China also has vulnerabilities, from the Strait of Hormuz blockade and energy security to chip controls, Trump needs wins he can show to voters in a way that Xi does not, according to Atli.
“Xi can afford to wait but Trump can't.”
But the two countries also depend on each other in critical areas.
The US needs Chinese rare earths, while Beijing needs American technology and buyers, as well as a stable global economy for its exports. Both sides know that abruptly severing those ties would hurt them both.
“What both leaders are really after is a stable balance, where competition and cooperation exist side by side,” Atli tells TRT World.
“That's more realistic and achievable than a permanent economic peace.”

But as for whether a war will actually break out, we in the armed forces and the army of the Islamic Republic of Iran have tried to make maximum use of the opportunity of the ceasefire, update our target bank, optimise our equipment, bring new equipment into our combat organisation, and use the reserves, experiences and lessons of the war period," he said.
"Regarding America, I think the Americans are not in a good position in the region, because their bases have suffered serious damage. Our observations show this, through aerial and satellite imagery and through field observations on the ground. Information tells us that American bases have suffered very serious damage, and most of these bases can no longer even be rebuilt."

Fuel and food supply for America now face problems because their important base, especially the Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain, has suffered serious damage and can no longer be rebuilt. They have been forced to prepare supplies from outside the region, from East Asia and from Diego Garcia base, and from this aspect the Americans have faced many difficulties and problems.
On morale, he said some US soldiers have committed suicide and that US forces are not in a good psychological state. "Our overall analysis is that the current situation for America is not a favourable one. From this aspect, the Americans may want to create a change to alter this situation and may commit an act of aggression."
But, he said, the reality is that they have no clear strategy.

He said the martyred Brigadier General Seyyed Abdolrahim Mousavi seriously pursued the strategy that Iran's military doctrine should move from defence to offense. "In this war we practically operationalised this strategy, where we targeted the positions of anti-revolutionary and separatist groups in Iraq's Kurdistan region."
He said that as the US president had announced, large quantities of weapons had been provided to separatists and anti-Iran groups so that, in parallel with the American attack, Iran's land borders in the west would also be attacked.
"This is in fact a kind of preemptive war. Before the enemy could commit aggression, it was targeted. And you have seen that until today, the anti-revolutionaries have not been able to carry out any operation against our land borders."

Budget : comment Matignon compte durcir l’accès des étrangers aux APL et allocations familiales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:20:48 UTC
23:20:48 KST

Dans une interview accordée mi-septembre au Figaro, Sébastien Lecornu avait anticipé les réactions à sa volonté d’établir un délai de carence pour certaines allocations versées aux étrangers. | Mael Ghazi/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — “Certains considéreront peut-être que c’est une mesure symbolique, les autres, de l’autre côté, hurleront sans doute à la mesure droitière.”
Dans une interview accordée mi-septembre au Figaro sur les grands axes de son budget, Sébastien Lecornu avait anticipé les réactions à sa volonté d’établir un délai de carence pour certaines allocations versées aux étrangers. Le Premier ministre avait alors pris soin de ne pas en dévoiler les contours.
A deux jours de la présentation du budget pour 2027, un projet d’article au projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale, consulté par POLITICO, permet d’en connaître le détail.
Advertisement
D’après la mesure, les ressortissants étrangers de pays tiers (soit hors Union européenne, espace économique européen et Suisse), devront justifier d’un an de résidence régulière dans l’Hexagone avant de pouvoir bénéficier de certaines prestations familiales.
Aujourd’hui, les étrangers en situation régulière peuvent bénéficier des prestations familiales, sans durée minimale de résidence, même si des délais existent déjà pour certaines aides comme le RSA (5 ans) ou l’allocation de solidarité aux personnes âgées (10 ans).
En plus des allocations familiales, l’article concocté par la direction de la Sécurité sociale et soumis au Conseil d’Etat prévoit que les prestations versées par la CAF telles que l’allocation de soutien familial (ASF), l’allocation de rentrée scolaire (ARS), la prestation d’accueil du jeune enfant (Paje) ou encore le complément familial soient soumises au délai de carence.
Trois prestations sont en revanche exemptées : l’allocation d’éducation de l’enfant handicapé (AEEH), l’allocation journalière de présence parentale (AJPP), destinée notamment aux parents d’un enfant gravement malade ou handicapé, et l’allocation forfaitaire versée en cas de décès d’un enfant.
En outre, le délai s’appliquera également aux aides au logement, comme les APL et les allocations de logement familiale et de logement social.
Le précédent de la loi immigration
Pour rédiger la mesure, le gouvernement s’est appuyé sur les observations du Conseil constitutionnel de janvier 2024 qui, au moment de la loi immigration portée par Gérald Darmanin, avait jugé qu’une mesure similaire avec un délai de cinq ans de résidence était disproportionnée.
Advertisement
A l’époque, la mesure avait été introduite dans le projet de loi par le groupe Les Républicains au Sénat. Le texte final avait été voté avec les voix du Rassemblement national.
La résurrection de cette mesure, “c’est un gros clin d’œil au RN”, analyse un haut fonctionnaire, jadis impliqué dans le suivi de la loi immigration.
A l’annonce de Lecornu, certains élus du parti dirigé par Jordan Bardella ont d’ailleurs salué l’idée. “On nous a dit depuis des années que c’était honteux, aujourd’hui on se rend compte que c’est possible”, a réagi le député Thomas Ménagé sur Franceinfo.
L’article sera immanquablement contesté par la gauche dans l’hémicycle, anticipe Boris Vallaud. “L’introduction d’un délai de carence pose un problème éthique et politique”, souligne auprès de POLITICO le président du groupe socialiste à l’Assemblée nationale.
“Au-delà de la rupture d’égalité et du caractère discriminatoire de cette mesure, on est en train de revenir sur un principe de notre Sécurité sociale selon lequel on est couvert dès lors qu’on réside sur le territoire national," abonde le député des Français de l’étranger Karim Ben Cheïkh (Ecologiste).
Des exemptions et un rendement symbolique
Le dispositif est plus étroit que ne le laissait entendre la première annonce de Matignon puisque la mesure ne s’appliquera ni aux réfugiés, ni aux bénéficiaires de la protection subsidiaire, ni aux apatrides, ni aux titulaires d’une carte de résident. Surtout, il ne concernera pas non plus les étrangers autorisés à travailler en France.
Advertisement
Le public cible se compose donc essentiellement de ressortissants de pays tiers nouvellement admis au séjour et dépourvus du droit d'exercer une activité professionnelle (visiteurs, stagiaires, retraités).
Dès la publication de l’interview de Sébastien Lecornu, avant même que les contours de la mesure ne soient connus, le collectif Alerte, qui regroupe une quarantaine d’associations de lutte contre la pauvreté, a exprimé une “profonde inquiétude et [une] incompréhension face à une telle perspective”.
D’après l’étude d’impact également consultée par POLITICO, le rendement potentiel de la mesure est estimé à “au moins plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros par an”.

Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:20:39 UTC
23:20:39 KST

European and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services.
Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry.
Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said.
Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign across Europe aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said.
Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated.”
Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”.
Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”.
Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”
Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”.
The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said.
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media.
Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”
About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.
Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this report
