Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:06:22 UTC
23:06:22 KST

Breadcrumb
'We must fight imperialism': Global Sumud Flotilla's Thiago Ávila takes his fight to Brazil's Congress
For more than two decades, Brazilian socio-environmentalist and Palestine solidarity activist Thiago Ávila has campaigned against what he describes as imperialism, colonialism and the exploitation of people and nature.
Now, after years of activism and high-profile participation in Gaza-bound flotillas, he is taking that political struggle into Brazil's electoral arena.
A member of the Global Sumud Flotilla's steering committee, Ávila has helped organise a movement that expanded from more than 40 vessels in 2025 to more than 70 by May 2026, bringing together hundreds of activists from around the world.
He was also among those detained after the flotilla was illegally intercepted by Israeli forces near Crete on April 30, 2026. Along with Spanish-Swedish activist Saif Abukeshek, he was held without formal charges at the Shikma facility in Ashkelon and deported on May 10, 2026, following international pressure and a hunger strike.
Now, Ávila is running for a seat in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with the green party REDE in São Paulo.
He says his potential term would bring his activism into parliament, with a particular focus on challenging what he describes as Israeli and Zionist influence over Brazilian policy.
"We believe that our candidacy and possible future term can accomplish an even more expressive role in the struggle for the Palestinian cause, in the fight against imperialism and colonialism," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"One of our key proposals is the rupture of all relations [with Israel]," he continues.
"We intend to establish a term that is vigilant to combat the Zionism lobby in our country, in our political process, and most importantly, in our elections. We are aware that Zionism uses scrutiny times to infiltrate, and that Brazil unfortunately has given in many ways, mostly associated with far-right-wing politicians."
Foreign influence in Brazilian politics
His remarks come days after ABIN, the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, forwarded a report on September 19 to the Supreme Electoral Court (TSE), the Presidency of the Republic, and the Ministry of Justice, pointing to the "risk of influence and interference from the United States of America in the upcoming Brazilian electoral process."
The information was released by Folha de S.Paulo and confirmed by O GLOBO. The report comes amid a wider pattern of closer US-Israeli alignment across Latin America, including the creation of the 'Shield of the Americas', a coalition of 18 Latin American countries plus the United States, which excludes Brazil's Lula and Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum.
The shift has also been reflected in relations between Israel and governments across the region.
Argentina's president Javier Milei has praised Benjamin Netanyahu and co-signed the 'Isaac Accords', a branch of the Abraham Accords aimed at furthering public diplomacy and cooperation between Israel and Latin American countries.
In Brazil, congresswoman Tabata Amaral of the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB-SP) registered bill 1424/26, which supposedly criminalises anti-semitism and includes criticism of Israel as an anti-semitic practice, despite anti-semitism already being a crime in Brazil since 1988.
On September 21, President Lula told CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour that he was "deeply concerned" about possible interference from the United States in Brazil's democratic election process.
As a counterpoint, the United States spokesperson, Amanda Robertson, denied that the United States or its allies had meddled in Brazilian democracy.
Brazilian Zionist backlash
Political candidates who publicly support Palestine and oppose Israel's genocide in Gaza, like Thiago, are commonly attacked by local Zionist organisations.
These include StandWithUs Brazil and the Brazilian Israelite Confederation (CONIB). Journalist Caio Blinder and academic Samuel Feldberg, who are linked to these organisations, have publicly described Ávila as a "professional activist" whose advocacy is motivated by the pursuit of publicity and political gain.
"This sort of attack is not exclusive to Brazil or to me," Ávila explains.
"They attack all those who report on what is done in Palestine, who report on the genocide, and who report on Zionist infiltration in a wide range of countries — similarly how they attacked United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, environmental activist Greta Thunberg, and other prominent figures in the debate for Palestinian liberation," he adds.
"I treat these attacks as part of the process. Threats against me and other advocates have increased dramatically, and our democracy has largely deteriorated due to the influence of Trump and Netanyahu. This is evident in the growing number of far-right leaders occupying positions of power. We must confront these hateful ideologies with all our capacity."
Pathway as a social-environmentalist
Despite support from a significant portion of the Brazilian-Palestinian community and his role in past flotillas to Gaza, Ávila rejects claims that his advocacy for Palestine is motivated by political gain.
He says that, in the electoral process, voters will primarily consider his work as a social-environmentalist rather than his activism in defence of the Palestinian people.
He also adds that his candidacy rests on the intersection of social justice and environmentalism, and rejects claims of appropriation, pointing to the recognition of his advocacy by Palestinian-Brazilian organisations such as the Palestinian Federation and the Palestinian Front of São Paulo.
"I've been an activist for 22 years now, and for 22 years I have been fighting against exploitation, oppression, and the destruction of nature in order to build a 'well-living' society," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"Both environmental disaster and the war machine that profits from genocide originate in the same system. American imperialism, which provides over 80% of the bombs Israel uses in Gaza, is also involved in environmental damage all around the world," he adds.
"It's not a coincidence that the US military, as an institution, is one of the most prominent sources of pollution for the whole planet," Ávila adds.
"In Brazil, some right-wing state governments, but also certain so-called progressive ones, purchase weapons, espionage software, drones and hypersurveillance technology from Israel's arms industry. These are, logically, tools used for mass exploitation, agricultural deforestation, poaching, mining and many other destructive practices," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"The billionaires who profit from these violations, and those behind the legal frameworks that allow this technology to flow into Brazil and circulate around the globe, are the same."
With elections approaching on October 4, and the country’s sovereignty to choose its own leaders at stake, the open question remains: will Brazilian voters pick their representatives based on the Brazil they want to build for the future, or on the Brazil foreign powers want to build for them?
Rogger Oliveira is a multimedia journalist covering geopolitics and social issues in the Middle East and North Africa. He has a previous background as a translator and interpreter working in English, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French

Asian Games | Two weightlifting world records fall as China takes two golds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:17 CST
23:06:17 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Two world records fell in weightlifting at the 2026 Asian Games on Tuesday as China claimed two gold medals, with Uzbekistan and Iran taking the other two titles.
Uzbekistan's Akbar Djuraev set a world record on his way to winning the men's 110kg title, lifting 197kg in the snatch before adding 226kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 423kg.
Turkmenistan's Shahzadbek Matyakubov took silver with 410kg, while China's Liu Huanhua claimed bronze with 405kg.
"This was our goal, to contribute our efforts to get a higher place in the medal table for our nation," Djuraev said. "I am very proud I could contribute to this."
Both Matyakubov and Liu entered the competition having dealt with injuries. Matyakubov was competing for the first time in two years after suffering a back injury.
"I have been injured for two years. A long time without competing. Two discs in my back [went] before the [2024] Asian Championships. I was in pain for a long time," Matyakubov said.
Liu, the 2024 Olympic champion in the men's 102kg division, competed despite a leg injury and failed his final clean-and-jerk attempt.
"I thought before the contest I would only manage one attempt each in the snatch and clean and jerk. My leg injury would not allow me to finish the competition," Liu said. "But then my coach told me to prepare for a second clean-and-jerk attempt, and that I might get a medal.
"I gave it everything today, 200 percent of my effort."
Liu said he had benefited from the guidance of senior teammates at the previous Asian Games and had now taken on a similar role with China's younger lifters.
"As I always say, give us a little time. We will grow rapidly. Have faith in China's weightlifting team," he said.
The day's second world record came in the men's +110kg division, where Iraq's Ali Ammar Yusur Rubaiawi lifted 219kg in the snatch.
Rubaiawi finished with a total of 465kg but had to settle for silver as Iran's Ali Davoudi took gold with 466kg. Bahrain's Gor Minasyan claimed bronze with 440kg.
In the women's +86kg division, China's Li Wenwen overcame a seven-kilogram deficit after the snatch to take gold.
Li snatched 140kg, with South Korea's Park Hyejeong leading on 147kg, before lifting 170kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 310kg. Li set three Asian Games records in the process.
Park took silver with 300kg, while Qatar's Ouisal Ikhlef claimed bronze with 273kg.
"Today I truly felt what it means when dreams come true," Li said. "I came here aiming for the gold. I told myself to stay composed and step onto the platform steadily."
Li, the 2024 Olympic champion in the women's +81kg division, withdrew from the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023 because of an elbow injury.
Earlier Tuesday, China's Wu Yan won the women's 86kg title with a total of 273kg.
Wu and Bahrain's Alina Marushchak both lifted 124kg in the snatch before Wu posted 149kg in the clean and jerk to secure gold. Marushchak took silver with 272kg, while 17-year-old Mahsa Beheshty of Iran claimed bronze with 259kg.
Competing at her first Asian Games, Wu said she took off her shoes and rested briefly after the snatch to help reset before the clean and jerk.
Asked about being tied with Marushchak after the snatch, Wu said she had been unaware of her rival's score.
"Watching opponents makes me tense," she said. "Weightlifting requires focusing solely on your own lifts." ■

Asian Games | Athletics roundup: China closes with three golds, Obiena sets pole vault Games record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:10 CST
23:06:10 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China added three more golds in the women's hammer throw, 4x100m mixed relay and women's 800m as athletics concluded Tuesday at the 2026 Asian Games, while the Philippines' Ernest John Obiena set a men's pole vault Games record of 5.91m.
In the women's hammer throw, China's Zhang Jiale set a Games record of 78.27m to win gold, with compatriot Zhao Jie taking silver at 74.83m and Japan's Joy Iris McArthur claiming bronze.
The Chinese duo faced little challenge, as no other contender in the field had a personal best beyond 71 meters.
Zhang said her focus after the Asian Games is now reaching 80 meters, a mark no women's Asian thrower has hit. "My teammate Zhao and I both want to push toward that and bring Asia closer to the world's best," she said.
China then won the 4x100m mixed relay, with Chen Jinfeng, Liu Guoyi, Shi Junhao and Chen Yujie clocking 40.78 seconds. Thailand took silver and India bronze.
It was the third gold of the Games for Chen, who had already won the women's 100m and the women's 4x100m relay, along with a silver in the 200m.
Chen said running the anchor leg from behind was one of the more nerve-testing moments of her Games, but she trusted her technique.
"I've raced the Thai anchor before, so I know her rhythm well. As long as I could beat her over the final 100 meters, I knew we'd be fine," she said.
"What I achieved at the Games is a real motivator. Now that it's done, I can already start looking ahead to the next one," she said.
In the men's pole vault, Obiena was the only competitor to clear 5.75m. After two failed attempts at 5.80m, he raised the bar to 5.91m and cleared it to break the Games record and take gold. China's Li Chenyang and Yao Jie finished second and third.
Uzbekistan's Sayfullaeva Barnokhon cleared a personal best of 1.90m to win the women's high jump. Kazakhstan's Kristina Ovchinnikova took silver and India's Pooja took bronze, while China's Lu Jiawen and Jin Ruoxuan finished fourth and 10th, respectively.
In the women's 800m, China's Wu Hongjiao won gold in 2:04.49, ahead of Bahrain's Nelly Korir and the Philippines' Victoria Bossong.
Running from a boxed-in position, Wu moved up early and, with no one willing to push the pace, settled into a rhythm that suited her.
"Everyone seemed to be waiting, so I just ran however felt comfortable," she said, adding that nerves only crept back in the final 100 meters.
It was Wu's first Asian Games title after years of near-misses. "I figured if I beat the faster entries, that's a breakthrough. If I ran a personal best instead, that's a breakthrough too," she said.
Looking ahead, Wu said Asian middle-distance runners need to "dare to believe" they can compete with the world's best.
In the men's 800m, Japan's Ko Ochiai set a Games record of 1:44.48 to win gold, ahead of Iran's Ali Amirian and Qatar's Abubaker Abdalla. China's Xi Xiaoheng finished fourth.
Bahrain's Birhanu Balew won the men's 5,000m in 13:30.79, ahead of Japan's Tomonori Yamaguchi and India's Gulveer Singh.
India won the women's 4x400m relay, with Bahrain second and China third. Host Japan closed out the athletics program with gold in the men's 4x400m relay, ahead of Qatar for silver and India for bronze. ■

During his life, Zou served as a member of the Political Bureau of the 14th CPC Central Committee, vice premier of China's State Council, and vice chairman of the Ninth NPC Standing Committee. ■

Operation Vivaldi Had a Secret Weapon—Ukraine Calls It “Griffin”

Operation Vivaldi Had a Secret Weapon—Ukraine Calls It “Griffin”
Ukraine’s 3rd Assault Brigade has begun air-dropping armed ground robots from heavy drones as far as 10 kilometers behind Russian lines, using the machines to hunt command posts, drone crews, supply hubs, and assault groups deep in the rear.
The tactic, known as “Griffin,” was employed during Operation Vivaldi, NC-13 strike UGV unit commander Mykola Zinkevych told Suspilne on September 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the operation, Ukrainian forces used robotic systems not only for direct strikes but also for deception, reinforcing vulnerable sectors, attacking command posts and warehouses, and intercepting Russian assault groups moving along logistics routes.
Robots also carried much of the operation’s less visible—but equally critical—work.
“80% of logistics during all stages of Operation Vivaldi were carried out by unmanned ground systems from other units of the 3rd Assault Brigade and the 3rd Army Corps. 90% of casualty evacuations were also carried out by unmanned ground systems from units of the 3rd Army Corps,” Zinkevych said.
The most unusual missions involved strike UGVs. Ukrainian troops equipped the robots with disposable grenade launchers, attached them beneath heavy bomber drones and flew them over Russian positions before releasing them deep in the rear.
Once on the ground, the machines continued toward their targets under their own power.
“We deploy the UGVs up to 10 kilometers behind enemy lines and then continue moving under their own power,” Zinkevych said.
The brigade calls the method the “Griffin” tactic, named after NC-13 serviceman Hryhorii Bach, call sign Griffin, who went missing near Andriivka in the Bakhmut sector in 2023.
Dropping the robots from the air allows Ukraine to bypass difficult terrain and frontline defenses while leaving Russian troops uncertain about where the machines may suddenly appear.
According to Zinkevych, the air-deployed UGVs have been used against operators from Russia’s Rubikon drone unit, command posts at company level and above, and Russian personnel moving along rear logistics routes.
In one case, their presence had an effect even before direct combat began. After a Ukrainian robot was dropped behind Russian lines, Russian troops reportedly canceled a planned mechanized assault because they believed a Ukrainian sabotage team had infiltrated the rear and was waiting to ambush their armored column.
The 3rd Assault Brigade also targeted Russian UAV operators and their launch sites during the opening phase of Vivaldi, combining strikes on Russia’s drone infrastructure with robotic missions deeper behind the line.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukrainian ground robots cleared 30 kilometers of routes in the Shandryholove sector in two nights during Operation Vivaldi.
The Third Army Corps stated that unmanned ground systems completed the difficult demining task entirely on their own.

Bail for RAF base suspects suggests no evidence of ‘terror’, say analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:05:58 UTC
23:05:58 KST

Bail for RAF base suspects suggests no evidence of ‘terror’, say analysts
Police released the RAF Fairford suspects on bail, which analysts say suggests no explosives were found.
When a woman driving home to her Gloucestershire village in England in the early hours of Sunday morning found her driveway blocked by three white vans, she immediately called the police.
The call triggered a whirlwind of dramatic events; within 15 minutes, armed officers had swooped on the scene, and a major incident was declared at the nearby Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, a base United States bombers have used to strike Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
- list 2 of 4Rubio, Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister hold talks on Yemen, Hormuz Strait
- list 3 of 4US-Iran talks continue, but ‘deal unlikely’ before midterm elections
- list 4 of 4Marco Rubio says UK airbase incident involved ‘foreign actor’
Some 85 homes were evacuated as a bomb disposal robot picked its way between the vans, and five British men in their 20s were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
As army explosives experts examined the vehicles and counterterrorism detectives began questioning the suspects, US President Donald Trump, some 5,800km (3,600 miles) away, was already hailing the arrests.
“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he told reporters on Sunday.
But Westminster was more cautious, with United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham urging people “not to speculate”.
Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects” any link, adding that such speculation would only “fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK”.
Then on Monday, all five men were released on bail, leaving Trump “surprised”. Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio went further, saying the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor”. He did not name one, though he noted that Iran had “openly threatened to attack American interests globally”.
The swift succession of arrests, claims and subsequent release has left a confused picture, raising questions about whether British authorities were indeed tracking the suspects – as Trump claimed – and whether the case is thinner than Washington suggests, say analysts.
But many analysts Al Jazeera spoke to said that the manner in which the suspects were released suggests that the UK government had little evidence, at least at this point, that the men were plotting a major attack.
From ‘World War III’ to ‘Four Lions’
Analysts said there were few signs of a sophisticated plot.
“If there had been any trace of explosives found in the vans, or any thoughts that these men were actually terrorists, they would not have been released,” Chris Phillips, a former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office, told Al Jazeera.
“It’s gone from World War III to Four Lions in four hours,” he said, referring to the 2010 British satire about a group of bumbling would-be suicide bombers.
Under the Terrorism Act 2000, police can hold terrorism suspects for up to 14 days without charge, he said, adding that officers who believed they had caught genuine attackers would use that time.
“You keep them, and you go through all their records and all their contacts and what they’ve been doing and what they’ve been talking about,” he said.
Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior Royal Air Force officer who served in Iraq, shares the same sentiment.
“If there had been any explosives, big or small, in those vans, then there is no way on Earth that the police would have released these individuals on bail,” he said.
Police have not said whether any explosives were found, with Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor stressing that the men “absolutely remain under investigation”.
Fuel thieves or ‘useful idiots’?
So, if not a terror plot, what was it?
One of the vans bore the logo “Fuel 2You”, which BBC Verify found no evidence of being a legitimate company.
Ashraf said many homes in the area, according to the internet, are not connected to the mains gas network and rely on heating oil stored in tanks in their gardens.
He said those tanks have become more valuable as fuel prices have soared during the Iran war.
“When you’ve got several hundred litres in gardens, that’s a bit of a killing for somebody,” he said, stressing that this was “an alternative and probably more plausible explanation” rather than a certainty.
“There’s absolutely nothing else at all, at the moment, suggesting that there is a link to any foreign government,” he added.
Phillips argued that the proximity to the base “may just be a complete fluke”.
“I’m absolutely certain there is intelligence that there are people in the UK that would love to attack,” he said. “But I’m not sure these guys are the ones.”
But not everyone is convinced.
Anthony Glees, emeritus professor of security and intelligence studies at the University of Buckingham, said the effort that went into the vans pointed to something planned.
“People do steal fuel, and students do do stupid things, but you wouldn’t go to the trouble and expense of taking three white vans to do so,” he said.
Instead, he believes the men were “useful idiots” who had “been hired at some expense” by a foreign state, not to carry out an attack but to stage one to “embarrass the British government”.
‘Narrative dominance’
If early indications suggest it was not a major terrorist plot, why, then, were Washington’s claims so emphatic?
For Ashraf, the explanation lies in the administration’s handling of the Iran war, which is driven by what he calls “narrative dominance”.
“This particular American administration hasn’t bothered with a strategy, a military strategy, or even a political strategy,” he said. “What it has worked on is a narrative strategy.”
On Trump’s claim that the men had been watched for “a long time”, he suspects a mix-up.
“What possibly has happened is that President Trump has been briefed about several groups, I would guess, that the Americans are tracking, which is normal,” he said.
He added that there may have been “some sort of conflation, which now the president has convinced himself is the same people”.
“Nobody’s going to tell the president he’s got it wrong,” he said.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, a longtime ally of Trump, posted on Monday that “Fairford proves my point on Iran and the IRGC”, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
He had linked the incident to Iranian agents arriving in small boats, before police confirmed all five men were British nationals from London.
For Ashraf, whether the claims hold up may matter little to Trump.
“Even if it’s proven that this is basically a criminal act and nothing to do with terrorism, what he’s successfully done, in the minds of a lot of people, and people like Nigel have amplified it, is just reinforced that association that’s been going on for a long time,” he said.
“That is a hit. That is success as far as they’re concerned.”
A ‘frightener’?
Police have not ruled out foreign involvement.
Taylor said investigators were “considering this from every possible angle”. That included the possibility of “activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.
Such plots are not new. MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said in October 2025 that the agency had tracked “more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots” in the UK in the space of a year.
Phillips explained how such recruitment typically works.
“They go onto the dark web, and they post, ‘Would someone like to do a job and make 10,000 pounds?’, as an example,” he said.
The person who carries out the job is often “four or five rungs down the line”, with no direct link to Iran or Russia.
Glees believes Fairford fits that pattern, and puts Iran “in pole position”, but he argued a real attack would have backfired on Tehran.
“If there had been an attack on RAF [Fairford], that would have been an attack on British soil, which would have meant Britain would have to be far more heavily involved in the war against Iran,” he said, adding, “Iran’s got no interest in that.”
Instead, he described it as “a frightener”, designed to embarrass the UK and perhaps make Trump feel the British “couldn’t be counted on”.
Ashraf is sceptical Tehran would take the risk at all.
He said Iran’s messaging has centred on the war being unpopular, even in the US, and that any plot endangering British or American civilians would undermine it.
If Iran had wanted to attack Fairford, he said, it probably would have assembled “a slightly more capable team”.

"Contempt for Science and Truth": Macron Condemns Russian Strike on Ukraine’s Science Academy
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned a Russian strike on Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences, describing it as the country's largest scientific research institution.
Macron made the statement in a French-language post on X on September 28. He stated that the regime of the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, had struck the academy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"These strikes are a new illustration of the hostile contempt of the Russian regime for science and truth," Macron wrote.
The French President noted that the attack added to "the barbarity of daily strikes that hunt down Ukrainian civilians."
The strike killed two scientists and injured several others. Across Kyiv, at least 19 people were injured in the broader Russian attack, including three children.
Macron declared that he shared the suffering of the victims and their families. "France and Europe will stand, for as long as necessary, alongside the Ukrainian people, who are resisting with courage," he added.
The strike is part of a broader pattern of Russian attacks on Ukrainian education and cultural sites in recent weeks.
On September 2, Shahed-type drones hit a Kyiv university during classes, while 160 students sheltered inside. Two days later, a drone damaged the 18th-century Consistory Building within the Saint Sophia of Kyiv sanctuary complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
By September 1, Russian attacks had damaged 4,650 educational facilities across Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 423 destroyed completely.

Legal aid chief denies stricter vetting as aid for policy challenges hits decade low
Legal Aid Department approved funds for just two challenges against government policies and decisions last year, down by 90 per cent from 2016
Hong Kong authorities approved only two legal aid applications for judicial review challenges against government policies and decisions last year, the fewest in the past decade, although its director has dismissed claims of tightened scrutiny or diminished access to justice.
The Legal Aid Department received 110 applications concerning judicial reviews of government policies and related organisations’ decisions last year, an almost 60 per cent drop from 2016, its annual reports show.
The department last year approved two legal aid certificates for such applications, down by almost 90 per cent from 2016.
In an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday, Director of Legal Aid Chan Chak-ming denied that the department had adopted a more stringent approach in vetting applications, following past criticisms of overly lenient approvals.

Should death penalty remain exception in rape cases, not the rule?
Every time a brutal rape case shocks the country, the demand returns almost immediately: give the harshest possible punishment.The anger is understandable. But the law applies a much narrower test. Not every rape case, however grave, crosses the threshold for the death penalty.India recorded 29,536 rape cases in 2024, according to the latest National Crime Records Bureau data. In Delhi, 1,058 rape cases were registered that year, while Delhi Police reported 1,901 cases in 2025.The figures come amid renewed attention on sexual violence, with a series of recent cases in Delhi and across the country bringing questions of punishment, deterrence and justice back into focus.While Indian law provides for stringent punishment, including the death penalty in certain rape cases, capital punishment remains restricted to specific circumstances.So when does a rape case cross the legal threshold for the ultimate punishment? What makes one case “rarest of rare”, while another results in life imprisonment?And should death remain an exception rather than the rule?
Why women's safety is back at the centre of debateA series of recent cases has once again put women’s safety under scrutiny.
In September, a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men posing as police personnel at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir in Delhi. The case triggered student protests demanding stronger measures for women’s safety, and police arrested the accused.In August, another 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by a bus driver and conductor after boarding a bus from Greater Noida. She was later dropped near Kashmere Gate. The National Human Rights Commission took suo motu cognisance of the case and sought reports from authorities.Against this backdrop, the Supreme Court on Monday took suo motu cognisance of recent rape incidents in Delhi-NCR, flagging what it described as a "systematic failure" to ensure basic public safety.Concerns have extended beyond Delhi.In Bihar, three incidents involving alleged sexual harassment and assault were reported within days. In Jamui, a teenage boy and girl were allegedly stopped and assaulted by a group of men on September 19, with three accused arrested after a video surfaced online. In Samastipur, a minor girl was allegedly assaulted and molested, while another case in Banka’s Mandar Hill area involved allegations of a woman being harassed and her male friend assaulted.The cases have also spilled onto the streets. Students and young people in the national capital are holding protests demanding safer public spaces, stronger policing and greater accountability.
2026 witnesses shocking incidents of sexual assault
When does rape become 'rarest of rare'?Indian law permits the death penalty in certain aggravated rape cases, including those involving minors and cases where the victim dies or is left in a persistent vegetative state, under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the POCSO Act.But the existence of the death penalty does not mean it follows automatically in the most brutal cases.Advocate Sumit Nagpal said courts consider factors including the brutality of the offence, injuries caused, the vulnerability of the survivor and the long-term consequences while determining punishment.Rupali Jain, who practises in the high court and Supreme Court, said the harm caused by rape, while grave, cannot by itself justify capital punishment."As harm is inherent in every rape, it cannot alone justify death. The court must also apply the 'criminal test', the offender’s age, antecedents, background, custodial conduct and prospects of reform, as reiterated in Manoj v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2022)," she said.The "rarest of rare" doctrine gained renewed attention following the 2012 Nirbhaya case. On December 16, 2012, a 23-year-old woman was gang-raped and brutally assaulted inside a moving bus in Delhi. She died from her injuries days later.Four adult accused were sentenced to death by the trial court in 2013. The Delhi high court upheld the punishment in 2014, and the Supreme Court confirmed the death sentences in 2017, holding that the case fell within the “rarest of rare” category.
Activist Yogita Bhayana in conversation with TOI
However, the Supreme Court has also held that the brutality or heinousness of an offence alone does not automatically make it a "rarest of rare" case. Courts must weigh aggravating circumstances against mitigating factors, including the possibility of reform and rehabilitation.But the death penalty is not automatic, even in cases involving extreme violence.The Bilkis Bano case offers another example of how courts apply the 'rarest of rare' test differently.In the Bilkis Bano case, 11 men were convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment for gang rape, murder and other offences linked to the 2002 Gujarat riots. Bilkis was 21 and five months pregnant when she was raped, and several members of her family were killed.The case shows why the "rarest of rare" test is not based only on how brutal or shocking a crime appears. Courts must also consider other factors, including the background of the accused and whether there is any possibility of reform.Activist Yogita Bhayana, however, argues that the impact of rape on the survivor should receive greater weight when courts consider the threshold."Every rape case is rarest of the rare in terms of the victim," she said, arguing that the legal system can focus heavily on physical brutality while overlooking the lasting impact on survivors.Bhayana said she believes the death penalty should remain available in rape cases and argued for greater weight to be given to the consequences of the crime for survivors while deciding punishment.What changes when the accused is a minor?The legal process changes significantly when the accused is under 18.Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a child aged between 16 and 18 who is accused of a “heinous offence”, including rape, can undergo a preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board.The Board looks at the child’s mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, whether they understood its consequences and the circumstances in which the alleged offence took place.
Minor victims in rape cases in India: NCRB data
Depending on that assessment, the case can be transferred to the Children’s Court, which then decides whether the child should be tried as an adult.Rupali Jain said the existing law already provides a framework for dealing with serious offences committed by juveniles, and the focus should remain on how it is implemented rather than simply lowering the age threshold.She also pointed out that the Juvenile Justice Act does not allow the death penalty, or life imprisonment without the possibility of release, for a child in conflict with law.However, activist Yogita Bhayana argues that the distinction between different degrees of brutality can be deeply troubling for survivors.“The miner will be treated as miner unless he brutally kills her, rape her in a very gruesome manner. Then otherwise, it will not be in the rarest of the rare category. So we need to change the whole thing,” she said, arguing that the system should focus more closely on the impact of the crime on the survivor and called for greater awareness and stronger mechanisms to deal with sexual offences.Does a harsher sentence always mean justice?For survivors, justice does not necessarily end with an arrest, conviction or sentence.Activist Yogita Bhayana said the distinction between "high-profile" and ordinary rape cases often comes from media attention rather than the nature of the crime or the survivor’s experience."There is no case which is high profile. What becomes media-highlighted becomes high profile," she said, pointing out that even Nirbhaya came from a humble, lower-middle-class family.She said survivors often continue to deal with trauma, repeated questioning and the pressures of the legal process long after public attention has moved on."Attention doesn’t mean justice," Bhayana said.
Two cases with different court sentences
Dr Vinodh Sreeram, senior psychiatrist & addiction specialist at Maarga Mind Care, Bengaluru, said rape can deeply alter a survivor’s sense of safety, relationships and ability to return to everyday life.He cautioned against judging trauma only by visible injuries or by how brutal an assault appears. Two survivors of similar incidents can experience very different psychological effects depending on factors such as age, past experiences, their relationship with the accused and the support available to them."The absence of visible injury should never be mistaken for the absence of psychological trauma," he said.On whether the death penalty can provide psychological closure, Sreeram said there is no single answer. Some survivors or families may see a severe sentence as justice, but "closure rarely comes from the sentence alone".Being believed, treated with dignity, protected from further harm and supported through recovery can be just as important, he said. Repeated questioning, cross-examination, delays and prolonged appeals can themselves become additional sources of distress.Why tougher laws alone may not be enoughRecent protests in Delhi have again brought demands for safer public spaces, stronger policing, better surveillance and greater accountability to the forefront.Advocate Sumit Nagpal said the biggest challenge is not necessarily the absence of laws, but the capacity to enforce them."The bottleneck is capacity, not the statute. India has roughly twenty judges per million people against a recommended fifty, and police strength sits well below sanctioned levels in most states. Until that gap closes, every reform stays on paper," he said."So the real agenda is unglamorous: more investigators, more courts, more forensic capacity, fewer vacancies. No amendment will substitute for that."
Delhi University students take out protest march amid rains to Miranda House college in north campus over women safety after Kalkaji gang rape.
Activist Yogita Bhayana said the biggest gap remains implementation. While reforms, awareness and gender-sensitisation efforts have increased, she said survivors continue to face inadequate support, delays in fast-track courts and a lack of sensitivity within the system.She also warned that repeated exposure to sexual-violence cases can make institutions become "immune" to such crimes."For them, they see it like an everyday thing," she said, arguing that continued training and sensitisation are needed to ensure sexual violence is not treated as routine.Dr Vinodh Sreeram said debates around harsher punishment must also account for the realities of reporting, particularly because many survivors know the accused and may face fear, stigma and family pressure.
A trauma-informed justice system, he said, should focus on sensitive questioning, privacy, timely trials and access to psychological support.“Justice is not only about the severity of punishment. It is also about ensuring that survivors are heard, protected, treated with dignity and given the opportunity to rebuild their lives,” Sreeram said.The death penalty is only one part of the debate. The larger challenge is to prevent such crimes, ensure quicker justice and make sure survivors get the support they need.

Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott was sentenced to seven years in prison on Tuesday after being convicted of sexually abusing two children.
The 49-year-old Scot, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, will also remain on the sex offenders register for life, according to a BBC report.
Dott had denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour involving a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.
Sentencing Dott at the High Court in Edinburgh, Judge Lord Harrower said he had robbed the victims of “a significant part of their childhood” and that his conduct bore the hallmarks of grooming.
The court heard Dott rewarded the children with treats, disguised abuse as games and warned them they would not be believed if they disclosed what had happened.
His abuse of the girl began when she was around nine and Dott was 16 or 17, while the second victim, a boy aged about eight, was abused around a decade later, the BBC report said.
The judge said the offences amounted to a “gross violation of trust” and had left the victims with lasting feelings of fear, shame and anger that affected their mental health into adulthood.
The sentence was backdated to Aug. 24, when Dott was remanded in custody.
Dott defeated Peter Ebdon to win his only world title at Sheffield’s Crucible Theater in 2006. He was runner-up on two more occasions, being beaten in the 2004 final by Ronnie O’Sullivan and losing to Neil Robertson in 2010.

Faces and bodies send matching signals of attractiveness, but voices tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:00:05 UTC
23:00:05 KST

People often judge a potential partner based on a combination of their face, body, and voice. A recent study reveals that while facial and bodily attractiveness tend to match up, a person’s voice provides an independent cue about their traits. These findings, published in Evolution and Human Behavior, suggest that our physical features send a mix of redundant and distinct messages to observers.
Evolutionary psychology proposes that human physical traits communicate genetic quality and health to potential mates or rivals. During the search for a partner, individuals evaluate physical attractiveness to gauge underlying fitness. During competition with rivals, individuals might assess physical dominance to determine formidability. Researchers study how these visual and vocal cues combine to form an overall impression of an individual.
One major theoretical framework is the “one ornament hypothesis.” This concept suggests that different physical traits, such as the face and body, are shaped by the same underlying biological factors. In this view, various body parts act as a single, unified signal of health or genetic fitness. If a person has robust immune function or developmental stability, it should reflect across their entire physical appearance.
The second major framework is the “multiple messages hypothesis.” This theory argues that different parts of the body convey entirely separate pieces of information. For example, a face might signal immune system strength, while a voice might indicate physical dominance. If this theory holds true, a person’s individual physical features would not necessarily correlate with one another in the eyes of an observer.
Researchers also suspect that sex hormones like testosterone and estradiol might drive the synchronized development of these physical traits. These hormones guide sexual dimorphism, which refers to the biological differences in physical characteristics between men and women. Higher testosterone in men and higher estradiol in women are thought to influence the development of traits that others perceive as attractive, healthy, or dominant.
To test these competing hypotheses, a research team led by Tobias L. Kordsmeyer of the University of Goettingen designed an experiment. They wanted to examine how independent raters perceived the attractiveness, health, and physical dominance of faces, bodies, and voices. The researchers also sought to test whether sex hormones act as a biological bridge linking these disparate features.
The study included 165 men and 155 women as evaluation targets. The research team collected standardized facial photographs, three-dimensional body scans, and short audio recordings from each participant. The facial photographs featured participants standing against a white wall with a neutral expression.
The three-dimensional body scans were rendered as digital figures that rotated over an eight-second duration. The researchers deliberately removed skin color and texture from these digital models, converting them to a uniform gray. This step ensured that raters would focus entirely on physical shape and proportions, removing skin quality as a potential confounding factor.
To collect voice samples, male participants were recorded speaking about positive aspects of their lives for one minute. Female participants were recorded reading a standardized text known as the rainbow passage. The researchers extracted five-second audio clips from the men’s recordings and used the second sentence of the passage (about 3.5 seconds on average) from the women’s recordings for the final evaluation.
A separate group of 400 independent raters evaluated the collected stimuli. To prevent their judgments of one trait from influencing another, the raters were divided into specific groups. A single rater only evaluated one type of stimulus, such as male faces, female bodies, or male voices. The raters scored the targets for attractiveness, health, and physical dominance using standardized rating scales.
The research team also gathered saliva and hair samples from the targets to measure hormone levels. They measured baseline testosterone and reactive testosterone in men. Reactive testosterone was captured shortly after the men engaged in a competitive task. For women, the researchers assessed baseline testosterone and estradiol levels across different phases of the menstrual cycle.
When analyzing the rating data, the researchers found positive correlations between how raters perceived faces and bodies. Targets whose faces were rated highly for attractiveness and health also tended to receive high ratings for their body shapes. The effects were of medium size, showing a consistent pattern across both male and female targets.
This pattern also held true for physical dominance, though it was only observed for male targets. Men with faces rated as physically dominant also had bodies rated as physically dominant. Female targets did not exhibit a coordinated rating for physical dominance between their faces and bodies.
These positive associations between the face and the body align with the one ornament hypothesis. Observers seem to interpret facial and bodily cues redundantly, picking up on shared information about the individual’s physical condition. Even without skin texture, the bodies provided enough shape information to align with the health and attractiveness ratings of the faces.
The results for vocal recordings painted a different picture. The researchers found very few measurable associations between how raters judged a target’s voice and how they judged the target’s face or body. Voice ratings appeared to operate independently from visual appearance.
An individual might possess a highly rated face or body, but this did not guarantee their voice would be perceived in the same way. This independence supports the multiple messages hypothesis. The human voice seems to act as a separate channel of communication, offering non-redundant information to observers rather than echoing visual cues.
The hormone analysis yielded unexpected results. The researchers found that adult hormone levels did not mediate the correlated perceptions of faces and bodies. While men’s baseline testosterone levels did show some positive associations with facial dominance and vocal attractiveness, the hormones did not serve as the underlying link for synchronized ratings across body parts.
The proposed mechanism of adult sex hormones bridging these distinct traits was not supported by the data. Adjusting for the targets’ body mass index or relationship status did not alter these outcomes. The correlations between traits remained robust even when accounting for body fat.
The study measured adult baseline and reactive hormone levels rather than developmental hormones. Physical traits like bone structure and vocal cord length are heavily shaped by organizational hormones during fetal development and puberty. Adult hormone levels might not accurately reflect the specific hormonal environment that originally sculpted these physical characteristics.
Additionally, the body scans lacked skin color and texture. Skin quality is a known biological indicator of physical health. Stripping this information away might have altered how raters evaluated the overall condition of the targets, even though it successfully isolated the role of physical shape.
The researchers measured subjective impressions of health, dominance, and attractiveness rather than objective medical data. The ratings reveal how people perceive others based on evolutionary psychological cues. They do not confirm whether the highly rated individuals were objectively healthier or physically stronger in reality.
Future investigations could incorporate developmental hormone tracking during adolescence to better understand how biology links physical traits. Researchers might also include other sensory cues, such as body odor or dynamic movement, to build a more comprehensive picture of human nonverbal signaling.
The study, “Correlated perceptions and underlying hormonal factors of bodily, facial, and vocal attractiveness, health, and physical dominance,” was authored by Tobias L. Kordsmeyer, Philine A.C. Rasokat, Julia Stern, Christoph Schild, and Lars Penke.

Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:00:01 UTC
23:00:01 KST

Rep. James Comer, chair of the House Oversight Committee, is expanding an investigation into insider trading on prediction markets and seeking information on what a trio of online platforms is doing to root it out.
The Kentucky Republican, in letters sent Tuesday and first shared with CNBC, requested documents and information from the CEOs of Hyperliquid Labs, Crypto.com and Aristotle Exchange Inc., which owns the platform PredictIt, that explain their identity verification procedures and how they identify and prevent insider trading on their platforms.
"As online prediction platforms grow and become more mainstream, some bad actors have exploited the platforms to make thousands of dollars by placing bets based on nonpublic information," Comer said in a statement. "The House Oversight Committee is investigating whether these platforms are fulfilling their legal obligations and doing enough to identify and prevent insider trading before it happens."
Prediction markets — which allow users to buy and sell binary event contracts on the outcome of future events, from sports games to elections and, in some cases, war and other global events — have drawn increased attention from lawmakers as they've surged in popularity.
Comer first opened an investigation into Kalshi and Polymarket, the two largest and most prominent prediction markets, in May, amid a series of highly publicized bets on world events. A committee spokesperson said that those investigations are ongoing and that the committee has received nearly 1,000 documents and five briefings from representatives of the two companies.
In April, a U.S. soldier was arrested for allegedly using inside information to place bets on Polymarket about the ouster of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January, netting roughly $400,000. And a May investigation by The New York Times found that more than 80 Polymarket users had made bets with suspicious characteristics, including trades placed hours before the U.S. and Israel struck Iran.
Former Rep. George Santos, a New York Republican who was expelled from the House by his peers in 2023, allegedly used Kalshi to bet on whether he would appear at this year's State of the Union address, in February, while also making a series of public statements in the lead-up indicating he would be in the crowd.
Kalshi permanently banned Santos in August and fined him $71,356 for his actions. Both Kalshi and Polymarket earlier this year announced they were strengthening their internal insider trading rules.
But trades that have drawn insider trading concerns have not been specific to the largest platforms.
Comer, in his letter to Hyperliquid CEO Jeff Yan, cited reports of "a substantial leveraged short position on the ... platform within minutes of a presidential announcement concerning a U.S. tariff policy in October 2025 that was not publicly known at the time the position was established."
"This transaction, precisely timed to a nonpublic government decision, executed on a platform with apparently no identity verification or mechanism to refer the responsible party to U.S. law enforcement, mirrors a pattern of insider trading the Committee is investigating across the prediction market sector," Comer wrote in the letter.
Spokespeople for Hyperliquid, Crypto.com and Aristotle Exchange did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.
Comer and the committee requested documents and communications from each company explaining their know your customer, or KYC, policies, and internal procedures to detect, investigate and report suspicious trading activity.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

PARIS – French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen on Sept 29 vowed to hit back at allegations of anti-Semitism targeting her de facto No. 2 Jordan Bardella, which have punctured her buoyant campaign at a time when she is riding high in the polls.
Le Pen, who is aiming to win the Elysee at her fourth attempt in 2027 in a far-right breakthrough that would send a shockwave across Europe, lambasted the Mediapart website that published the claims and said Bardella has her “total confidence”.
Bardella, who has vehemently denied the making the comments dating back to 2013, said the report marked the start of a “total war” to derail Le Pen’s campaign and said he was taking legal action against Mediapart.
The 31-year-old is the leader of Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) party and is tipped to be prime minister if she wins the presidency. A savvy user of social media, he has helped the RN make inroads among the youth vote.
Le Pen reaffirmed she had “total confidence” in her young lieutenant and vowed the RN would “counter-attack” after the allegations.
She warned “our opponents will do absolutely anything – including the most disgusting things – to try to derail this momentum” ahead of the 2027 election for a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
‘Kill my political career’
A poll published on Sept 28 suggested that Le Pen would easily lead the first round of voting in the elections in 2027, and would defeat any challenger in the second round run-off to win the Elysee.
She is planning to stand despite a conviction for a fake jobs scam in the European Parliament, a case Le Pen also says was falsified by opponents.
“Now, I think it’s Mediapart that needs to be told to put on its Kevlar vest, because there will obviously be a response to the way they are behaving,” she said.

Responding to suggestions the allegations could have come from individuals expelled from the RN in a purge of extremists, he said: “Either Mediapart orchestrated this, or Mediapart itself was tricked by powerful figures behind the scenes with an interest in destabilising the presidential campaign.”
He denounced what he called a bid to “kill my political career”.
Israel visit
Mediapart’s investigation is built on comments in private chats allegedly written by Bardella in the summer of 2013 when he was 17 or 18 years old. Mediapart maintains it authenticated the comments. It did not specify where the messages had been written nor publish screenshots.
According to the report by Mediapart, Bardella wrote, among other comments, in a chat: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so.”
He was also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”.
Bardella has been a key player in Le Pen’s project of “de-demonisation” to make the RN into an electable force and rid the party of the legacy of her father, the late Jean-Marie Le Pen, who founded and led what was then known as the National Front (FN) and repeatedly made anti-Semitic remarks.

France’s public debt reaches 119% of GDP, highest since 1946
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:58:53 UTC
22:58:53 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
France’s public debt rose to 119% of gross domestic product at the end of June, its highest level since 1946, according to figures released Tuesday by the national statistics agency INSEE.
Debt reached €3.5955 trillion (about $4 trillion), up €59.6 billion ($67.6 billion) from the end of March. The debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 117.5% in the first quarter, INSEE figures showed.
The ratio also surpassed the 117.8% peak recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, Le Monde reported.
The rise adds pressure on Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s government ahead of its presentation of the draft 2027 budget on Thursday. The government projects public debt will reach 119.3% of GDP by the end of this year and 121.7% in 2027.
Higher borrowing costs are also adding to the burden on public finances. Economy Minister Roland Lescure said on Sept. 21 that the government expects debt-servicing costs to reach €91 billion in 2027.

Spanish government approves measures to ease housing crisis after outcry over eviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:58:36 UTC
22:58:36 KST

Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week.
Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible.
Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028.
A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements.
Hundreds of people remained camped out in one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.
It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree.
Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.”
She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.”
The Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees.
“It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.”
The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.
“Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.”
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.”
Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction.
Underlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband.
Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative.

Nearly 16,000 people were displaced in Yemen in one week as fighting intensified along the country’s western coast and south, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The latest displacement comes as Yemen faces an already dire humanitarian crisis, with more than 5.2 million people internally displaced even before the latest escalation, and more than 22 million people in need of humanitarian assistance.

Spain plans stricter rules on asylum seekers in Ceuta, draft decree shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

22:57:46 KST

Spain plans stricter rules on asylum seekers in Ceuta, draft decree shows
MADRID, Sept 29 - Spain is planning to override standard migration procedures and tighten rules on asylum seeking for migrants who arrived in its North African enclave of Ceuta in July's mass crossing, a draft decree seen by Reuters showed, prompting outcry from legal experts and NGOs.
The decree, designed to speed up applications and deportations for the over 10,000 migrants who remain in the tiny territory, would mark a major strategic shift for Spain's leftist, pro-immigration government, a staunch advocate of multilateral rules and institutions, as it struggles to contain the political fallout from the border crisis.
Spain's Interior Ministry declined to comment on the draft.
More than 70,000 people illegally crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta via land and sea in late July in an unprecedented rush, rattling European leaders and exposing the limits of a recent overhaul of migration rules intended to tighten borders.
Under the measures in the draft, first leaked to Spanish newspaper El Pais and not yet confirmed, migrants appealing against a rejected asylum application must do so from outside the country if it is deemed safe by the EU, as is the case for Morocco, regardless of their personal circumstances.
The decree, which would apply retroactively to migrants arriving since the mass crossing of July 30 and 31, also permits the government to skip a standardised review of asylum requests by a commission including representatives from the UN refugee agency.
Migrants' applications would be withdrawn if they were unreachable for five days and anyone deemed to have behaved in a "violent or threatening" manner would have their right to remain immediately revoked.
Asked in a news conference about plans to shorten timeframes for processing migrants, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analysing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" due to questions of international law.
Spanish lawyers and NGOs decried the draft measures in statements to Reuters and other media, with 13 NGOs, including Spain's Commission for Assistance to Refugees (CEAR) and Oxfam, describing them as a "grave threat" to Spain's commitment to human rights conventions. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

IDF will keep killing Hamas commanders as long as terror group keeps controlling Gaza - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:56:22 UTC
22:56:22 KST

The IDF said on Tuesday that it had “struck in northern Gaza and eliminated the terrorist Izz al-Din Bik, commander of the Northern Gaza Brigade in the military wing of the Hamas terrorist organization.”
This is one of the several recent strikes on Hamas officers and commanders of Hamas units linked to Jabaliya, Rafah, and other areas. The northern brigade of Hamas was destroyed several times in combat, which raises questions about the nature of the continued attacks on these commanders.
On the one hand, the continued strikes on commanders may show that Hamas is not only appointing new leadership, but it is actively rebuilding itself. Most Hamas commanders who were alive on October 7, 2023, have now been eliminated. The IDF has also claimed to have defeated many of these units in the past. For instance, the northern Brigade of Hamas, which had several battalions, was said to have been defeated by January 2024, and then again in late 2024 and 2025.
What did the IDF say about the recent strike?
“Izz al-Din Bik had served in this position since the elimination of Ahmed Abu Ghandour, after previously serving as the brigade’s military intelligence chief,” it reported. “As part of his role, Izz al-Din Bik was responsible for managing the activities of the brigade’s terrorists and directing them to advance and carry out terror attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians. In addition, he operated to restore the brigade’s force buildup, which had suffered severe damage throughout the war.”
The military noted that “the terrorist posed an immediate threat to IDF troops and Israeli civilians and was eliminated in a precise aerial strike.”
Let’s look back at some other eliminations in Gaza City and Northern Gaza. In May 2026, the IDF said that they had “eliminated the terrorist Imad Hassan Hussein Aslim, the deputy commander of the Gaza Brigade and the commander of the Zeitoun Battalion in Hamas’s military wing, who commanded the battalion’s terrorist infiltration into Israeli territory during the brutal October 7 massacre.”
In July, they reported, “in the northern Gaza Strip earlier this week, the IDF eliminated the militant Raed Hani Mohammed Al-Amsi, an aerial surveillance platoon commander in Hamas’s aerial array.”
In August, the IDF said it “struck in the Al-Shati area in the northern Gaza Strip and eliminated Bilal Ibrahim Saleh Raqi‘i, a commander in Hamas’ military wing’s anti-tank array.”
It’s clear that the IDF is continuing to carry out targeted strikes on Hamas in northern Gaza. This is after almost three years of war. During this war, Hamas attacked Israel from areas such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as near Erez and along the coast on October 7. In the wake of the attack, the IDF waited until late October to begin operations. When the IDF did strike, it sent the 162nd Division down the coast of Gaza toward Shati and Gaza City.
By mid-November, the IDF said it had defeated 10 Hamas battalions in northern Gaza. The claim at the time was that Hamas only had another 14 battalions left.
By late March, the IDF claimed it had “dismantled” 20 of Hamas’ 24 battalions.
By April 2024, six months into the war, the IDF claimed it had eliminated 12,000 terrorists in Gaza. It said it had eliminated five Hamas brigade commanders, 20 battalion commanders, and 100 company commanders. In northern Gaza, a total of 30 commanders had been killed.
By July 2024, the last time the IDF gave a full assessment of those eliminated, it claimed to have “eliminated six brigade commanders, over 20 battalion commanders, and approximately 150 company commanders.”
What is the goal?
The question this raises is: What is the goal of the continued eliminations of Hamas commanders? Usually in war, the goal is not to get to some kind of objective. The objective is reached by defeating enemy units. Historically in war, the great commanders and great battles were often won not by eliminating every enemy commander but by defeating or outmaneuvering the enemy. Sometimes in battles, the enemy would be put in such a difficult position on the battlefield that they would be defeated without a major battle.
This is not always the case. Hannibal often won major, bloody battles against the Romans but was unable to defeat Rome. Huge numbers of Romans died at Cannae, for instance, but Rome prevailed. Napoleon was a great commander, but even though he may have outmaneuvered his enemies in the campaign of 1814, for instance, he ultimately did not win the war. Similarly, America’s Stonewall Jackson was a brilliant commander, but even his genius could not bring victory.
What does history teach us in these cases? Sometimes total war and wars of attrition are necessary to sap an enemy’s strength. This was the case in the US Civil War. However, the First World War showed that mass killing on a front line can go on for years. Vietnam taught that insurgencies can go on for decades. Winning tactical battles doesn’t always win wars.
What is happening in Gaza?
Hamas continues to control around forty percent of Gaza. It has lost almost all the men it fielded on October 7. It has lost almost all its commanders as well. In many cases, Hamas units have had their leadership eliminated two or three times. Most Hamas units appear to exist only on paper. Yet, Hamas has shown in the past that even when the IDF believed units, such as those in Rafah or Jabalia, had been dismantled, they returned to fight again and again.
Hamas continues to control all 2 million civilians in Gaza. It doesn’t have to recruit very many people to maintain a force of 10,000 or so fighters. This is the challenge today.
Without separating the civilians from Hamas, so Hamas can’t recruit and arm them, it will be hard to remove Hamas. The American-backed peace plan, created by US President Donald Trump, envisions providing civilians in Gaza with an alternative government. This would likely reduce Hamas’s ability to recruit. Until that happens, it appears Hamas will remain in Gaza and continue to recruit, and its commanders will continue to be targeted.

“This is typical of the state. When they start to be pushed back into a corner politically, militarily and now economically, you are seeing how the state will start to push back and crack down on internal repression. So this is an example of internal repression,” he said.
“It’s to change the narrative, to show that they are still in control. Repression is what these people do so well, and it is done solely to threaten and coerce people back into submission. These people have no shame. They will do anything to their people to ensure that they maintain total control,” he added.
Ejei’s demand also followed insistence by Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, an Iranian politician and relative of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, that the Islamic Republic was unable to focus on policing women’s clothing because of “wartime conditions.”
In recent months, prosecutors and law enforcement authorities have increasingly targeted businesses over alleged violations of the mandatory hijab rules. Cafes, restaurants and other commercial establishments have been shut down or threatened with legal action over women appearing without headscarves on their premises or for allowing other behaviors viewed as un-Islamic.
Last Sunday, authorities announced an investigation into a music event and incidents involving women without headscarves at a hotel in Nowshahr, according to Iran International. In May, authorities sealed the historic Ameri House Hotel in Kashan over alleged hijab violations. In July, the public prosecutor of Kohgiluyeh County announced the closure of 10 cafes and teahouses in Dehdasht for allegedly failing to observe religious standards.
The pressure on businesses comes as many companies and individuals already struggle to survive Iran's high inflation, a weakening currency, and broader economic pressures. The renewed enforcement of hijab rules therefore extends the impact of the Islamic Republic’s morality policies beyond individual women, with businesses also facing closures and legal action if they themselves do not police the behavior and clothing of their customers.

Why ‘Washington Post’ columnist Shadi Hamid excuses Hamas, demonizes Israel, Jews - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:56:10 UTC
22:56:10 KST

When Gaza-born activist Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib penned a devastating op-ed in The New York Times on September 4 decrying Hamas’s destructive role in the Gaza Strip, Washington Post columnist Shadi Hamid was incensed (“For Gaza to Recover, Hamas Must Be Expelled”).
Hamid invented on X/Twitter that “pro-Israel hardliners” support Alkhatib because he “justifies the killing of Palestinians as unfortunate fact or a necessary evil.” Hamid’s assault against Alkhatib is a gross distortion of Alkhatib’s vision for a bright future for the people of Gaza.
“A Palestinian miracle on the Mediterranean is within reach if Gaza rejects Islamism, Jihadism, Hamas, and stale nationalist notions, all of which have left it devastated,” Alkhatib wrote, laying out the path forward for the fruitful development of the coastal territory.
But a thriving future in which the Gaza residents can pursue peaceful lives free from the ruinous rule of Hamas is apparently not Hamid’s shared vision. Since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacre, Hamid’s columns and social media posts have rationalized Hamas, demonized Israel, and marginalized Jews politically.
On October 31, 2023, Hamid published a column in The Washington Post explaining that Hamas isn’t evil. The essay – written three weeks after Hamas launched a cross-border raid and murdered 1,200 people and abducted 250 others – exonerated murder, abduction, and rape carried out in the name of Palestinian “resistance.”
Noting that Palestinians had become convinced “that nonviolence doesn’t work,” Hamid argued that Hamas’s violence was a legitimate expression of Palestinian frustration.
But in what world does frustration justify mass murder?
Moreover, in his essay, Hamid ignored the inconvenient history of Palestinian leaders Yasser Arafat and Mahmoud Abbas rejecting peace deals. He left out Hamas’s ideology, codified in the organization’s charter, which advocates killing Jews.
He was silent on the inculcation of hate in Palestinian schools. And he also ignored Hamas’s hijacking of international aid to raise an army, dig tunnels, and build a rocket arsenal.
By ignoring the threat that Hamas posed to Israel, Hamid was free to accuse Israel of using excessive violence and committing war crimes in its war against Hamas. Over the course of a year and a half, Hamid argued his case, often using discredited information that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
The tolerance for hatred
In his May 28, 2025, Post op-ed, Hamid wrote: “A genocide is happening in Gaza. We should say so.” He rehashed charges that Israel deliberately starved the residents of Gaza.
But a UNICEF study released this summer showed that acute malnutrition in Gaza ranged from 0.2% to 0.8% (pre-war, the rate was 0.8%), which is significantly lower than the malnutrition rate for many surrounding countries such as Egypt (2.9%) and Jordan (2%).
Hamid also argued that the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide’s definition of genocide, which emphasizes intent, fits Israel’s actions in Gaza.
But as David Bernstein, a law professor at the Antonin Scalia Law School of George Mason University, noted, the established international legal standards requiring genocide intent mandate that “[a] state’s conduct must be inexplicable except as an attempt to annihilate a protected group.”
Bernstein detailed that given that Israel provided “a plausible explanation for its conduct [namely the elimination of a very real terror threat], the inference that the campaign is aimed at destroying Palestinians as a group cannot be the only reasonable interpretation.”
Claims of Israeli excesses have fueled harassment of Jewish students on campus and created a toxic atmosphere for Jews in general.
Hamid has also been involved in efforts to marginalize Jews politically. In his opposition to vice president candidate Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Hamid wrote in 2024, “It’s simply a fact that Josh Shapiro holds hardline pro-Israel views that are well outside the mainstream of the Democratic Party. None of the other leading VP contenders have shown such disregard for campus protesters, comparing them to white supremacists.”
Shapiro’s pro-Israel views are hardly hardline. They are centrist, maybe even Left of Center, and well within the American Jewish consensus. While he didn’t say so explicitly, Hamid implied that no Jew holding mainstream views of Israel should be welcome in the Democratic Party.
When he started at the outlet in October 2023, he was a member of the editorial board. The first Washington Post editorial after October 7 described the terror as “clarifying.” To the editorial board, the cataclysmic attack demonstrated extensive preparation. Yet, October 7 and its aftermath have been clarified in another way too.
Three years after the worst mass-killing of Jews since World War II, one of America’s most prominent newspapers has a columnist who excuses the terrorist perpetrators, demonizes Israel, and considers most Jews unfit for mainstream politics. The tolerance for hatred is indeed clarifying.
The writer is a US media researcher for CAMERA (Committee for Accuracy in Middle East Reporting and Analysis, the leading organization exposing and countering anti-Israel narratives in the media, online, and in schools. Learn more at CAMERA.org and on social media @CAMERA4Truth.
