Libyan leader Haftar's airplane was in Abu Dhabi at same time as Netanyahu's visit - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:56:04 UTC
22:56:04 KST

Data from flight-tracking websites showed that a Libyan Airbus A319, registration P4-KH5I9, flew from Benghazi to Abu Dhabi on Sunday, at the same time that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was in the UAE to meet Emirati President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Italian outlet Il Folgio reported on Tuesday.
The plane has been used by Saddam Haftar, son of the leader of the Benghazi-based Libyan National Army, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, and candidate for the Libyan presidency.
Additionally, state flights from Morocco, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar appeared to land at the UAE's Al Bateen Executive Airport, southeast of Abu Dhabi, on Sunday while Netanyahu was on the ground.
Il Foglio's report implies that Haftar and Netanyahu also met in the UAE, although neither Israeli officials nor pro-Haftar Libyan sources have corroborated this at the time of writing.
Notably, the UAE has been a major backer of Haftar and the LNA throughout the Libyan Civil War. After the conflict cooled in 2021, Haftar's LNA remained in control of large parts of eastern and southern Libya, but international organizations do not widely recognize it as the de facto government of Libya.
Israeli officials, Haftar have previously met, according to reports
This is not the first time that the Haftars have reportedly met Israeli officials. In 2021, officials from Israel's intelligence Ministry reportedly met with Saddam Haftar, who, as a senior military commander and deputy LNA leader, has authority to act as a proxy on behalf of his father on the international stage.
Later, in November 2021, Saddam Haftar reportedly flew to Ben-Gurion Airport to discuss potentially normalizing relations with Israeli officials. The visit, which was first reported by Haaretz, was a brief stop while traveling from Dubai to Libya, reports at the time noted.
According to reports at the time, Haftar had previously contacted Mossad's international relations division, known as "Tevel," which coordinates with countries with which Israel has no diplomatic relations.
Khalifa Haftar reportedly requested Israeli "military and diplomatic assistance" in return for normalization, according to Haaretz at the time.
Additionally, Khalifa Haftar's private jet reportedly landed in Israel in January 2022, where it remained for two hours before returning to Cyprus, as noted by The Jerusalem Post at the time.
Days before Khalifa's visit, the internationally recognized Libyan Prime Minister Abdul Hamid al-Dbeibah and then-Mossad director David Barnea met in Jordan to discuss normalization and security cooperation, according to Saudi and Libyan media reports. However, Dbeibah's office denied that any such meeting happened.
Yonah Jeremy Bob and Lahav Harkov contributed to this report.

Another child of Jolie and Pitt has dropped father&apos;s surname
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:53:44 EEST
22:53:44 KST

Another child of Jolie and Pitt has dropped father's surname
Kyiv • UNN
A Los Angeles court allowed 21-year-old Zahara to change her name from Jolie-Pitt to Jolie. She had been using her mother's surname for years.
The daughter of actors Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie, Zahara, has shortened her previously hyphenated surname. UNN reports this, citing E! News.
Details
Twenty-one-year-old Zahara has officially renounced her father's surname, and a Los Angeles court in the United States granted her request to retain only her mother's surname.
"After reviewing the case materials, the court hereby rules as follows: as there are no objections, the petition for a name change is granted," reads a court document filed on September 28 and obtained by E! News. "The order has been signed and entered. The petitioner's name is changed from Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie," the document states.
Zahara filed a petition to change her name in June, nearly a month after graduating from Spelman College in Atlanta with a Bachelor of Arts degree in psychology.
In July, she published notice of her intention in the Los Angeles Daily Journal, fulfilling California's requirement that a name-change petition be published in a local newspaper so that anyone who objects to the name change could submit a written objection before the final hearing.
Although Zahara's legal name change has only just been finalized, she has already been using her mother's surname for many years. When she joined the Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority in 2023, she introduced herself in an intake video as Zahara Marley Jolie.
And at her graduation ceremony earlier this year, she was again introduced as Zahara Marley Jolie when she walked onto the stage to receive her diploma.
Addendum
Zahara is the second of Brad and Angelina's six children to receive permission for a legal name change, choosing to remove the surname of the star of "F1 The Movie" from her name. The former couple's 20-year-old daughter, Shiloh, received similar permission in 2024 after filing a petition on her 18th birthday.
Since then, her siblings, 25-year-old Maddox and 18-year-old Vivienne, have also taken similar steps this year. Approval of their name-change requests is currently pending.

Denmark plans new animal welfare agency, more inspections and tougher penalties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:53:05 UTC
22:53:05 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

World’s largest ship by gross tonnage passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:52:55 UTC
22:52:55 KST

Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.
Denmark’s government will establish a new animal welfare inspection agency and increase inspections by 50% under an emergency package presented Tuesday, following criticism of enforcement failures and a backlog of about 1,500 follow-up visits.
The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.
Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.
The package follows sharp criticism in April 2026 from the National Audit Office, which scrutinizes public spending and administration. A Justice Ministry review published in early September found that about 1,500 follow-up inspections from 2025 and the first half of 2026 remained outstanding.
Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.

The Danish government plans to allocate an additional DKK 22 billion to the Armed Forces in 2027 as part of its upcoming budget proposal, according to Berlingske.
Defense investment is then expected to increase to around DKK 40 billion in 2030.
The government expects Denmark to meet NATO’s target of spending 3.5 percent of GDP on military defense before 2030. According to NATO figures cited by Berlingske, Denmark is already spending 3.4 percent of GDP on defense in 2026 when funding from the Ukraine Fund is included.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said the government’s first budget would require cuts in some areas to finance other priorities.
“There is something we need to have a little less of, so that in return we can invest in the community, in welfare, in security, and in a competitive business sector,” he told Berlingske.
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr said support for Ukraine would continue to form part of defense spending in the coming years.
“This is both about defending Denmark and Europe, while at the same time we also protect welfare. The Danish economy is strong enough to do both,” she said.
Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt said continued donations to Ukraine would require support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
NATO members agreed in 2025 to increase the alliance’s military spending target to at least 3.5 percent of GDP, replacing the previous 2 percent target.

A majority in the Climate, Environment and Technology Committee at Copenhagen Municipality approved a new plan Monday afternoon.
According to it, the city has moved a step closer to introducing a zero-emission zone in part of Vesterbro, where petrol and diesel vehicles would generally not be allowed to drive.
“It is really good that Copenhagen is now getting its first zero-emission zone. It is good for the climate and for reducing local air pollution,” Kristine Ammitzbøll-Bille of De Radikale, the Danish Social Liberal Party, told TV 2 Kosmopol.
The proposal was originally larger but was changed after 768 consultation responses from residents, businesses and interest groups.
Around 80 percent of the responses were either critical or reserved about the plan.
The revised version exempts all of Vesterbrogade, the area around Copenhagen Central Station, Skelbækgade and part of Halmtorvet.
Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.
Fewer trains between Copenhagen and western Denmark until Tuesday morning
Fewer trains will run between parts of Denmark until at least 10 a.m. Tuesday after an overhead wire fell between Sorø and Slagelse.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said Monday afternoon that repairs were underway.
DSB, Denmark’s national passenger rail operator, said InterCityLyn and InterCity trains are still running between Copenhagen and Esbjerg, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
Although the overhead wire fell on the westbound track, trains can still use the other track.
Replacement buses are also running between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. DSB said earlier Monday that it had ordered 50 buses.
The disruption was initially expected to last until 8 p.m. Monday, but Banedanmark later extended the estimate until 10 a.m. Tuesday.
A train that stopped beneath the fallen wire also had to be evacuated. Another train was connected to it and pulled it to the nearest station.
Banedanmark said it would investigate why overhead wires have fallen repeatedly on the same section. A damaged overhead line near Sorø also caused cancellations and delays in mid-September.
“We are well aware that this is not the first time we can see a fallen overhead wire on the same section within a relatively short time,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Smidt Sigsgaard said.
Another overhead wire was also torn down at Copenhagen Airport on Monday, causing reduced service and delays.

Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.
If the exemption is not extended again, higher taxes will therefore take effect from the beginning of 2027.
The additional revenue would help finance government plans including free dental care, lower taxes and changes to agriculture.
An expert group is currently examining possible changes to car taxation, including models for permanently removing registration tax on electric cars. Its recommendations are expected in the second half of 2026.
DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ organization, criticized the government’s plan.
Thomas Sørensen, director of DI’s automotive branch, called it an “own goal to let taxes on electric cars rise from the new year.”
According to FDM, Denmark’s main association for car owners, a VW ID.4 Style could cost around DKK 10,300 more in tax, while a Tesla Model Y Long Range with all-wheel drive could face an increase of nearly DKK 28,000.
Mobility Denmark, an industry association representing the automotive sector, also criticized the proposal.
“Danes have embraced the green transition, and now the government wants to make some of the popular electric cars tens of thousands of kroner more expensive. It simply does not add up,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Around 50 rail replacement buses have been ordered to operate between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. The first buses have already started running.
DSB has also sent staff to the stations in Slagelse and Ringsted to help passengers affected by cancellations and delays.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s rail infrastructure, is at the site and working to repair the fault.
At 2:51 p.m., DSB’s traffic information showed that the company was unable to operate all scheduled trains between the regions.
InterCityLyn and InterCity services between Copenhagen and Esbjerg are still running, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
DSB is advising travelers to check the journey planner before traveling.
Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”

Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.
British singer Rod Stewart will perform at Royal Arena in Copenhagen on 6 June 2027 as part of his “The Final Encore” tour, concert promoter Live Nation Denmark said in a press release.
The 81-year-old singer said the time has come to end his career on the road.
“After more than six decades, ‘The Final Encore’ will without doubt be my last tour,” Stewart said.
“I have sung the music I love since I was 19 years old, and I have had the privilege of taking it around the entire world to all of you. It has given me a life that is far more fantastic than I could ever have imagined,” he said.
Stewart had to interrupt his “One Last Time” tour in August this year after having a stent inserted into a coronary artery, according to a statement from his representative reported by CNN.
A stent is used to keep a narrowed coronary artery open, including in cases where the artery has been affected by atherosclerosis.
Stewart began making music as a teenager. His career took off in the late 1960s, when he became a member of several rock bands, including The Jeff Beck Group and The Faces.
He released his first solo album, “An Old Raincoat Won’t Ever Let You Down,” in 1969.
His major breakthrough as a solo artist came in 1971 with “Every Picture Tells a Story,” which included the song “Maggie May.”
Another of his best-known songs is “Da Ya Think I’m Sexy?” from his ninth solo album, “Blondes Have More Fun,” released in 1978.
Stewart is also known for recording his own versions of songs by other artists, including Cat Stevens’ “The First Cut Is the Deepest,” Van Morrison’s “Have I Told You Lately” and the Sutherland Brothers’ “Sailing.”
His latest album so far, “Swing Fever,” was released in 2024 in collaboration with pianist and composer Jools Holland.
“The Final Encore” will begin in Dublin on 23 April and end in Hannover, Germany, on 24 July.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.
“There will be no cost to the US,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, with the words “no cost” written in capital letters.
Asked how that could be the case if the US will finance new bases, Løkke said:
“You’ll have to ask him about that.”
“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.
“That is, after all, completely obvious,” he said.
Pituffik Space Base was previously known as Thule Air Base and has around 150 US military personnel stationed there.
Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.

Germany's Foreign Minister called Putin's belligerent imperialism the greatest threat to Europe
Kyiv • UNN
Johann Wadephul urged people not to question the threat posed by Moscow. He criticized Fico's doubts about NATO guarantees.
Russian imperialism poses the greatest threat to Europe, and questioning this is irresponsible. Germany's representative Johann Wadephul said this in Slovakia on Tuesday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"The greatest threat to the freedom of our continent comes from Moscow. The greatest danger to Europe is the bellicose imperialism of (Russian President — ed.) Putin," German politician Johann Wadephul said during a meeting with his Slovak counterpart, Juraj Blanár.
"Questioning these facts is not only a sign of a lack of solidarity, but also simply irresponsible."
The publication adds that Slovakia, whose government is headed by left-nationalist Prime Minister Robert Fico, has expressed doubts about the European Union and NATO's response to the war that began after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Fico maintains warm relations with Moscow, including holding meetings with Putin, and is also clashing with the EU over measures aimed at ending supplies of Russian oil and gas, which Bratislava still needs.
This month, Fico criticized unnamed Western politicians for seeking to foment a conflict between NATO and Russia after the "failed" strategy of defeating Moscow.
He also said that Europe was closer to war than ever and expressed a desire to keep Slovakia from participating in the conflict.
In a television interview over the weekend, he said he did not believe that partners would send troops to help Slovakia in the event of war. Fico noted that he would prefer to remain neutral, but that NATO membership obliges him otherwise.
To add
Slovak opposition parties criticized Fico for questioning Slovakia's commitment to the principle of NATO collective defense.
Wadephul said on Tuesday that states must rely on security guarantees, and that doubts about NATO's ability to deter threats endanger "all of us."
He also recalled that the EU had already faced "systematic obstruction" from Hungary during the tenure of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, whose 16-year rule ended in an electoral defeat earlier this year. Orbán often obstructed the adoption of EU measures concerning Russia.
Earlier this year, Slovakia — together with Hungary and the Czech Republic — refused to participate in the EU's lending program for Ukraine, and in the past delayed the imposition of sanctions against Russia over energy policy issues.
Wadephul said that "blockages" in Brussels weaken the EU.
"Ultimately, this does the most harm to the side that resorts to blocking," he noted.

Economic sentiment and employment expectations across the EU and the euro area showed a mild decline in September due to lower consumer confidence.
The European Commission reported that the Economic Sentiment Indicator fell by 0.4 points to 97.9 in the EU and by 0.5 points to 97.9 in the euro area.
The Employment Expectations Indicator also receded during the same period, as it dropped by 0.6 points to 98.3 in the EU and by 1.3 points to 97.5 in the euro area.
Lower confidence reported by consumers drove the overall decline in sentiment, even though managers in the industry and construction sectors expressed higher confidence.

Managers raised their selling price expectations sharply in the construction and industry sectors, while consumers' inflation expectations for the next 12 months increased by 1.8 points.
The Economic Uncertainty Indicator grew by 1.2 points to 18.4, which broke a four-month downward trend that started after its peak in April.

When violence becomes routine: Israel reels from week of crime

Unknown Publisher

13:48:05 UTC
22:48:05 KST

Murders, shootings, explosives, grenade attacks and deliberate vehicle rammings — In recent days, hardly a day has passed without a serious or unusual criminal incident somewhere in Israel, from Holon to Rahat and Netanya to the Galilee. 
These are some of the main incidents reported over the past several days.
Monday: 15-year-old wounded by explosive device
- An explosive device detonated Monday afternoon in the yard of an apartment building in Holon’s Jesse Cohen neighborhood, south of Tel Aviv. A person known to police lives in the building and investigators believe he was the intended target. Police were trying to locate him to obtain his account of the incident. A 15-year-old boy was moderately wounded in the blast.
- More than 10 people were arrested in Rahat, a predominantly Bedouin city in southern Israel, during police raids targeting two families involved in a feud that has included gunfire.
Sunday: 16-year-old girl wounded by grenade
- A 16-year-old girl was moderately wounded when a grenade was thrown at a home in Ma’alot-Tarshiha, a city in northern Israel. Police said the incident was criminal in nature.
- Police arrested two boys, ages 15 and 13, after they allegedly filmed themselves making an obscene gesture at police officers and kicking a police vehicle in Tel Aviv, then uploaded the videos to TikTok. The two were taken for questioning at the Holon police station and later released under restrictive conditions.
Saturday: Driver hits police vehicle, injures officer
- In Netanya on Saturday night, police officers spotted a vehicle they considered suspicious and ordered the driver to stop for inspection. Police said the driver ignored their instructions, continued driving and collided with a police vehicle. An officer was moderately wounded in the crash and the driver sustained minor injuries. The driver was arrested.
Friday: Killings in Kabul and Haifa
- Mohammed Samer Yassin, a resident of Tamra, was shot and killed in the Arab town of Kabul in the Western Galilee. His cousin, Jawad Yassin, was killed in February last year. Police said the shooting was criminal in nature. Yassin was the 177th person killed in Israel’s Arab community since the beginning of the year.
- Yonat Maswada, a woman in her 30s, was found in critical condition on Haifa’s Ha’atzmaut Street and taken to Rambam Health Care Campus, where she was pronounced dead. Her partner, Ali Maswada, was arrested. A court on Monday extended his detention until Thursday. His attorney argued that she had inflicted the injury that caused her death herself.
Thursday: Man opens fire on building, then is shot
- A man in his 30s opened fire with a long gun at a building in Yafa an-Naseriyye, an Arab town near Nazareth, and was shot by police following a pursuit. He was taken in critical condition to the English Hospital in Nazareth, where he was pronounced dead.
- Police arrested a 28-year-old resident of Modi’in who is suspected of planning to distribute cannabis across Jerusalem. The suspect is the son of a well-known Israeli singer.
Wednesday: Fragmentation grenade explodes in Kfar Shmaryahu
- An IDF fragmentation grenade exploded overnight in Kfar Shmaryahu, an affluent community north of Tel Aviv. Neighbors reported hearing a powerful explosion. Police bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene and collected evidence. A preliminary investigation indicated that the incident was criminal in nature.
Police pushed back on the suggestion that the recent cluster of violent incidents reflected a broader surge in crime, saying its data showed declines in several major categories compared with the same period last year.
According to police, Israel has recorded 22 fewer killings since the start of the year than during the corresponding period last year. Vehicle thefts have fallen about 27%, break-ins at businesses about 12% and burglaries of homes and vehicles about 8%, police said, adding that robberies have also declined.
Police said officers responded immediately to the incidents cited, making arrests, conducting searches and collecting evidence. In Rahat, five suspects were arrested over the weekend and police seized an M-16 rifle, two handguns, magazines and hundreds of rounds of ammunition. Ten other people were arrested or detained in a separate operation connected to the violence there.
In Haifa, police noted that a suspect had been arrested and remained in custody. In Yafa an-Naseriyye, police said officers confronted and shot an armed man after seeing him fire a long gun at a residential building.
Investigations into the other incidents remain underway, police said.
“A cluster of incidents occurring within a few days should not be taken as evidence of a nationwide trend,” police said, adding that crime trends should be assessed over longer periods and on the basis of broader data.
Police said they would continue operations targeting violent offenders, organized criminal activity and illegal weapons in an effort to prevent further violence and bring suspects to justice.

Iranians stagger under soaring costs of seven months of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:47:59 UTC
22:47:59 KST

Iranians stagger under soaring costs of seven months of war
LONDON, Sept 29 - Iran's leaders may radiate bullishness in their war with the United States, but life is becoming ever tougher for ordinary citizens unable to afford basic necessities or rent as a US blockade cuts the state's financial lifeline - oil exports.
From an engineer forced out of Tehran by high rent to a woman forced to stop smoking because of the price of cigarettes and carers struggling to buy medicines, all areas of daily life are affected.
"I'm forced to sell my items with a very small and negligible profit, yet I can't close my business because then I'd be unemployed," said Behnam Riazi, a restaurant owner interviewed on camera in Tehran.
Riazi cannot raise his prices because his customers cannot pay more - any most anyway buy only necessities now.
How far economic strains may push Iran towards diplomatic compromise is unclear, as it tightens its own stranglehold on Gulf energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil and gas prices in the US and around the world.
ECONOMIC MISERY MAY SPUR DIPLOMACY
However, the latest burst of diplomacy was partly spurred by economic strains, US, Middle Eastern and Iranian sources said last week. Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed fears of unrest, and cracked down ruthlessly on rumblings of dissent.
In January, over a month before the US and Israel began their war on Iran, authorities killed thousands of demonstrators exasperated by years of cumulative economic distress.
But now, all those Reuters spoke to said they had too many daily worries to think about protesting.
Hediyeh, a housewife in her 60s in northern Iran, survives on her husband's civil service pension. She can barely afford medicine or even the adult diapers needed by her elderly mother, who has Alzheimer's disease.She wanted to buy her grandson a new bag for his first day at school this autumn, but it cost five or six times what she had expected, and in the end she could only buy him a notebook and pencils.
Like most of the Iranians Reuters interviewed by phone or messaging app, she did not want to be identified, fearing punishment for speaking to foreign media.
A.J., a teacher who asked only to be identified by his initials, also said he cannot always afford the medicine his mother needs.
He has already moved in with his mother and siblings in a northern village, leaving Tehran after schools moved online because of the war, but fears he will no longer be able to afford to return if in-person teaching resumes.
In Sanandaj, capital of Kurdistan province, 34-year-old psychotherapist Nazanin has given up smoking because of the cost after having previously found it impossible to do so, she said.
Those who can afford to bypass the usual ways of obtaining goods or services through the black market are finding it has become more pervasive, though the cost has gone up.
One man said he had paid $200 in hard currency to a surgeon to get around the bureaucratic process needed for an operation.
Another said police requests for bribes were growing more frequent, and that he had had to pay more than before after being stopped at a checkpoint without identification papers.
JOBS BEING CUT IN PRIVATE SECTOR
An architect, who only gave his initials A.A., said even wealthier Iranians were cutting back: "All of them have become poor relative to the lifestyle they used to have."
His car had a puncture last week and he is having to drive on a spare tyre for the two weeks it takes to get a cheap replacement; he can no longer afford those available immediately.
He worries that Iran is heading for fuel shortages, which could disrupt supply chains and cause wider economic havoc.
Already, the war is causing heavy job losses across the private sector.
M.H., a woman in Tehran who also asked to be identified only by her initials, said she had lost her job this month in the procurement department of a local business even though her one-year contract had only been renewed the previous day.
She now has to return the money the company had paid into Iran's social security system for the coming year. Her family has strictly prioritised spending, with food at the top.
"Thank goodness we can still afford the internet, so we can stay connected online, maybe watch a film," she said.
Bijan, 40, a former engineer who now offers tuition to students to make money, said he and his wife had left their Tehran flat and moved to an area he described as "half slum" outside the capital.
The couple have exhausted their savings and plan to move to another city where they hope to live more cheaply.
Shop owners see the slide in living standards better than most. Ramin Yousefnia said in an on-camera interview in Tehran that all the customers in his grocery shop had cut down.
"Something they used to buy five or 10 of, they can only buy two of now," he said. "Don't even get me started on savings. This is the reality." REUTERS

Over 300,000 refugees in Chad risk losing access to basic services amid funding crisis: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:41:39 UTC
22:41:39 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Over 300,000 refugees in Chad risk losing access to food, healthcare, and education as a funding crisis threatens registration and other critical protection services, the UN refugee agency warned Tuesday.
Dominique Hyde, UNHCR's director of external relations, told journalists in Geneva that 319,000 refugees face delays in registration, leaving them without vital documentation needed to access basic services and potentially exposing them to a greater risk of detention.
The funding shortfall could also leave up to 200,000 women and girls without access to safe spaces and programs designed to prevent and respond to violence, while as many as 233,000 children could lose access to child protection services.
Hyde warned that programs aimed at helping refugees become self-reliant are also under threat.
In Chad, livelihoods, vocational training and business development opportunities are at risk for nearly 400,000 refugees and members of host communities, she said.
"These programs, they matter because that humanitarian assistance was never intended to be permanent," Hyde said.
She stressed that allowing refugees to work, earn an income and participate in local economies helps them support themselves and contribute to host communities, freeing humanitarian assistance for those who need it during the first days of an emergency.
The impact of the funding crisis extends beyond Chad.
In Ethiopia, the number of safe houses for survivors of gender-based violence has more than halved in a year, while newly arrived families in Burundi risk losing services including family tracing and psychosocial support, Hyde said.
In Afghanistan, assistance for returnees has also been sharply reduced as more than 1 million Afghans have returned or been deported this year.
UNHCR said the cuts come amid a broader funding crisis, with its income falling from $5.2 billion in 2024 to $3.9 billion in 2025. By the end of July, the agency had received only 32% of the funding it requires for 2026.
The agency also cut its workforce by 33% last year, closed 140 offices, and generated $135 million in efficiencies as it reduced costs and prioritized critical activities.
"Prioritization has limits," she warned, adding that an increasing share of the funding UNHCR receives is tightly earmarked.

EU to Trump: We will keep pushing for global AI safety rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:39:11 UTC
22:39:11 KST

EU to Trump: We will keep pushing for global AI safety rules
EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Washington’s opposition to global AI regulations won’t stop Brussels from moving forward on a new international safety system.
The European Commission will continue to seek an international agreement on AI security, despite U.S. resistance, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Tuesday.
"The U.S. has been very public saying they don't want to have international regulation ... because they have concerns that it's hindering innovation,” Virkkunen said on the stage of the RAID Conference in Brussels in response to questions by POLITICO.
U.S. President Donald Trump has brushed away concerns about AI existential risks as a "hoax," and declared his opposition to global regulations. The EU takes a different view, having offered its support for last week's initiative for an international safety body to monitor AI led by Finland and Norway, and signed by 20 other countries.
Advertisement
"We have a different approach because we think that, if you are regulating in a pro-innovation manner, it's also a good basis for innovation that people have trust in those technologies," said Virkkunen, the EU Commissioner responsible for technology.
She praised the EU’s landmark 2024 AI Act as a strong regulatory basis for tackling challenges posed by AI bots.
Calls to slow down technological development and strengthen international governance have grown as reports of AI agents going rogue come to light. On Tuesday, OpenAI reportedly said it would not release its latest model out of safety concerns, while rival Anthropic will note AI's "risk to humanity" in its upcoming IPO documents.
"This summer, we have seen AI agents act in a ways we maybe never thought possible," Virkkunen noted. "Agents escaping their environment, agents inserting malicious code and agents using deception on humans."
The Finnish-born European Commissioner told the audience that discussions are already taking place in international forums such as the G7, because "people have serious security concerns, because there are no international rules about the safety and security."
"The European Union will continue to promote this internationally. We should have agreements about the safety and security of AI. At the same time, we continue to enforce our rules," she said, also calling for greater cooperation in the meantime among national AI safety organizations.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who is joining a meeting of artificial intelligence officials in Washington later Tuesday, said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that he favors "striking the right balance" with the technology and hopes guardrails will be "voluntary."
"I hope it's voluntary," Johnson told CNBC Tuesday before meeting with the executives and President Donald Trump. "We'll find out what comes out of the meeting today. I think that that's where they're headed. I think they see the handwriting on the wall, and I think they want to ensure investors, you know, consumers, the American public, that they're going to do this in a very safe way, and and that will, I think, put us in the right place."
Johnson's comments come amid pressure from industry executives and fellow Congress members to act fast on legislation to set a regulatory structure for AI and to impose government limits intended to prevent it from causing harm. The speaker is set to meet with executives including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet's Sundar Pichai.
Congress is still in the early stages of regulating artificial intelligence, and the legislative branch is due to be away from Washington and out of session starting at the end of this week and until after November's election.
That time away from Washington gives the issue a sense of urgency, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said. "God forbid — we're going to break this week — if we have an incident," he said on "Squawk Box."
Warner, who built his fortune as a tech entrepreneur, said he is not an AI "doomer," but he thinks there are real risks that rogue agents could pose to national security and critical infrastructure. He plans on Tuesday to seek unanimous consent — an expedited method of passing broadly popular legislation on the Senate floor — on legislation that would establish a federal AI safety board to review frontier models at least 45 days before public release. The legislation is unlikely to pass.
AI executives have recently warned that the technology they built poses catastrophic risks if it goes wrong and urged Washington to act to slow down the advance of the frontier technology. But AI also undergirds the economy, driving market gains amid other headwinds as the technology promises productivity gains and new breakthroughs.
OpenAI, which has a developer day on Tuesday, said late Monday, it had decided not to release an upcoming artificial intelligence model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after determining it did not adequately meet the company's safety standard.
Proposals on AI safety have been flying around Capitol Hill in recent weeks. Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that its technology poses "catastrophic or existential risk to humanity," which is likely to keep the drumbeat strong for regulation.
Some regulatory proposals include installing independent auditors inside frontier labs, introducing new liability laws and standing up regulatory reviews for AI models.
Asked whether the AI companies he meets with bring up potential exemptions from liability in potential regulations, Johnson said "it doesn't come up."
"Of course products liability law applies here directly, and we're going to make sure that that keeps everybody in check," he said.

WADEPHUL SAYS OBSTRUCTION IN BRUSSELS IS SELF-DEFEATING
Slovak opposition parties have criticised Fico for calling into question Slovakia's commitment to NATO collective defence.

Russia is reaping the benefits of tensions in the Middle East through oil exports, but there is a caveat - Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:35:37 EEST
22:35:37 KST

Russia is reaping the benefits of tensions in the Middle East through oil exports, but there is a caveat - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Over four weeks, Russian oil exports rose to 3.71 million barrels per day. The value of shipments reached nearly its highest level since the start of the invasion.
Russia shipped the largest amount of oil in a month and a half, while a surge in prices pushed the value of these cargoes to almost the highest level since the beginning of the Russian Federation's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But the benefits for the Kremlin are offset by its ban on diesel fuel sales abroad. Bloomberg reports this, UNN writes.
Details
In the four weeks through September 27, overseas oil shipments rose to 3.71 million barrels per day, according to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. This is the highest figure since early August.
At the same time, average prices for the key Urals and ESPO grades reached their highest level in more than three months amid disruptions to oil supplies from Saudi Arabia caused by repairs to a key oil pipeline that was attacked at the beginning of the month.
Oil prices rise amid risks of supply disruptions from the Middle East29.09.26, 08:46 • 3928 views
Russia, the publication writes, "is reaping the benefits of tensions in the Middle East, as increased oil supplies combined with rising oil prices replenish Moscow's war chest" for the Russian Federation's war against Ukraine. The inflow over the past four weeks was slightly below the record set in early May, the publication writes.
However, proceeds from oil sales are only part of the story and are likely to be partially offset by a decline in oil-product supplies, the publication notes. Although Russia raised its forecast for oil exports in 2026 by approximately 150,000 barrels per day, it reduced its forecast for oil-product supplies by approximately 500,000 barrels per day.
Drone strikes continue to disable Russian oil refineries. This is forcing Moscow to redirect for export oil that cannot be refined domestically, increasing supply volumes, the publication writes. However, shortages of key fuel types forced the Kremlin to suspend overseas sales of most diesel fuel, which had averaged about 1 million barrels per day before the intensification of the strikes. The ban is expected to be extended through October.
Russian oil shipments
In the week through September 27, about 37 tankers loaded 27.9 million barrels of Russian oil, according to vessel-tracking data and reports from port agents. This compares with 24.99 million barrels on 32 vessels the previous week.
Loading operations in Novorossiysk have resumed, but some tankers are spending considerably more time at the berths than usual, according to satellite images obtained by Bloomberg.
Weekly shipments can be volatile, affected by weather, maintenance, sanctions, military activity, and departure times.
One shipment of Kazakh oil of the Kebco grade was made from Novorossiysk during the week. This month, Moscow redirected all Kazakh oil shipments through the Black Sea port, freeing up more capacity for its own supplies at Ust-Luga on the Baltic, which is considered safer, the publication writes.
The volume of Russian oil aboard vessels increased again last week, reflecting the rise in shipments. Vessels carrying Arctic oil to China usually transfer their cargoes to other vessels. These transfers typically take place east of Singapore from vessels bound through the Red Sea, and near Nakhodka or Zarubino for vessels traveling via the Northern Sea Route. Most Sokol cargoes are also transferred, usually in Kozmino Bay. These loadings can cause delays, increasing the amount of oil at sea.
Export value
Over the four-week average, Moscow's gross export value rose to $2.39 billion per week in the 28 days through September 27, which was $290 million per week more than in the period through September 20 and the highest figure since the period through May 24. The increase was driven by a combination of higher prices for Russia's main oil grades and a moderate increase in shipment volumes, the publication indicates.
On a weekly basis, the value of exports jumped by approximately $180 million, with the increase in supply more than offsetting the decline in prices for Urals crude, which converged with global benchmarks. The weekly value stood at $2.75 billion, the highest figure since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Supply by destination
"China and India remain by far the largest buyers of Russian oil," the publication writes. However, it is not always possible to determine the final destination of individual cargoes until they have traveled a significant part of the route, so many of the latest tanker shipments, listed with intermediate destinations such as Suez or Port Sudan, are marked as "Unknown Asia."
The volume of Russian oil supplies to Asian buyers, including those without a final destination, increased to 3.61 million barrels per day in the 28 days to September 27, compared with 3.4 million barrels for the corresponding period to September 20.
