====================================================================================================

Gulf countries seek alternative export routes amid Hormuz crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:30:16 UTC
22:30:16 KST

Gulf countries are looking to find alternative oil and gas export routes due to the security crisis in the Strait of Hormuz after the joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran at the end of February prompted Tehran to close the vital waterway in retaliation, exposing vulnerabilities in the region’s energy infrastructure.
The Strait of Hormuz typically handles around 20% of global oil supplies, and its closure led to varying outcomes depending on the alternative infrastructure capacities and vulnerabilities among Gulf nations.
Only Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have active pipeline infrastructure able to bypass the strait, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain rely on maritime transit via the strait and have no alternative export capacity, while Oman benefits from its unique geographic location outside the chokepoint.
Kuwait suffered massive economic disruptions, having no immediate bypass options, with its daily crude production plummeting from a pre-war level of 2.6 million barrels to a low of 573,000 in May after its storage facilities maxed out.
Kuwaiti crude exports partially recovered to 1 million barrels per day by September while still remaining below 36% of pre-war levels.
Even though Kuwait is in talks with Saudi Arabia on long-term pipeline bypass projects, such multi-year infrastructure solutions do not offer immediate relief to the country’s short-term economic dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar is in a similar situation, facing a structural crisis as one of the world’s largest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG), which cannot be transported via pipelines in its liquefied state.
A Qatari commercial vessel suffered direct attacks, and escalating regional tensions prompted Doha to scale back operations at its Ras Laffan plant.
The prolonged maritime transit suspension is estimated to have led to a shortfall of around 30 million metric tons in Qatar’s 2026 LNG export targets, analysts say.
Constructing new facilities outside the strait is not possible for Qatar, as country officials said they will not pursue bypass pipelines. Instead, the Qatari government is mediating US-Iran diplomatic talks alongside Pakistan to restore maritime security and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
At the same time, Bahrain suffered direct infrastructure damage in addition to logistical bottlenecks amid the maritime blockade.
The Sitra BAPCO refinery, Bahrain’s only oil processing plant, was forced to idle its 400,000-barrel-per-day capacity as its storage tanks maxed out.
The situation worsened when drone and missile strikes set fire to storage tanks and severely damaged them at the Sitra facility on April 5, further crippling the Bahraini energy economy.
In contrast, the UAE navigated the crisis mostly unscathed, relying on its Habshan-Fujairah oil pipeline, which is also known as the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP).
The 360-kilometer (223.7-mile) ADCOP transports up to 1.8 million barrels of crude per day directly from Abu Dhabi to the Gulf of Oman.
The UAE is planning new infrastructure investments to double its bypass capacity amid its push to reach its production goal of 5 million barrels per day by next year, having recently withdrawn from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to evade quotas of up to 3.5 million barrels per day.
The situation in Saudi Arabia showed the vulnerabilities of multi-billion-dollar bypass systems.
Saudi Arabia relies on the 1,200-kilometer (745.6-mile) East-West Crude Oil Pipeline to transport up to 7 million barrels per day to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Drone strikes by Iranian-backed Yemeni Houthi militias on Sept. 11 damaged the pipeline’s pumping stations, which led Saudi Aramco to shut down the system and cancel October deliveries to at least two European refineries.
Riyadh was forced to reroute its shipments back via the Strait of Hormuz to meet its contractual obligations, causing its daily transit via the waterway to rise from 700,000 barrels in August to 2.9 million barrels this month.
The East-West pipeline resumed limited operations last week, but experts estimate it will take up to eight weeks to repair the damaged pumping stations, leaving the route vulnerable to future Houthi attacks.
Meanwhile, only Oman has been able to turn this regional crisis into an advantage through its Sohar, Duqm, and Salalah ports along the Arabian Sea, serving as a secure transshipment hub for other Gulf producers making ship-to-ship oil transfers.
Crude exports from Hormuz-reliant Gulf nations fell 36.4%, costing $15.2 billion in lost oil revenues during the first month of the crisis alone, according to the Turkish Center for Energy Strategies and Policy Research (TESPAM).
Texas-based think tank Baker Institute confirmed these economic impacts in a recent report, which showed that the lack of alternative export infrastructure concentrated the most severe effects of the crisis squarely on Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain.

What Did Chinese Analysts Think of the Trump-Xi Summit?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

22:30:00 KST

Both in China’s official media and in the world press, the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump last week – their second so far this year – generated usual, predictable descriptions: “ambiguous,” “highly symbolic,” “historic summit,” and so on. However, a section of China’s strategic affairs community – definitely not the pro-U.S. faction – has taken exception to Trump’s “dramatic,” “personal diplomacy” hospitality in welcoming Xi. Cautioning Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leadership to tread carefully with the untrustworthy, capricious, and unpredictable Trump, a skeptic in China’s “leftist” media even observed, “It’s possible they’re [the U.S.] trying to lull China into a false sense of security.”
U.S. watchers in mainland China are split into two factions: pro-U.S. (qin-Mei) and anti-U.S. (fan-Mei). The qin-Mei faction among the Chinese intelligentsia, as expected, celebrated Trump personally greeting the Chinese leader at the airport, as well as the grand welcoming ceremony and the meticulously arranged state banquet at the White House.
“The U.S. side welcomed the Chinese leader with a level of courtesy rarely seen in recent years,” a qin-Mei-leaning Chinese language media outlet reported as Xi returned home.
Some scholars in China highlighted the “historic” and “diplomatic” significance that Trump served Xi the same wine that former U.S. President Richard Nixon used during his visit to China in 1972. In an interview with a popular digital e-paper published from Shanghai, Professor Wu Xinbo, the director of the Center for American Studies at the city’s Fudan University, noted, “The serving of the same wine Nixon used during his China visit in the early 1970s indicates that the current China-U.S. relationship is at an important and historically significant juncture, and President Xi’s visit is historic and a milestone.”
Further, it was widely reported in China that following a tea reception held at the White House for Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, Trump remarked: “The United States was very pleased with this visit, and that the visit has been very productive.” Asked why Trump placed such importance on Xi’s visit, Wu said: “Interactions outside of formal talks, whether it’s taking a walk, having tea, or visiting culturally and historically significant sites, can create a relaxed and informal atmosphere for the leaders of both countries.”
Notably, Wu was invited to attend the state banquet welcoming Trump in Beijing earlier in May this year. Hence, it is understandable that he attaches great importance to opportunities leaders create beyond formal meetings.
At another level, some scholars in China, especially economists, see the current friction in China-U.S. relations arising out of “imbalance” in the economies of the world’s two largest powers. Addressing the issue of the need for “balance” and “equilibrium” between China and the United States at a recent economists’ forum on the eve of Xi’s Washington visit, Professor Ju Jiandong of Tsinghua University in Beijing said: “The currently existing extreme pattern of China doing manufacturing and the United States doing finance is inherently unstable, which is the root cause of the competition between China and the United States.” The Tsinghua professor recently published a controversial book, “The Great Power Competition and the Restructuring of World Order,” in which he argued that the “only way for China and the U.S. to avoid a lose-lose situation is to move from hegemonic iterations to competitive coexistence.”
In sharp contrast, scholars belonging to the fan-Mei faction in China have become more suspicious of the United States given Trump’s “rare, dramatic” personal touch in welcoming the Chinese leader. Scholars in this camp pointed out two examples of Trump going out of his way to impress. One, Trump made a great show of personally greeting Xi at the airport, at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington, D.C. The last time a U.S. president personally welcomed a foreign leader in this manner was 11 years ago, when Barack Obama met Pope Francis at the airport in 2015. Earlier, in 1962, John F. Kennedy had similarly welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.
The other dramatic event that particularly drew attention from the Chinese skeptics was Trump making some startling remarks at the banquet welcoming the Chinese head of state. Citing reports widely circulated in Chinese media, one commentary noted Trump “shamelessly” declaring that the relationship between the two countries has never been as harmonious as it is now. Reacting adversely to the word “harmonious,” the commentary called it “a remarkable attempt by U.S. President Trump to whitewash the current state of the relationship.”
Three factors explain this skepticism targeting Trump and his theatrics while hosting Xi. First, as mentioned, China’s skeptics are apprehensive of China being lulled into a false sense of security. Characterizing Trump as a leader who is “two-faced and hypocritical,” these scholars assert that Trump cannot be trusted. They want CCP leaders to always be vigilant of “untrustworthy” Trump. As the commentary cited above put it: “Trump acted this way towards Russia, and he did the same toward Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela. Regarding China, he has repeatedly attacked over the years, displaying the same ugly nature of a two-faced and hypocritical person.”
Second, some in China suspect Trump’s lavish reception of Xi was a tactic to sow discord between China and Russia. It is argued that Trump has always been outspoken about breaking up the close relationship between China and Russia, seeking to isolate them. These Chinese scholars further argue that before his “dramatic” hospitality toward Xi, Trump was on record in making efforts to cultivate the most “harmonious” Russia-U.S. relationship possible. However, that attempt backfired, resulting in domestic criticism and accusations of collusion with Russia. Now, he’s elevating the China-U.S. relationship to an unprecedented level.
Some in China are even drawing parallels between Trump’s statement praising unprecedented harmony in China-U.S. relations at present with the historic scenario of the United States and China joining forces against the Soviet Union.
“This baseless accusation is not without purpose; its direct effect is to place China-U.S. relations above China-Russia relations, while still maintaining a strong intention to dismantle them,” scholar Zhang Zhikun argued.
Third, some Chinese skeptics are putting forward what appears to be bizarre logic: Trump’s attempt to “whitewash” China-U.S. relations are aimed to stabilize ties so that the United States can act without restraint. Scholars advancing this argument acknowledge that a section of the media and political elite in the United States is highly critical of Trump’s “subservient” approach toward Xi. However, given Trump’s capricious and ambitious nature, it is extremely difficult to fathom the U.S. leader’s true intentions. The fan-Mei faction vehemently argues that “he [Trump] is using appeasement to stabilize [relations with] China, allowing the U.S. to act with greater impunity and wage war around the world.”
To sum up, it is quite clear Trump has succeeded in further deepening the divide between rival qin-Mei and fan-Mei factions among Chinese foreign policy experts, especially the U.S. watchers in China. They interpret the summit – and its implications for China – quite differently.
The two Chinese factions do have one thing in common: they share the viewpoint that changes in Sino-U.S. relations will inevitably lead to corresponding changes in relations among countries around the world. Many Chinese scholars agree that any change in the highly complex China-U.S. relations will not affect Taiwan and Japan, as the two have “secured” their respective interests vis-a-vis the United States. However, some Chinese scholars are of the opinion that changes in China-U.S. relations will lead North Korea to gravitate toward Russia and India toward the United States.

Unknown

2026-09-29

22:26:46 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
NATO will strengthen lower-cost counter-drone defenses so it does not have to deploy advanced fighter jets against inexpensive threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said Tuesday.
“We will strengthen cheaper counter-drone defenses so we are not using high-end jets against low-cost threats,” Rutte said at a joint news conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius at NATO headquarters.
He said repeated drone incidents along the alliance’s eastern flank showed how the threat was evolving. NATO was reinforcing its integrated air and missile defenses through a “multilayered, 360-degree approach” and adapting its posture against drones through initiatives such as Drone Edge, he added.
Rutte cited an incident two weeks ago in which Italian jets deployed by NATO from Lithuania’s Siauliai Air Base shot down a drone that had violated Lithuanian airspace, calling it “collective defense in action.”
Sinkevicius said air defense and preparedness on NATO’s eastern flank were among the main topics of their talks. He said Lithuania remained on track to host a permanently deployed German brigade by the end of 2027.
The two leaders also reaffirmed support for Ukraine. Rutte said Russia’s hostile actions were intended to weaken NATO’s resolve, but pledged that the alliance would “do even more for Ukraine, and not less.”

The case against five participants in a scheme to steal cars in the EU has been sent to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:26:41 EEST

The case against five participants in a scheme to steal cars in the EU has been sent to court
Kyiv • UNN
Five Ukrainians will stand trial for stealing five expensive cars in France as part of the international Matador operation. They face up to 12 years in prison.
Ukrainian law enforcement agencies have sent an indictment to court against five members of an organized group who were part of an international scheme to illegally seize expensive cars in EU countries. This is reported by the Prosecutor General’s Office, according to UNN.
Details
The investigation was conducted as part of the international special operation Matador. According to the investigation, the group included more than 50 citizens of various countries, each of whom performed a specific role.
In May 2024, law enforcement officers conducted around 70 searches in France, Spain, Poland, Latvia, Germany, and Ukraine. In October 2025, the group members were notified of suspicion. The investigation established that from December 2022 to May 2023, the group members rented cars from French rental companies using forged driving licenses. They subsequently handed them over to other members, who altered the vehicles’ identification data and blocked GPS signals.
After that, the cars were transported for legalization, resale, or dismantling for spare parts. As part of the proceedings, the illegal seizure in France of five cars was established: Mercedes-Benz C-Class, BMW 218, Audi E-tron, BMW 420i, and BMW 530 XDrive
The five accused will stand trial for the illegal seizure of vehicles, forgery and use of knowingly forged documents - under Part 5 of Article 27, Part 3 of Article 289, Part 3 of Article 27, and Parts 3 and 4 of Article 358 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The sanctions under these articles provide for imprisonment for up to 12 years.

Aysu Bicer

The UK government has confirmed that national museums in England will continue to offer free admission to all visitors, including overseas tourists.
“Everyone will continue to enjoy universal free admission to our world class national museums in England,” the government said in a statement Tuesday.
Earlier this year, the government had considered introducing admission fees for overseas visitors as a way to boost museum finances but decided against the move.
However, it said charging international visitors could deter domestic audiences and that “the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector.”
National museums contribute more than £1 billion ($1.3 billion) a year to the UK economy and attract visitors from around the world.
“Seven of the UK’s ten most visited museums are national museums,” the government said.
In 2025, 7.1 million people visited the Natural History Museum, while 6.4 million visited the British Museum.
The government said it would work with Arts Council England and the sector to develop “a long-term strategic plan for the future of museums.”
“Further details will be released in due course,” it added.

US completes Iraq pull out after 2 decades, leaving void for Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

U.S. forces are scheduled to withdraw from their final bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies, who now hold deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.
Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal – agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump's administration even as it wages war against Iran – could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other U.S. enemies to stage a comeback, including the Daesh terrorist group.
"Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition's departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a counterweight to Tehran's influence in Iraq," said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specializing in studying armed Shiite groups aligned with Iran.
He predicted that the pro-Iranian militia groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also "seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making."
Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the U.S. withdrawal as "a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honorable Iraqis and a crushing defeat for the American project."
"On Sept. 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country," he told Reuters. "Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people."
While the eventual departure of U.S. forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature.
"We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time," Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, told Reuters.
"All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the (U.S.-led coalition) leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear."
American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple dictator Saddam Hussein and went on to occupy the country, install a Shiite-led government and fight a yearslong counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011.
They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat Daesh in a major war from 2014 to 2017.
Around twice as many Americans died in "Operation Iraqi Freedom" as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt U.S. withdrawal in 2021.
In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield.
The United States killed a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran's allies repeatedly fired on U.S. bases, sometimes drawing reprisals.
In this year's war against Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
"Lasting security will prevail in Iraq" once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran's Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said Monday.
Iran "welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it," he told Iran's parliamentary news service. "Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops."
Washington has accused Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighboring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence.
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish-majority region, say the U.S. pullout also risks giving new life to Daesh, who, despite the defeat nearly a decade ago, retains a sleeper cell network.
At their height, the terrorists occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former U.S. military base.
A lack of U.S. intelligence, logistical support and drones will give Daesh a chance to regroup, said Sirwan Barzani.
"For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by (Daesh) sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September," he said. "This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale" of the fighters.
Iraqi security forces said a suspected Daesh cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout. The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials.
Daesh "is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks," said Col. Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

Experts say use of modified Iranian defence system could alter the balance in the fight for the Red Sea.
Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government has alleged that the Tehran-backed Houthis have modified Iranian air defence weapons into loitering cruise missiles with the assistance of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The Yemeni government has warned that the capability of such missiles – which operate on a heat-tracking system, it alleged – in practice threatens civilian air traffic over Yemen and the crucial Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia as they fight Yemeni government forces. On Thursday, Riyadh said it intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu port area on the Red Sea.
The Houthis also said they attacked “a sensitive target” in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group used ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones in the two operations.
The Houthis were in open conflict with Yemen’s government and a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states from 2014 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire was declared in 2022, but fighting has reignited in recent weeks with the Houthis taking the Red Sea coast of Yemen along with the strategically important city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
In July, the armed group declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, essentially opening yet another theatre in the US-Israel war on Iran.
Since the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz during the war, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative export route for the region’s biggest oil player, Saudi Arabia. Its East-West Pipeline, which carries oil from its eastern oilfields to the western port of Yanbu is only just restarting operations after damage inflicted by a drone attack this month.
So what do the Houthis’ latest missile capabilities mean for the region?
What has the Yemeni government said?
Brigadier General Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, said the Houthis are using Iranian air defence weapons that pose a danger to all aircraft.
Al-Nazili said the weapons have been modified with the assistance of IRGC experts and are being used to strike aircraft and cruise missiles.
“These missiles move around for a period of up to 25 minutes per missile and operate using a thermal-tracking system and attack any heat source without the ability to distinguish between military or civilian targets,” he said in a statement.
“This constitutes a direct and serious threat to the safety of civil aviation and the lives of passengers,” al-Nazili added.
Why does Yemen’s government think regional airspace is under threat?
Al-Nazili noted that aircraft belonging to the United Nations or humanitarian organisations travelling via air routes over Yemen and the region could potentially be in danger.
“Threatening the airspace over the southern Red Sea and turning it into a danger zone for civilian aircraft and passengers represents an escalation that goes beyond the scope of Yemeni airspace safety alone,” he said.
Al-Nazili also said “this dangerous escalation coincides with the threats” by Iranian officials, including Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, to target aviation services in the region after the US sanctioned Iranian airlines.
Rezaei had initially warned that regional airports could lose flights if they joined US restrictions on Iranian aviation. Two days later, his office later clarified that Tehran was not planning military retaliation over the restrictions although it said nonmilitary countermeasures against specific airports remained possible.
Using “Iranian weapons from Yemeni territory poses a direct threat to international air navigation routes and cannot be considered a purely domestic Yemeni issue,” al-Nazili said, calling on international authorities to take “urgent and decisive action”.
Have the Houthis modified Iranian weapons systems?
Eleonora Ardemagni, a senior associate research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, told Al Jazeera that while there is no conclusive evidence that the Houthis have modified an Iranian air defence system, “a series of things suggest this can’t be ruled out.”
“The Houthis have often demonstrated to be able to innovate despite the warfighting scenario, so the evolution of threat capabilities is a constant for the group,” she said.
Ardemagni said years of research have established that “the Houthis don’t receive assembled missiles from Iran but Iranian-origin components to be assembled, so they have significant expertise in assembling weapons.”
She referred to an incident in June 2025 when the Yemeni government-aligned National Resistance Forces, led by Tareq Saleh, seized a 750-tonne shipment of weapons and military equipment bound for the Houthis, including hundreds of advanced cruise, antiship and anti-aircraft missiles, according to the US military’s Central Command.
In July this year, several media reports, including from the Reuters news agency, said an Iranian Mahan Air flight directed to Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, was carrying IRGC commanders, military advisers and weapons. Al Jazeera could not independently verify this report. “The flight was forced to land in Houthi-controlled Hodeidah at last, the same governorate from which the Yemeni government now states the Houthis would launch cruise missiles,” Ardemagni told Al Jazeera.
Brigadier General Mohammed Al-Kumaim, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, said the Houthis are no longer content with using Iranian ballistic missiles and drones but have begun employing advanced air defence technologies based on “loitering” cruise missiles.
Al-Kumaim noted that these missiles can remain in the air for up to 25 minutes, tracking the flight path of targets from their electrothermal emissions.
Yemeni military and strategic expert Ali Al-Dhahab told Al Jazeera that the effect of these loitering munition projectiles is to create a “permanent threat” to any moving object in the air, which could temporarily restrict military air movements.
AI giant Anthropic has also identified a weapons-development cell in northern Yemen reportedly linked to the Houthis that used its Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for a guided rocket and several missile programmes.
What are the Houthis’ known missile capabilities?
The Houthis have a multilayered missile force, ranging from short- and medium-range ballistic missiles to antiship cruise missiles and modified surface-to-air missiles.
Research into the armed group’s arsenal suggested it has evolved substantially from the inherited Yemeni military stockpiles it seized when it took Sanaa in 2014, including Soviet- and Chinese-designed missiles, and has incorporated Iranian-designed missiles.
Here is what we know the Houthis have in their missile arsenal, based on their recent statements:
- Palestine-2: a two-stage, solid-fuel missile unveiled by the group that the Houthis claim is hypersonic with a range exceeding 2,000km (1,245 miles)
- Toufan: one of their long-range systems, said to have an estimated range of 1,350km to 1,950km (840 to 1,210 miles). An International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) assessment said the Toufan appeared to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr.
- Burkan series: short- to medium-range ballistic missiles based on Iranian designs
- Quds series: cruise missiles cited by Houthi spokespeople after strikes on oil and economic facilities in the region
- Older inventory: The Houthis have historically possessed or modified older variants of missiles that include the Scud-B/-C, Tochka and Qaher-1 ballistic missiles as well as C-802 antiship cruise missiles.
What does this mean for the Red Sea and the Yemen war?
As far as the regional aviation sector is concerned, Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that “critically, air traffic around Yemen is almost nil, and that reduces the propensity of inadvertent threats to passenger airplanes.”
However, “these same missiles are being launched northwards into Saudi Arabia, where there is commercial traffic,” Ahmad added.
That Houthi threat, therefore, poses “a huge dilemma for the Saudis, who will be very reluctant to close off airspace but equally be mindful of the risks of allowing air traffic through when missiles are inbound”, Ahmad said.
He added that the Houthis have “demonstrated that they can hit targets at distance. The attack near Tel Aviv airport last year is but one example.”
When the Houthis’ arsenal is analysed in the context of the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait, “any missiles that the Houthis have in their armoury can easily decimate ships at will on a much narrower waterway,” Ahmad said.
Yemeni military strategist Al-Kumaim said the introduction of these supposedly new missiles “adds another capability to the military operations theatre south of the Red Sea” and is part of a broader Iranian strategy to exert pressure on regional airspace and energy supply chains.
Analyst Ardemagni noted that Yemen’s government and Saudi Arabia “have an interest in raising the alarm bell for regional security as much as possible given the current ‘loneliness’, in terms of regional and international allies they are experiencing since the Yemen war has reignited”.
She added that if new cruise missiles are demonstrated, “it would certainly contribute to redesigning Red Sea balances in favour of nonstate armed actors.”

Slovak school stabbing kills teacher, injures two
Bratislava – A knife-wielding schoolboy killed a teacher and wounded another and a pupil in an attack in north-western Slovakia on Sept 29, authorities said.
The attack occurred at around 7am GMT (3pm, Singapore time) in the village of Staskov close to the Czech border.
A 13-year-old schoolboy was detained over the attack, police said, adding he was being investigated for murder.
“This morning, after the first class, a school pupil launched a knife attack,” Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok told reporters.
A 61-year-old woman died of her injuries, while a 44-year-old “with a stab wound to the chest” and a girl were hospitalised, emergency service spokeswoman Petra Klimesova told AFP.
The schoolgirl was “in a serious, critical condition, in a state of heavy neuralgic shock” after the attack, Health Minister Kamil Sasko told reporters.
Sutaj Estok said later the injured teacher’s life was not in danger.
Police said the situation in the village was “under control”.
Asked by journalists, Education Minister Tomas Drucker declined to say whether the attack was due to bullying.
‘Tragic incident’
Nationalist Prime Minister Robert Fico expressed his “sincere condolences” and said he was following “the tragic incident in the village of Staskov with great concern”.
“Personally, I am deeply saddened by this,” he said in a statement.
President Peter Pellegrini said he was “shocked that this is yet another case in which a student attacked teachers and a classmate”.
“Aggression and an atmosphere of intolerance – spread primarily by social media and, unfortunately, by some politicians as well – are literally poisoning the public sphere and influencing the behaviour of our children in schools,” he said.
He urged “all citizens to act in a way that calms the atmosphere, rather than further radicalising it”.
In January 2025, an 18-year-old killed a fellow pupil and a teacher in a knife attack and wounded another pupil at a secondary school in the town of Spisska Stara Ves in north-eastern Slovakia.
In 2020, a teacher was stabbed to death and several others wounded at an elementary school in central Slovakia, the first violent attack at a school in the central European EU and NATO member of 5.4 million people. AFP

Iran downplays possible role in Houthis’ recent Yemen victories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:20:34 UTC
22:20:34 KST

Iran downplays possible role in Houthis’ recent Yemen victories
Iran has long been accused of links with the Houthis in Yemen, but how far do these links go?
Tehran, Iran – Strategic military victories in Yemen by the Tehran-allied Ansar Allah, also known as Houthis, have directed attention towards Iran’s role in the war against the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
According to recent US media reports, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) helped direct an offensive in western Yemen that solidified Houthi control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the port city of Mocha.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
- list 2 of 4Iran touts Hormuz attacks as oil flows increase despite tensions
- list 3 of 4Rubio, Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister hold talks on Yemen, Hormuz Strait
- list 4 of 4Hormuz and Yemen: Iran offers de-escalation at a price others will pay
The Houthis gains on the coast coincide with Iran’s disruptions of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to pressure Washington to lift its naval blockade, US media have reported in recent weeks.
IRGC advisers worked with front-line commanders, assisted with communications and satellite-intelligence analysis, and promised ongoing military support to the Houthis, according to unnamed officials and soldiers cited.
Iranian authorities have not commented on details of the latest allegations but have broadly denied directing the Houthis. They and the Houthis have long stressed the Yemeni group’s independence, despite their geopolitical views often converging.
The IRGC said it viewed the Houthis recent advances in Yemen as a “divine triumph” that followed years of steadfastness.
Earlier this week, President Masoud Pezeshkian rejected a connection between Iran and Houthi actions during an interview with Al Jazeera. He also urged Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the Houthis to negotiate to end the war. But he did offer Iranian assistance in resolving their years-long conflict, which has included Houthi missile and drone attacks on cities in Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier this month rejected a charge by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Houthis are a proxy of Iran. It also highlighted the dire humanitarian consequences of a Saudi blockade on Yemen.
In mid-July, an Iranian passenger aircraft attempted to break the blockade by landing in the Houthi-run airport in the capital Sanaa. The aircraft was redirected after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government bombed the airport shortly before it was due to land.
The aeroplane ended up touching down in Hodeidah, and a Houthi official denied government allegations that the plane carried IRGC personnel.
Iran’s authorities said the plane carried a Houthi delegation which had participated in the funeral of slain Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as well as a number of Yemeni nationals who had received medical treatment in Iran.
Houthi capabilities
This September, the Houthis captured Mocha, Dhubab and Mayyun (or Perim) Island, giving them command of Yemen’s west coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It also cut the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s access to the Red Sea.
In September 2024, a confidential United Nations report leaked to US media claimed that, with the help of the IRGC, Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists, the Houthis had grown “from a localised armed group with limited capabilities to a powerful military organisation”.
Members of the Houthis were receiving tactical and technical training outside Yemen and members were travelling on fake passports to Iran, Lebanon and Iraq, the report alleged.
Iran played an important advisory and logistical role, although it is important not to overstate it, Yemen expert and political risk researcher Nicholas Brumfield told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has had advisers embedded with the Houthis for years, the IRGC [and Hezbollah] is involved in senior Houthi decision-making, and Iran continues to supply weapons and technology to the Houthis,” Brumfield said.
“That said, the west coast offensive reportedly involved 76,000 Yemeni fighters that the Houthis raised using their own governance apparatuses, and there is increasing evidence of the Houthis possessing domestic military industrial capabilities.”
Intense fighting in Yemen has focused on strategic high ground around Taiz and Lahij, including the Kahboub Mountains, as the Houthis seek to consolidate their recent gains and government forces attempt to recoup losses.
With Yemeni government forces now positioned in more favourable mountainous terrain with air support, the Houthis are not expected to repeat the same rapid advances they achieved in September.
This was achieved through their ability to deploy large numbers of fighters with strategic backing against relatively untested government-linked forces in Mocha.
They also exploited continued divisions among Yemeni government-aligned forces, including technically compromising their communications and command-and-control, and the unwillingness or unpreparedness of Saudi Arabia to provide air support during the coastal campaign.
Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan travelled to Washington for talks with Rubio on Tuesday, while UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed is scheduled to visit Riyadh after an invitation by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman. The UAE withdrew from Yemen after Saudi-backed government forces launched an offensive against Southern Transitional Council (STC) separatists, long accused of being supported by Abu Dhabi.
It is unknown why these meetings are taking place, but they come after conflicting reports about the level of support Washington is providing Saudi Arabia regarding Yemen. The US also reportedly declined Saudi requests for strikes in Yemen to support the government.
Disrupting the Bab al-Mandeb
Since taking over Yemen’s west coast, the Houthis have stressed that they have no plans to disrupt Red Sea trade, but will continue to target Saudi-linked vessels.
US President Donald Trump said his administration had established contact with the group and was assured they would not target international shipping, at a time when global markets are in flux over disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
But since Yemen’s war restarted, the Houthis have successfully targeted several Saudi tankers and are believed to be behind disruptions to the critical East-West oil pipeline, as well as targeting multiple Saudi cities.
Both the Houthis and Tehran denied Saudi allegations that the Yemeni group was responsible for the launch of a drone towards the holy Muslim city of Mecca.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told the UN General Assembly that any threat to Muslim holy sites in Mecca and Medina would constitute a “red line that must never be crossed”.
Pakistan and Turkiye, which have a defence pact with Riyadh, have so far refrained from entering the conflict despite sustained Houthi attacks on their ally Saudi Arabia.
The developments in Yemen have come as experts say Iran and the US appear to be on a course for military escalation, even as they maintain contact via mediators such as Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye to reach a deal on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemen expert Brumfield said that despite attempts to distinguish the two parties, it is fair to describe the Houthis as a very close ally of Iran.
“There is a great deal of trust between them and Iran, they’ll go out of their way to help Tehran, and the strategic alignment between the two is such that they rarely have irreconcilable interests,” he said.
But the implications of acknowledging clear Houthi-Iran links would put Riyadh in a difficult position, as Saudi Arabia has suffered from Houthi attacks, as well strikes from Tehran-backed Iraqi militias.
“Earlier in the war, this vulnerability pushed the Saudis to be incredibly conciliatory to Iran even amid intense attacks, and it may be Riyadh simply has no option but to capitulate or cut a deal after the Houthis’ west coast advance, especially without major external support from the US or its Mecca Agreement allies,” Brumfield said.
The other choice for Saudi leaders would be to follow the UAE in adopting a more hardline stance against Iran and its allies. A major escalation would be the involvement of Saudi ground forces in Yemen, “something Riyadh has been very hesitant to do for over a decade”.

In Hungary, two former ministers in Orbán’s government were detained in a corruption case
Kyiv • UNN
Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták are suspected of misappropriating state funds and bid-rigging. The expenses for Péter Szijjártó’s flights are also being investigated.
In Hungary, two former ministers in Viktor Orbán’s government—Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták—were detained. They are suspected of corruption offenses related to the distribution of public funds and government contracts. TVP World reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
It is reported that former Minister of Culture and Innovation Balázs Hankó and former Minister of National Development Miklós Seszták were taken into custody on Monday, several hours after Parliament stripped them of their parliamentary immunity.
The detentions took place several months after Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s Tisza party ended Orbán’s 16-year rule in the April election.
Commenting on the detentions, Magyar wrote on Facebook on Monday: "After Orbán’s unworthy game of hide-and-seek and most pathetic performance in history, by the end of the first serious day of Operation Cleansing Fire, two former ministers have ended up in the hands of law enforcement."
Corruption cases
Hankó is involved in an investigation into the distribution of funds from Hungary’s National Cultural Fund—a state fund that finances cultural projects and institutions.
According to prosecutors, from September 2025 to March 2026, 17.3 billion forints (€47 million) was improperly distributed through 1,079 grants. Some of the funds were reportedly used for an election campaign and personal needs.
Hankó denies any wrongdoing and calls the proceedings politically motivated. He voluntarily went to the tax authority to give testimony.
His former state secretary, Veronika Varga-Bajusz, was also taken to law enforcement authorities and reportedly questioned as a suspect, although there is currently no confirmation that she was officially detained.
Seszták, who served as development minister from 2014 to 2018, is suspected of receiving a total of €34 million in bribes connected to government contracts, including agreements involving the state-owned bus company Volánbusz. He denies committing any crime.
His case was transferred to Hungary’s newly created National Office for the Recovery and Protection of Assets, which is part of Magyar’s government’s broader anti-corruption campaign. Seszták became the first person taken into custody on the orders of this agency.
Flights of former foreign minister under investigation
A separate investigation also concerns travel expenses incurred by former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó.
Documents from Hungary’s Foreign Ministry obtained by the Hungarian news website 24.hu show that in 2022–2026, the ministry paid €781,000 for eight private jets that Szijjártó ultimately did not use. In each case, a private jet was booked for Szijjártó, but he later flew on a Hungarian military aircraft, while the state paid a cancellation fee for the booking.
Szijjártó, who left politics in July to work for Chinese automaker BYD, essentially did not comment on the allegations. When asked by journalists earlier this month, he said that he now works in the international corporate sector.

Art Goes Underground in Zaporizhzhia as GOGOLFEST Returns 30 Km From Frontline
The international contemporary art festival GOGOLFEST Pokrova will take place in Zaporizhzhia from October 1 to 4, with most of its program moving underground in response to the security conditions of the frontline city.
Recognized among Europe’s five leading festivals by the EFFE Awards, the event will hold 95% of its program in underground venues to avoid disruptions from air attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This year’s Zaporizhzhia edition, titled TimeCode, will explore Ukraine’s past, present, and future through a program spanning theater, music, performance, digital art, and public discussions.
At the center of the festival will be Futurum, a large-scale performance directed by Vladyslav Troitskyi that will connect 15 underground schools across Zaporizhzhia through a live digital broadcast.
“Holding the largest contemporary art festival 30 kilometers from the frontline in Zaporizhzhia today means developing practical tools for safe interaction for a new generation instead of allowing Ukrainian cultural life to be paralyzed, as our enemy wants,” GOGOLFEST Program Director Anna Basova said.
She added that the project would create a precedent by connecting the city’s underground educational spaces into a single digital network for one evening. Together with Ukrainian theater director Vladyslav Troitskyi and Ukrainian band DakhaBrakha, children living under the daily threat of Russian attacks will explore a new form of technological art, while the project could serve as a model for safely engaging young audiences in cultural activities in frontline communities.
The festival’s theater program will likewise take place in protected spaces. DakhTrio will present the Ukrainian premiere of the chamber opera Skovoroda. Shevchenko. Stus, which combines academic, folk, and rock influences. According to organizers, most of the compositions based on works by Ukrainian poets Vasyl Stus and Hryhorii Skovoroda will be performed on stage for the first time.
The international program will include Swiss performer Madeleine Bongard’s Be My Margaret! (or in the strangeness of loneliness), a solo production based on interviews with French writer Marguerite Duras. Following 39 performances across Europe in English and French, the production will be presented in Ukrainian for the first time.
The underground music program will focus on contemporary Ukrainian electronic and experimental music. SI Process, the electronic project of drummer and sound producer Stanislav Ivashchenko from the Brave! Factory community, will present a special program adapted to the acoustics of shelters. Ukrainian musician Stas Koroliov and director Anastasiia Vesna will also present a collaborative experimental project combining alternative music, songwriting, and performance.
Beyond its artistic program, GOGOLFEST Pokrova will host discussions and workshops featuring analysts, urban planners, architects, and sociologists. Topics will include the transformation and postwar reconstruction of public spaces in frontline communities, strengthening local communities during crises, and the future of Zaporizhzhia.
The program will also feature The Future. Zaporizhzhia After, a panel bringing together local leaders, architects, and international experts.
The festival comes as Ukrainian cultural projects continue to adapt to the realities of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian documentary Landing, which follows a skateboarding community in the frontline city of Okhtyrka, has been selected for the official program of the international SUOMFORNIA film festival in Helsinki, Finland.
The film chronicles the community’s efforts to establish “Krytka,” Okhtyrka’s first indoor skatepark, in 2024 amid the full-scale war.

China's external debt rises in Q2 amid active cross-border trade

22:19:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's external debt rose in the second quarter of 2026 amid active cross-border trade, while the latest available debt-risk indicators were within internationally recognized safety thresholds.
Outstanding external debt stood at 2.4982 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of June, up 86.1 billion dollars, or 4 percent, from the end of March, data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) showed on Tuesday.
The increase was mainly driven by relatively active cross-border trade, with both corporate trade credit and intercompany lending rising, said Li Bin, deputy head and spokesperson of SAFE.
Li said China's external debt remained generally stable in the second quarter.
China's goods imports and exports reached 13.61 trillion yuan (about 2.02 trillion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter, up 18.4 percent year on year, the fastest year-on-year growth for any quarter since the third quarter of 2021, according to data from the General Administration of Customs. Trade value in June alone rose 24.2 percent year on year, marking 17 consecutive months of growth.
Yuan-denominated external debt accounted for 56 percent of the total at the end of June, up 1 percentage point from the end of March, while medium- and long-term debt held steady at 41 percent.
SAFE said in July that the share of yuan-denominated external debt had risen while medium- and long-term debt had remained broadly stable at over 40 percent in recent years, with currency and maturity mismatch risks seeing significant declines.
Moderate external borrowing allows Chinese companies and banks to tap both domestic and international markets, diversify financing channels and improve operational efficiency, while risks stemming from excessive debt levels require continued monitoring, SAFE said.
At the end of 2025, China's outstanding external debt was equivalent to 11.9 percent of gross domestic product, below the 20-percent international safety threshold cited by SAFE.
Separate data released on Tuesday showed that China's external financial assets continued to exceed its external liabilities. External financial assets stood at 12.1804 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of June, against liabilities of 8.3555 trillion dollars, leaving net external financial assets of 3.8249 trillion dollars. ■

TRIPOLI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Libya's High State Council (HSC) has said the House of Representatives (HoR)'s amendments to the presidential election law were "unconstitutional" and called for further institutional consultations on the electoral framework.
The HSC issued a statement on its Facebook page late Monday night detailing its opposition.
The council asserted that any modification to the rules, conditions, and timelines for electoral competition must be carried out through a clear, agreed-upon institutional process.
The move came as the HoR issued Law No. 4 of 2026 on Monday, amending provisions related to the presidential election framework, such as allowing military personnel and dual nationals to run for office under updated terms.
The HSC's stance comes just before the one-month deadline for ratifying the UN-facilitated agreement on presidential and parliamentary elections in Libya.
In April, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) began engaging a smaller group of Libyan representatives known as the "4+4" committee, as part of its political roadmap. The discussions focused primarily on resolving disputes over the electoral framework.
In June, the UNSMIL said the participants had reached an understanding on the presidential election law.
On August 30, under UNSMIL facilitation, the 4+4 participants signed an agreement, vowing to restructure the Elections Commission and resolving outstanding legal and constitutional issues affecting presidential and parliamentary elections.
On Spet. 3, the UNSMIL presented the agreement to the HoR and HSC leadership, giving one month to approve it.
The HSC leadership objected to the agreement's existing form, with the dispute focusing on the legal process for approving the electoral rules and the Elections Commission's composition, rather than on the principle of holding elections.
On Sept. 14, the HoR voted unanimously at a session in Benghazi to adopt the 4+4 agreement, saying it was consistent with its existing position on several electoral issues.
Libya has been divided politically and institutionally for years, while the United Nations and Libyan parties have been seeking to reach a consensual framework paving the way for national elections, resolve contentious issues related to the presidential election law, and appoint a new board of the electoral commission to oversee the overall electoral process across the country.
The country's political system remains divided among competing legislative, executive and security institutions. The eastern-based HoR is the country's main legislative body, while the Tripoli-based HSC is a separate consultative institution with an important role in major political and institutional arrangements. The dispute between the two over electoral legislation forms part of a broader division between rival authorities and power centers in western and eastern Libya. ■

Defeat in Nagoya, questions in Tehran: What next for Iran’s U23s?
TEHRAN - Iran’s U23 football team suffered another major setback at the Asian Games, crashing out of the 2026 tournament in Nagoya after a humiliating 4-1 defeat to North Korea.
The result was more than a disappointing night for Hossein Abdi’s side. It was another warning sign for an Iranian Football Federation that has repeatedly failed to build a clear, long-term plan for one of the country’s most important national teams.
 
 The most worrying aspect is that this was not a squad lacking talent. Several players were regulars for their Persian Gulf Pro League clubs, and the team had been assembled with the stated ambition of using the Asian Games as a step towards the 2028 Olympics. Abdi himself had spoken about the importance of international matches and building chemistry before the tournament.
 
 Yet the team looked increasingly disconnected as the tournament progressed. After a promising opening win, Iran failed to secure qualification against China and then produced a chaotic performance against North Korea. Abdi accepted responsibility and described the result as unacceptable.
 
 That responsibility, however, cannot end with the coach.
 
 Abdi certainly deserves scrutiny. He knew many of these players from their earlier youth-team years and had several preparation camps and overseas training periods. Whatever the logistical difficulties surrounding player availability and preparation, the final performance raised legitimate questions about tactical organization, defensive structure and the team's ability to respond under pressure.
 
 But changing the coach again risks missing the larger issue.
 
 Iran's Football Federation has repeatedly struggled to establish a stable process for selecting U23 coaches and preparing teams well in advance of major tournaments. The pattern has become familiar: a coach is appointed relatively late, preparation is compressed, expectations remain high and, after failure, the entire project starts again with a new name.
 
 Now the federation faces another decision. Names such as Afshin Ghotbi, Farhad Majidi, Yahya Golmohammadi and Mojtaba Hosseini have been mentioned, while the possibility of a foreign coach has also been discussed. Yet the crucial question is not which name appears on the shortlist. It is what criteria and long-term plan will determine the appointment?
 
 Japan will host the 2028 AFC U23 Asian Cup, which will also serve as Asia's qualification tournament for the Los Angeles Olympics. Iran therefore have a clear target and a reasonable amount of time to prepare.
 
 What it needs now is not simply another coach. It needs a defined project: a clear football philosophy, transparent selection criteria, continuity between youth levels, regular international fixtures and measurable objectives.
 
 Otherwise, Iran's U23 team will remain trapped in the same cycle; appoint, prepare, fail, replace and repeat. And another promising generation of players will once again pay the price for a problem that is much bigger than the man standing on the touchline.

CAS launches program for breakthroughs at science frontiers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:46 CST
22:18:46 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) announced on Tuesday the launch of a new program aimed at achieving breakthroughs at the frontiers of science and producing major original research achievements in key fields.
At a press conference held in Beijing, Zhou Qi, CAS vice president, said the program focuses on major scientific questions that will drive a paradigm shift in research and open up new frontiers, harnessing shared access to major scientific infrastructure and AI-empowered scientific research to organize leading talent into systematic, institutionalized research campaigns.
These efforts are designed to support China's pursuit of original, trailblazing breakthroughs on major frontiers of science and in core technologies, Zhou said.
The first batch of 10 projects under the program was unveiled at the media event, targeting research in fields such as the synthesis of new elements, the nature of dark matter and dark energy, microscopic measurement of chemical bonds and the creation of synthetic cells.
Meanwhile, a list of priority areas for the next batch was also released, with key support to be directed toward the fields of physical sciences, life sciences, Earth system sciences, and space sciences.
Wei Zhixiang, director of the Bureau of Basic Science Research of the CAS, said this program will deeply integrate the coordinated use of major scientific facilities with AI empowerment, centering on the directions of "the extremely macroscopic, the extremely microscopic, extreme conditions, and highly convergent interdisciplinary frontiers."
Outstanding scientists from within and beyond the CAS, as well as around the world, are encouraged to join the program and make full use of the large-scale scientific facilities, AI platforms and networks of the CAS, Wei said.
Li Yuhui, deputy director of the Bureau of Basic Science Research of the CAS, said the program will focus on key difficulties in national security, people's health, and major engineering projects, promote breakthroughs in fundamental theory, and encourage scientists to seek new growth areas in the "uncharted territories" at disciplinary boundaries.
The program will use AI to conduct deep mining of massive literature and experimental data, identify key problems approaching the critical point of breakthrough, and then carry out rapid verification through automated experiments by scientific facility clusters.
Yang Weijin, deputy director of the Bureau of Basic Capacity for Science and Technology of the CAS, said major scientific and technological infrastructures can provide ultimate research means for frontier research and for tackling core technologies, and serve as strategic support platforms in the era of big science.
China has deployed 77 major scientific and technological infrastructures. The CAS now operates 43 of them, accounting for 56 percent of the national total, according to Yang. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- India's Neeru Dhanda made history as the country's first woman to win an Asian Games trap title on Tuesday, while China secured another shooting gold in the women's trap team event at the 2026 Asian Games.
Neeru, 26, entered the women's trap final as the top qualifier after hitting 118 of 125 targets and beating Qatar's Ray Bassil in a shoot-off for first place.
Neeru battled China's Sun Yunong for gold in the final, with the pair tied at 14-14 before Sun missed two targets in the following series. Neeru finished with 28 hits, surpassing the previous Asian record of 24, to take the title.
Sun claimed silver with 26 hits, while Hajar Abdulmalik took bronze.
"Neeru missed, as they all did, but she kept grinding away," coach Peter Wilson said. "We have worked a lot on staying in the present, but the brain likes to trick you into the future."
"I was able to play to my strengths today, but there are still some technical details I need to improve," Sun said. "Overall, I'm fairly satisfied with my performance."
Sun, Liu Shanshan and Zhu Jingyu combined for 346 hits to win the women's trap team title for China. India took silver with 328, while Kuwait claimed bronze with 325.
The victory increased China's shooting gold medal tally to 16, matching its total from the Hangzhou Asian Games.
In the men's trap team event, Kuwait won gold with 355 hits, while Qatar and Kazakhstan took silver and bronze with 349 and 348, respectively. China finished fourth.
Kuwait's 48-year-old Khaled Almudhaf won the men's individual title with 26 hits, one ahead of Chinese Taipei's Yang Kun-Pi. China's Qi Ying took bronze.
It was Almudhaf's first individual gold medal in eight Asian Games appearances.
"I'm an ambassador for older people to see that they can win even at this age," Almudhaf said. "This is a sport where you can shoot when you are older." ■

URUMQI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- International coffee chain giant Starbucks on Tuesday opened two stores in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, marking its debut in the region and the latest expansion in China, its second-largest market after the United States.
The stores are located in Urumqi, the regional capital -- one in the iconic Grand Bazaar and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport.
The Grand Bazaar flagship store boasts a distinctive design inspired by traditional bazaar canopy silhouettes, with interiors featuring Xinjiang elements like Atlas silk and ethnic musical instruments. Both stores have rolled out locally inspired menus and exclusive drinks, such as the milk-skin-flavored salty milk tea.
"Entering Xinjiang not only marks a further expansion of our store network, but also allows us to engage deeply with this vibrant market and build sincere, lasting connections with our customers there," Molly Liu, chief executive officer of Starbucks China, said in a written statement.
Zhang Yu, an official with the regional administration for market regulation, said Xinjiang has made the "first-store economy" -- a gauge of urban commercial vitality and consumer appeal -- a key lever for boosting domestic demand and consumption.
Zhang added that Xinjiang will continue to improve support policies for first stores, enhance approval efficiency and optimize the business environment.
The openings follow Starbucks' partnership with Chinese venture capital firm Boyu Capital to operate its retail business in China. According to the agreement signed in November last year, Boyu and Starbucks will operate a joint venture with Boyu holding up to a 60-percent interest in Starbucks' retail operations in China, while Starbucks will retain the remaining 40-percent interest in the joint venture, and continue to own the Starbucks brand and license the brand and intellectual property to the new entity.
The latest expansion comes as Starbucks is restructuring its North American business, with the company announcing plans last week to close 250 underperforming coffeehouses in the region.
Starbucks entered the Chinese mainland in January 1999, opening its first store in Beijing. As coffee culture took root and gained popularity, the chain steadily expanded its footprint across China. By Sept. 27, 2026, Starbucks operated 8,342 stores on the Chinese mainland, up 331 from the end of fiscal 2025, according to its fiscal 2026 data.
The Chinese mainland is now Starbucks' second-largest market after the United States, where the company operated 16,933 stores as of June 28, 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 third-quarter results.
Its long-running expansion reflects how foreign brands are seeking opportunities in China's growing consumer market.
The State Administration for Market Regulation said China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year. Separate data from the Ministry of Commerce showed nearly 4,800 foreign-funded enterprises increased investment in China in the first half of 2026. ■

China firmly opposes any action of Philippines to harm China's sovereignty, rights: FM spokesperson

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China firmly opposes any action of the Philippines that harms China's sovereignty and rights and interests, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday.
Guo made the remarks at a regular press briefing in response to a query related to a so-called updated "maritime chart" by the Philippine National Maritime Council, which includes islands and reefs in China's Nansha Qundao such as Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao.
"Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao are part of China's Nansha Qundao and Chinese territory. China has indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters," Guo said.
Noting that the scope of Philippine territory is defined by several international treaties, Guo said that China's Nanhai Zhudao, including Nansha Qundao, lie beyond that scope.
The Philippines has illegally occupied several islands and reefs in Nansha Qundao, claimed the so-called "Kalayaan Island Group" beyond its own territory and issued a so-called "maritime chart," which includes relevant islands and reefs of China's Nansha Qundao, Guo said.
"Those actions seriously violate China's territorial sovereignty and the UN Charter and relevant international laws, and are illegal, null and void," he said.
"China firmly opposes any action of the Philippines that harms China's sovereignty and rights and interests. China will continue taking necessary measures to firmly defend its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea," the spokesperson said. ■

Ukraine’s New Battlefield Robot Drove, Swam and Hauled Ammo for 40 Km on Its First Mission
Ukraine has deployed a domestically produced amphibious unmanned ground vehicle on a frontline logistics mission for the first time, delivering ammunition and supplies across more than 40 kilometers of mixed land and water terrain, the Defense Ministry reported on September 29.
During the mission, Ukrainian troops used the robotic platform to move both ammunition and provisions to forward positions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The route stretched more than 40 kilometers and required the system to travel across both dry ground and water.
That capability addresses a persistent logistics problem on parts of the Ukrainian front, where rivers, canals, marshes and other water obstacles can break up supply routes and make conventional ground transport more difficult.
Standard unmanned ground vehicles are not always able to cross such terrain, while aerial delivery is not practical for every type of cargo or mission.
The amphibious UGV is designed to solve that problem with a single platform.
It can move across difficult terrain on land and transition directly into water without requiring a separate transport system or additional vehicle.
Before entering service, the platform spent several months undergoing modifications and testing in cooperation with Ukrainian troops, allowing developers to adapt it to battlefield requirements.
“The Brave1 defense innovation cluster provided grant support for the system, helping bring the solution to practical use,” Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
The September mission marked the first known operational use of the Ukrainian-made amphibious UGV for frontline logistics.
Its successful 40-kilometer run suggests Ukraine is continuing to push robotic systems beyond reconnaissance and combat roles and into one of the war’s most dangerous jobs: moving supplies to frontline positions without exposing soldiers to the same level of risk.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces converted a Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carrier into a remotely controlled attack vehicle and used it to destroy fortified Russian positions during offensive operations in eastern Ukraine.

Australian household spending up 6.8 pct in Aug. year on year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:37 CST
22:18:37 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australian household spending was 6.8 percent higher in August than a year earlier, while remaining unchanged from July, official statistics showed on Tuesday.
Household spending rose 1.1 percent in July and 0.9 percent in June, both from the previous month, according to data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Recreation and culture spending fell 1.4 percent in August after months of higher spending associated with major sporting events, ABS head of business statistics Tom Lay said in a statement.
Spending on clothing and footwear, recreational goods, food, health and furniture also declined, Lay said.
These falls were offset by a 2.3 percent increase in transport spending, driven by higher fuel spending and new vehicle sales, particularly electric vehicles, as households responded to rising fuel prices, he added.
Fuel spending rose 8.1 percent in August after the full restoration of fuel excise duty on Aug. 3, following temporary relief introduced by the federal government in April, according to the ABS.
Excluding fuel spending, total household spending would have fallen by 0.3 percent in August, the ABS said.
Experimental data showed the volume of fuel spending fell 0.5 percent in August, following a 4.6-percent decline in July, it added. ■

China Focus: China brings childcare closer to families
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:18:25 CST
22:18:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- As demand for formal childcare continues to grow among Chinese families, young parents are looking for more affordable, convenient and trustworthy services.
China's National Health Commission (NHC) has said efforts are under way to make childcare more accessible, affordable and quality-assured. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for faster development of affordable childcare, including more publicly provided places and a wider range of services.
For many families, the first hurdle is price. In 2023, childcare cost an average of 1,978 yuan (about 293 U.S. dollars) per child a month nationwide, excluding meals. In first-tier cities, monthly fees topped 5,500 yuan, pricing out many families.
In Baiyin, northwest China's Gansu Province, the city's First People's Hospital runs a childcare center where full-day care costs 750 yuan a month, including three meals and two snacks a day.
Baiyin received 100 million yuan in central government funding in 2024 to support affordable childcare. First-time users can also apply for vouchers allowing their children to try a nearby center free for two weeks.
Similar efforts to lower costs are under way elsewhere. Nine provinces have introduced childcare subsidies since 2021, while 1,315 county-level regions have offered support ranging from construction and operating subsidies to family vouchers. Over the same period, average fees for full-day childcare fell 29 percent nationwide.
Broader family support is also expanding. Since 2025, families have been eligible for 3,600 yuan a year for each child until the age of three. Parents can also deduct 2,000 yuan per child each month from taxable income for children under the age of 3.
Location matters too, especially for families with very young children. Ma Liejian, vice president and member of the Secretariat of the All-China Women's Federation, has called for qualified kindergartens to extend services to younger children and for communities to offer full-day, half-day, hourly and temporary childcare close to home.
In Beijing, 562 public kindergartens have added nursery classes this year, creating more than 10,000 new places for children aged 2 to 3 and giving more families access to childcare closer to home.
Baiyin is following a similar approach. As of April 2025, the city's Baiyin District had 15 registered childcare providers, 13 of them nursery classes in kindergartens, offering a total of 1,360 places.
Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, is building a "15-minute childcare service circle" using community space, kindergarten classrooms and workplace facilities.
Proximity alone, however, does not solve the problem for parents whose working hours fall outside a conventional childcare day. Yang Fan, vice dean of Renmin University of China's School of Population and Health, said more flexible services, including hourly and holiday care, could better meet the needs of parents in flexible employment or shift work.
At a technology park in Shanghai's Yangpu District, an on-site childcare center offers full-day, half-day and hourly care. One project manager said he once booked temporary care through an app just two hours before an unexpected client meeting.
In rural Pingdu in east China's Shandong Province, a childcare center converted from unused village property near agricultural greenhouses operates around the clock, giving farming families an option outside conventional daytime hours.
For parents of very young children, trust can matter just as much as price or convenience.
The same hospital-run center in Baiyin accepts babies as young as three months. Opened in 2021 with 100 places, it has more than 20 certified caregivers. It keeps health records for children and draws on hospital resources for visits by medical experts and multidisciplinary services.
Safety is also receiving greater attention at the national level. A draft law on childcare services, submitted to China's national legislature for a first reading in December 2025, includes provisions governing the licensing of childcare providers, staffing, monitoring and emergency response.
Zhang Li, deputy dean of the Law School at the China University of Political Science and Law, said the proposed licensing system would allow regulators to screen providers before they begin operating. Requirements for public information disclosure, she said, could also improve transparency, help parents better understand the services on offer and strengthen their confidence in sending children to childcare centers.
The draft law's proposal to gradually incorporate inclusive childcare services into the scope of basic public services would strengthen the public-service role of childcare and the government's responsibility for its provision, providing legal support for more stable long-term development, according to He Dan, director of the China Population and Development Research Center under the NHC.
In Baiyin, Guo Jianna and her husband are both busy with work, and all three of their children have spent time at the childcare center run by Baiyin's First People's Hospital.
Shortly before 5 p.m., Xu Xiaoqin, who oversees the center, began getting the children ready for dinner. By the time Guo arrived to pick up her 2-year-old daughter, the girl had eaten and was ready to go home.
"With professional caregivers looking after them, my family and I feel reassured," Guo said. ■
