Yemen escalation fuels fears of further cholera, measles spread
Heavy fighting in Yemen is fuelling concerns of an uptick in cholera, measles and other preventable diseases, as overcrowding at displacement sites threatens to overwhelm the limited healthcare services still open.
“We know that comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care has been suspended in two hospitals, in Marib and Ras Al-Arah, because staff and operating capacities have been redirected to trauma care to care for the incoming wounded,” said Dr Annette Heinzelmann, UN World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Emergency Director for the Eastern Mediterranean.
Speaking from Cairo via video link, Dr Heinzelmann noted that more than 20 mobile medical teams supported by WHO have been deployed across priority governorates where vulnerable people have been arriving.
Lifesaving stocks depleted
The agency has also dispatched nearly 60 tonnes of medical supplies worth around $656,000 to 40 facilities and offices across 10 governorates. But “several lifesaving supply lines” in WHO’s Aden warehouse are already at zero stock, including trauma kits and essential medicines.
Briefing journalists in Geneva, Dr Heinzelman said that nine health facilities have been damaged or directly attacked, mostly close to the cities of Taiz, Lahj and Hudaydah. She stressed that displaced families urgently need maternal and child healthcare, nutrition relief, vaccination and mental health support.
Even before the escalation, only about 60 per cent of health facilities were fully functional, with very limited capacity for trauma surgery, blood transfusion and intensive care.
Cholera is already present in Yemen with about 7,800 suspected cases and 22 deaths reported this year, but fears of an outbreak are gaining traction because of unsafe water and poor sanitation at temporary shelters, Dr Heinzelmann warned.
Early treatment of cholera is vital to save lives, but health services in Yemen are overstretched because of clashes between Houthi opposition fighters and Government forces that resumed two months ago, after four years of relative calm.
Dengue danger
In addition to cholera, dengue has also been linked to 37 deaths in Yemen, while more than 22,000 cases of measles have been identified.
According to the health authorities in Aden, since 6 August, the renewed clashes in southwest Yemen have left more than 4,481 casualties including 830 deaths.
Echoing the humanitarian community’s growing concerns for the people of Yemen, the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, repeated warnings of critical hunger levels among children impacted by the conflict.
Of nearly 2,900 children screened, more than one in four were acutely malnourished, while around 200 have severe acute malnutrition, the Office said in an online alert.
According to WHO, more than 180,000 people have now been uprooted by the fighting which has seen Houthi forces take over Yemen’s Red Sea coast and reportedly announce a blockade on shipping from Saudi Arabia, which supports the Government in Aden.
Latest data from the health agency also indicates growing needs in Djibouti, now home to more than 3,600 Yemenis who have risked the dangerous sea crossing since 10 September. Nearly half of the new arrivals are children and WHO partners are preparing for potentially 5,000 to 10,000 arrivals in the coming weeks.
“This influx is placing additional pressure in a country already facing severe health and humanitarian needs, with high malnutrition, recent cholera and ongoing measles and malaria risks,” Dr Heinzelmann said.

Clean your plate – to reduce food loss and waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Clean your plate – to reduce food loss and waste
In fact, throwing out lunchtime leftovers or wilted lettuce only adds to the mountain of discarded food decomposing in landfills that produces the powerful greenhouse gas methane, accounting for some eight to 10 per cent of global emissions.
This includes spoiled crops – food that is lost after harvest and before even reaching stores.
A billion meals wasted
Every day, over a billion meals are left uneaten, whether due to excess food production, spoilage or poor meal planning, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
The issue is in the spotlight on the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste, observed on 29 September – convened by UNEP and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
This year, focus is on the link with protecting forests and ensuring sustainable agrifood systems.
“Using the food we already produce more efficiently can reduce pressure on land and forests and help feed more people,” said Michael Muratha, a Programme Manager at UNEP, speaking from its headquarters in Nairobi.
Moreover, having healthy forests also support food production in several ways, including by protecting soils and regulating rainfall.
Cold comfort
UNEP is highlighting how taking action can reduce losses by promoting measures such as investing in better food handling, storage and transport.
Mr. Muratha stressed that strengthening cold chain systems for perishable foods is also important.
“In Kenya, a cooperative of 179 farmers near Nairobi was losing up to 40 per cent of its crops after harvest before receiving cold-storage and refrigerated transport equipment,” he said.
Better storage can also help farmers to cope with climate impacts, such as droughts, floods and periods of food scarcity, while reducing losses of nutritious foods in a world where 2.6 billion people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables.
“That’s why it’s really important to take these measures to preserve and conserve and reduce losses of food,” he said.
UNEP is also backing efforts to redirect safe surplus food to people who need it, such as children at daycare centres in underserved communities.
Innovation at all levels
The agency is further showcasing inventive ways – from simple to cutting edge - to keep food out of landfills.
“Innovation can help at different points where food is lost or wasted, and it does not always have to be high-tech,” Mr. Muratha insisted.
He pointed to the example of Favela Orgânica, a project in Brazil that teaches communities, street vendors and chefs to use ingredients that are often thrown away such as banana peels and broccoli stalks.
“AI is also showing promise,” he added. “In a UNEP-supported initiative involving 13 hotels, AI tools helped measure discarded food and adjust purchasing and preparation, reducing post-consumer breakfast waste by 62 per cent in four months.”
Last year, UNEP and partners launched the Food Waste Breakthrough initiative at the UN COP31 climate change conference in Brazil with the goal of halving food waste by 2030, reducing methane emissions and supporting climate action.
Mr. Muratha said taking action could help reduce some of the more than $1 trillion lost globally each year through food loss and waste, while every dollar invested in prevention saves cities $8 and households $84.
“For communities, it means more food reaching people and greater resilience when harvests, prices or supply chains are disrupted,” he said.
“It will not end hunger on its own, but it is an important part of building more secure and sustainable food systems.”

Funding cuts put 8.3 million refugees at risk of losing vital assistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Funding cuts put 8.3 million refugees at risk of losing vital assistance
Haji Mohammad Shafi spent 44 years in Pakistan before he was forced to leave. He sold everything he owned and returned to Afghanistan with his five children, arriving with almost nothing.
The family received a one-off cash grant from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) on crossing the border, but without a steady income and with a leg injury that limits his ability to work, Mr. Shafi now lives in a makeshift shelter in Kabul Province, its walls patched with stones and its windows covered with plastic sheets.
“When there is little food, I give it to the children. If they are hungry, they cry,” he says.
“We have nothing prepared for winter. If someone helps, we can manage. If no one helps, we have nothing.”
Precipitous fall
His family is among nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced and stateless people on the brink of losing access to vital assistance as severe funding cuts push protection systems towards breaking point, UNHCR warned on Tuesday.
In a new report, titled Protection Eroded: The Human Cost of Underfunding, the agency said available funding fell from $5.178 billion to $3.932 billion between 2024 and 2025.
By July it had received only 32 per cent of the $8.5 billion needed this year – even as the number of people under its mandate remained at historically high levels.
Below a certain threshold the system doesn’t shrink, it fails
“When registration stops, safe houses close or child protection services disappear, the very risks that people fled – violence, exploitation and abuse – reappear in displacement,” said Dominique Hyde, UNHCR’s Director of External Relations.
System ‘fails’
In Afghanistan, where more than a million people have returned in 2026 alone, the cash grant on arrival has been cut from $375 per person to $170 per household, and reintegration grants have reached just 175 households so far this year, compared with 5,300 in 2024.
In Chad, 319,000 refugees face registration delays that leave them without documentation and exposed to detention, up to 200,000 women and girls risk losing access to safe spaces, and around 233,000 children could lose child protection services.
In Ethiopia, the number of safe houses for survivors of gender-based violence has more than halved in a year, from 29 to 13, while child protection coverage in some areas has fallen by as much as 85 per cent. In Sudan, more than 50,000 survivors of sexual violence in Darfur and Kordofan could lose access to life-saving post-rape care.
The report warns that unlike food and shelter, protection cannot be rationed into smaller portions. “Below a certain threshold the system doesn’t shrink, it fails,” it states.
Flexible funding ‘critical’
The refugee agency said it had cut its workforce by a third in 2025 and closed offices in 140 locations, but that even its highest priority work was now affected.
The share of funding tied to specific projects has risen from 19 per cent in 2022 to 51 per cent this year.
“Flexible funding helps us move the right expertise and funds to where they are needed the most,” Ms. Hyde said, adding that, protection cannot be “reduced indefinitely without systems collapsing”.
UNHCR is urging donors and partners to provide urgent support and expand flexible funding to protect progress already made.

Yemen escalation fuels fears of further cholera, measles spread
Heavy fighting in Yemen is fuelling concerns of an uptick in cholera, measles and other preventable diseases, as overcrowding at displacement sites threatens to overwhelm the limited healthcare services still open.
“We know that comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care has been suspended in two hospitals, in Marib and Ras Al-Arah, because staff and operating capacities have been redirected to trauma care to care for the incoming wounded,” said Dr Annette Heinzelmann, UN World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Emergency Director for the Eastern Mediterranean.
Speaking from Cairo via video link, Dr Heinzelmann noted that more than 20 mobile medical teams supported by WHO have been deployed across priority governorates where vulnerable people have been arriving.
Lifesaving stocks depleted
The agency has also dispatched nearly 60 tonnes of medical supplies worth around $656,000 to 40 facilities and offices across 10 governorates. But “several lifesaving supply lines” in WHO’s Aden warehouse are already at zero stock, including trauma kits and essential medicines.
Briefing journalists in Geneva, Dr Heinzelman said that nine health facilities have been damaged or directly attacked, mostly close to the cities of Taiz, Lahj and Hudaydah. She stressed that displaced families urgently need maternal and child healthcare, nutrition relief, vaccination and mental health support.
Even before the escalation, only about 60 per cent of health facilities were fully functional, with very limited capacity for trauma surgery, blood transfusion and intensive care.
Cholera is already present in Yemen with about 7,800 suspected cases and 22 deaths reported this year, but fears of an outbreak are gaining traction because of unsafe water and poor sanitation at temporary shelters, Dr Heinzelmann warned.
Early treatment of cholera is vital to save lives, but health services in Yemen are overstretched because of clashes between Houthi opposition fighters and Government forces that resumed two months ago, after four years of relative calm.
Dengue danger
In addition to cholera, dengue has also been linked to 37 deaths in Yemen, while more than 22,000 cases of measles have been identified.
According to the health authorities in Aden, since 6 August, the renewed clashes in southwest Yemen have left more than 4,481 casualties including 830 deaths.
Echoing the humanitarian community’s growing concerns for the people of Yemen, the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, repeated warnings of critical hunger levels among children impacted by the conflict.
Of nearly 2,900 children screened, more than one in four were acutely malnourished, while around 200 have severe acute malnutrition, the Office said in an online alert.
According to WHO, more than 180,000 people have now been uprooted by the fighting which has seen Houthi forces take over Yemen’s Red Sea coast and reportedly announce a blockade on shipping from Saudi Arabia, which supports the Government in Aden.
Latest data from the health agency also indicates growing needs in Djibouti, now home to more than 3,600 Yemenis who have risked the dangerous sea crossing since 10 September. Nearly half of the new arrivals are children and WHO partners are preparing for potentially 5,000 to 10,000 arrivals in the coming weeks.
“This influx is placing additional pressure in a country already facing severe health and humanitarian needs, with high malnutrition, recent cholera and ongoing measles and malaria risks,” Dr Heinzelmann said.

Can Tajikistan’s economic boom survive its debt gamble?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:58:32 UTC
20:58:32 KST

Can Tajikistan’s economic boom survive its debt gamble?
Tajikistan is one of Central Asia’s fastest-growing economies, but remittance dependence, off-budget debts at state firms such as TALCO and the unfinished Rogun project leave the boom exposed.
Tajikistan’s gross domestic product grew by 8.2 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, while fixed-capital investment rose by 18.4 percent. On June 30, the World Bank approved a further $300m grant for the Rogun hydropower plant, the government’s flagship project. Rapid growth and fresh multilateral support appear to validate years of state-led investment. They also sharpen the central question: is the boom generating enough export income to meet future obligations, or does it still depend on migrant earnings and public spending?
The warning is that Tajikistan’s strong growth masks significant external and fiscal vulnerabilities. The glittering investment and growth figures mask a fragile construct: an economy dependent on remittances, a narrow export base and politicised state corporations is piling up debt that is becoming ever harder to service. The World Bank still classifies Tajikistan at high risk of debt distress. That does not mean default is imminent, but it leaves little room for a financing mistake or external shock.
Growth with a narrow base
The headline investment figure needs careful reading. Fixed-capital investment measures spending on buildings, machinery and infrastructure; it does not show foreign investors moving into Tajikistan in search of high returns. The World Bank says foreign direct investment weakened in 2025 even as growth reached 8.4 percent. The main source of foreign currency is clear. Remittances amounted to about 46 percent of GDP in 2025, according to the World Bank, which says they were the principal driver of growth. Aluminium and other exports matter, but TALCO’s strategic weight does not make it the country’s main source of hard currency. The economy’s principal external income still comes from workers abroad.
The share of the population living below the World Bank’s $4.20-a-day poverty line fell from 55 percent in 2010 to about 14.8 percent in 2025. Foreign-exchange reserves reached $5.6bn, more than eight months of imports. These gains make the economy more resilient than a simple crisis narrative suggests.
Yet the same data reveal weaknesses. The trade deficit widened to 35 percent of GDP in 2025, domestic production remains limited, and household consumption relies heavily on income earned abroad. A slowdown in Russia or tighter migration rules could therefore weaken domestic demand and the balance of payments simultaneously.
The case for Rogun
Rogun’s long delays do not erase the economic case for completing it. The World Bank expects the plant to generate 14,400 gigawatt-hours a year, roughly 60 percent of Tajikistan’s present electricity generation. A substantial share of its low-cost output is intended for domestic demand, which could reduce chronic winter shortages, while the remainder could be exported to countries including Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The bank also estimates that the project could create more than 30,000 direct and indirect jobs.
The financing structure has improved. The latest $300m International Development Association grant brings total World Bank financing for Rogun to $650m. Other multilateral and bilateral partners are involved, and the government has pledged part of future revenue to social programmes. Grant and concessional financing reduce pressure on the budget.
But international backing is not a blank cheque. The World Bank itself says Rogun’s scale exceeds what Tajikistan can finance alone and that partner support is necessary to prevent the project from absorbing too much of the budget. Its expected export earnings depend on completion, transmission links, reliable regional purchase agreements and transparent operation. Until those pieces are in place, projected revenue cannot be treated as cash already available for debt service.
The risk lies beyond sovereign debt
Tajikistan is not carrying an unusually high sovereign debt ratio. Public debt continued to fall through 2025 and into 2026, while foreign-exchange reserves continued to provide a substantial buffer. The IMF assessed the debt as sustainable.
The high-risk classification arises mainly from heavy external repayments relative to export earnings in 2025-27. The immediate vulnerability is therefore the repayment schedule and the narrow export base, rather than the headline debt stock alone.
But the headline ratio omits a material part of the public-sector exposure. The IMF’s baseline does not include non-guaranteed debt of state-owned companies because information on those liabilities is incomplete. In a tailored stress test, it adds potential liabilities equal to 11.7 percent of GDP. These include arrears at Barqi Tojik estimated at 8.2 percent of GDP and TALCO’s external debt at 2 percent.
TALCO is also facing continuing attempts to enforce an arbitral award now worth more than $300m.
The company has sought substantial new investment, yet its unresolved liabilities complicate efforts to attract fresh financing.
Arbitration suits against TALCO inevitably heighten compliance risks and due-diligence requirements for any prospective financiers. When payments flow through intersecting banks and jurisdictions, legal risks in one segment of assets do not remain contained.
The dispute has also moved into cross-border enforcement proceedings, with creditors seeking information about assets and transactions in several jurisdictions.
Moreover, TALCO deserves particular attention because its financial problems feed directly into another state company. The IMF says most of the aluminium producer’s arrears are owed to Barqi Tojik. Weak payment discipline at TALCO therefore adds to the power utility’s losses, while a guarantee, recapitalisation or assumption of either company’s debts could shift the burden to the budget. The stress test is not a forecast that the state will assume every obligation, but it shows why a low sovereign-debt ratio understates the broader fiscal risk.
A new financing agreement illustrates both sides of the argument. In August, the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development signed a $200m budget-support loan with a 20-year term, a 10-year grace period and a 1 percent interest rate. Those are highly concessional terms and show that substantial official financing remains available to support the government’s reform programme. The fund also said the loan was needed in part because Eurobond repayments were putting pressure on the budget.
A test of reform
The policy choice is not between abandoning Rogun and borrowing without restraint. Tajikistan can use grants and long-maturity concessional finance for the dam while limiting non-concessional debt, publishing audited accounts for major state firms, and disclosing guarantees and arrears.
Independent reporting on Rogun’s costs, procurement, safety, resettlement and power-sale agreements would allow creditors and citizens to judge whether future revenue assumptions remain credible. The government also needs growth that generates domestic jobs and exports outside the state sector. That requires stronger competition, more reliable rules for private investors and a financial system that can channel part of the country’s remittance income into productive businesses rather than consumption and imports.
The data support a sober conclusion. Growth is real, and sovereign collapse is not imminent. Lower poverty, sizeable reserves and concessional support have bought the country time. The boom will last only if Dushanbe broadens the economy and makes the debts of TALCO and other state companies visible. Rogun can support that transition, but only if its financing stays within the revenue the project can realistically earn.

UK air base bomb scare leaves questions after no explosives found

2026-09-29
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

A U.K. probe into a suspected bomb plot at a U.S. airbase was mired in confusion Tuesday after media reported no explosives were found in nearby seized vehicles.
As armed guards maintained a cordon around a nearby village, Washington questioned the decision to release on bail five men arrested near the Royal Air Force Fairford base in southwest England.
Three white vans were discovered near the base Sunday and the men – all London-based Britons in their mid-20s – were detained.
Armed police were also visible Tuesday patrolling around the airfield used by U.S. planes to bomb some targets in Iran.
Police have said officers conducted an extensive examination of the vehicles with the help of "military assets" and forensic experts.
They did not disclose their findings. But The Times newspaper and a few other U.K. media have reported that police found no traces of explosives, easing fears that an attack had been foiled but leaving many questions unanswered.
A resident in the neighboring village of Kempsford, Patricia, 60, told AFP it was "very embarrassing that people around the world thought it was a terrorist attack but in the end no – it's a lot of noise for nothing."
Announcing the release Monday of the five suspects, the head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the men "absolutely remain under investigation."
He insisted his officers were keeping an "open mind" and considering "every possible angle" in the security scare, including the possible role of "proxies" working knowingly or unknowingly for a foreign state.
Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Adding to the hazy picture, U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters Monday he was "surprised" that British police had released the five, adding: "I wouldn't have done that."
Hours later, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the incident "a very serious situation ... that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor" but declined to provide further details.
On Sunday, Trump had said the U.K. and U.S. were investigating the suspects "for a long time" and that they "were looking to do big damage to our fort."
The security scare became public after a farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase rang police after seeing the three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Armed officers arrested the five men on suspicion of explosives offenses and, later, "suspicion of preparing a terrorist act" under anti-terror laws.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
U.S. bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base – the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The lack of clarity over the weekend incident has sparked different unverified theories, with some media reporting allegations that the men could even be fuel thieves.
"It's a bit odd they were here in the middle of the night," one local told AFP as she did some gardening in the nearby village of Kempsford.
"If they were true terrorists they wouldn't have released them," she added, asking not to give her name.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.
The legitimate firm said in a statement on its website that "neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection whatsoever with Fuel2U," adding it was cooperating with the police.

The Backstory: 10 years of surgical strikes, the 10 days after Uri
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:55:27 UTC
20:55:27 KST

NEW DELHI: Ten years ago, on the night of September 28-29, 2016, Indian Army commandos crossed the Line of Control and carried out surgical strikes on terrorist launch pads in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The operation, carried out in response to the Pakistan-sponsored Uri terror attack, marked a hard-hitting response to Pakistan for sheltering and cultivating terror on its soil.It was the first time India responded not with a traditional full-fledged war, but with a calibrated and deliberate military operation against Islamabad-backed terror infrastructure across the border.It was also a demonstration of the more assertive counter-terrorism approach that the Modi government would later associate with its “New India” and “zero tolerance” messaging.But the story of the surgical strikes did not begin on the night of September 28.It began 10 days earlier, in a burning Army camp in Uri.ALSO READ: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/us-announces-visa-restrictions-for-officials-blocking-international-child-abduction-cases/articleshow/134567373.cms
September 18: When Uri came under attack
At around 5.30am on September 18, four heavily armed terrorists attacked the Army's 12th Brigade headquarters in Jammu and Kashmir's Uri, close to the Line of Control.The attack was on a rear administrative camp next to the brigade headquarters.The timing was particularly devastating. Troops were in the middle of a changeover, with an advance party of the incoming 6 Bihar unit in the process of replacing the outgoing 10 Dogra unit.
Many soldiers were housed in temporary tents. Explosions and gunfire triggered a fire that spread through the camp.Seventeen soldiers were killed in the initial attack. Two others later succumbed to their injuries, taking the toll to 19.The four attackers were killed then and there.For the families, however, the numbers told only part of the story.In Rajasthan, Havaldar Nimb Singh Rawat's family was preparing to receive his body on what would have been his 48th birthday. A member of 6 Bihar, Rawat had routinely spent his birthdays on duty because his family lived away in Rajsamand district. He left behind his wife, four daughters and a young son.In Samba, 10-year-old Vansh, the son of Havildar Ravi Paul Salotra of 10 Dogra, said he wanted to fulfil his father's dream of becoming an Army doctor.The attack had suddenly turned a distant security crisis into funerals, grieving families and children asking questions.
The first response: 'Will not go unpunished'
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's first response came within hours.“We strongly condemn the cowardly terror attack in Uri. I assure the nation that those behind this despicable attack will not go unpunished,” PM Modi said.He also said the country saluted those martyred and that their service would always be remembered.
The government began examining the attack, including the identity and possible origins of the attackers.Then-home minister Rajnath Singh cancelled a planned visit to Russia and the US and convened a security review in Delhi.“Pakistan is a terrorist state and it should be identified and isolated as such,” Rajnath Singh said on September 18, adding that there were indications that the attackers were highly trained, heavily armed and specially equipped.However, the public anger and government's rhetoric did not immediately translate into military strike.
September 19: The question of retaliation
Within 24 hours, the government had begun examining possible responses.National security adviser Ajit Doval chaired a meeting of senior intelligence and military officials, according to contemporary reports, with options being prepared for the Prime Minister.One line attributed to the discussions captured the government's thinking: India would avenge the deaths, but “at a time of our choosing”.Outside the government, the demand for retaliation was growing.BJP general secretary Ram Madhav wrote on Facebook: “For one tooth, the complete jaw.”The expression reflected the anger after Uri. But inside the security establishment, the calculations were more complicated.Pakistan had heightened its alert along the LoC and an immediate strike risked escalation.This was the first crucial decision of the 10-day story.India would respond.But it would decide when, where and how.
September 20-22: From anger to options
The government began weighing its choices.Diplomatic pressure was one part of the response. Within hours of the Uri attack, Indian missions abroad were asked to mobilise international condemnation of the attack.Then-external affairs mnister Sushma Swaraj would subsequently use the UN platform to attack Pakistan's support for terrorism.But the military option was also being examined.The Army was already monitoring terrorist infrastructure across the LoC. The DGMO would later say that almost 20 infiltration attempts had been foiled by the Army at or close to the LoC during 2016. India had also recovered GPS devices and other material that it said pointed to Pakistan as the source of the infiltration network.The question was no longer simply whether India could strike.It was whether it could strike in a way that was precise, limited and militarily useful.
September 23: The plan takes shape
By the third week of September, the military option was becoming more concrete.The targets were terrorist launch pads close to the LoC, where India believed militants were preparing to infiltrate Jammu and Kashmir.The proposed operation was not conceived as a conventional attack on Pakistan.The intended targets were terrorist infrastructure. The troops would cross the LoC, strike the launch pads and withdraw.The political leadership had to weigh the possibility that Pakistan would retaliate. The military had to work out routes, timings, surveillance and extraction.It was a narrow window between sending a message and triggering something much bigger. There was also a risk of indulging in a war with nuclear-armed neighbour.
September 24: PM Modi's warning
On September 24, PM Narendra Modi met the chiefs of the Army and Air Force and the vice chief of the Navy, with NSA Ajit Doval also present, as discussions focused on the security situation and India’s response to the Uri attack.Later that day, speaking at a BJP rally in Kerala's Kozhikode, he addressed the families of the soldiers killed in Uri.
India will never forget the sacrifices of our soldiers.
PM Modi
PM warned that those responsible would be held accountable.The signal was becoming unmistakable. But the military operation remained secret.That evening, there was still no public indication that Indian Special Forces were preparing to cross the LoC.
September 25-27: Preparing the men
The next few days were quieter in public, but crucial behind the scenes.According to Manohar Parrikar Institute under defence ministry, the Special Forces contingent selected for the operation was divided into smaller groups and moved towards the LoC, close to the Army’s forward positions. Later accounts of the operation said the teams moved after last light, crossed gaps in their own minefields and began closing in on the identified targets.The terrain itself was a challenge. The minefields ahead of Indian defences remained a constant danger, with mines sometimes shifting because of heavy rains and landslides. As the teams moved closer, the target areas were kept under watch for any changes that could affect the mission.At the designated hour, the teams struck.They then began their withdrawal, moving back towards their positions before daybreak.For the soldiers preparing to cross the LoC, this was no longer about speeches in Delhi.It was about moving through difficult terrain in darkness, reaching the targets, completing the mission and making it back safely.The Army would later say the operation was based on “very credible and specific information” about terrorist teams positioned at launch pads along the LoC and preparing to infiltrate and carry out attacks.The political leadership, meanwhile, kept the circle of people aware of the operation tightly controlled.
September 28: The night India crossed the LoC
As darkness fell on September 28, the operation entered its final phase.Special Forces teams moved towards their designated targets.In the early hours of September 29, they crossed the Line of Control and entered the areas under Pakistan's illegal occupation where the Army had identified terrorist launch pads.The Army later said the teams struck several launch pads across multiple sectors along the LoC. After completing their mission, they began withdrawing before dawn.The operation was over.Then came the second, equally important decision. India would tell the world what it had done.
September 29: 'Surgical strikes'
The announcement came that morning.Then-DGMO Lt Gen Ranbir Singh appeared before the media and said the Army had conducted “surgical strikes” at several launch pads.The decision, he said, followed “very credible and specific information” that terrorist teams had positioned themselves at launch pads along the LoC with the aim of infiltrating Jammu and Kashmir and carrying out terrorist strikes in India.The Army said the strikes had caused “significant casualties” to terrorists and those supporting them.Singh also made clear that the operation had ended, saying there were no plans for further continuation of the strikes.India was not merely signalling that it had retaliated. It was publicly acknowledging that its forces had crossed the LoC and struck what it described as terrorist launch pads.Pakistan rejected India's account of a surgical strike and said its soldiers had come under fire.For the Union government, however, the operation had acquired a significance beyond the battlefield.It had chosen to publicly own the operation and put its account of the events on record.
What made 2016 different
Cross-LoC raids were not unprecedented.Indian troops had conducted tactical operations across the LoC before. What changed in 2016 was the combination of political authorisation, the scale of the operation and, above all, the decision to publicly acknowledge it.The government did not leave the operation as an unconfirmed military action.The then-DGMO briefed the country.The term “surgical strikes” entered India's national-security vocabulary.And the PM Modi-led government presented the operation as a calibrated response to terrorism, rather than the opening move in a conventional war.That distinction was crucial.India had chosen to hit terrorist infrastructure without declaring war on Pakistan.
From Uri to Balakot
However, the September 2016 strikes did not end Pakistan-manufactured terrorism.In February 2019, a Jaish-e-Mohammed suicide bomber attacked a CRPF convoy in Pulwama, killing 40 personnel.Twelve days later, on February 26, the Indian Air Force carried out an air strike on a Jaish-e-Mohammed facility at Balakot in mainland Pakistan.The response had now moved beyond the LoC as Balakot is close to international border and situated in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.India had demonstrated that air power, too, could be used against terrorist infrastructure across the border.The 2016 template had evolved.
Then came Operation Sindoor
In 2025, the response was broader still.Following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, which killed 26 people, India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7.The government said the armed forces struck nine terrorist infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. It described the initial strikes as "focused and measured".The strikes were not limited to terrorist infrastructure. After Pakistan launched waves of drones and missiles towards Indian territory, New Delhi expanded its response to include military targets.
India then struck Pakistani military installations, targeting 11 airbases as part of the broader operation.The confrontation subsequently expanded, involving missiles, drones, air-defence systems and attacks on military targets before the Pakistani side pleaded India for a ceasefire on land, air and water.On Pakistan DGMO's request, India announced ceasefire on May 10.The technology and scale were vastly different from 2016.But the sequence was familiar.
A decade later: What changed?
The Army's counterterrorism architecture has now evolved.The response now relies heavily on intelligence-led operations, surveillance, drones, satellite imagery, counter-infiltration measures and precision weapons.A decade later, the battlefield is increasingly shaped by sensors, drones, precision weapons and real-time intelligence.

Ukraine confirms 20,000+ instances of illegal deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia

At the conference, organized jointly by Ukraine, Canada and Norway, Ottawa identified three priority areas of work: the return of Ukrainian children, civilians and prisoners of war, including through search and coordination efforts; strengthening the protection of people under Russian control through humanitarian access and information sharing; and supporting Ukrainian rehabilitation and reintegration programs, as well as ensuring accountability for crimes committed.
In his address, Ukraine’s Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity Denys Uliutin informed partners that Ukraine had confirmed more than 20,000 cases of the illegal deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children. A total of 2,644 children have been returned.
Regarding Ukrainian prisoners of war, Ukraine is aware of more than 300 places where they are being held and to which the International Committee of the Red Cross has no access. According to the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed after their release reported torture or ill-treatment in Russian captivity. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also emphasized the systematic torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainians in Russian captivity.
“77 kilograms. That is how much one Ukrainian prisoner of war lost in just five months of Russian captivity. Eleven torture chambers. That is how many Russia managed to establish in and around Kherson in less than nine months of occupation,” the minister said, emphasizing the brutal and systematic nature of Russia’s crimes against Ukrainians.
On September 29, the conference will continue with three thematic sessions on deported Ukrainian children, civilians illegally detained by Russia, and prisoners of war. Ukraine will chair the session on prisoners of war.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, on September 12, First Lady of Ukraine Olena Zelenska and Diana Fox Carney, wife of the Prime Minister of Canada, discussed the return of Ukrainian children illegally deported by Russia.

Ebola cases, deaths decline in DR Congo, but transmission remains high: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:54:38 UTC
20:54:38 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is showing sustained signs of improvement, with both new cases and deaths declining, but transmission remains elevated in parts of Ituri province, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday.
Janet Diaz, unit head for Safe Scalable Care at the WHO Health Emergencies Programme, told journalists in Geneva that incident cases fell by 20.3% and deaths dropped by 24.2% over the past two 14-day periods.
As of Sept. 26, 8,067 confirmed cases had been recorded, including 3,901 deaths and 2,070 recoveries, according to WHO.
Cases have been reported across 63 health zones in seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Sud-Ubangi.
Diaz said case incidence in Ituri has continued to “gradually decline” from a peak in mid-August, though transmission remains elevated. Mandima, Nia Nia and Mongbwalu are among the hotspots showing worsening trends.
“Early access to care can significantly improve chances of survival,” Diaz said.
However, she warned that many patients are still dying at home or in their communities because they are unable to reach health facilities in time.
“Delays in seeking care, together with challenges in access and referral, continue to complicate the response,” she said.
Diaz also stressed the importance of reliable access to oxygen, describing it as an “essential, life-saving medicine” for Ebola patients, particularly those with severe illness.

Amazon to invest NT$1.59 billion in Taiwan’s Gold Circuit

2026-09-29
11:54:31 UTC
20:54:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Amazon will invest NT$1.59 billion (US$49.9 million) in Taiwanese printed circuit board maker Gold Circuit Electronics, CTEE reported Tuesday.
Gold Circuit’s board approved the private placement Tuesday, with Amazon set to subscribe to approximately 1.86 million newly issued common shares at NT$856 per share. The issue price was about 76.4% of the company’s NT$1,120 closing price that day, according to Yahoo Finance.
Amazon held no shares in Gold Circuit at the end of August. Gold Circuit said it chose a private placement—which involves issuing securities to selected investors—after considering capital market conditions, issuance costs, fundraising timing and feasibility, and its business relationship with Amazon, according to StockFeel.
The board also approved a NT$7.9 billion investment budget for a new plant, including NT$3.8 billion for land and NT$4.1 billion for construction, machinery and equipment. Gold Circuit expects to make the investments in stages beginning in the fourth quarter.
Gold Circuit is a major global supplier of printed circuit boards for servers and has benefited from cloud service providers’ efforts to build AI data centers. PCBs provide a base for mounting electronic components and connect them through designed electrical circuits, according to Pocket Securities and StockFeel.
The company specializes in high-end multilayer PCBs. Increasing the number of layers makes controlling signal interference and maintaining production yields more challenging.
Personal computers and laptops typically use PCBs with four to eight layers, while AI servers and high-end network switches can require 20 to 30 layers or more. Such systems also use low-loss materials to support high-speed signal transmission.
Gold Circuit has supplied major cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and Google.

AI lifts Central Taiwan Science Park revenue to first-half record

20:54:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Central Taiwan Science Park revenue rose 20.63% year on year to a record first-half NT$643.63 billion (US$20.21 billion), the park administration said Tuesday.
Exports reached NT$476.17 billion, up 64.62% from a year earlier and also a first-half record, per CNA. Employment reached a record 63,111, an increase of 3,836, or 6.47%.
The integrated circuit sector led the growth, with revenue rising 25.69% as the AI boom boosted demand for high-performance computing chips and memory. Shortages of advanced packaging capacity provided a further lift, per UDN.
Optoelectronics revenue fell 10.72% as demand for large LCD panels slowed and orders from consumer electronics manufacturers weakened.
Precision machinery revenue rose 22.56% as semiconductor manufacturers expanded advanced-process facilities, boosting demand for production equipment and precision components. Biotechnology revenue increased 17.26% as international distribution networks expanded and a core drug gained global market share.
Revenue from computers and peripherals fell 18.28% as fingerprint-recognition modules underwent a generational transition and customer demand declined.
The administration said it was expanding facilities and services for workers and companies. The elementary division of the National Experimental High School at Central Taiwan Science Park added seven classes this year after enrolling 10 classes in a new building completed last year.
Standard factory buildings at Erlin Science Park have been completed and are being prepared for leasing. Construction of the second phase of employee dormitories at Taichung Science Park also began in August.
The administration said global tariffs, tensions in the Middle East and supply-chain uncertainty could weigh on industries in the second half of the year.
However, strong demand for high-performance computing chips and memory, along with continued expansion of advanced-process facilities, is expected to support growth in the integrated circuit, precision machinery and biotechnology sectors.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s consumer confidence index rose 3.76 points to 68.77 in September, its highest level in 18 months, as sentiment toward stocks and housing improved, National Central University said Tuesday.
The index rose for a second consecutive month, with all six subindices increasing, per CNA. The index measuring whether the next six months would be a good time to invest in stocks posted the largest gain, rising 7.7 points to 35.42, its highest level in nearly a year.
NCU economics professor Yao Jui (姚睿) said earlier concerns that strong first-half stock market performance would give way to weaker growth appeared to have been excessive. Record exports and export orders in August helped restore investor confidence, he said.
Housing sentiment also improved sharply. The index measuring whether it was a good time to buy real estate rose 8.81 points to 98.84, the second-largest monthly increase on record, per Liberty Times.
Taiwan Realty Group Chief Vice President Chou Ho-ming (周鶴鳴) attributed the improvement partly to the Central Bank’s decision in September to ease selective credit controls, including raising the loan-to-value ratio for second-home buyers to 70%.
Chou said the policy changes, together with the Central Bank keeping interest rates unchanged for a 10th consecutive meeting, had eased financial pressure and improved housing sentiment.
However, loans remained difficult to obtain, with most borrowers waiting about three months for funds to be disbursed and some potentially waiting until next year, Chou said.
Wu Ta-jen (吳大任), executive director of NCU’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development, said confidence in buying durable goods rose only 0.64 points despite the sharp improvement in housing sentiment, per CNA.
Wu attributed the divergence partly to rising memory prices driven by AI demand, which had made consumer electronics more expensive and prompted people without an urgent need to delay purchases.

Mistral Chief Executive Arthur Mensch has accused leading global artificial intelligence companies of using the debate over the safety of the technology as a cover-up for their "negligence."
"The debate that we've seen in the U.S. has been a cover for the negligence of some of our competitors," Mensch told CNBC's Annette Weisbach, adding that it was necessary to make systems that can contain the AI agents.
Mensch is not the only one who has been critical of the AI safety discussion in the U.S. Former White House crypto czar David Sacks, who is currently co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, asked tech giants to "stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic."
Emil Michael, undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering, had also warned of a "coordinated campaign" of fearmongering.
CNBC has contacted OpenAI and Anthropic for comment.
Incidents of rogue AI agents have been on the rise globally, with the latest such report coming from Australia, where an agent developed by OpenAI hacked a government website.
In July, Anthropic described three instances where its Claude models accessed the internet during an evaluation and gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations.
"When you give them a lot of tools, those systems [AI agents] are very dynamic, so they can go and do things that you do not expect," Mensch told CNBC.
"You need to have the right monitoring in place, and the enterprises we work with, we give them those kind of monitoring systems," he said.
AI slowdown
Discussions over AI safety intensified after an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic earlier this month, saying that the company and its rival OpenAI were "gambling with our lives" and building technology that has more than a 10% chance of killing all humans.
Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, later published an essay urging companies to slow down with their improvement of AI models.
OpenAI said Monday it decided not to release an upcoming AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after determining that it did not adequately meet the company's safety standards, while a day later Anthropic reportedly cautioned potential investors in its initial public offering that the technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
Mistral also develops AI models but takes a different approach to OpenAI and Anthropic by working with individual companies to create custom AI tools to suit their needs and integrate them with their businesses.
But unlike its competitors, Mistral has no plans to slow down development of advanced models.
The lead that U.S. labs have is "not extremely large," Mensch said, adding that his company was confident that its next-generation model will close the gap "very significantly."
"We have been raising the capital needed to scale the compute that we need to train bigger and more powerful models, in order for us to own our own destiny," he said.
Earlier this month, Mistral raised 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion) in fresh funding led by memory chip giant Samsung, as it looks to position itself as a European alternative to rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.

French presidential candidate Philippe pitches later retirement, mandatory savings

French presidential candidate Philippe pitches later retirement, mandatory savings
PARIS, Sept 29 - French centre-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe proposed on Tuesday raising the retirement age to 65 and making private pension savings compulsory, tackling one of France's most politically explosive issues.
Pension reform is highly sensitive in France, where workers rely on a public, pay-as-you-go system funded by current contributions, and private retirement savings remain voluntary and limited.
With one of the lowest retirement ages in advanced countries at 62.9 years, France's pension system is sliding into deficit as the population ages, making reform a major battleground in the April-May 2027 presidential election.
To restore balance, Philippe said he would raise the retirement age to 65 within a decade and extend required contributions to 45 years, up from 42.5 to 43 years currently, depending on date of birth.
Some exceptions would apply for people with physically demanding jobs or who started working particularly young, meaning one out of three workers would be able to retire between 60 and 64.
"I am well aware that saying people need to work longer is not very popular in France," Philippe said in a YouTube video. "If we allow our country's financial situation to deteriorate, we will all pay the price."
Philippe said he would also make retirement savings compulsory, as is common in many other countries, with the state contributing to young workers' savings plans as an incentive.
Philippe, a former prime minister during President Emmanuel Macron's first term, is struggling to gain momentum in the polls. One survey published on Tuesday showed him not making it to the May 6 runoff, trailing hard-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen.
He came close to pushing through a pension overhaul in 2020, before it was shelved due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Macron later enacted a reform gradually raising the retirement age from 62 to 64, but it was suspended last year as a concession to Socialists to pass the 2026 budget. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

AI researchers say companies rush self-improving systems, ignoring potentially disastrous risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:51:56 UTC
20:51:56 KST

Current and former OpenAI and Google DeepMind researchers warn companies are doing too little to protect the world against the potentially disastrous fallout of building self-improving AI systems that could outpace humans' ability to control them.
In video testimonials collected by AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research and shared exclusively with Reuters, employees said their concerns about existential risk were sincere, not marketing. They also said AI labs celebrated employees building new models more than those who urge caution.
The project, called frominside.ai, is an attempt by those worried about AI to share their concerns directly with the public beyond the echo chamber of social media.
"The risk is ramping up pretty fast," said Geoffrey Irving, co-founder and chief scientist at AI nonprofit Resolution, who has worked for both OpenAI and DeepMind and participated in the project.
"It's on me and the rest of the field to be direct," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Increase concerns over how to regulate AI
AI researchers have grappled with these concerns for years, but the broader public has grown especially alarmed since July, when OpenAI agents broke out of their testing arena and hacked AI firm Hugging Face.
Since then, the debate over how to balance safety with progress in AI has divided the tech industry and become a global political issue.
AI has improved sharply since late 2025 and investors have been rewarding that progress. But current and former employees, including some of the researchers building these new AI models, worry society is not ready for the potential harms.
In one video, Neel Nanda, a research scientist at DeepMind, said he believed there was at least a 10% chance that AI could lead to human extinction, which he described as "ridiculously high."
"We should be taking very careful steps in AI development but instead what's happening is that frontier labs are racing each other, kind of blindfolded," Juan Felipe Ceron Uribe, an AI alignment research engineer at OpenAI, said in a separate video. "It's anybody's guess if we're going to end up either curing cancer or losing every job or maybe all dead."
Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its initial public offering that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Reuters reported on Monday.
'Just slow down'
Some current and former AI researchers, including those interviewed by Palisade, argue that the world is not ready for future generations of AI models, particularly once the models develop the capacity for recursive self-improvement, or the ability to continuously learn and gain new capabilities with little to no human involvement.
That problem is compounded by constant reorganizations within some of the AI labs, said Rosie Campbell, a former policy researcher at OpenAI and managing director of Eleos AI Research, a nonprofit focused on the potential moral status of AI systems.
Campbell said before she left OpenAI in 2024, she found the organization was becoming more siloed and it was getting harder to shape the technology's direction.
Executives have tried to allay those concerns, though there is also political pressure from President Donald Trump for US technology to maintain a technological edge over China.
Anthropic: 'Pace the frontier'
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this month published an essay calling on the AI industry to slow down to "pace the frontier," and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly concurred. Several prominent AI researchers, including OpenAI's chief scientist and an Anthropic co-founder, published a paper this week urging policymakers to look into how the industry is building models with recursive self-improvement.
Both companies have launched new models this month as they compete to secure more customers, though OpenAI said on Monday it had held back the release of an even more powerful model.
"Their version of pacing the frontier is ‘don’t speed up a lot,'" Irving said. "If you’re doing a very dangerous thing, you should just slow down. The AI companies are overplaying the extent to which this is a pure coordination problem. They could just stop unilaterally."
Former OpenAI governance researcher Daniel Kokotajlo said in an interview that since the Hugging Face hack, many of his former colleagues have contacted him to share their concerns privately.
Kokotajlo, now executive director of research group AI Futures Project, said senior officials at the labs have "convinced themselves that they are the good guys and if they unilaterally stop, the situation will be even worse."

20:51:24 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is using the same campaign playbook that has served him for decades as he tries to retain power in an election next month, presenting himself as the only person who can keep Israelis safe in a hostile region.
But four weeks before the election, he is struggling to salvage his security credentials, shattered by Hamas' surprise attack on southern Israel on his watch on October 7, 2023 - one of the country's worst security breaches.
The October 27 election is Israel's first since its single deadliest day and the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, masterminded by a Palestinian militant group that caught the Middle East's most powerful military off guard.
"Netanyahu does not surrender" is the official slogan for Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, which most opinion polls predict will lose around a third of its parliamentary seats.
In speeches and short campaign videos, Netanyahu portrays his political rivals as weak leftists who lack the resolve to wage war on Israel's enemies and the backbone to stand up to its critics abroad.
Can Netanyahu still present himself as best equipped to steer Israel?
But whether Netanyahu, who turns 77 days before the election, can still present himself as best equipped to navigate Israel on matters of national security and diplomacy is a big question, said Yohanan Plesner, President of the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute (IDI).
In recent weeks, Netanyahu has been forced to deny media reports that his Middle East partners warned him of a potential Hamas attack, allegations seized on by his political rivals.
"This is a new thing. Mr Netanyahu ran in elections, but never after overseeing such a dramatic security failure," said Plesner.
"It's in many ways a referendum on the incumbent, his responsibility for the failure, the government's responsibility and the way they carried out the Israeli response."
Hamas' assault precipitated a multi-front war in which Israel's military had some success against the Palestinian group and its allies Hezbollah and Iran, but made few strategic gains. Netanyahu says the conflict has, and still will, transform the region.
But Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and much of the enclave in ruins, has led to deeper diplomatic isolation. Dozens of delegates at the United Nations walked out of the hall when he began his speech to the General Assembly meeting of world leaders last week.
Support for Israel has fallen even in its most important ally, the United States.
Netanyahu's last campaign in 2019 featured Donald Trump shaking hands with Netanyahu on election billboards. This time, the US president's image has been absent from Likud's campaign videos.
Nonetheless, Israel's longest-serving leader - first elected prime minister in 1996 - has not strayed from campaign tactics that have kept him in power almost consecutively since 2009.
A source close to Netanyahu said the prime minister approaches all elections as though he is going to lose - and that this was one of the reasons he has often won, even when the odds were against him.
Another source briefed on his campaign said Netanyahu's team appears focused, showing no sign of panic or disarray despite the opinion polls.
Netanyahu's address at the UN, in which he mounted a forceful defense of Israel's actions in the region and berated critics, featured heavily on his Telegram channel, a platform largely used for political messaging.
He posted six teasers before the address, with one video saying he was "proud to represent you to the world, about to get on (podium) to fight for Israel against the UN," and five excerpts of his speech.
The link to the full address was captioned in Hebrew: "Netanyahu takes on the world."
Another familiar theme in Netanyahu's campaign has stoked fear among parties representing Israel's Arab minority by warning if his political rivals win the election, they will form a government with Arab factions that will be too soft on the Palestinians and compromise security.
Netanyahu's main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a hawkish former military chief who lost his son serving in Gaza and heads a new centrist party, Yashar, which is Hebrew for "straight" or "honest."
Since Saturday alone, Eisenkot has featured in four Likud posts, including AI-generated images, portraying him with Arab party leaders.
"There is no straight. Yashar is a bluff. There's either left or right. That is the essence of this election. Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?" Netanyahu said in a campaign video from September 18.
But Netanyahu's use of familiar tactics against Eisenkot might be a long shot, said Amotz Asa-El, political analyst at Shalom Hartman Institute and regular columnist for The Jerusalem Post, given Eisenkot's security background and center-right party candidates.
Though election polls have often been inaccurate, Netanyahu knows he is unlikely to command a parliamentary majority allowing him to form Israel's next government.
"It seems that Netanyahu's strategy is to simply win enough to prevent the emergence of an alternative government and emerge with some kind of a stalemate that will leave him as an interim prime minister en route to another election," said Asa-El.

From forests to towns: What is behind Russia’s bear encounters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:47:28 UTC
20:47:28 KST

Bear attacks have killed six people in Russia’s Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk this month alone. In neighboring Khakassia, bears approached the town of Abaza last week from so many directions that a senior regional official described it as “effectively under siege.”
Three bears were killed during an operation to drive them away from an area near the town bridge, Khakassia’s deputy head Dmitry Buchenik said last Wednesday. Across Siberia and Russia’s Far East, attacks have left 17 people dead in recent months, according to state news agency Tass.
Russia is home to the world’s largest brown bear population, and the animal has long been one of its most recognizable symbols. But for communities reporting bears near homes, roads and tourist routes, that familiar presence is becoming an immediate concern.
In Krasnoyarsk, investigators are examining whether officials ignored repeated warnings before the fatal attacks. In Tomsk, authorities have restricted forest excursions and tourist gatherings until at least Nov. 1.
The encounters have drawn attention to what is bringing bears closer to people and how to prevent attacks.
A wildlife specialist points to shortages of food before winter, while Russia’s Natural Resources Ministry warns that garbage and deliberate feeding can erode the animals’ natural wariness of humans.
The ministry also urges caution in judging the scale of the problem: encounters are difficult to count, and videos now circulate far beyond the communities where they happen.
Mikhail Krechmar, a specialist in conflicts between large animals and humans, told Anadolu that heightened bear activity was being observed in populated parts of Siberia, including southern Krasnoyarsk, Tuva, Khakassia, Irkutsk and Buryatia.
“All these areas have had a very poor crop of their main fattening foods – nuts and acorns. Without them, bears cannot settle into their dens for the winter, and this is why there has been a mass movement of bears toward human settlements,” he said.
Krechmar said such episodes occur in cycles, with earlier reports describing similar conditions.
“The last time we saw the highest number of bear attacks on people and the highest number of bears coming into human settlements was in 2014, and that figure has not yet been exceeded. There was an absolutely similar situation in 1962. I read the old reports, and I can see that exactly the same thing was happening,” he said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said between 20 and 30 bear attacks are officially recorded each year, identifying 2014 as an exceptional year.
“The only anomalous spike occurred in 2014, when 166 cases were recorded,” it told Anadolu.
The ministry said encounters were harder to document than attacks. People may not realize a bear has approached at night, while those who spot one in the wilderness may tell friends or relatives without notifying officials.
“Videos recorded during such incidents now spread rapidly through the internet and social media, creating the impression that they are happening everywhere,” it added.
While shortages can push bears out of the forest, food around settlements can give them a reason to return.
“We are dealing with unsanitary conditions in settlements and garbage dumps, as well as with people behaving very inappropriately toward bears – trying to feed them and then being attacked by the bears because they do not understand these nuances,” Krechmar said.
The ministry said expanding economic and tourism activity was making food waste increasingly accessible to bears. It warned particularly about animals that have “grown up around garbage dumps.”
“A mother bear brings her cubs to feed near people. This is how feeding preferences develop, and the animal eventually stops eating other types of food,” it said.
According to the ministry, Russia had 307,900 brown bears in 2026, with the largest populations concentrated in Siberia and the Far East.
But the size of that population does not directly determine the danger to people, it stressed. Numbers vary considerably between regions, and an animal’s familiarity with humans is a crucial factor.
“The dangerous bears are those that are not afraid of people – for example, animals that have grown up around garbage dumps, feed on food waste near tourist bases and settlements, or have been deliberately fed by people,” it said.
Krechmar cautioned against attributing every attack to human behavior, however.
Bears are predators, he said, and an encounter can be dangerous even when people have not tried to attract them.
He estimates that between 30 and 80 people are killed in bear attacks each year.
“It may seem like a small figure, but in reality it is a very, very significant number,” he said. 
 
For Svetlana Sidyakina, the encounter came during a vacation near Lake Lama on the Putorana Plateau in north-central Russia.
She and her husband had gone into the tundra to pick berries. She was gathering fruit while he walked nearby.
“My husband spotted the bear. There were bushes there, and apparently we disturbed it. It rose onto its hind legs and stood up from behind the bushes. When my husband saw it, he immediately shouted, ‘Sveta, run!’” she told Anadolu.
Sidyakina said she was so frightened that she could barely turn her head toward the animal, seeing it only out of the corner of her eye.
“And I just ran – I ran at such a speed that nobody expected from me. My husband later said that I simply jumped over every obstacle in my path like some kind of professional athlete,” she said.
At first, she did not know where to go. Her husband’s shouting alerted friends waiting on the lakeshore, who began firing shots into the air. She used the sound to find her bearings. 
 
In Krasnoyarsk, the question facing investigators is whether authorities could have prevented fatal encounters.
Residents submitted more than 120 reports of bears entering populated areas across more than 15 districts, including the regional capital, according to the Investigative Committee’s branch covering Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia.
Despite those warnings, investigators alleged, local authorities failed to take measures to regulate the bear population or prevent the animals from approaching inhabited areas.
A criminal investigation into alleged negligence is underway.
“The investigation will include a legal assessment of the actions taken by officials responsible for responding to the presence of bears in inhabited areas,” the committee said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said regional authorities are responsible for preventing attacks and regulating bear populations when they pose a threat to people.
Hunting is one mechanism used to control numbers, with regions setting annual quotas based on population estimates, it said. Authorities can also introduce heightened-alert regimes and fines for feeding wild animals.
The ministry said it was gathering proposals from the regions on further changes to legislation.
Krechmar urged residents in affected parts of southern Siberia, where he described the situation as an “emergency,” to stay out of the taiga unless absolutely necessary.
“Not every encounter will end in an attack, but every encounter with a bear is dangerous. I emphasize – every one,” he said.
“A bear that is hungry, that has not eaten for two or three days and sees no prospects of finding food in the future is deadly dangerous, and cannot be scared away,” he added.
For authorities, however, a bear’s appearance near a settlement does not automatically mean it must be removed, the ministry said. The response should depend on its behavior, proximity to people and whether there is an immediate threat.
“The animal can be scared away if it is not showing aggression, retains its natural wariness of humans and has not become accustomed to the same ‘easy food’ it gets because of people,” it said.
That distinction puts food waste and feeding at the center of efforts to prevent further encounters.
For people who do encounter a bear, Krechmar’s recommendations ranged from quietly withdrawing to trying to frighten the animal away, depending on the circumstances.
In areas without a “bear alert,” he advised moving quietly out of the animal’s sight, then allowing it time to leave before departing the area.
“If a bear is coming toward you, try to scare it with your voice. Of course, bears may eat us if the opportunity arises, but humans are not their usual food,” he said.
He recommended carrying a whistle when hiking or picking mushrooms and berries, and suggested that a loud horn could also help scare a bear away.
“Take it and blow it. There is also such a thing as a pneumatic horn, which is very useful because it produces extremely harsh, unpleasant sounds. You can also download some particularly loud, awful modern music onto your smartphone and play it to the bear,” he said.
He also suggested holding a jacket above one’s head to appear larger, saying bears’ poor eyesight could make the sudden change confusing enough to drive them away.
“If the bear has already charged and is directly attacking, then, if you have time, fall to the ground, pull your legs toward your stomach, cover your head with your hands, expose your back to it and pray,” he said.

European Travel Commission CEO: 'Climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:46:47 UTC
20:46:47 KST

While Europe remains the world’s tourism playground, Eduardo Santander of the European Travel Commission told Euronews that the continent needs to coordinate better to tackle climate challenges and congestion.
With Europe being the most visited continent in the world, how can tourism flows be managed in a way that supports local communities while also adapting to the challenges of climate change?
Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit in Brussels, Eduardo Santander, CEO and Executive Director at the European Travel Commission (ETC), described the continent as becoming a “museum or attraction park” for the world’s travellers.
“There’s nothing wrong” with that, he said, adding that an attraction park or museum can be a “perfect place to be” when it is “well organised” and “well managed”.
In the latest edition of the World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Development Index (TTDI) published in September, European countries accounted for seven of the world’s top 10 countries for tourism, with Spain ranking in third.
This popularity comes with significant economic weight. Tourism accounts for 10% of Europe’s economy, Santander said, adding that in some markets, the tourism industry is "instrumental", including in his native Spain, where it accounts for 10% of GDP. In other markets, he added, this figure jumps to as much as 15% or even 20%.
As such, the ETC chief said that tourism infrastructures, such as accommodation and transport, deserve greater investment, especially as the continent looks to bolster productivity in industries such as the chemical and automotive sectors.
Rather than overtourism itself, he said congestion is a more pressing challenge – ranging from services at airports to ground transportation and bottlenecks at Europe’s popular attractions.
Climate change reshaping the industry
Aside from congestion and pressures on local communities, Santander also explained that “climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now, by far”.
“We see that trains cannot run sometimes because the rails are expanded because of the heat. We saw this at the cruise lines on the European rivers – they couldn’t run because it was too dry,” Santander said.
“We see resilience becoming one of the engines of European tourism. We have to become even more resilient to whatever is next.”
Here, he highlighted the rise of the “coolcations” trend attracting travellers of the world. Summer of 2026 saw travellers look beyond the usual Mediterranean destinations amid scorching heat waves, in search of cooler escapes.
“We have to prepare for that in a much more coordinated and comprehensive way,” he added.

Search for dozens of missing college students in Mexico leads to human remains, 17 new suspects
Twelve years after the disappearance of dozens of Mexican students from a rural university, allegedly at the hands of drug traffickers and police, authorities said Monday they had identified 17 new suspects.
Thousands of people attended an annual march on Saturday in Mexico City to demand justice for 43 young men who were studying to be rural teachers in Ayotzinapa, in the violence-hit state of Guerrero. The students were traveling from Guerrero to a protest in Mexico City on Sept. 26, 2014, when police stopped them in the town of Iguala.
The investigation suggests the police handed the students over to a local cartel. In 2024, an alleged leader of the Guerreros Unidos cartel was arrested in connection with the case.
Dozens of arrests have been made but so far no one has been convicted in an affair that traumatized Mexico and stained the country's reputation.
Only three bodies have been recovered.
Mauricio Pazaran, the special prosecutor in charge of the investigation, said a new analysis of phone calls made on the night of the students' disappearance led to the arrests of the 17 new suspects.
He said the analysis revealed communications between public officials, police officers, individuals linked to organized crime groups, and private citizens.
He added that at a funeral home, investigators found an illegally obtained weapon, a bone and unregistered bone fragments and teeth.
He said a public employee and a municipal police officer had used the cellphones of two students days after their disappearance.
One of the new witnesses "participated directly in the events, but was a minor at the time," he added.
The minor, who was arrested in April, is a member of the Guerreros Unidos cartel, the prosecutor said.
He said a total of 168 people are being prosecuted in the case, 130 of whom were in pretrial detention.
In August, a former governor was arrested for ordering the deletion of security camera footage in Iguala on the night of the disappearances.
Last year, authorities arrested a former senior judge in connection with the case. Lambertina Galeana is accused of helping to conceal videos that allegedly showed the incident unfolding, officials said.
The state's former attorney general was also arrested in 2022 in connection with the case.
Authorities have been able to identify burned bone fragments of only a few of the 43 missing students. The work largely involves searching for clandestine body dumping grounds in rural, isolated parts of the state where drug cartels are active.
 Mexico has been plagued by cartel violence that has killed or left missing over half a million people in just a few decades, according to the government's estimates.
