A year ago Andy Burnham had a tough business reception at Labour’s party conference. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, with clear ambitions to replace Keir Starmer, had rattled the City of London with his comment that Britain should be less “in hock” to bond markets.
Returning to the annual gathering in Liverpool a year later as prime minister, the mood is different. Labour is pushing to repair relations with corporate Britain and reassure City bond traders against a jittery backdrop amid the Middle East war.
At a private reception on Monday night hosted by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), HSBC and National Grid, John Healey told executives the government would do “our bit” to support firms struggling with rising costs. The chancellor said his budget next month would also have fiscal discipline at its core.
“I very much welcome the chance as chancellor to work with you,” he said.
Over bottled beer and glasses of wine overlooking the River Mersey, one executive praised the chancellor: “Can I just say, bloody wonderful speech of yours at conference today. Really determined to achieve success; it went down very well.”
For most bosses, however, there is a caveat: the 28 October budget. Labour gained a reputation after its return to government in 2024 for love-bombing bosses before then raising taxes on firms.
“Ask us on 29 October [how business feels]” said the CBI chief executive, Rain Newton-Smith.
She said that while Burnham appeared to be in listening mode, Labour faced difficult decisions at next month’s budget.
“When you get a change [of administration], you’re sort of changing mid-flight, and that allows you to think what was working, what wasn’t. Without denigrating the previous [administration], they’ve sort of said, ‘“Look, we need to get change, but also, how can we be responsive?’”
In previous years there had been a clamour among businesses to attend Labour’s annual conference – held for three years running in Liverpool – to the point it was jokingly dubbed the “Davos on the Mersey”, referring to the annual gathering of the global elite in the Swiss ski resort.
Starmer had run a strategy before his landslide election victory to win corporate endorsements to burnish Labour’s credentials in City boardrooms. But within his first months in office relations had soured, after Rachel Reeves sprung £40bn of tax increases – centred squarely on employers – in her first budget.
This year, delegates said there appeared to be fewer top bosses at Labour’s “business day”, where executives paid £6,000 a ticket to attend an exclusive breakfast reception hosted by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, followed by a “fireside chat” with Burnham.
However, corporate Britain was still evident en masse, with companies including Mastercard, HSBC and Heathrow among those paying thousands to sponsor fringe sessions and private networking events.
After smaller sessions focusing on policy, executives were ushered into the main auditorium to hear the chancellor’s speech, including Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, and the bosses of the “B5” group of leading business trade bodies.
In the auditorium the chancellor gave little away about the budget, despite striking a markedly different tone to Burnham’s “in hock” comment from a year earlier – insisting that he and the prime minister were “in lockstep” in their commitment to balance the books.
“There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said.
Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said Healey’s speech was “significant” because the chancellor had acknowledged that private enterprise was vital for helping the UK economy to grow.
However, she warned that companies still faced severe headwinds. “[The government’s] strategy is unlikely to succeed while the everyday cost of doing business is still soaring. Firms are being asked to invest while facing a tsunami of rising costs from employment, energy and business rates,” she said.
Lobbyists said there appeared to have been a concerted effort to ensure senior ministers spent time with business leaders and to match them more directly with the relevant sector.
One external affairs chief at a FTSE 250 retailer noted a marked shift in willingness to listen to business concerns, highlighting the work of the prime minister’s special adviser for business relations, James Carroll.
Varun Chandra, who had been Starmer’s chief business investment and trade adviser and who stayed on under Burnham, was also orchestrating meetings at the private CBI reception on Monday night.
One minister said the business leaders they had met in Liverpool welcomed the renewed sense of optimism projected by the new government – in contrast to what some saw as Starmer’s downbeat attitude.
Businesses have welcomed individual initiatives, such as Burnham’s tax cut for pubs and clubs; but are yet to understand what “Manchesterism” might mean if applied UK-wide – and remain concerned about the possibility of tax rises in next month’s budget.
Steve Rigby, the chief executive of the family-owned property and technology company Rigby Group, said Labour’s approach to business had improved from two years ago, but he was reserving judgment until the budget in a month.
“The PM and Jonathan Reynolds are visible and engaged, whether they are listening to our concerns will become clear in the budget,” he said. “You can buy tickets to get into the right rooms, where proper access [to the politicians] is possible – but you have to work hard to get it.
“Really we are in a holding pattern until the budget. The signs are good – we like the boring, no-leaks approach from Healey [so far]. However, businesses have absorbed about as many tax rises as they can, which is what the main focus will be over the next month.”

Rights groups warn Spain’s planned Ceuta deportation decree threatens asylum protections

Alyssa Mcmurtry

Human rights organizations on Tuesday urged Spain to abandon a proposed decree to accelerate deportations from Ceuta, warning that it would undermine asylum protections.
In a joint statement, organizations including Oxfam and the Spanish Commission for Refugees said the proposal would create an "exception to the right to asylum based on place and time."
The government has been preparing the measure following a mass crossing into Ceuta in late July, when nearly 80,000 people crossed into the small Spanish African enclave.
El Pais newspaper reported Saturday that officials were aiming to bring the proposal before the Cabinet on Tuesday, although the text remained under development.
According to the newspaper, the Interior Ministry-backed proposal would shorten administrative and judicial procedures to speed up asylum decisions and returns to Morocco.
More than 10,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, according to government figures cited by El Pais.
The organizations warned that the draft would allow some asylum-seekers to be removed before decisions on their applications and restrict their ability to invoke protection against being returned to danger.
They said this threatened the principle of non-refoulement, which protects people from being sent to countries where their lives or physical safety would be at risk.
The groups also criticized a provision under which asylum applications would be ruled inadmissible if submitted more than seven days after notification of a return, expulsion or refusal-of-entry order.
People could miss that deadline because they lacked information about asylum or faced difficulties accessing initial screening procedures, the organizations said.
They also warned that a proposed five-calendar-day deadline for appealing unfavorable decisions would undermine access to legal assistance.
They said it would leave insufficient time to appoint a lawyer, examine the case file and consult the applicant with an interpreter where necessary.
The statement also criticized the removal of safeguards involving the UN refugee agency's role in assessing applications.
The groups urged the government to withdraw the proposal and honor its commitment to implement the EU's migration and asylum pact in the least harmful way possible for asylum rights.

To the people voting for Nigel Farage: is this really the finger you want on the red button? | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:42:24 UTC
20:42:24 KST

Another week, another chance for Nigel Farage to demonstrate his literally hysterical leadership inabilities. For a guy who supposedly valorises the wartime British spirit, Nigel would genuinely have had to have been interned during that conflict on account of his serial predilection for spreading panic and unverified information at any given chance. The weekend incident near RAF Fairford was simply the latest in a long line of occasions that make you suspect the poster on the wall at Reform HQ reads simply: “Lose Cool and Start Shitposting.”
Despite its popularity now, the famous “Keep Calm and Carry On” poster from the second world war was almost certainly never displayed in that conflict. Although more than 2m copies of it were printed, it was in fact held in reserve in case a really serious crisis hit. Which, when you consider even the blitz apparently didn’t clear the bar, it is almost impossible to conceive of in our era where comparatively minuscule incidents force certain party leaders into more than 24 hours of madly irresponsible and emotional online incontinence.
Many of you may find you have a low tolerance for shrieks of “We have the right to know absolutely everything, immediately!” from a congenitally secretive guy who notoriously declined to declare the £5m he was given from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and, since that weird “gift” has been uncovered, has been in a prolonged tantrum that has caused him to snap at any attempts to discover more about what might have motivated it. “None of your business,” ran one particularly ill-judged attempt by Farage to put the issue to bed. “What’s it got to do with you?”
I do find my finger hovering over the “What’s it got to do with you?’ button with increasing regularity when Farage appears on screen to insert himself into moments of obviously active sensitivity. The clearly nuanced and potentially complex Fairford investigation – still ongoing, despite the release on bail of the five men arrested – was a case in point, although on Monday Nigel did attempt to set it out in a madly precipitous video on what he called “the Fairford plot”, captioned: “Fairford proves my point on Iran and the IRGC.” Does it? OK, thanks Jack Ryan.
Anyone who judges that this intemperate psychological liability should have access to the nuclear codes and other top-level information must have a subconscious wish for their answer to the question “where do you see yourself in five years’ time?” to be “living in Britain’s catacombs and distilling drinking water from my own urine”. It’s unclear whether a Prime Minister Farage would just bottle everything or shoot first and ask questions later, but the most likely metaphorical outcome in any given scenario may well be him shooting the wrong person first, then refusing to answer questions later.
Furthermore, as always with Nigel, it’s worth highlighting his insistence on rising to only the occasions from which he feels he might personally benefit. And so it is that he will have an awful lot to say about the horrific murder of Henry Nowak, but nothing or next to about those of Jo Cox or Sarah Everard. Whatever may or may not have happened at Fairford feeds into what we have to call, with heavy irony, his two-tier approach to public life. After all, for a guy who supposedly worries about illegal activity that could bear the hallmarks of foreign sponsorship, Farage strangely didn’t have a lot to say about the Ukrainian and Romanian nationals who were recruited via a Russian-speaking pseudonymous Telegram user to commit arson on property connected to Keir Starmer and on a car he had previously owned, back when Starmer was prime minister. Even after they were found guilty, the Reform leader didn’t seem to find this sort of darkly intriguing activity worthy of comment. Things he did find worthy of comment that same month included disputes over flying the St George’s cross flag and AI scam videos.
The thing about attaining the very highest office in the land is that you have to be prime minister of all the things, all the time. It is difficult to see how someone as cynically selective as Farage could somehow become the sort of leader able to speak for a nation. Or, just as importantly, the sort of leader able to realise when it’s time to shut up for a nation.
Far more troubling still is the gathering sense that Farage is too mentally weak for the role, and would go to pieces in very short order once plunged into the realities of life in Downing Street. Perhaps his declining poll ratings mean worrying may be unnecessary. But he’s increasingly a set of walking psychological red flags: emotional, quick to temper, incapable of rising above the self-serving.
Amazing that there is a psychological screening test to determine whether you are up to appearing on a reality TV show these days, but you could ascend to the office of prime minister without submitting to anything similar. At least 20% of would-be Big Brother contestants are deemed mentally unfit to participate during the casting process each year. And looking at the five main party leaders this week, you’d think a similar percentage had the potential to absolutely implode were they to enter the Downing Street house. Perhaps our politics needs new duty-of-care guidelines, so that the office of British prime minister is psychologically guardrailed to the same level as, say, a dating show like Love is Blind.

Jewish dreidels, an icon, and a 19th-century cross — an attempt was made to take cultural valuables out of Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:39:36 EEST
20:39:36 KST

Jewish dreidels, an icon, and a 19th-century cross — an attempt was made to take cultural valuables out of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv customs officers confiscated 19th-century cultural valuables bound for the United States and Estonia. No permits for their export were provided.
Kyiv customs officers prevented the export of 19th-century cultural valuables from Ukraine—dreidels, an antique icon and a cross. An expert examination confirmed that the items are cultural valuables. The State Customs Service of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
The dreidels and cross, which were headed to the United States, and the icon, which was headed to Estonia, were discovered during customs control of international postal shipments. Given their signs of antiquity, customs officers sent them to the National Museum of the History of Ukraine for an expert examination to determine whether they belonged to cultural valuables
According to the experts’ conclusion, the three small spinning tops are dreidels, traditional to Jewish culture. They are an attribute of an ancient game that children play during the celebration of Hanukkah. The sides of the dreidels bear Hebrew letters that form the phrase "A great miracle happened there."
The history of this game is connected with events in the 2nd century BCE. In 167 BCE, the Syrian king Antiochus significantly restricted the rights of Jews to observe religious commandments and banned the study of the Torah. Jews were forced to study it secretly, hiding in caves. According to tradition, children were left near the entrance and, upon noticing guards approaching, began playing noisily with dreidels so that the adults would have time to hide the Torah scrolls.
The discovered dreidels are of archaeological origin. Similar items are represented in Ukraine’s museum collections only to a very limited extent.
The metal icon of the Holy Mother of God "Joy of All Who Sorrow" is an example of 19th-century Old Believer cast-copper artwork. Such icons were worn as amulets or hung near the head of sick people.
The eight-pointed cross that was discovered is an altar crucifix. Such crosses became an obligatory attribute of priests, who put them on during ordination.
Under current Ukrainian legislation, permits are required to export cultural valuables abroad. No such documents were provided to the customs officers.

Türkiye plans to digitally archive centuries-old Turkish music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:38:23 UTC
20:38:23 KST

Türkiye is preparing a digital archive of centuries-old musical works, historical scores and performance recordings that will be made freely accessible to the public in 2027.
The project, led by the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Fine Arts, will bring together scores from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods, along with religious hymns, gazels, concert recordings and stage performances.
The archive aims to give musicians, researchers and the wider public access to Türkiye’s musical heritage through a single online platform.
Omer Faruk Belviranli, director general of Fine Arts, said that the directorate oversees 29 orchestras, choirs and musical ensembles, including six state symphony orchestras and the State Polyphonic Choir. Other ensembles specialise in traditional Turkish music, folk music, folk dances and music from different regions.
Archiving performances
A separate project is also under way to digitally record artistic productions by the directorate’s ensembles.
“Works we produce must definitely be recorded. If it is visual, there must be a video recording; if it is audio, they must definitely be recorded through the YouTube channel,” Belviranli said.
He said 15 of the directorate’s 29 units have professional recording studios and that an existing archive of performances will be transferred to an online platform.
“We currently have an archive. All that remains is to bring this archive to life and transfer it to the YouTube channel, or whichever channel we will publish it on, in accordance with our minister’s instructions,” he said.
The digital archive will also include historical musical notation reflecting centuries of Turkish musical tradition.
“Turkish music is a sea,” Belviranli said. “We have in our possession, in the form of an archive, very special scores inherited from the 700-800-year-old Seljuk and Ottoman tradition to the present day, Hamparsum notation, scores written in Ottoman Turkish and many more.”
Hamparsum notation is a historical system developed during the Ottoman period to record Turkish music.
“We will definitely transfer all of these to the archive and make them available to those interested,” he said. “We will create a digital sea that our listeners can access free of charge, where everyone interested can see everything with one click and gain access to the details of the archive.”
Belviranli said an exact number of works could not yet be given, but the archive would cover the programmes of the directorate’s 29 units and eventually include tens of thousands of works.
He said the recordings would allow people to study individual pieces and performances, while stressing that digital access would not replace the experience of attending a live concert.
“Music lovers will be able to listen to the concerts digitally through our archive, but being at concerts is like watching the same match. Watching it on television and going to the stadium to watch it are very different,” he said. “Being able to feel that atmosphere, that spirit, is very important.”
The directorate also plans to continue sending musical ensembles abroad. Belviranli said it had received requests from at least 42 countries for performances marking October 29, Türkiye’s Republic Day.
He said foreign audiences accounted for nearly 80 percent of spectators at some overseas programmes, particularly those featuring traditional music, whirling dervish performances, Turkish World music and folk dances.
“We are striving to be a bridge carrying the past into the future,” Belviranli said.

PARIS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- France's public debt rose by 59.6 billion euros (67.7 billion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter of 2026 from the previous quarter, reaching 3.59 trillion euros (4.08 trillion dollars), or 119 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) said Tuesday.
According to Insee, France's public debt had already increased by 75.8 billion euros (86.1 billion U.S. dollars) in the first quarter, standing at 117.5 percent of GDP.
Under the Maastricht Treaty, which entered into force on Nov. 1, 1993, member states adopting the euro are required to keep their public budget deficit below 3 percent of GDP and public debt below 60 percent of GDP.
According to data released by the French Ministry of Economy and Finance on Sept. 19, the country's public debt will continue to rise, reaching 119.3 percent of GDP in 2026, and is projected to rise further to 121.7 percent in 2027, more than double the European Union's 60-percent limit. ■

Spain’s government on Tuesday agreed on two housing decrees that would extend protections against evictions until 2030 and temporarily restrict residential property purchases by so-called “vulture funds.”
The measures, agreed by the governing Socialist Party (PSOE) and its junior coalition partner Sumar, would prohibit such investment funds from purchasing homes until 2028 and regulate seasonal and room rentals, according to Europa Press.
Existing rental contracts due to expire before Dec. 31, 2028, would also be extended for two years.

The government requested an extraordinary session of Congress on Friday in an effort to secure immediate parliamentary approval of both decrees, the report said.
The Cabinet meeting began about an hour late Tuesday amid last-minute negotiations, as Sumar pushed for regulations covering room rentals and automatic contract extensions, two demands also raised by the Madrid tenants’ union.
The agreement comes amid protests over Spain’s housing crisis following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid home where she had lived for 71 years.
Hundreds of people have been camping in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol demanding stronger tenant protections after police removed her from the property last week.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday cited her case while promising urgent action.
“Patriotism is also preventing an 87-year-old woman, who has spent 70 years faithfully paying her rent in the same home, in the same neighborhood, from ending up on the street after a lifetime in that house,” Sanchez said.

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's service sector has maintained strong growth momentum this year, contributing 66.1 percent to the country's economic growth in the first half (H1) of 2026, up 5.9 percentage points from the same period a year earlier, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) said on Tuesday.
Since April, the business activity expectations index for the service sector has remained above 55 percent for five consecutive months, well clear of the 50-percent threshold that separates expansion from contraction, according to Li Chunfang, an NDRC official.
The sector has maintained positive momentum, underpinned by supportive policy expectations, growing market confidence, resilient consumption and vibrant opening up, Li noted at a press conference.

Over the past six months, relevant authorities have rolled out 81 supporting measures, while more than 60 percent of the key tasks have seen notable progress. A total of 27 provincial-level regions have also convened meetings or issued policy documents to promote development in the service sector.
With services now forming the bedrock of the Chinese economy, the country has elevated this sector's strategic importance to new heights.
In April, China held a conference focused on the service industry, the first of its kind at the national level, indicating a stronger policy focus on the development of a sector serving as both the largest pillar of China's economy and a major source of employment.
Official data showed China's service sector had surpassed 80 trillion yuan (about 11.87 trillion U.S. dollars) in added value last year, making up 57.7 percent of the country's GDP.
During Tuesday's press conference, Li said China is stepping up efforts to deepen the integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services. Building on two rounds of national pilot programs launched since 2020, authorities are guiding local governments in carrying out a new round of pilot projects to promote closer integration between the two sectors.
Financial support has continued to expand. By the end of the second quarter of 2026, outstanding medium- and long-term loans to the service sector in domestic and foreign currencies stood at 76.22 trillion yuan, up 6.4 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than overall loan growth, the People's Bank of China revealed.
Authorities are also seeking to make better use of existing land and buildings for development of the service sector, and cultivate more internationally competitive "China Services" brands.
Li said China will continue to strengthen resource support, improve policy measures, and accelerate their implementation to further expand the capacity and enhance the quality of its service sector. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Riding the waves: how outrigger canoeing is forging community on Hong Kong's waters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:36:10 CST
20:36:10 KST

by Xu Shumin, Liang Jiajun
HONG KONG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- While Hong Kong is globally renowned for its towering skyscrapers and relentless urban tempo, a growing legion of paddlers heading out into the dawn sees a different face of the metropolis.
For the paddlers, the city is defined by maritime routes threading from Deep Water Bay to Sai Kung and Lamma Island, nurtured by a vibrant network of clubs and enthusiasts dedicated to outrigger canoeing.
In late August, a 43-member Hong Kong delegation returned from the 2026 International Va'a Federation (IVF) World Sprint Championships in Singapore -- a testament to how the sport has evolved from a niche weekend pastime into a sophisticated, competitive discipline on the international stage.
Originating in the Polynesian islands and also known as the Hawaiian canoe, the craft features an outrigger float (ama) attached to the main hull via lateral spars (iako), creating a distinctive, wave-resistant structure.
Paddlers sit single-file in the slender craft, paddling rhythmically on one side before switching. Once an indispensable means of survival for island traversal and open-ocean fishing, it has evolved into a dynamic global water sport.
Watch a six-person canoe (OC6) slice through the foam, and the precision borders on telepathic. At the core of the frenzy is a simple, clipped bark: "Hut!" Calling the rhythm from seat three is 63-year-old Martha Levin. With every cue, all six paddlers cleanly alternate sides in lockstep, setting the vessel's trim and cadence.
Born in Hong Kong, Levin spent years abroad before returning in 1995. Seeking a way back to the emotional fabric of her hometown, she threw herself into water sports at the Victoria Recreation Club, where she now serves as chair.
"I was captivated during a race in Hawaii, looking out at hundreds of boats taking to the ocean alongside leaping dolphins," Levin recalled, her eyes brightening. "Right then, I was hooked. I was completely in love with the sport."
To Levin, Hong Kong's waters offer a diverse year-round training ground: calm, warm waters in the summer contrast with winter swells that can surge up to two meters. "Hong Kong is really my home," she said. "It feels like a way of life to come back here to the team, the camaraderie."
In Levin's eyes, outrigger canoeing is never a solo pursuit. In the same vessel, young corporate professionals in their 20s paddle shoulder-to-shoulder with mothers in their 50s; broad-shouldered powerhouses sit alongside petite teammates whose endurance keeps the rhythm steady. Each must juggle demanding careers, family commitments, and intensive regimens.
"It's more than just me, so everyone makes the effort to show up on time," she noted.
This distribution of power in a six-seater is almost constitutional. Seat three is the metronome, responsible for the switch commands, while seat six, the steersperson at the stern, reads the sea, sets the strategy, and commands the boat's overall course.
Steering from the stern is Alex Miranda, a native of Brazil who now serves as the paddle sports head coach at the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club. Now in his 50s, Miranda remains a fixture across diverse maritime communities and disciplines.
For him, stepping into a canoe represents a deliberate return to nature and community. "You get really focused and all the distractions of everyday life just kind of clear out," he said.
On the open water, there is no margin for complacency. Paddlers must remain hyper-focused, continuously synchronizing their strokes, assessing the hull's trim, and reading changes in the wind and swell. To accommodate varying goals, the club runs structured programs on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays catering to all age brackets.
Miranda and his peers also look beyond local shores, aiming to expand outrigger canoeing into other cities across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. "The Greater Bay Area already has good paddlers coming from the tradition of dragon boating, so they can combine that with outrigger paddling and try something slightly different to grow the sport," Miranda said.
While the sport once drew predominantly middle-aged participants, Miranda has noticed an influx of younger faces filling the docks.
Take Tommy Yiu, a 31-year-old local resident, who cut his teeth on university dragon boating before crossing over to outrigger canoeing in 2024 on a colleague's whim.
Unpredictable weather and shifting currents frequently threaten to throw a canoe off course. Once accustomed to tackling problems single-handedly, Yiu found that battling adversity on the sea taught him humility and team trust. "Survival and speed only come when you surrender your ego and trust your crew entirely," he reflected.
"The moment you set foot inside the boat, your pedigree, your job title, your socio-economic status -- it all evaporates," said 50-year-old crew member Wang Xiaoxin. "Everyone is reduced to the same basic weight, pulling toward the exact same marker."
A mainlander relocating to Hong Kong, Wang found herself in an emotional low two years ago. Multiple sports failed to lift her spirits until her husband recommended outrigger canoeing. The expansive horizon and welcoming community won her over on her very first outing, anchoring her immediately.
"I was an incurable late-riser," she laughed. "Now, dragging myself out of bed at 5 a.m. is second nature, purely because of the camaraderie of my teammates," she said. Recalling her first Round the Island race in Hong Kong, she remembered encountering towering waves near Po Toi Island. Relying purely on mutual trust, the crew persevered through the chop and crossed the finish line.
As a professional jewelry designer, Wang discovered that the resilience she gained on the water seamlessly translated into her daily craft. The rigorous mindfulness required during dawn paddles mirrors the stillness and precision demanded when handcrafting delicate jewelry, the two disciplines feeding into one another.
At the World Championships in Singapore, Wang saw competitors with disabilities racing flat out, and paddlers in their late 70s cutting through the water. "It made me embrace the passage of time and realize that we should never place limits on our lives," she said.
As the session winds down, paddlers rinse the salt from their skin, change into work attire, and disperse into the glass towers in town, the workshops of industrial estates, and lecture halls.
Hong Kong will always have its gleaming skyline, but just beyond the shore, there are waves, winds, and fellow paddlers moving forward as one. ■

====================================================================================================

‘Just like that, I lost my girls’: the mother who feels betrayed by the family courts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

On the afternoon that Sarah’s daughters were taken away from her, they had been due to go to a paddling-pool party. It was July 2020 and, with the easing of lockdown restrictions in England, the girls – then nine and six – were excited about seeing their friends again after months apart. Sarah had just bought them matching swimsuits: blue with sequin unicorns.
But the girls never made it to the party. Three days before, Sarah had received a call from her solicitor. “I could not comprehend what I was hearing,” she says. “My legs started shaking.” Her solicitor explained that she had been called a “narcissist” in evidence presented to the family court, which claimed she was an immediate danger to herself and her children. Both of her girls could be removed from her with immediate effect.
“I kept saying to him: ‘It makes no sense.’” Sarah had committed no crime. Her children’s social workers, teachers and other professionals with whom they were in contact had seen no problem with her parenting. The girls had spent lockdown with their mother “doing maths and fishing for tadpoles. They were safe and happy.”
The person who had “diagnosed” Sarah was an unregulated psychologist, Melanie Gill, whom at one point the judge wrongly referred to as “Dr”, although she had never attained any qualifications that merit that title. Gill has a third-class degree in psychology and a diploma in child forensic studies, which she was awarded instead of a master’s degree because she did not finish her dissertation.
Sarah attended an urgent court hearing via a video call on the morning of the party. It lasted 50 minutes. On the basis of Gill’s evidence, the judge told her that her daughters would have to live with their father and that she had two hours to get them ready to leave. Instead of the paddling pool that afternoon, she told them they would be going on a “two-week holiday with Daddy”.
When their father arrived, the children refused to go with him. “The girls were clinging to me and had to be dragged off kicking and screaming. All the neighbours came out to see what was happening.
“And just like that, I lost my girls.”
That was more than six years ago. Apart from two brief occasions, Sarah has not seen her daughters unsupervised since. Most of the contact has happened fortnightly in public places such as hotel lounges. She has missed birthdays, first boyfriends and academic achievements. She wasn’t consulted when it came to choosing secondary schools or GCSE options. No one told her when one of her daughters received hospital treatment. “I’ve effectively been stripped of all parental responsibility,” she says.
Fighting this has cost her £85,000 in legal bills. Her share of the cost of supervised contact with her daughters has reached £13,000. She is close to bankruptcy. And still she is asking how one unregulated court expert using a theory that official guidance in England and Wales now says is a “harmful pseudo-science” could wield so much power over her life.
Sarah was a teenager when she and her ex got together. “He was the first person I’d ever loved,” she says. They were happy at first, but Sarah says he was controlling and prone to angry outbursts. “It was my first sexual relationship and I didn’t understand it was wrong.”
They married and had children, then she left her job to care for them. After this, she says, he took increasing control of their finances.
By 2018, the couple’s marital disputes had escalated. The police had been called to their address several times and Sarah was becoming increasingly depressed. After she took an accidental overdose and was admitted to hospital, a referral was made to social services, who recorded that the children had witnessed domestic abuse and were showing signs of anxiety.
“He was furious with me that social services were involved,” she says. While they were still living together, Sarah’s ex made an application to the family court to try to stop her from taking the children.
She says that the abuse escalated and she fled the family home with her daughters under police escort. Sarah had reported the allegations of abuse against him and later secured a non-molestation order (a type of protective order) from the family court. In response, Sarah’s ex claimed that she had tried to kill herself (which she denies, supported by hospital records) and that she was “alienating” the children from him. In one statement, he wrote: “I’m being prevented from seeing them even though I’m a hands-on dad.”
In July 2018, a district judge in the family court made limited findings against both parents. They included that Sarah had slapped her ex, thrown things at him, shouted and sworn at him and sent him abusive texts. The judge accepted, too, that her ex had been “nasty” and “intimidating” and had “inadvertently” trapped Sarah’s arm in a door. A court order was made for the children to share their time equally between the parents.
A few months later, however, the girls appeared to be struggling. Sarah’s elder daughter told her GP that her father had smacked her on the bottom and she complained of recurring abdominal pains. Court papers state that the elder daughter later told teachers, social workers and her GP that she and her sister were sent outside by their father in the “cold and dark” and that they took shelter in a wendy house for a while before sneaking back inside.
The next day, according to court papers, the younger daughter recorded a video while hiding under her bed covers. In the audio, her sister and her father could be heard arguing. The elder daughter later reported to her teacher and GP that, during the row, her father had thrown her around, causing her to hit her head and chest, leaving a bruise. The children’s school contacted social services. The girls refused to see their father for eight weeks.
Sarah, meanwhile, made an application to change the shared care order and the girls’ contact with their father was suspended by the court. In April 2019, a social worker fed back to the court that the children were sometimes “scared when with their father”.
Her ex responded by applying for sole custody. He claimed Sarah had been influencing the girls to express negative views about him and that his elder daughter was lying. The court requested that the local authority prepare an independent report. The social worker who wrote the report recommended the children live with their mother and see their father regularly, including on alternate weekends. The social worker said she saw nothing to suggest the girls were being influenced by their mother. She wrote of Sarah’s elder daughter: “This is not the behaviour of a child who has been influenced by a parent.”
Sarah’s ex objected to the report and said he wanted a second opinion from a psychologist. The judge agreed, saying that the social worker had not been trained in “parental alienation” since 2010. Since that time, he said, things had “significantly moved on”.
They certainly had. Parental alienation syndrome was a concept created in 1985 by the New York psychiatrist Richard Gardner. It was based on the theory that a parent can brainwash a child to turn them against the other parent, leading the child to wrongly believe they are being abused. The theory was widely rejected for lacking scientific credibility and by the mid-1990s had begun to fall out of use.
By the 2000s, however, it had resurfaced and the idea of “parental alienation” gained traction as a litigation tactic in the family courts – to much concern. In April 2023, a UN report called parental alienation a “pseudo-concept” weaponised by abusers to discredit abuse claims. The NSPCC has also issued warnings about the concept, while the UK government has said it “does not recognise ‘parental alienation syndrome’ as a diagnosable condition”.
Gill is one of the fiercest proponents of “parental alienation”. By her own estimate, she has given evidence in family courts in England, Wales and Northern Ireland “probably 150 to 200 times” over the past 15 years. During that time, she has given evidence that has been pivotal in the removal of at least a dozen children from their mothers, according to an investigation by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). This includes cases where fathers had been found by the court to be coercive and controlling or to have engaged in domestic abuse. It was Gill whom Sarah’s ex asked for a second opinion.
Sarah had her concerns: “I had seen something that connected her to a fathers’ rights group. My instincts were that there could be some kind of bias.” She wasn’t aware at the time that Gill wasn’t registered with any regulatory body. “Of course, I would have objected on those grounds had I known.” Instead, she says her lawyers told her it would serve her case to be amenable. “I was given the impression the judge didn’t like me and I should not complain,” Sarah says. “Not for one second did I imagine how badly it could go.”
Expert witness psychologists can hold significant power and influence in the family courts in England and Wales. They are duty-bound to act impartially and, since the rules were tightened by law in July, should be registered with the regulator, the Health and Care Professions Council. However, before July, judges could appoint whomever they wished. Gill, who describes herself as “an attachment specialist, psychologist and forensic consultant” working “exclusively as an expert witness”, was appointed in September 2019 to make an assessment of Sarah’s family and was paid £10,688 to do so.
Her views have troubled others working in the field. Dr Jaime Craig, a consultant clinical psychologist and the chair of the Association of Clinical Psychologists UK, believes Gill has an assessment process that assumes “there’s no such thing as domestic abuse”. Gill rejects mainstream clinical psychology and has described her own approach using “attachment science” as being able to “get to the truth of what happened in the past”.
Gill did not respond to requests for comment, but a spokesperson previously told TBIJ that she was well qualified to perform the role of expert witness and had years of specialist training.
In a 2023 case, she told a court: “I have been challenged and questioned on my qualifications in every single private law case I have ever undertaken and I have never been criticised.” Gill claims to be the victim of a “witch-hunt” and her supporters say she has been unfairly hounded by the media and “radical feminists”.
Sarah says her assessment process with Gill was “confusing and difficult”. “She asked whether I’d ever experienced abuse, so I opened up about some of my father’s behaviours towards me – and my ex-husband’s,” she says.
Sarah has fond memories of her father from when she was a young child. While he later became abusive, her mother was always a protective figure. “Despite being subjected to abuse from my father at times, my mother was always a safe, steady, wholesome presence. I told Gill this, but she claimed I was neglected, which I was not in any sense.”
Gill concluded that Sarah’s “narcissism could make her prone to vengeful anger” and went on to recommend “schema therapy”, which is commonly used to treat personality disorders, despite Sarah having never been diagnosed with one. Gill also said there was extensive evidence the children were being alienated from their father by Sarah. There was no mention in Gill’s report of the 2018 court findings of abuse, or the elder child’s specific allegations against her father.
Gill recommended that, in order to safeguard the girls, they should live with their father and receive therapy. After this, Sarah did not see her children for four and a half months.
As family court proceedings are held in private and speaking about them could be in contempt of court, Sarah was not even allowed to explain to close friends why her children were no longer with her. She was, she says, “effectively gagged”.
Sarah is keen to point out that although there were periods where her children refused to see their dad, they always wanted a relationship with him. “They were not alienated; they just didn’t want to live with him,” she says. “I have now become the victim of precisely what I was accused of.”
In August 2020, the decision that the children should live with their father was made permanent at a review hearing. Gill wrote a second report and told the court that the children’s attachment to their mother resulted in them “presenting negative information to her and others to align themselves with her views”.
She said the social worker, the GP, the school and other professionals to whom the children had made negative reports about their father would not have seen these “attachment issues” as “they cannot be identified just by looking at what is happening on the surface”.
She said Sarah’s contact should not progress to unsupervised until she had undertaken schema therapy, which is not widely available on the NHS, costs anywhere from £80 to £200 an hour for private treatment and can take “up to two years”.
Giving evidence, the social worker tasked with writing an independent safeguarding report said, despite Gill’s recommendations, there was “insufficient evidence” to “deny the children contact” with their mother. But the judge found the social worker’s evidence was lacking in the area of “attachment issues”. By contrast, he found Gill’s evidence to be “compelling” and said the picture she painted of the mother fitted “entirely” with his view of her.
In her own evidence, Sarah said Gill’s recommendations had gone against the view of all the other professionals who had dealt with the family. She said she did not agree schema therapy was appropriate for her, as she had not been diagnosed with a personality disorder.
She questioned Gill’s expert status and mentioned her links to a fathers’ rights group. The judge said these criticisms “smack[ed] of desperation” and that Gill’s CV was “impressive”. Sarah’s evidence, he said, was seeking to “portray herself entirely the victim”. Meanwhile, he described the father as “willing to learn” and “wholly child-focused”.
Sarah’s ex did not reply to requests for comment. Previously, he rebutted all the allegations made against him and said that he cooperated throughout court proceedings at a “considerable personal, emotional and financial cost, and with the children’s welfare and best interests at the forefront of my mind and decision-making”.
In court, the judge acknowledged that removing the children from their mother was a “draconian step” taken with “some considerable misgivings”. But he added: “The decision was … based entirely on the expert recommendation and nothing is before the court today to suggest that decision was wrong.”
Sarah’s face lights up when she talks about her daughters. She describes them as sweet, funny, kind little girls – even though her elder is now taller than she is. During previous supervised visits, they talked fondly of school friends Sarah has never met.
The elder is creative and crochets toys and bags. When they still lived together, she would ask Sarah to choose her clothes, but now she is finding her own style. “She’s enjoying cutting up her T-shirts and being an individual,” she says. Her younger sister, meanwhile, loves Taylor Swift and the colour pink.
After the children were taken away, Sarah clung on to the home she had occupied with her daughters after leaving her marriage. “It had been a sanctuary for us,” she says. “If they came back, I wanted it to be familiar.”
When she got home after her daughters were taken away, it felt as if they had died, she says. They had left in a hurry and their toys were exactly as they had left them. “That’s where they stayed for years,” she says, describing the lounge littered with Lego constructions and collections of feathers, shells and pebbles. In the sisters’ bedroom, Sylvanian Family characters were set up as part of a classroom scene. A cupboard had been converted into a doll’s house. One day, Sarah opened it to find a miniature dolly tucked up in bed.
The contact she has had with her children feels far from home. It takes place under the eye of a supervisor, who writes down everything that is said. The contact notes are kept and could later be produced as evidence if required by the court. “The implicit message is that I’m a danger,” says Sarah. “We can’t even go to the toilets without the supervisor.”
On one such loo trip, her elder took the opportunity to whisper that she had started her period. “She clearly didn’t want her sister to hear, so all I could do in response was to give her a hug,” says Sarah. “She was deprived of the intimacy of that mother-daughter moment. So I went home and wrote her a letter telling her about my own experiences.”
In the end, Sarah did not send the letter. She did not want the details of her own first period to be read by the court and her ex, as every card, gift or piece of correspondence had to go through him for approval. Later, she was upset to learn that her daughters were self-harming.
There may now be hope for Sarah. In December 2024, the Family Justice Council (FJC), an advisory body sponsored by the Ministry of Justice, published official guidance that said court-appointed experts should be regulated and should not be asked to look for “parental alienation”, which cannot be diagnosed and which the FJC considers “harmful pseudo-science”. Instead, judges should identify any “alienating behaviours” as factual matters, but only after ruling out domestic abuse.
Then, in a high court ruling in July 2025, a senior judge acknowledged that there were “concerns” about Gill and ruled that the findings in Sarah’s case, based on Gill’s evidence, lacked a “solid foundation”. The judge added that “what the [district] judge expressed to be findings based on Ms Gill’s assessment should not stand as such in any further assessment” and that Gill’s use of “attachment science … makes it very difficult to retain any of what she says as a base for future decision-making”. The judge said there should be “an investigation about the current situation so as to inform … what sort of relationship … the children can have with their mother in the light of their own best interests, wishes and feelings”.
It was a watershed moment, not only for Sarah, but also for other mothers who believe their children have been unjustly removed on the advice of Gill. A transparency order issued by the family court means Sarah can finally talk publicly – albeit under a pseudonym – about her ordeal for the first time.
Since Sarah’s successful legal challenge, another mother has been vindicated after getting Gill’s evidence overturned on similar grounds. In February, the then president of the family division, Sir Andrew McFarlane, issued “firm guidance” around court experts that said courts should no longer use unregulated experts. On 20 July, rules barring unregulated psychologists such as Gill from family courts in England and Wales (unless in exceptional circumstances) came into force.
However, for families such as Sarah’s, the damage has already been done.
Sarah hopes her years of “living in limbo” may soon come to an end. But despite having Gill’s evidence overturned, it has not proved so simple. She should now be allowed to return to a full relationship with her daughters. However, her girls have said they want the supported contact to continue. Sarah fears that therapy provided to the girls on Gill’s recommendation has reinforced the notion that she is a danger to them.
“Their trust in me appears to have been destroyed by whatever they have been told in line with the Gill narrative,” says Sarah. She has seen disclosures from the girls’ schools showing that they were told she was “mentally unwell” and “high risk”.
At a hearing in April, an officer from the Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service, who had assessed the girls, told the court he supported their request for continued supervised contact, even though there were no safeguarding concerns. He confirmed that they had not been told the truth about why they were removed, nor that their removal from Sarah was based on flawed expert evidence, since overturned by the high court.
Sarah’s barrister challenged his report and successfully argued that a new properly trained and regulated psychologist should be brought in to deal with the complex and delicate situation. “They need to know the truth, because their perception of me is based on a lie,” says Sarah. “For all intents and purposes, my motherhood ended the day their father took them away. I will never get back the lost time with my daughters.
“Of course, I’ve been at rock bottom,” Sarah continues. “There have been times when I knew if I spoke out I’d be further punished – maybe lose them completely … But I wasn’t going to let this be a self-fulfilling prophecy; I didn’t want to give any credence to Gill’s theories.
“All I want now is a chance of a future as a family, rather than the strangers we’ve become.”
Sarah is a pseudonym

Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

To what extent is the “the story about the analytic turn” in philosophy a story about politics?
There’s been an increased discussion in recent years of externalist explanations of philosophy, and one such explanation that has gotten a fair amount of attention lately is the idea that McCarthyist anti-communism in the United States in the middle of the 20th Century played a significant role in analytic philosophy’s emerging dominance in the discipline at the time.
In the following guest post, Sander Verhaegh of Tilburg University, shows how the picture is quite a bit more complicated than that, casting doubt on how much the “McCarthyist thesis” can explain.
The post grew out of research Professor Verhaegh conducted for his just-published book, Logical Positivism: An American History (also here and here).
Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look
by Sander Verhaegh
How to explain the analytic turn in American philosophy? One controversial thesis, regularly discussed in the blogosphere, is that analytic philosophy’s dominance is a product of McCarthyism. On this view, anti-communist repression forced philosophers to abandon socially-engaged, humanistic modes of inquiry, and to a replace them with a technical, ‘politically neutral’ approach. John McCumber develops the theory in two of his books and the hypothesis recently resurfaced in publications by Christoph Schuringa and by Robert Hanna, who likens postwar analytic philosophy to “McCarthy-style anti-communist, big-capitalist politics”.
Critics have pushed back hard. Richard Hudelson and Robert Evans argue that McCumber “fails to give a historically or philosophically coherent account” of the analytic turn, while E. J. Spode compares Schuringa’s book to “A Turd in the Punchbowl”. Some contend that the McCarthyist thesis ignores simultaneous analytic turns in Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, such that it offers an “American explanation for … a pan-Anglophone phenomenon”. Others point out that some of the best-known analytic philosophers of the period, Bertrand Russell and Rudolf Carnap, were hardly the apolitical figures the thesis requires; while the most notorious anti-Communist witch-hunters, Arthur Lovejoy and Sidney Hook, were humanist philosophers who had studied with William James and John Dewey.
In this post, I discuss archival evidence that sheds new light on the question. In the last eight years, I spent much of my research time in archives for a book on the history of twentieth-century American philosophy, working through a wealth of material from the period: departmental records, diaries, correspondence, personnel files, and hundreds of newspapers and magazines. The book, Logical Positivism: An American History, reconstructs how émigré positivists and their American students and allies rose to dominance at private and public universities; and it shows that the story about the analytic turn is more complicated than the McCarthyist thesis suggests. In what follows, I argue that the Cold War did play a role in the development of American philosophy, albeit in various unexpected ways ignored by proponents of the McCarthyist view. At the same time, I argue that it was not the only factor, let alone a sufficient explanation, for the analytic turn.
The McCarthyist Thesis
Before discussing the evidence, let us get clear about the explanandum. Though there seem to be as many variants of the McCarthyist thesis as there are historians who have written about the period, no one argues that analytic philosophy itself is a product of the Cold War. Proponents and opponents agree that the analytic tradition predates the McCarthy era, in Europe and in the United States, even if anti-communist pressures may have changed its character in the 1950s. The central question is not to explain analytic philosophy’s presence. It is to understand its hegemonic position by the early 1960s, since American departments and journals of philosophy had been dominated by non-analytic schools and movements before the Second World War.
Naturally, it is difficult, if not impossible, to sharply define what does and does not count as ‘analytic philosophy’. Still, even a cursory look at the composition of American philosophy departments, curricula, and journals, as well as lists of APA presidents and Carus lecturers reveals that something changed in this period. Nor is this an ahistorical projection. At the time, philosophers regularly observed and discussed the rapid transformation of their discipline (more on this below), even if it took a while before ‘analytic philosophy’ became the generally accepted label for the newly dominant approach.
Second, if we are to evaluate the McCarthyist thesis, we need to get clear about the supposed victims of anti-communist repression. Few people will deny that (former) communists and Marxist scholars were pushed out of the profession. The central question is whether the Red Scare also affected pragmatists, phenomenologists, and ‘continental’ philosophers more generally. McCumber and Schuringa answer in the affirmative, arguing that anti-communist pressures blocked out any alternative to the Cold War paradigm; Joshua Rayman and James A. Good deny that pragmatism was a target. George Reisch, finally, argues for the more subtle thesis that McCarthyism played a role but affected analytic and non-analytic philosophers alike. Whereas many logical positivists and their American allies had been politically engaged in the 1930s, they turned to the “icy slopes of logic” in the years thereafter.
Finally, we need to get clear about the mechanisms through which the Cold War reshaped American philosophy. Since only a few, relatively minor philosophers were direct victims of McCarthyite investigations, proponents need a story about how the Red Scare affected the composition of journals and departments of philosophy. Most agree that anti-communist pressures created “a “climate of fear”, stimulating philosophers, journal editors, and university administrators to self-curate to prevent public controversy. But some add that there were carrots as well as sticks: Analytic philosophers were showered with funding and cushy advisory positions at institutes like RAND Corporation. Lastly, McCumber believes that there are conceptual connections between analytic philosophy and Cold War ideology. He argues that while pragmatists dealt with context-dependent problems of men, analytic philosophers saw truth as a property of sentences independent of context, thereby echoing the absolutist modes of thinking that were dominant in the period.
Analytic Philosophy Before the Red Scare
Let us turn to the evidence, starting with the state of American philosophy before the Cold War. Now, even if we accept that the McCarthyist thesis seeks to explain analytic philosophy’s dominance, not its existence or emergence, the timing is awkward: Analytic philosophy already had a solid foothold in the 1920s and 1930s. When Herbert Feigl, the first of the logical positivists to emigrate to the United States, arrived at Harvard in September 1930, it was already considered a flourishing “center” for logic-infused philosophy. Feigl found American colleagues developing ideas that were, in his words, “barely distinguishable” from the Vienna Circle’s scientific world conception, and he regularly attended meetings of a group of talented young philosophers, including W. V. Quine, Susanne Langer, and Nelson Goodman, writing that they were “almost always discuss[ing] logic” and it was “almost like in Vienna!” (letters from Dec. 6, 1930 and Apr. 5, 1931).
Harvard was not an isolated case. Even if American departments were dominated by non-analytic philosophers at the professor level, there is much archival evidence that the new generation had started to adopt the style of philosophy that was in vogue in Cambridge, Prague, Vienna, Warsaw, and Berlin. C. I. Lewis wrote that “logical posi[vi]sm easily takes the first place in the interest and the discussions of our students” (letter, Dec. 1934). Cecil Currie was surprised how much the analytic movement had “caught on among the younger generation” (letter, May 1944), and an advisor for Princeton’s department wrote about “the trend which takes the students at this time to Wittgenstein and other positivists” (letter, Apr. 1947). Even Kant-scholar Charles Hendel, who deeply opposed the trend, wrote that “we ‘older boys’ have to take cognisance … of the enthusiasm and conviction of the younger logicians” (letter, May 1951).
These historical eye-witness reports are supported by bibliometric studies. A network analysis of the most-mentioned philosophers in American journals in the 1940s, for example, reveals that the literature of the period can be divided into at least two, roughly equally-sized clusters of discussion: (1) a set of literature mentioning mostly émigré positivists, Cambridge analysts, and young American philosophers such as Ernest Nagel and Charles Stevenson; and (2) a cluster mentioning American professors who felt that the focus on “logical clarity is producing a kind of sterility that has largely destroyed [philosophy’s] cultural value” (letter by Charles Cory, 1945). The most striking difference between the two clusters is a demographic one: The median birth year of U.S.-based philosophers in what we would now call the ‘analytic’ cluster is 1899, whereas the median birth year of the U.S.-based philosophers in the second cluster is 1882— a difference of seventeen years!
Considering this generational divide, it is much less puzzling that analytic philosophy boomed after the Second World War. In the 1930s, analytic philosophy was already popular among students and junior scholars. But this was not reflected in the hiring of the period. American universities faced severe budget cuts due to the Great Depression (in the 1930s) and the War (the 1940s), so there was little space to hire analytic philosophers. Only when departments could expand in the 1950s, they had the opportunity to catch up. Coincidentally, this is exactly the period when the older generation, educated in what they called “the Golden Age of American Philosophy” (the 1900s and 1910s), retired. In consequence, it was the new, more analytically-minded generation that could steer American philosophy in a different direction, a period when the U.S. student population grew from 2.7 million to 8.0 million in two decades. A study of the growth of eleven prominent philosophy departments estimates that they increased from 6.3 to 17.3 faculty on average, meaning that there was much space for new hires.
Appointments in the McCarthy Era
Even if the timing and the swiftness of the analytic turn are partly explained by a generational shift and a fifteen-year dip in the job market, this does not entail that McCarthyism played no role in the process. So let us turn to academic hiring in more detail. Now, if the anti-communist climate of fear was an important factor in the analytic turn, one would expect deans, department chairs, and university presidents to reflect on the risks involved in hiring pragmatists, humanists, and existentialists irrespective of the candidates’ political ideas and activities. Yet, in my archival research on the hiring procedures of ten departments of philosophy, including both private (Columbia, Cornell, Harvard, Princeton, and Yale) and public universities (UC Berkeley, UMich, UMN, UIowa, and UPenn), I have not found a single example of a philosopher or administrator raising doubts about a candidate because of their philosophical affiliation.
Of course not every meeting is recorded. Moreover, it is well-known that repressive environments can be governed by tacit agreements on how to avoid public controversy. Yet it seems unlikely that the supposed political risks involved in appointing a pragmatist or a phenomenologist did not leave a single trace in thousands of pages of dossiers about possible hires, particularly since administrators often did voice concerns about other ‘liabilities’ involving race and religion. When Yale considered hiring Paul Weiss, the head of department openly shared his worry that he would be a risk because he was likely to have some of the “deficiencies that Jewish people labor”, most notably a “lack of social discretion” (letter, Oct. 2, 1945). And when Princeton was searching a new full professor, the president was openly warned not to appoint a Catholic because members of “the Roman hierarchy” could not “avoid being illiberal” (letter, May 1948). While the records show that some candidates were considered a liability because of their race or religious affiliation, I have encountered no discussions of potential hires who were considered a risk because they were pragmatists or phenomenologists.
Second, it is important to note that all these departments kept hiring non-analytic philosophers. In some cases, it was even an explicit criterion that a position should be filled by a pragmatist or continental philosopher. Jacques Barzun, provost at Columbia, urged the philosophy department to establish “a balance between ‘analysts’ and ‘humanists’” (letter, May 1960) and when Princeton could appoint two full professors, the president and the department agreed that one of the appointees had to be “broadly humanistic in his philosophical orientation” and that the other should be “logical and scientific in his outlook” (memo, Dec. 1954).
Naturally, these conclusions do not apply to philosophers who were suspect because of their political activities. Irving Copi’s personnel file at the University of Michigan contains a letter from William Frankena, defending the former Troskyite because he had “entirely renounced his questionable connections, opinions, and activities” (letter, Sep. 1948). And when the University of Minnesota refused to renew the contract of Forrest Wiggins in 1951, the department’s first Black instructor publicly announced that it was because his “Communist line” had cost the university money in the state legislature (Star Tribune, Dec. 13, 1951).
Cultural Momentum
Finally, let us turn the broader cultural conversation about philosophy. The standard focus on McCarthyism is rather one-sided because it has led historians to overlook other important elements of America’s cultural moment. The 1950s were not just marked by Cold War anxieties. It was also a decade of cultural optimism about science and technology. Science had not just helped the United States win the Second World War. It had also improved the life of average Americans through the introduction of new medical treatments such as polio vaccines, synthetic antibiotics, and ultrasound monitoring; as well as exciting consumer products such as portable television, credit cards, and long-playing vinyl records.
In order to understand the analytic turn, in particular the success of logical positivism, one has to incorporate this cultural optimism about modern science. Today, logical positivism is often associated with the dark sides of science and technology. Positivism is equated with the value-free conception of science that helped universities justify research that was used to sow death and destruction in Vietnam. But it is important to realize that these associations only emerged in the late 1960s, when the protest generation identified positivism as the ideology of the military-industrial complex. In the 1950s, logical positivism was still widely regarded as a model of modern scientific thinking, even in popular newspapers and magazines. Wallace David, a minister and gay rights activist, could note that we live “in a scientific age” and describe himself as a member of the “school of ‘logical positivism’” (ONE Magazine, June 1954). An Alabama newspaper could positively comment on a proposal to add logic to the state school curriculum, noting how comforting it would be to “listen to sermons or to political speeches and be able to say with the logical positivists that they fall short” (The Anniston Star, Mar. 15, 1957). And a political columnist could praise John F. Kennedy’s actions during the Cuban Missile Crisis because he displayed “a harshness of which the intellect only of the logical empiricist intellectual is capable” (Times Argus, Dec. 3, 1962). None of these references reflect any real engagement with positivist views or arguments. But it does provide a window on analytic philosophy’s cultural momentum: logical positivism came to exemplify a modern scientific attitude in a period when ninety-four percent of U.S. citizens felt that science was making their lives “healthier, easier, and more comfortable”.
Pragmatism, meanwhile, often got negative press, in particular during the Sputnik crisis of 1957. After the USSR successfully launched the first satellite, American media were quick to blame the school system, noting that Russian children spent much more time studying science and mathematics. And some of them held the pragmatists responsible considering their outsized influence on American education. E. F. Hutton commented that the Russians “make their kids study!”, noting that Americans did the same “before John Dewey and his followers said children should never be made to do anything” (Houston Chronicle, Feb. 23, 1958). Admiral H. G. Rickover agreed, proposing to replace Dewey’s idea that “the school is primarily a social institution” with a new, more rigorous “education process” centering on the collection of “factual knowledge” (Omaha World-Herald, Mar. 24, 1958). Analytic philosophy was considered new and exciting and pragmatism old-fashioned and outdated, even if pragmatist ideas and perspectives still played an important role in shaping the views of analytic philosophers like Hilary Putnam, W. V. Quine, Ernest Nagel, and Richard Rorty.
* * *
McCarthyism severely affected the lives of Marxists and (former) socialist philosophers. Yet it played a very limited role in the development of American philosophy. Anti-communist witch-hunts may have led philosophers to be more careful in their political pronouncements. But there is no evidence that the Red Scare significantly impacted the composition of departments of philosophy. At the same time, it would be a mistake to conclude that Cold War culture was not a factor in the analytic turn. Although analytic philosophy had been on the rise since the 1920s, demographic and economic developments had halted its representation in philosophy departments. When analytically-minded philosophers finally had the opportunity to reshape the profession, the conditions were ideal: higher education was growing, the job market was booming, and the American public celebrated science, professionalism, and ‘neutral’ expertise.

Malaysia repatriates nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:29:20 UTC
20:29:20 KST

Faisal Mahmud and Riyaz ul Khaliq
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Malaysia began repatriating 1,476 Myanmar nationals Tuesday aboard three Myanmar naval vessels.
The group comprises 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys, and seven girls, age between eight and 60, Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported, citing Home Ministry deputy secretary-general Makhzan Mahyuddin.
The returnees were drawn from 14 immigration detention depots and identified by Myanmar before their names were submitted to Malaysia through an Aug. 13 diplomatic note.
Malaysia says the program is voluntary and being conducted under procedures agreed with Myanmar.
The returnees underwent health checks and identity verification before being transported to the Royal Malaysian Navy base in Lumut.
They are being repatriated aboard the Myanmar naval vessel UMS Moattama, accompanied by UMS King Sin Phyu Shin and the hospital ship UMS Thanlwin, according to Bernama.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim last month announced that Myanmar agreed to accept 5,000 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia, with the Home Ministry subsequently beginning identification and screening.
Later, Anwar said he planned to invite Myanmar military leader Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia for further negotiations on gradually returning refugees while seeking guarantees for their safety and access to medical care.
"People ask why we do not simply send them back. Send them where? Myanmar had refused to accept them before," said Anwar, according to New Straits Times news outlet.
"Now, because of our good relations with Myanmar, they have agreed to take back 5,000 from Malaysia," said Anwar in Simpang Durian town in Jelebu district of Negeri Sembilan state on July 29.

This year's Pacific hurricane season is shaping up as more severe than usual, as a Super El Niño, an extreme version of a recurring weather pattern, wreaks devastation, in the form of historic droughts and flooding.
Hurricane Polo made landfall on Mexico's Baja California peninsula on Tuesday, cutting power and causing flooding as the sea breached coastal defences.
The Category 3 storm is the latest in a busy storm season turbo-charged by the El Niño weather phenomenon which has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.
Polo hit just south of Las Barrancas, a small fishing village in Baja California Sur state on Mexico's west side, the US National Hurricane Centre (NHC) said, warning of life-threatening winds and flash flooding.
As Polo approached, strong winds churned the sea and waves off Puerto San Carlos, a fishing port of nearly 6,000 people in Baja California Sur.
AFP reporters noted that the sea had already breached several sections of a sand barrier, causing water to pour into the street.
The town's power supply was cut, palm trees swayed violently in the wind and Mexican authorities ordered residents to take shelter.
Juan Manuel Sarabia had boarded up the facade of his home and reinforced it with wooden beams.
"It's coming with full force," the 53-year-old whale-watching and fishing guide told AFP.
On Tuesday, Polo had sustained winds of up to 175 kilometres per hour, the NHC said.
'Very severe damage'
This year's Pacific hurricane season is shaping up as more severe than usual, as a Super El Niño, an extreme version of a recurring weather pattern, wreaks devastation, in the form of historic droughts and flooding.
Meteorologists have issued Polo-related warnings of heavy rain and flooding in parts of 10 US states including Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Colorado. Several of the states are experiencing drought.
The head of Mexico's meteorological service, Fabian Vazquez, said storm surges and heavy rains could cause "very severe" damage.
Some 169 shelters have been opened across Baja California Sur.
At one high school near the sea, shopkeeper Maria Palomino was preparing to ride out the storm on a mattress on the floor.
"If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," the 57-year-old said. "We'll be among people we know."
Only a handful of homes and businesses in the town were boarded up or sandbagged against flooding.
A passing police officer told AFP he believed the entire town should have been forced to evacuate.
"Everything is going to flood," he said.
Military deployment
The military has deployed nearly 7,000 troops in Baja California Sur state, where classes were suspended and public servants have been ordered to work from home, where possible.
Laura Velazquez, National Coordinator of Civil Protection, said all maritime activities were suspended in the area.
El Niño raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall.
In addition to Polo, meteorologists are monitoring Rachel, a tropical storm also brewing in the Pacific off Mexico that is expected to run parallel to the coast and is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane mid-week.
