Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 29, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:30:13 CST
19:30:13 KST

CCTV: Today marks the 54th anniversary of the issuance of the China-Japan Joint Statement. As China-Japan relations face grave difficulties, how does China see the historical significance of the four political documents between the two countries, including the joint statement, and how are they still relevant today?
Guo Jiakun: Today 54 years ago, the older generation of Chinese and Japanese leaders, with extraordinary political vision and courage, signed and issued the China-Japan Joint Statement, which marked the normalization of relations between the two countries. In the joint statement, Japan explicitly noted that it is “keenly conscious of” and “deeply reproaches itself” over its responsibility for war and that it “recognizes the Government of the People’s Republic of China as the sole legal Government of China.” The statement also notes that the Government of Japan “fully understands and respects” the position of the Chinese government that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People’s Republic of China. The four political documents between China and Japan, including the joint statement, laid the political and legal foundation for China-Japan relations, and established the rules for properly settling major issues of principle, including history and Taiwan. There should be no distortion or regression, still less sabotage, regarding these principles.
Today, more than half a century later, China-Japan relations once again face a severe situation. The root cause is that the political foundation of the bilateral relations has been gravely undermined. The incumbent leader of Japan not only refuses to reflect on the history of aggression, but also claims that a contingency in Taiwan will constitute a “survival threatening” situation for Japan. This is a blatant challenge to China’s state sovereignty and against the aspiration demonstrated by the normalization of China-Japan relations and the political commitments Japan made to China. Japan keeps peddling the so-called “external threat” narrative, using it as a pretext to speed up remilitarization. The move poses a challenge to the postwar international order and threatens regional peace and stability.
History has repeatedly shown that only by staying true to the spirit of the four political documents can China and Japan keep the relationship on the right course. Just as Foreign Minister Wang Yi noted in the meeting yesterday with Takeshi Iwaya, head of the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade, the pressing priority for Japan is to correct Japanese leader’s erroneous words and deeds on the Taiwan question. Japan should adopt a correct attitude on historical issues, and form an objective and rational perception on China. On this day of historic significance, we once again urge those running the government of Japan to seriously reflect on and correct their wrongdoings, and take real actions to return to the purpose and mission of the four political documents.
TASS: The spokesperson of Kremlin expressed that the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen will provide a good opportunity for a trilateral meeting of leaders of Russia, China and the U.S. What’s China’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: As this year’s host of APEC, China stands ready to work with all parties for fruitful outcomes of the APEC “China Year,” and contribute to the economic growth in the Asia Pacific and beyond.
For your question, I have no information to share at the moment.
Shenzhen TV: It’s reported that the Philippine National Maritime Council on September 25 unveiled an updated maritime chart, which includes islands and reefs in China’s Nansha Qundao such as Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao. What’s China’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: Zhongye Dao and Mahuan Dao are part of China’s Nansha Qundao and Chinese territory. China has indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters. The scope of Philippine territory is defined by several international treaties. China’s Nanhai Zhudao, including Nansha Qundao, lie beyond that scope.
The Philippines’ illegal occupation of several islands and reefs in Nansha Qundao, designation of so-called “Kalayaan Island Group” beyond its own territory, and so-called “maritime chart,” which includes relevant islands and reefs of China’s Nansha Qundao, seriously violate China’s territorial sovereignty and the UN Charter and relevant international laws. Those actions are illegal, null and void.
China firmly opposes any action of the Philippines that harms China’s sovereignty and rights and interests. China will continue taking necessary measures to firmly defend its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea.

====================================================================================================

Timnit Gebru Believes There Is No ‘Existential Threat’ From AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Going rogue. Breaking containment. Misalignment. P(doom). As the industry booms, an entirely new vernacular has emerged in the debates over how consequential artificial intelligence really is.
Within that new parlance, two phrases have become focal points: stochastic parrots and existential risk. And at the center of those is one prominent AI researcher who has never stood down from a fight, Timnit Gebru.
Gebru came into the public eye several years ago after sparring with Google over a research paper she coauthored that called out biases in the company’s AI, saying that LLMs basically parroted their training data and risked perpetuating biased viewpoints. The contested paper resulted in Gebru’s departure from the company, and led her to found an institute that investigates harms perpetuated by technology and supports the creation of unbiased tech tools. She has also authored a new book, Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, expected to ship early next year.
More recently, Gebru has spoken out against a faction of the industry that believes AI is so powerful it could destroy humanity. In turn, some members of that community, including an Anthropic cofounder, have alleged that Gebru’s earlier research about stochastic parrots is no longer relevant, and that AI does have the ability to “think” or reason. (In an interesting twist, or you might say horseshoe, Gebru’s beliefs about the cult-like aspects of AI’s effective altruism community have now aligned her with right-wing entities who have also lambasted these EA groups.)
The AI debate is no longer just about the technology itself, but about ideological groups and strategic narratives, and Gebru believes these narratives are a “harmful distraction” from the real issues with AI. I recently spoke with Gebru about what she believes these arguments are distracting from, and also got her response to critiques that her earlier research underestimates the AI of today.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
LAUREN GOODE: Timnit, thank you so much for being here.
TIMNIT GEBRU: Thank you for having me.
I'm gonna assume that a lot of people know this already, but for those who don’t, a few weeks ago, a young AI researcher at Anthropic stepped down, and in his resignation post on X he indicated that a lot of people within the company feel that we are facing this major existential risk with AI. A few people responded, and there was this whole pile-on and discourse about the real threats of AI.
When you and I spoke in the immediate aftermath, you said you felt that that particular narrative was a distraction from the real problems we’re facing with AI. Can you unpack that a little bit?
I would even go farther than that and say that it’s dangerous. It’s not just a distraction, but it’s harmful.
Before I answer your question, I want to give a little brief history of how this narrative has been going for a long time. Elon Musk and Peter Thiel have been saying this is going on since 2013. Prominent people have been saying that AI is an existential risk to humanity. It is exactly the same rhetoric every three years.
For example, the Future of Life Institute …
Wait, what is that?
The Future of Life Institute is an institute that was founded by Max Tegmark, a physicist at MIT now, and Jaan Tallinn, a billionaire who led Anthropic's Series A funding.
He was a Skype cofounder, correct?
Yes. Jaan Tallinn also funds METR, which is an auditor, a so-called third party, whose report about OpenAI’s so-called rogue agents hacking Hugging Face went viral.
So to the public it might seem that there are so many different entities coming together saying the same thing. But the same billionaires who founded and funded Anthropic, the ones who stand to benefit from its IPO more than anybody else, also founded and funded the institutions warning about the, quotation marks, “existential risk” of AI. They also founded and funded the third parties that are being heavily cited right now as if they are an independent entity.
Tell us why you thought the “machine-god narrative,” as you put it, is a distraction.
It’s even more than a distraction. It’s harmful. The reason I was telling you all these facts is that these people, the funders, the founders, the investors who stand to benefit and profit the most from these companies IPO-ing are saying this, that they have been the ones seeding this narrative going back multiple decades.
So people should ask why. If I stand to get lots of money from a particular thing, why do I seem to be the person saying this particular company might build something that kills us all? It sounds counterintuitive.
This is why I really have a lot of respect for [former Federal Trade Commission chair] Lina Khan, because one of the things she said is that there’s no exception to the current laws we have for AI companies, and they talk as if there is an exception. You’re saying that whatever you’re building is so powerful that it's beyond anything we’ve seen before.
Right. It’s self-aggrandizing. It’s saying we’re the future-makers here, but the future’s gonna be really scary if we can’t continue to build this.
You have to pay attention to what they say in the news cycles. When they say that AI can cause an existential risk, they also say that AI can stop climate change, bring us world peace, and eradicate poverty.
AI can do all of these things because it’s powerful. It can bring us utopia, but also if the wrong people do it and we don’t have guardrails or whatever, it can also just kill us all. So the same people believe these things. There’s only a few people who might be in one of these camps.
When you’re telling people that you have super powerful machines, what you’re speaking to, first of all, is to your investors. You’re saying, “You wanna get your hands on these super powerful machines.” You’re talking to governments saying, “You don’t want your adversaries to get their hands on these super powerful machines. You wanna get your hands on these super powerful machines.” And you're also telling any regulating bodies that whatever regulation they’re thinking about should be about these fictional super powerful things.
If I’m talking about potentially eradicating all of humanity, things like pollution, data centers, they sound kinda small potatoes, right? You're talking about copyright protection for artists, actual lawsuits that are going on right now? The government should not waste its time thinking about this stuff. And if you waste your time regulating us on these small topics, you risk China getting its hand on the super powerful machines. And you don't want that. Trust us, we can build a machine-god that can help us, and we’re telling you we wanna be regulated.
Right.
That’s the first one. The second issue is you can always abdicate responsibility.
In our prior conversations, we’ve talked about the use of certain language or phrases to describe this modern era of AI and how you take issue with some of them. So, for example, in our previous conversation, you said something about autonomous weapons. After that was published, you told me you later regretted saying that because you would’ve phrased it differently. We’ve talked about P(doom). We’ve talked about how when you say that agents have gone rogue, such as in OpenAI scenarios, that you’re essentially removing culpability from the engineers who built those tools.
I wonder if there are groups that are actually more aligned than they realize around safety and transparency, but who are deploying different phrases to describe what is essentially the same thing.
One of the reasons that I regret saying these words is not that I have any issue with the term “autonomous weapons.” It’s a legal term. Even land mines are considered autonomous weapons, legally. It’s just that people in the so-called existential risk camp have co-opted it to mean something different.
When I said the term, I knew. I’m like, “Huh, I wonder if this is gonna be taken in that way.” And it was, because the people talking about existential risks of AI took it to mean what they’re saying, right? Which is like some kind of a superhuman, superintelligent machine doing stuff on its own.
I happened to be at the UN General Assembly this past week. I was part of a side panel conversation, so I was not allowed into the General Assembly nor the Security Council. But a lot of top tech leaders spoke. Both Sam Altman and Dario Amodei talked about the need for global cooperation to address the existential risks to humanity. Dario reportedly said, “If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole.” His competitor, Sam Altman, said, “We could lose control of the future to AI.” So explain how it is that these folks who have these companies that have commercial interests in selling AI are now here on the world stage at the UN saying, “I don’t know. There could be some risks here.” Is this part of regulatory capture? Are they gonna be looking for ways to self-govern before there’s an actual regulatory crackdown on this?
Absolutely, it’s part of regulatory capture.
What can be done? What kind of governance do you think is needed for AI?
So this regulatory capture has been happening for a long time.
In 2023, same thing. Sam Altman said the same thing. We need world cooperation, et cetera, et cetera. The EU AI Act regulated, and then he threatened to pull out of the EU. So you just have to see what they’ve actually done. When there’s regulation that actually regulates them for real things that they’re doing and holds them liable, they threaten to pull out or they lobby super hard to water down that regulation.
On the other hand, they’re going around telling these multilateral bodies that there has to be world cooperation, et cetera, et cetera. And then again, what is this doing? It is selling themselves as organizations that are creating so-called superintelligence, right? So that’s already marketing.
They’re also making everybody scared of anybody else who might be creating such things. So they don’t want open-weight models from China. They don’t want this competition. I am not following Chinese regulation that closely, but they’re not talking about existential risk. They’re talking about deepfakes, and they’re talking about real things that need to be regulated.
So the first one is marketing yourself as creating super powerful, unprecedented things for which we don’t have existing regulation, which is not true. We have existing regulations. But the second one is what they’re doing when someone tries to enforce the existing regulation, they either threaten to pull out or they lobby hard so that they don’t have this existing regulation. So the reason I keep on going back to 10 years ago, five years ago, three years ago, is that it’s the same. In my book, I say it’s “the same movie on repeat with different heroes.”
So what is the solution for governance right now if you had to propose it?
Very, very simple things. First of all, I’m not a legal scholar, but former FTC commissioner Lina Khan outlined five things. One is deceptive marketing practices. You know, there’s a law for deceptive marketing practices, and you can go after companies for that.
Two is transparency, documentation. Before you put something out there, you should be able to tell us where all the data came from and actually document it. This simple thing they don’t do. I’m gonna tell you that they will fight tooth and nail to do the simple thing of documenting data.
Labor exploitation of data workers, that’s another one that they don’t wanna talk about.
We are here in the world, in the clouds talking about superintelligence, where you have hundreds of millions of people around the world painstakingly labeling data, even pretending to be chatbots.
Right. 404 Media recently reported that the new Meta Muse chatbot, when you go to use that for some use cases, actually has a person on the other end responding.
Yeah, very simple. Data transparency, labor exploitation, you should not be able to steal data from people. Even the first three things I talked about, data transparency, documentation, labor exploitation, if they had to abide by laws like that and they were not allowed to steal data and not document it—right now, the market calculation is not working, but with these additional measures, it just would not work whatsoever. You would automatically slow them down and have to make them accountable for something.
Back in 2021, you coauthored a paper that was titled “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots.”
Google had approved it initially, then it was being reviewed. There were parts of it that were in dispute. At some point you said, “Look, if you want me to remove my name from this, I’m not gonna be a part of this.” You ended up decamping from Google. That paper was later presented at the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, and people still reference it.
Can you briefly explain, for someone who’s never heard of stochastic parrots before, what it has to do with the AI we’re using today, what it means?
Stochastic parrots is a metaphor to help people understand what large language models do. Large language models are models that are trained on vast amounts of textual data on the internet, and they are trained to output the most likely sequences of text given their training data. They power most of the chatbots we see today, whether it’s Claude or ChatGPT.
When I wrote this paper ChatGPT hadn’t even come out yet, but we saw the race to build larger and larger language models. So it’s the danger of building larger and larger language models that we were describing in this paper.
That they would essentially parrot people?
So, to parrot is to repeat back without understanding, right? So there was this whole existential risk narrative happening back then too, if you can believe it. You know, OpenAI had claimed that GPT-2, the precursor to GPT-3 that powers ChatGPT, was too dangerous and too powerful to release. There was this whole conversation about whether GPTs can be ethical or are they creative and all this stuff. So we really wanted to ground the conversation in the real issues.
One of these issues is the environmental catastrophe, which a lot of people are now seeing, and that was one of the main sections that Google people were unhappy with. The environmental cost. The other one is not documenting your data because you say you have too much data to document.
The other one is deceiving people into believing that there is a mind behind the textual outputs that they’re interacting with. That’s where we really wanted to explain that these systems are parroting the patterns of their training data.
Mm-hmm.
It’s very dangerous when you’re outputting text like that because when you have plausible-sounding text or very fluent text, there’s so many different kinds of issues that can occur besides you believing that there’s a mind behind a machine. In that paper, we gave an example of this Palestinian man writing “good morning,” which was translated to “attack them.”
Because of that grammatical correctness there were no cues that the translation could be wrong, and people believed the translation. So the other issue of believing there is a mind behind the machine is what we call automation bias. You over-trust automated systems, and if you believe that this thing is an all-knowing machine, then you’re gonna over-trust the errors that you get, right?
It’s funny. I must be too much of an elder millennial because you say that there’s too much automation trust, and I’m so distrustful. If I call the bank and it’s a robot I’m like, “Nope, nope.”
“I don’t want to talk to it.” Exactly.
One of Anthropic’s cofounders, Jack Clark, recently posted something on X. He basically put stochastic parrot in quotes and said it was a memetically fit cognitive virus that spread from 2021, when your paper was out, to 2025.
It temporarily blinded many gifted people to the nature of AI progress, burned up crucial years of research, he says. He later says the use of this frame causes people to materially underestimate what AI systems can and can’t do.
When you saw Jack’s post on X, what was your initial response to that?
I was not surprised, let me just tell you.
This is a talking point that [effective altruists are] telling lawmakers now, because every time I said something, they were like, “Oh, you should not take seriously someone who still takes the stochastic parrots thing seriously in 2026.”
The idea is that the research is outdated, right?
Yeah. And it’s not. It’s so ludicrous that we’re even saying this, because these are definitions of what large language models are.
What large language models are has not changed, will never change. Large language models are large language models. Now, you might have large language models in a separate system. They now have reinforcement learning agents. But our paper was about large language models, and that’s never changed.
And these chatbots still have large language models as a basis. It’s so ridiculous that Jack Clark is talking about overestimating systems, because what I’m seeing is the examples that I just told you. It's over-trusting these systems, not having checks and balances, and ending up misdiagnosing someone’s breast cancer to the wrong side.
There’s a direct line between LLMs being stochastic parrots, essentially, and giving a medical misdiagnosis using an AI tool because why? How does one lead to the other?
The stochastic parrots, they don’t understand what’s inside the text, so you cannot expect them to be factual.
Even if you see something like the AI Overview. I was calling an oncologist friend of mine to ask about a specific medication and whether it was appropriate for a specific use, because I read the academic paper saying that it was not, and I wanted confirmation. And my oncologist friend was like, “Oh, look at the Google Overview. It says that it’s appropriate.” But it turned out not being.
I encounter that all the time with Google AI Overviews.
Because they are stochastic parrots trained to give you the most likely sequences of text based on their training data.
Emily M. Bender has been trying to say this in so many languages for a long time.
Also one of the coauthors on your paper, correct?
Yeah. To say that the research is outdated is ludicrous because right now, as we are hyping up superintelligence and all that, there are news stories that are going unnoticed, which are about the complete opposite scenario that is actually happening in the real world.
My understanding is that some of the biggest critiques people have had about focusing on research from that era is that it may not be incorporating the thinking or the reasoning or even the recursive intelligence …
There is no reasoning. There is no recursive intelligence.
Is there none? How is there none? This is something that, by the way, at the Berkeley AI conference earlier this summer I heard someone from Google talking about recursive intelligence.
Of course they are!
The New York Times just did a big story about how the scientists and researchers right now, that’s what they’re looking towards, recursive intelligence, the AI learning from other AI. Is that a reality? It sounds like you’re saying that’s not a reality.
No, because there’s one problem with AI researchers, which is aspirational naming and aspirational stuff. So machine learning, that’s aspirational naming.
But machine learning is real.
But the naming is aspirational. The machine is not necessarily there.
So just because there’s curriculum learning in AI, it’s a field. But let me give you a paper from my former manager, Samy Bengio, who is a superstar in machine learning, not as famous as his older brother Yoshua. I ask him, “Aren’t you tired of your whole life being, like, debunking the whole reasoning thing every single paper you write?”
He quit after I got fired from Google, and he’s now head of machine learning research at Apple. If you look at almost every single paper that they have, it’s showing how if you change the benchmarks on reasoning slightly, the whole thing breaks down. It’s not reasoning.
Got it.
Let me give you another example. Just because your models, the stochastic patterns that you trained to print out certain tokens, you call them chain-of-thought reasoning. You didn’t know that they were thinking, you don't know it's a chain, you just know that these are tokens that are being printed out, but you call them chain-of-thought reasoning. Now you’re saying that they’re reasoning already.
One of the biggest crises that we have right now is actually sound scientific research. So if you look at my work, if I ever have access to the data, the code, the training data, and the evaluation data, which none of these companies give you those things—you don’t even know if they ingested that benchmark during training or not.
If you ingest a benchmark during training, it’s like studying to the test. It’s like me coming to an exam knowing what the answers to those 10 questions are already, studying that, and writing it down, right? Every time I have had access to these things, I have shown how their claims are not correct.
But then with Samy Bengio and his team’s paper, what they showed—and this is from 2025—is that you just change the benchmarks a little bit, tweak it a little bit, and it all breaks down, showing that you were just relying on the patterns. Now, some people, when I give them this example, they’re like, “Well, but we’re talking about 2026 models.”
Guess what? Real evaluation in science takes time. We should not be going from press releases to lawmakers parroting those press releases and journalists repeating those claims. If you wanna do real research and evaluation, ask for the training data, the evaluation data, and the methodology so we can all reproduce it.
So the thinking, reasoning, recursive intelligence—it sounds like you still see that as something that is purely human. It’s the way our neural processes work, but the AI doesn’t work that way yet. That’s what you believe.
I don’t know if it’ll ever … Like intelligence, that’s aspirational naming. Just to take people back to these hype cycles, I sometimes play this game. I tell them a claim that was made and I say, “Is this 1954 or 2024?”
What would you say is the biggest part of your own thinking, your own research, that has evolved since the early 2020s of AI until now that has surprised you the most?
I have to be actively making space for the kinds of models that I think should be built and building them, and ignore the noise. That’s the conclusion I’m getting to.
That’s your biggest learning, your biggest takeaway.
Yeah.
There is so much noise online right now, it’s hard to get any deep work done if you’re just literally paying attention to whatever the AI guys say.
Even if your research, at this point, is all about debunking what they’re saying, you know? It gets tiresome.
Right.
It’s not fun to do that. It’s more fun to think about the future you wanna have, the technological advancements you wanna have, and work on that.
What would you say gives you the most hope right now for the future of AI?
I want to tell you that we have a list called the AI Resist List, where we talk about people resisting, in the ways that they should resist: in media capture, narrative, data centers, funding, et cetera.
And so we list the ways in which they’re resisting, and also people creating alternative tech futures that don’t kill our environment, that don’t exploit labor, or steal data, and instead are actually actively helping their communities, and these ideologies are spreading, right? You see one small organization somewhere doing something, you get inspired by them, you do something different.
So, I have hope that there are a lot of people tired of what they’re seeing, and they’re actually in small circles doing something different. I believe in human agency and collective power to imagine a better future and stop bad things from happening and ban things if they are bad, right?
My belief in human agency, I think, is what gives me hope.

"The message to Moscow is clear" - Rutte makes a new statement on NATO's support for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Rutte said that Russia had not broken NATO's unity, despite sabotage and drones. The Alliance is strengthening its defence and support for Ukraine.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called on allies to remain calm and continue supporting Ukraine. He noted that Russia has failed to undermine the alliance’s resolve and halt its support for Ukraine, despite the growing number of acts of sabotage and drone incidents targeting NATO. Rutte said this at a press conference on September 29, UNN reports.
Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and halt our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine. Our message to Moscow is clear. We will do more for Ukraine, not less
He noted that "repeated drone incidents on our eastern flank have demonstrated the evolving threat, and we are strengthening our integrated air and missile defense".
"We are adapting and strengthening our posture against drones," the NATO Secretary General said.
Speaking about hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledged that they "have an impact," but, in his words, NATO has "all options for responding: sometimes visible, sometimes not."
"I am not saying that these malicious actions in the gray zone do not have an impact. They can have an impact, and sometimes they have an obvious impact. What I mean is that we have all options for responding. Sometimes visible, sometimes not, not always public, not always 'tit for tat'," Rutte said.
At the same time, he called on the allies: "Continue strengthening NATO."
"And finally, (...) continue supporting Ukraine, because the best response to any actions in the gray zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine, not less. Because ultimately, they want to divide us so that we lose focus on Ukraine and start discussing among ourselves what is happening, why, and how it all fits together," the NATO Secretary General stressed.
Remain calm, continue and support Ukraine, support it more, not less, just as we are doing, also thanks to the European Union and the loan to support Ukraine
He also announced "excellent news": "We have reached the threshold of 10 billion when it comes to PURL funds. This is vital for the items supplied from the United States to Ukraine and financed by Canada and European allies, including the European Union, which plays a major role here."
"So all of this is extremely important. We (...) must not be naive about Russia. But they know that we are stronger, and we must ensure, by continuing our investments, that we will also be stronger in two, three, and five years. And that is exactly what we are doing," the Secretary General said.

How Netanyahu's lies at the UN lost the world but won Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

Breadcrumb
How Netanyahu's lies at the UN lost the world but won Israel
Since 7 October, support for Israel throughout the world has plummeted. In the US in particular, its favourability has dropped from +51% to -16% according to a CNN poll. That's a 65% decline over the past eight years. Most of this happened since 2023, when Israel launched its genocide against Gaza.
Since then, it has devised various strategies to arrest the phenomenon. In 2026, it budgeted $730 million for what's euphemistically called "public diplomacy" (i.e., hasbara). This is part of an Israeli "global intifada" in defence of genocide, which often invokes overused tropes such as "blood libel" and "support for terrorism," etc. This is little more than empty sloganeering based on lies.
Israel paid nearly $50 million to Trump's former digital mastermind, Brad Parscale, to create an AI army of social media bot accounts spouting pro-Israel propaganda. They created their own fake think tank, AI-populated website, and articles.
The battle has raged from world capitals to international fora. This also played out at the annual UN General Assembly meeting in NYC last week. Israel's UN ambassador Danny Danon called for the arrest of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, after the latter repeated his call for Netanyahu's apprehension under an International Criminal Court arrest warrant.
Similarly, when London's mayor, Saddiq Khan, in a 2025 Eid al Fitr message called the Gaza assault a "betrayal of humanity," the Israeli embassy accused him of spreading "Hamas propaganda." It's no accident that both are Muslim and both are courageous champions of Palestinian victims.
Mamdani fired back: “I have been clear about the way that I see the world...When it comes to Benjamin Netanyahu, I have described him as I believe him to be: a war criminal and an architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people."
Netanyahu replied vitriolically: "Shame on you, Mr Mamdani. Shame on you for supporting the Hamas terrorist monsters who butchered our people."
He vowed to "tell the truth" about Mamdani during his speech. As if the NYC mayor was hiding some scandalous secret. What was truly scandalous was that the perpetrator of a genocide could take the podium of an international body to spew his lies. But not to worry, few listened. Only a few diehard delegates remained in the hall. The rest walked out in protest.
To any other leader of any other country, it would be an abject embarrassment. To an Israeli leader, it's a badge of honour.
Outside the UN hall, tens of thousands protested with banners proclaiming "End the Genocide." Among them was award-winning Hollywood actress Hannah Einbinder. She proudly held this banner aloft.
After she was arrested, the proud Jewish anti-Zionist stated on her Instagram story: “If the pictures of my friends and me getting arrested in protest of Netanyahu’s shameful visit to New York draw attention to anything, let it be to the devastating genocidal war Israel is waging against the people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon — to the settler attacks, the home demolitions, the bombing of people as they sleep”.
Netanyahu is always at his best (at least for an Israeli audience) when he's the pugilist, showering blows on Israel's enemies: David battling global Goliath. However, in this case he may win a skirmish via video or a snappy soundbite. But he can never win the war. In fact, he's already lost it.
The Israeli leader also attacked French President Emmanuel Macron for denouncing Israel's West Bank mass murder, in which 1,100 Palestinians have been murdered since 7 October, along with 65 villages depopulated and 5,000 inhabitants ethnically cleansed.
Israeli apologists were in high dudgeon over a single word in a single sentence in the text of his speech. They claim Macron said: "Hamas has never operated in the West Bank”. But this was a mistranslation. He actually said: “Hamas has never dominated the West Bank.” Nevertheless, the hasbara brigade – all apparently members of the Académie Française – decided that Macron actually said Hamas never "was active" there.
And what a field day they had! Parsing a single word to bash a European leader with the temerity to call out Israel for its crimes. This is Israeli apologetics at its most banal. Rather than strength, it signals desperation. Nothing says hopelessness like a leader speaking to an empty hall.
In Europe, Israel and its allies launched additional attacks on progressive foreign leaders who've called Gaza a "genocide" and spoken in support of Palestine. They include the UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, who've announced a sweeping ban on financial and commercial support for Israeli settlements. The chief rabbi accused them of "mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric” betraying a “dangerous obsession with the Jewish state.”
After Berlin's Left Party victory in the municipal elections, Social Democratic Party (SPD) political rivals accused it of antisemitism.
This Israeli campaign offensive has two goals. They seek to distract from the Gaza genocide and the worldwide cratering of support, including the increasing demands among US Democrats for cutting military aid and a ban on settlements. They are also working to feed "red meat" to Likud's domestic constituency ahead of October's national elections.
The Israeli right hates two things in particular: Palestinians (and Arabs in general); and foreign "meddling" in Israel's affairs. This also includes international bodies like the United Nations, the International Criminal Court, and the International Court of Justice. Netanyahu is banking on the "they all hate us" mantra to unite the right and bring it out to the polls.
This campaign is political theatre. The Israeli leader is using an international campaign to win a domestic election. He clearly doesn't care that he's hated so deeply abroad that anything and everything he says elicits disgust, rather than agreement. No one except the die-hard Zionist few can stomach his lies, which are part of a desperate attempt to staunch a self-inflicted wound that can never be healed.

NHRC seeks reports over alleged use of minors in scripted social media videos in UP’s Etah
NEW DELHI: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Tuesday took cognizance of a complaint alleging the repeated use of minor children in "scripted, objectionable and politically sensitive" social media videos linked to a purported coaching centre in Etah, Uttar Pradesh.A bench headed by NHRC member Priyank Kanoongo issued notices to the senior superintendent of police and district magistrate of Etah, Meta India’s managing director and country head, and the secretary of the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY), seeking action taken reports within two weeks, news agency ANI reported.
The complaint raised concerns over the children’s dignity, privacy, psychological well-being, parental consent and possible exploitation. The NHRC has directed Etah police to identify the children involved and ensure their protection and counselling.The police have also been asked to identify those controlling the social media account and examine the role of adults involved in scripting, recording, uploading or facilitating the videos. The commission directed that appropriate legal action, including registration of an FIR, be taken if a cognizable offence is found.
The NHRC has separately asked Meta to explain how content featuring minors was repeatedly uploaded and circulated, what steps were taken to restrict or remove it, and whether any monetisation or commercial benefit was generated from the content.

Iran's Ghalibaf warns no country can sell oil if Tehran is blocked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:26:58 UTC
19:26:58 KST

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned on Tuesday that no country in the region would be able to sell oil if Iran were prevented from doing so, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
“The US and other countries should know, as we have said, that in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf said.
His warning comes as Iran faces severe restrictions on its oil exports amid the ongoing conflict with Washington and US sanctions.
Iran’s Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in August that the country’s oil exports had fallen to zero, saying Tehran was no longer exporting crude because of the war and sanctions.
The US military, meanwhile, said on September 19 that more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz in recent months with US military assistance, while stating Iran had exported “zero barrels” under what Washington calls its “ironclad blockade.”
“If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Ghalibaf said.
Rejected proposal
Earlier this month, Ghalibaf warned that US energy infrastructure and assets around the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could face Iranian retaliation if Washington attacked Iran’s oil and gas facilities.
Ghalibaf also referred to recent remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning the Strait of Hormuz and the passage of vessels through the waterway, describing them as a repetition of earlier US claims.
Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal commercial traffic within seven days, saying Tehran’s conditions were unacceptable and claiming Washington already had “total control” of the waterway.
Under Tehran’s proposal, Washington would release frozen Iranian assets, lift oil sanctions and end the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, after which Iran would move to reopen the strait and talks on a final agreement would begin.
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz restricted while demanding that Washington fulfil commitments under a June memorandum of understanding.
Iran says that the waterway will not fully reopen until Iran’s conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Qatari mediators will present the US with new ideas discussed with Tehran on how to meet Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Swift retaliation on ‘adventurism’
Ghalibaf also warned Washington against further pressure on Tehran, saying Iran will not retreat in the face of what he described as “air or commercial blockades.”
His comments come as Washington has expanded economic pressure beyond Iran’s oil and maritime sectors to civil aviation.
“The leaders of the White House should know that Iran, a wise nation that has made history, will never retreat because of lines being drawn, speeches, or air or commercial blockades,” Ghalibaf said.
He added that Iran’s response to “any threat or adventurism” would be “regrettable and swift.”
In February, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continue to escalate between the two sides.

Robert F Kennedy Jr laid out an expansive vision for collecting, sharing and analyzing US health information at a Maha event hosted by a close ally and outspoken anti-vaccine activist.
Medical and lifestyle data, from doctor’s visits to exercise, should be connected and shared with the government and independent researchers, where it can be searched by AI – including potential links between vaccines and health outcomes including autism and mortality, suggested Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine skeptic.
“We need to use America’s health data to determine whether the food we eat, the chemicals we encounter, the vaccines that we’re administering, the other environmental and lifestyle exposures are contributing in one way or another to the chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said at an event with the Maha Institute on Monday, with about two dozen people tuning into the live stream.
The Maha Institute is headed by Mark Gorton, who called himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference” two weeks ago. The institute was co-founded by Tony Lyons, whose publishing house gave $4m to Kennedy through various Maha foundations with funding from political contributions and health-related corporations, according to reporting by the New York Times.
Kennedy has focused on pulling together data from all of the agencies he oversees, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).
Trump speaks after meeting with AI company executives
Speaking after a meeting with several AI company executives, Donald Trump said that there “was a lot of commonality in this room”.
A reminder that some of those at today’s meeting include Open AI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
When it comes to further guardrails on development, the president said that “tremendous self-regulation” should be the path forward, compared with the calls that there should be greater congressional oversight.
On the topic of datacenters, Trump insisted that the structures – which are used to house thousands of energy-intensive servers for tech companies – “are going to be very popular”.
This, despite frequent polling which shows that an overwhelming majority of Americans do not approve of more datacenter construction in their communities.
“The areas with datacenters have become very rich,” Trump claimed, without citing any evidence. “People have become very rich. Their taxes have gone down, not up, and a lot of good things have happened.”
In fact, several areas that are the site of datacenter development have raised concerns about water quality, noise pollution and potential impact on their electricity bills.
Jack Smith faced Senate lawmakers on the judiciary committee for a contentious hearing that saw a number of Republicans accuse the former special prosecutor of perjury, and conducting a political witch-hunt against Donald Trump when he secured two indictments against the president that were later dismissed when he took office. Many GOP lawmakers hurled insults and accusations, with little evidence, at Smith. The former special counsel stood by his findings, and said that his investigations found “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that Trump engaged in criminal activity. He also fended off allegations about the legality of procuring call toll records – and explained several times what these are and aren’t – outlined the persistent attacks he and former colleagues have faced from lawmakers and the president in the years since he prosecuted Trump and defended himself against the accusations that his work was politically motivated. Democrats, meanwhile, blasted their colleagues for peddling “the Big Lie” and called the hearing a “farce”.
In Washington, Trump said the US ‘can’t stifle’ AI as he unveiled a new tool to streamline federal government information. The president made his views on any guardrails on AI development clear again, after previously branding the calls as a “hoax”. Also today, Trump met with several AI company CEOs at the White House, alongside Republican House speaker Mike Johnson.
Trump also used the opportunity – now a little more than a month away from the midterm elections – to repeat his claim that the war with Iran will be over “very soon”. This despite another week of stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran via mediators. “They’re failing very badly,” the president said. “They will not have a nuclear weapon. And oil prices are going to be tumbling down, just like they were before.” He again referred to the conflict as a “little excursion”. A reminder the war is now in its seventh month, and has caused a global energy crisis that has seen the average price of a gallon of gas increase by a dollar.
A Republican senator blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with the Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it.
Smith pushed back against a number of Josh Hawley’s accusations, including the process the former special prosecutor went about to get records from the National Archives, which included text messages between White House officials and 44 members of Congress
“That was a request for White House phones,” Smith said, noting that these happened to have contacts with members of Congress in it. “It was also inaccurate to state that our indictment happened on 2 October. We indicted that case in August [2023],” Smith said, noting that he and his team and consulted with the Public Integrity Section of the justice department, who “ultimately concurred” that they had “followed the election year sensitivities policy”.
Hawley accuses Smith of attempting to 'interfere' with presidential election through Trump investigations
Josh Hawley – a Republican senator and fierce Trump ally – launched into his critiques of Smith from the jump.
“Your investigation, so-called, your prosecution, so-called, was nothing other than an attempt to interfere politically in a presidential election in the United States of America,” Hawley said, repeating many right-wing conspiracies about Smith’s motivations. “You twice indicted a presidential candidate.”
When Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, asked Smith about whether there was anything he would have changed in the way he handled his investigations into Donald Trump, the former special prosecutor said that he learned, throughout his inquiries, that if he only stuck to confining his comments to the courtoom “people can unfairly malign your team and unfairly malign you and your case”.
He added:
There are things being put out daily that are patently untrue … I’m not advocating that prosecutors in the future start going on the internet every day responding to comments … I do agree that prosecutors in the future need to learn to be able to communicate to the outside world because I believe strongly we did our investigation the right way, but I limited myself in who I talked to about that.
Jack Smith tells Darline Graham her brother would have 'likely' been a witness in the case against Trump
Ariana Baio
Republican senator Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham, used her time questioning Jack Smith to accuse the former special counsel of adding “stress” to her brother’s life through subpoenas.
The South Carolina senator, appointed to replace her brother who died in July, told Smith that he should be “ashamed” of himself and that it made her “sick” to think that Smith’s subpoenas of Lindsey Graham’s phone records would have stressed him out.
“Do you really believe that Lindsey was going to destroy evidence that was not even in his possession?” Darline Graham asked.
But Smith responded, saying Lindsey Graham was “a patriot” and was not the target of his investigation.
“He likely would have been a witness in our case,” Smith added.
Cory Booker rails against Republicans 'gaslighting' public by perpetuating lie that Trump won 2020 election
Back at the hearing, Democratic senator Cory Booker accused Republicans of “a farce”, levelling that they were “gaslighting” the public by “continuing to perpetuate the big lie in America that Donald Trump was somehow cheated out of the 2020 election.”
This big lie has gone on [long] enough. We have people who are serving at the highest offices in the land that repeat the big lie. We have people running for office in the Republican party that can’t even tell the truth.
And today’s farce – today’s gaslighting – cannot obscure the mountain of evidence and what Americans saw with their own eyes.
A visibly frustrated Booker lamented that this was unfair to Jack Smith and his family, but also to the American people who continue to struggle with problems including high gas prices, lack of health insurance coverage, and childcare costs.
The New Jersey senator ended, addressing Smith:
What do the Republicans in control of Congress do with their closing statement before an election? They carry out the big lie. They persecute prosecutors. They do Trump’s bidding. They choose Trump over truth, corruption and crimes over the constitution, and I’ve had enough of it.
This hearing is a farce. And I’m sorry for what you and your family are enduring as a result.
Utah Republican blocks bill to ban Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center without Congress’s approval
Joseph Gedeon
Away from the hearing for a moment, a Republican senator last night blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress.
Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with the Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it.
“First, he destroyed its programming, and now, he wants to destroy the building itself,” Merkley wrote in a statement. “All because the law says Trump can’t put his name on the building.” He called the president’s threats “straight out of the authoritarian playbook”.
Murkowski, who chairs the appropriations subcommittee that funds the center, said last week that lawmakers had authorized and funded substantial renovation work, but “what was not authorized is a demolition of the Kennedy Center”.

Ted Cruz angrily questions Jack Smith, says Javert from Les Mis would look in 'astonishment'

How AI is becoming a new battleground in Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:20:52 UTC
19:20:52 KST

Breadcrumb
How AI is becoming a new battleground in Israel's election
East Jerusalem - Like a scene from an action movie, Israeli political party leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Avigdor Lieberman descended an elevator shaft, tore off their spy gear, and tried to break into the prime minister’s office.
When their attempts failed, Eisenkot said to Lieberman in Hebrew, “I have the master [key],” and the video cut to Israeli MP and leader of the United Arab List (Ra'am), Mansour Abbas, waving a giant set of pliers with a sinister grin.
In fine print in the top right-hand corner of the video, it reads 'AI: This content was created through a digital medium and is not original.'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu posted the AI-generated video on his X account with the caption, “Eisenkot will form a left-wing government with [Israeli Democrats’ leader] Yair Golan and the Arab parties”.
It’s one of a myriad of images Netanyahu and other Israeli politicians have shared ahead of Israel’s national elections scheduled for 27 October.
In fact, Netanyahu’s Likud Party leads in the amount of AI-generated content they’ve distributed throughout this election cycle.
According to the “Ze Be AI” project by Israel’s Open University, 13 per cent of content published by politicians and political parties was created with artificial intelligence. Of that number, 70 per cent of the AI content came from Likud.
Highlighting their opponents’ willingness to work with Palestinian parties is a common theme for these AI campaign adverts.
AI becomes a new political weapon in Israel
In a video posted by Itamar Ben Gvir, Israel’s National Security Minister and leader of the Jewish Power Party, former police officer Yoav Segalovitz is seen wearing the flag of the Al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ military wing, while handing out pastries to a smiling queue of Palestinian prisoners.
In the preceding scene, Abbas kisses Segalovitz while draping him in the green sash. Segalovitz joined Abbas’ party last month, prompting Ben Gvir to release the AI-generated video with the caption, “Marhaba (hello in Arabic), ya Segalovitz. The Eisenkot brothers and [former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali] Bennett are proud of you,” in Hebrew.
Another AI video, posted by Bezalel Smotrich, Israeli Finance Minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, portrays a phone conversation between a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, with the West Bank resident warning that Smotrich is going to Judaize the Naqab (Negev) and Galilee, just as he did with the West Bank.
“Over here it is all lost. They don’t let you run wild anymore and build without stopping,” the character, Ahmed, says.
Using AI, Smotrich, Ben Gvir, and Netanyahu are attempting to instil fear in Israeli voters that their opposition - in collaborating with Palestinian parties - will lead to terrorism, and that under their leadership, Israel’s expansionism will thrive.
In response to several controversies surrounding the use of AI-generated campaign materials, including a Likud video showing Eisenkot running into the arms of Abbas after snubbing an individual resembling his son, who was killed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, authorities have stepped in.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has mandated the aforementioned AI label to be displayed on all AI-created campaign content that “could appear to have been authentically documented when it was not,” meaning not all AI images have to be disclosed.
“It's not real, it's an AI. So when we cannot tell what is true and what is generated any longer because of AI slop, people’s minds become very weary. They don't have the energy to start determining what is real and what is not,” Dr Sharon Haleva Amir, a communications professor at Bar-Ilan University, told The New Arab.
“What it causes is that you can no longer say what is true and what is false in the general sense - to an ad or a statement or an agenda. You just don't believe anything anymore.”
Changing the way Israelis vote
A month after Israel’s last election, in November 2022, ChatGPT debuted, and subsequently unleashed a swarm of AI tools into the public sphere.
Almost four years later, this is Israel’s first election in the age of AI and will test how much influence the technology has - not just over day-to-day lives, but politics as well.
“These things meddle with your brain in ways that the people don't understand or perceive in real time,” Haleva Amir said. “From a democratic point of view, AI pulls the rug out from under your feet because this is not really your decision. Your mind is being played with.”
And with AI distorting reality, Dr Tal Elovits, a political analyst and communications lecturer at Reichman University, explained it reinforces the scepticism that Israeli society was already experiencing in the aftermath of the coronavirus pandemic and Hamas’ 7 October 2023 attack.
“Conspiracy theories that are blending with political campaigns and with the generated AI content, which looks good, have a tremendous effect,” Elovits said. “It makes the whole information environment become untrustworthy. For the general public, if you don't know where the truth lies, if you don't know how you can search for the truth, it makes political convincing and political competition very, very difficult.”
In addition to increasing the level of distrust in the public, AI also risks compromising election integrity.
“One of the affordances of AI-generated content is that you can prepare a lot of versions. Different people can receive different ads,” Haleva Amir said.
“Like we have with search engine optimisation, today there are also firms that do large language model [LLM] optimisation, and in this way, we cannot even know what people are being fed with because these things are behind the scenes.”
AI has become so advanced that its messages are no longer simply tailored to individual commercial interests.
“We are no longer talking about a single ‘campaign ad’ for everyone, but an emotional pressure point that speaks directly to the fears, anger, or hopes of a specific individual,” Dr Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, head of the Israel Democracy Institute’s in the Digital Age Program, wrote.
As politicians use AI to influence, Israeli voters are expected to use it in their decision-making.
Through a survey, the Israeli Internet Association found that a quarter of Israelis are considering or intending to use AI to determine who they should vote for.
“If the information is not correct and since people do not check anymore, then the [LLMs] can circumvent the way voters think,” Haleva Amir told The New Arab.
While AI has sparked alarm in the run-up to the election, it also poses a threat on Election Day as robocalls could disseminate false information to voters.
Similar to Netanyahu’s infamous 2015 rallying cry that falsely claimed, “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls,” AI bots could spread propaganda designed to manipulate votes.
Possible violations, like these, of the Central Elections Committee’s new AI law can be reported to the committee through a petition and if the material does breach the law, the content will be removed. Experts stress, though, it’s a little too late once the material is published.
“The content itself is already living online. It already has multiplied itself,” Elovits said. “So the damage was already done even before the committee was able to discuss if it's illegal.”
Amid weak election oversight, Haleva Amir advises that the public should become more informed on the capabilities and dangers of AI.
“Laws will not be enough or sufficient because technology always exceeds the law,” Haleva Amir said.
“The real answer to all these things should come from the people…by raising awareness and educating people and giving them tools to criticise and reflect and understand AI literacy.”
Jessica Buxbaum is a Jerusalem-based journalist covering Palestine and Israel. Her work has been featured in Middle East Eye, The National, and Gulf News
Follow her on Twitter: @jess_buxbaum

Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with surprise performance

Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with surprise performance
- Published
Celine Dion has opened Paris Fashion Week with a surprise performance of her 2002 hit I'm Alive, underneath the city's famous Eiffel Tower.
The Canadian star, who was diagnosed with a rare neurological disease called stiff person syndrome in 2022, took to the runway at the end of L'Oreal's annual show.
The singer, who wore a ruched full-length velvet black gown, was later joined by famous ambassadors for the French brand, including Viola Davis, Simone Ashley, Aja Naomi King and Eva Longoria.
Dion recently performed a comeback show in the city earlier this month, her first since her 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short.
Paris Fashion Week, showcasing women's spring/summer collections, runs until 6 October.
Actress Viola Davis was feeling the love from the crowd as she joined Dion under the stars in the French capital.
Kendall Jenner also modelled at the show, wearing a sheer black halterneck dress with thigh split and an ivory corset underneath.
Supermodel Cara Delavingne, meanwhile, walked the runway in a sparkling red sheer dress with train.
Pop star Rihanna brought her usual fashion credentials to Paris on day one, with a shimmering, glamorous copper two-piece worn over sheer black lingerie.
She was on the front row of the Matières Fécales fashion show - the label behind Zendaya's angel wings dress at The Odyssey premiere in New York this summer.
Wicked star Cynthia Erivo was also in the French capital at a Tiffany and M.A.D - Musée des Arts Décoratifs - event.
Other labels showing in Paris over the next week include Louis Vuitton, Tom Ford, Schiaparelli, Givenchy, Jean Paul Gaultier, Balenciaga and Loewe.
The fashion world is keeping a particularly close eye on Dior and Chanel, after both signed up new artistic directors last year.
Matthieu Blazy took over as Chanel's creative director in early 2025, while Jonathan Anderson began the same role at Dior last summer.
This week should see the pair continue to solidify their strategies for the two brands. Expect some serious aesthetic rivalry on the runways.

Era of Iraq without US troops begins as combat presence ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:20:13 UTC
19:20:13 KST

Breadcrumb
End of an era as US-led coalition forces withdraw from Iraq
Baghdad and other Iraqi provinces hosting military bases used by foreign and US forces are entering a new chapter with the end of the "combat and operational presence" of US forces and the international coalition.
Baghdad no longer has any field barracks or combat camps after Lt Gen Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and head of the Iraqi government, announced that the Victory military base, located near Baghdad International Airport west of the capital, is now completely free of US personnel as part of the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq.
A new framework based on the bilateral security and political relationship between Baghdad and Washington is set to follow after the withdrawal.
Iraq says it will work to cover the shortfall in military aviation capabilities that will follow the departure of the international coalition, stressing that there will be no foreign combat forces or military bases in the country after 30 September.
Years of US forces in Baghdad
For years, the US military and security presence was distributed across strategic sites inside and around Baghdad, including the Victory military base complex, the largest operations management centre near the capital.
Victory housed headquarters for the general staff, reconnaissance centres, and facilities securing air and logistical transport, as well as advisory headquarters in Baghdad's "Green Zone", the government district.
These forces focused on coordination through the Joint Operations Command to protect the area around the US Embassy and nearby institutions.
In Anbar province in western Iraq, Ain al-Asad airbase was a vital artery for air support, radar systems and supplying equipment and support to fronts near Baghdad.
Harir Airbase in Erbil, the centre of the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq, emerged as a hub for technical support and logistical movements in the north. Its various roles included intelligence gathering, intelligence coordination through unmanned aircraft, providing air cover, training and equipping Iraqi forces, and carrying out targeted strikes against remnants of the Islamic State.
Iraqi government military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced on Monday, 28 September, that the international coalition forces had begun withdrawing from the base, saying in press statements that the withdrawal would be completed by 30 September.
Under the 2008 security agreement between Baghdad and Washington, US forces completed their full withdrawal from military bases and cities in December 2011.
The final convoys crossed the southern border into Kuwait, with Baghdad announcing at the time that it had taken over the sites and bases from the Americans and established national sovereignty.
But Iraq soon became compelled to submit an official request to Washington for training and air support after Islamic State occupied about 30 per cent of the country in 2014, amid a security and military collapse of the Iraqi army and armed forces that continues to raise questions without answers.
As a result, the US-led international coalition was formed, comprising 89 countries and international organisations such as the European Union and NATO.
US advisory and combat groups returned to scattered bases, including in Baghdad and Anbar.
The role of the international coalition and US forces in the war against Islamic State from 2014 to 2017 contributed to providing air cover and carrying out direct strikes against the group's headquarters and movements, as well as coordination through reconnaissance aircraft, intelligence gathering and identifying field targets, and training Iraqi military forces, equipping them with modern equipment and weapons, and providing advice on managing battles.
The role of Iraqi forces and Popular Mobilisation Forces brigades was to conduct direct ground combat and carry out raids and operations to liberate villages and cities that had been under the group's control.
But the assassination of Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi Al-Muhandis, deputy head of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, and Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani near Baghdad International Airport on 3 January 2020 marked a decisive strategic turning point like the relationship between armed factions close to the "Axis of Resistance" and US forces and the international coalition in Iraq.
These factions chose to apply political pressure and launch continuous and systematic military campaigns.
This translated into parliamentary demands to expel foreign and US forces as "occupiers", alongside moves to launch strikes and attacks against the US Embassy in Baghdad and vital military bases, including "Victory, Asad and Harir", using missiles and drones.
These attacks led to a state of isolation and heightened security precautions inside headquarters and bases.
The movement of US forces in the field was restricted, and Washington was often forced to redeploy its forces and withdraw some personnel from secondary bases, consolidating them in more heavily fortified camps.
The tensions pushed forward negotiations to restructure the military presence and shift it entirely towards an advisory and bilateral framework.
Baghdad and Washington announced the end of combat missions at the end of 2021, with the missions changing from combat to advisory and training roles, without ground combat forces on the ground.
This followed lengthy rounds of dialogue conducted by the Joint Higher Military Committee between the two sides, which established timetables for evacuating sites, dismantling combat infrastructure and returning full management of the airspace and bases to Iraqi military forces.
In this context, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said the international coalition had handed over all its bases and headquarters to the authorities and that there would be no coalition combat or training forces after the end of this month.
Maan added that Iraqi security forces were ready to take over the security file and capable of managing it after the international coalition withdrawal.
He said in a press statement that "relations with coalition countries after their withdrawal will become bilateral".
Optimism and objections
For his part, Ali Al-Fatlawi, a member of the Coordination Framework alliance, said to The New Arab, "Iraq's sovereignty is indivisible, and we see ending any US military presence inside Baghdad and its bases as an inevitable step that has been long awaited."
"Previous experiences, beginning with the 2011 withdrawal and the return under the pretext of the Islamic State in 2014, taught us that real stability is not achieved through the presence of foreign forces but through complete reliance on Iraqis," he said. "the withdrawal of the international coalition's combat forces and the complete clearing of Baghdad and its headquarters of any field barracks is a national achievement that reflects the high readiness of Iraqi forces".
"The security situation today is under the full control of our security institutions, and what the agreement stipulated is a smooth and carefully planned transition from a direct military and field role to an equal bilateral security relationship based on training, arms supplies and intelligence sharing to ensure that Islamic State threats do not return," he added.
"Clearing the capital of signs of foreign and US military presence represents a pivotal turning point in the history of security alliances in the region," researcher Adnan Al-Kinani told TNA. "This shift from a field combat presence to institutional partnership tests the state's ability to control the pace of the domestic security scene and remove political and weapons-related pretexts."
"Iraqi forces now face the challenge of proving their direct field capacity to manage the vacuum and sustain stability without direct foreign support," Kinani added.
Despite optimism in Baghdad over the departure of US forces and the announcement of a three-day public holiday after 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day", the Kurdistan Regional Government has openly expressed its concerns over the US withdrawal.
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described the US military withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful" and said it would leave Washington's Kurdish allies without protection.
He warned that US President Donald Trump risked repeating the mistake of the administration of President Barack Obama, which withdrew in 2011 before being forced to return.
Barzani warned in an interview with the Financial Times that "the US withdrawal is happening at a particularly turbulent time in the region".
"We are weak, and we are under attack. To be left alone now without any proper defence system is shameful," he continued. "And when we are prevented from buying the sufficient weapons needed against these missiles, drones and advanced systems, we naturally become more vulnerable by design."
