China Focus: China's retirees embrace seasonal home rather than check-in tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:58:01 CST
18:58:01 KST

GUIYANG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Every year by late June, 66-year-old Li Donglai resettles into his summer routine in Anshun, a city in southwest China's Guizhou Province. This is not a tourist holiday, but a seasonal life away from his own home.
Li, from Chongqing, spends more than two months in Anshun each year, drawn by its mild summer weather, nearby hospitals, and everyday conveniences. He buys vegetables at the local market, takes walks around the neighborhood, and heads out to explore attractions within reach.
"I used to think retirement meant staying at home, looking after my grandchildren and remaining in my hometown," he said. "After experiencing seasonal living elsewhere, I realize I can actively choose how to spend my later years."
Li is one of a growing number of Chinese retirees who have moved beyond check-in tourism -- a rushed way of sightseeing. They choose the same place to stay for weeks or months each year and build everyday routines there. What begins as a trip becomes a way of living for part of the year.
MOVING WITH SEASONS
For many retirees, it is the thermometer, not the hometown, that decides where the year is spent.
Zhao Tianlong, who runs a seasonal-living center in Yunnan, sees the effect in his clients every year. From June to September, retirees from hot regions such as Hunan, Sichuan and Chongqing head to cooler Yunnan cities like Kunming and Dali. From November to March, retirees from northern China head south to escape the cold.
Places in Guizhou, Yunnan, Guangxi and Hainan have become popular destinations, combining comfortable climates with well-developed healthcare, transportation and everyday amenities. In Yunnan alone, local reports show seasonal-living visitors topped 5.51 million in 2025, up 41.4 percent from a year earlier, and stayed an average of 83 days.
Li Ying'an, 74, is one of many Chongqing residents who flee the summer heat. He describes life back home as "living in a steamer." He and his wife compared several cities' climates, healthcare and living costs before settling on Qujing in Yunnan, where they have now spent 11 summers.
Liu Yufen, from northeast China's Jilin Province, spends her winters in China's southern island province of Hainan to escape the cold and ease her joint pain. "Take a walk in the park next door in the evening, and you'll hear Northeastern accents everywhere," she said.
FINDING NEW CONNECTIONS
Beyond accommodation, food and sightseeing, seasonal living is also meeting a deeper need for companionship and social connection.
Wang Fei, who heads a department serving seasonal residents in Anshun Economic and Technological Development Zone, puts it simply: climate brings retirees to a destination, but social connections can keep them there.
For many seniors, retirement can mean a shrinking social circle. Zhao Tianlong said many older people living in high-rise apartments in cities barely know their neighbors, while their children are busy with work and their own families. As a result, they often spend much of the day alone or with their spouse.
To bring people together, Zhao has organized paper-cutting, calligraphy, poetry recitation and table tennis at his center. Similar activities have become common in seasonal-living communities, giving retirees opportunities to pursue their interests while making new friends.
"Compared with staying in a nursing home, seasonal living gives us more freedom and flexibility. We can decide how to spend our time, socialize and have fun," said Li Ying'an, who formed an arts group in Qujing with fellow retirees from Sichuan and Chongqing. The group rehearses in parks and performs at local events throughout the summer.
DEVELOPING NEW MARKET
What began as a seasonal escape is now developing into a broader market.
According to a report released by the China National Committee on Aging, China recorded 84.316 million senior-living stays from July 2024 to June 2025, averaging 7.026 million a month. The figure counted monthly stays of people aged 60 and above who spent more than 14 days in a city outside their home province, for up to six months a year.
Ge Lei, secretary-general of the China Tourism Association, attributes the trend to China's aging population, rising demand for higher-quality experiences and a more supportive policy environment.
At the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of the population. The figure is projected to surpass 400 million around 2035.
"This group of people has the time and financial means to enjoy retirement, a strong sense of how they want to live, and a growing demand for wellness and leisure stays away from home," Ge said.
Policy support has also helped the sector take shape. In 2021, China included senior tourism and seasonal retirement living in its national development plan. Yunnan, Guizhou, Hainan and other provinces have also introduced local action plans to promote and regulate the sector.
As the market grows, destinations are increasingly vying for a share. Jilin, for example, will allocate 100 million yuan (14.83 million U.S. dollars) a year for three consecutive years from 2027 to develop itself as a summer destination for retirees. Kaifeng in Henan Province aims to build partnerships with more than 100 cities by 2027 to share resources and visitors.
After seeing the trend unfold in Anshun, Wang believes seasonal living among retirees is moving from a niche choice to a mainstream way of life, and one that is becoming a normal part of retirement in the years ahead. ■

The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:58:00 UTC
18:58:00 KST

The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
Enceladus may be naturally sorting and concentrating chemicals from its hidden ocean, potentially making the search for signs of life much easier.
- Date:
- September 29, 2026
- Source:
- Institute of Science Tokyo
- Summary:
- Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.
- Share:
Saturn's moon Enceladus is covered in ice, but beneath that frozen shell lies a global ocean. Near the moon's south pole, fractures in the crust release water vapor and ice particles into space. Those particles give scientists an unusual way to study an alien ocean without having to drill through kilometers of ice.
An international team that includes researchers from the Earth-Life Science Institute (ELSI) at the Institute of Science Tokyo has now investigated what happens to that ocean water as it moves from beneath the surface and eventually becomes the tiny ice grains detected in space.
Cassini Found Surprisingly Diverse Ice Grains
Between 2004 and 2017, the Cosmic Dust Analyzer on NASA's Cassini spacecraft measured the composition of individual ice particles in Saturn's E-ring. That ring is continually supplied with material erupting from Enceladus.
A team led by Prof Frank Postberg at Freie Universität Berlin examined 961 mass spectra from salt-rich grains known as Type 3 particles. If the grains were simply small samples of the same ocean water, scientists might expect them to contain broadly similar mixtures of salts.
Instead, the grains varied dramatically.
Some were especially rich in sodium chloride, while others contained higher amounts of carbonates, phosphates or potassium chloride. One particularly striking pattern was that chloride and carbonate rarely appeared together in the same sodium-rich particle.
That raised a basic puzzle. If all of these grains came from the same ocean, why did their chemical compositions differ so much?
Recreating Enceladus' Ocean Droplets in the Lab
To explore that question, Professor Yasuhito Sekine and colleagues at ELSI created laboratory droplets containing the major salts thought to be present in Enceladus' ocean.
The researchers froze droplets of different sizes under different cooling conditions, then studied how the chemical elements were distributed once the droplets had solidified.
The results showed that the speed of freezing plays a major role.
In droplets about 200 micrometres across, salts became separated into different regions when freezing occurred relatively slowly, at approximately 10 K per minute or less. When the droplets froze more quickly, their chemical ingredients remained much more evenly mixed.
"What surprised us was that the diversity seen by Cassini could emerge from droplets originating from essentially the same ocean water," said Sekine. "Our experiments show that when relatively large ocean droplets freeze slowly, different salts can separate within them. If those frozen droplets are later broken apart, they can produce much smaller ice grains, each with very different chemical compositions."
A Slower Journey Through Enceladus' Ice
The findings may also reveal something about what happens inside the moon's icy crust.
Earlier studies generally assumed that seawater spray from Enceladus freezes quickly and moves rapidly toward space soon after leaving the ocean. The new experiments point to a different scenario.
The droplets may initially move much more slowly through the underground vent system, following complicated pathways through fractures in the ice before they approach the surface.
The researchers suggest that ocean spray first forms droplets ranging from tens to hundreds of micrometers in size. As those droplets move slowly through deeper sections of the vents, they gradually freeze, giving salts enough time to separate into different regions.
Closer to the surface, conditions change. Gas begins moving faster, and the frozen droplets can slam into the walls of narrower icy channels at high speed. Those collisions may break the droplets into much smaller pieces.
Each fragment can come from a different salt-rich region within the original frozen droplet, creating grains with very different chemical compositions. Those fragments can then escape into space and become part of Saturn's E-ring.
"The Cassini data showed us that these salt-rich grains are far more chemically diverse than an average ocean composition would suggest," said Postberg. "Combining those observations with the freezing experiments gives us a physical explanation: Cassini may have sampled fragments of larger frozen ocean droplets, each preserving different components that became separated during their journey towards the surface. The abundance of each individual component in the ocean is then reflected in the number of fragments in which a particular component is found."
Enceladus May Naturally Concentrate Key Compounds
The discovery could be especially important for future missions to Enceladus.
As droplets freeze and break apart, individual compounds can become concentrated in particular grains. The process does not only separate different salts. Earlier work has also shown that organic substances can become separated from one another and appear at elevated concentrations in certain particles.
That could make future analysis considerably easier.
Compounds that are highly diluted in Enceladus' ocean and mixed with many other substances may become much easier to detect when concentrated into individual ice grains.
On Earth, laboratories often spend considerable effort separating and concentrating chemicals before analyzing a sample. Enceladus appears to perform both of these "sample preparation" steps naturally: The chemical components become separated, and some end up concentrated within a fraction of the ice particles.
Possible Implications for Prebiotic Chemistry
Slow freezing could have another important consequence.
As ice crystals grow, small pockets of liquid brine may remain trapped between them. Salts and organic compounds can become highly concentrated inside those pockets.
That concentration could matter for prebiotic chemistry, which involves chemical processes that may precede the emergence of life. One major challenge in such chemistry is bringing molecules that are normally very dilute into close contact with one another.
Because much of the material erupted from Enceladus eventually falls back onto the moon, this freezing, concentration and recycling process could potentially happen again and again.
Understanding how Enceladus forms its ice grains therefore does more than explain Cassini's unusual measurements. It offers new clues about the hidden environment beneath the moon's surface and may help future spacecraft correctly interpret the particles they collect while searching for evidence of habitability and possible signs of life.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Institute of Science Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Frank Postberg, Zenghui Zou, Yasuhito Sekine, Minori Koga, Jürgen Schmidt, Mark Fox-Powell, Fabian Klenner, Jon K. Hillier, Nozair Khawaja, Toshihiko Kadono, Melih Çakar, Sascha Kempf, Ralf Srama. Cassini CDA observes compositional segregation of Enceladus’ ice grains from slow freezing and fragmentation of oceanic spray. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (39) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee7256

Ukrainians increased tax payments for their luxury cars by half - where the most was paid
Kyiv • UNN
In January–August 2026, local budgets received UAH 237.5 million in transport tax — 58.7% more than last year. Kyiv paid the most.
Transport tax revenues to local budgets in Ukraine from owners of expensive cars increased by almost 59%, reaching more than UAH 237 million in 2026. UNN reports this, citing data from the State Tax Service of Ukraine dated September 29.
Details
In January–August 2026, transport tax revenues to local budgets increased by 58.7% compared with the same period last year. In total, taxpayers paid UAH 237.5 million. Last year, this figure was UAH 149.6 million.
Where the most was paid
The largest amounts of transport tax were received by the budgets of:
-  Kyiv – UAH 68.1 million; 
-  Dnipropetrovsk region – UAH 21.3 million; 
-  Odesa region – UAH 17.9 million; 
-  Kyiv region – UAH 17.5 million. 
Who pays transport tax
The owner of the car to whom the vehicle is registered is the transport tax payer. The actual user of the car, including a lessee or a person who uses it under a power of attorney, is not liable for this tax.
Transport tax is paid on passenger cars that are no more than 5 years old, provided that their average market value exceeds the threshold established by law. In 2026, this is more than UAH 3.2 million.
The list of passenger cars subject to transport tax in 2026 has been published on the official website of the Ministry of Economy, Environment and Agriculture of Ukraine.
The tax rate is fixed and amounts to UAH 25,000 per year for each car that is subject to taxation.
Transport tax is part of the property tax and is credited in full to local budgets. Communities may use the funds received to finance socially important measures and develop local infrastructure.

Video shows Iranian police beating, sexually humiliating teenage detainee

Video shows Iranian police beating, sexually humiliating teenage detainee
A video posted in mid-September showing Iranian police officers beating and sexually harassing an arrested teenage boy has caused widespread outrage in Iran. Experts say such mistreatment of people accused of common crimes is frequent in Iran, but the footage provides rare visual evidence of what they describe as a recurring practice within the police force.
On September 17, 2026, a 78-second video was widely shared on social media. The footage appears to have been recorded by a police officer present at the scene. The Observers team geolocated the video to the courtyard of a police station in Tabriz, capital of Iran’s East Azerbaijan province, where most inhabitants speak a dialect of the Azeri language.
At least five Iranian police officers and another man in civilian clothes can be seen in the video. Four officers punch and kick the teenage boy, while two subject him to sexualised humiliation.
At one point, one officer pulls the boy’s trousers partly down. The officers then mock him as two of them slap and grab his buttocks.
The dialogue heard in the video is in Azeri. Subtitles have been added in Persian.
Policeman: Do you see him? He goes around pulling knives on people. He’s the big thug in the neighbourhood! We haven’t seen your ass yet. Oh, he’s got a white ass, the big thug in the neighbourhood! Don’t move, you thug.
Victim: I’m not a thug. Why are you doing this?
Policeman: It’s so white [a reference to the teen’s buttocks]. He’s going to be raped at this police station.
On September 18, police in East Azerbaijan province said the incident dated back to June 4, when the teenager was arrested following a street fight. They said the boy was 17 at the time of his arrest. They did not say whether he had been charged or convicted in connection with the incident.
By cross-referencing multiple sources, including other videos of police stations in Tabriz available on social media, FRANCE 24 was able to geolocate the footage.
The video was recorded in the courtyard of Police Station No. 14, in a poor neighbourhood in southwest Tabriz.
A day after the video was posted, widely circulated on social media and picked up by Iranian media – prompting public outrage – Fars News, an Iranian news agency close to the Revolutionary Guard Corps, published a video report titled “A glimpse of the Tabriz criminal’s violent conduct”.
In the report, Fars News interviews several people who say they were attacked with a machete by the teenager seen in the video. The report portrays him as a source of insecurity in the neighbourhood.
According to the police statement, the teenager had prior convictions for involvement in street fights, harassment and drug dealing. Police said the incident was under investigation and that none of these allegations justified the officers’ improper conduct. They said all the officers involved had been disciplined and suspended until further notice, with any additional punishment dependent on a court ruling. The police did not specify whether the officers were disciplined before or after the video emerged on September 17.
‘We are seeing more and more sexual harassment in recent years’
Niki Mahjoub is an Iranian independent journalist based in Europe who has covered social issues in Iran for more than three decades.
 The police not only fail to hide some of this misconduct, they sometimes even display it openly.
Parading people accused of violent crimes through cities while beating and publicly humiliating them is a common punishment for those the authorities call “thugs”.
In recent years, the situation has escalated. The authorities have even published videos showing suspects who were shot with live ammunition during their arrest.
We are also seeing more and more cases of sexual harassment in recent years. We do not know whether this means such incidents are becoming more frequent, or whether social media has simply made it easier for information about them to emerge. This is the first video evidence we have seen of a form of sexual harassment that we know has happened repeatedly.
As horrific as this is, in this particular case we are talking about a teenager – a child under the age of 18 – who requires particular protection and treatment.
Read more'We will shoot the thugs': Iranian police crack down on crime
“Human Rights groups have documented systematic sexual harassment”
 Personally, I have worked as a journalist for decades, and for as long as I can remember, violence has been part of the Iranian police culture.
They have even coined an expression for it: “technical interrogation”, which in practice means severe violence that can extend to psychological and sexual abuse.
But there are no statistics or comprehensive studies on violence against people accused of ordinary crimes in Iran. To some extent, this may be because many of those accused face charges such as robbery, rape or other violent crimes, and even human rights activists have often kept their distance from them.
Several human rights groups, for example, have documented systematic sexual harassment and abuse of young women and men arrested during protests in Iran, including in January 2026 and during the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement in 2023. But we do not have comparable documentation for people accused of ordinary crimes.
The few testimonies we do have about what common criminals experience in prison or detention often come from political prisoners who encountered them behind bars and later had a platform to speak publicly about what they had witnessed.
Figures such as Narges Mohammadi, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, have testified about people imprisoned for ordinary crimes whom they met in detention and who had been subjected to severe violence, sexual harassment and rape.
In one case highlighted by Mohammadi, a woman imprisoned for an ordinary crime was allegedly raped by her interrogator and later underwent an abortion in prison.’
“This is a PR effort”
Mahjoub is not convinced by the police statement saying the officers will be held accountable:
 ‘I don’t believe there will be any real consequences. The simple question is: if they really care about this kind of abuse, why didn’t they prosecute these officers before the video went viral?
I believe this is a PR effort aimed at containing the public reaction. Personally, I don’t remember any case in which a political prisoner or someone accused of an ordinary crime pursued accountability for this kind of violence and achieved any meaningful result.’
Police Station No. 14 in Tabriz has previously been linked to at least one other publicly reported case involving alleged human rights violations. In 2023, Iranian security forces violently arrested a local activist and two members of his family and detained them at the police station for a day without medical care.

But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance.
Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance.
“If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen.”
Some evacuated residents reportedly return home although others are hesitant to do so
Residents in the Cotswold village of Whelford were told yesterday they were able to return home after being advised to temporarily evacuate to a local leisure centre.
About 85 households in Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning as a precaution due to the major police incident declared around RAF Fairford.
One local resident has since told the BBC that while most people have now returned home, others are hesitant to do so.
“I haven’t gone home as I want to wait until I know more about what the hell happened, as it feels super dodge to me,” the resident told the BBC, adding that police are advising people not to take any photos and to stay inside their properties.
A cordon remains in place around three vans which are being examined by counter-terrorism police near RAF Fairford, two days after the incident.
Here are some of the latest images from the scene that have been sent to us over the newswires:
Iran has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. But Iran’s embassy in London yesterday strongly rejected any speculation linking the country to the arrests of the five suspects near RAF Fairford.
The Guardian’s defence and security editor, Dan Sabbagh, has looked into the claims of a possible Iranian link to the alleged RAF Fairford plot. Here is an extract from his analysis:
RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring.
The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”…
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed.
What we know about the suspected plot at RAF Fairford
Vikram Dodd
Five men arrested over a suspected plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back. The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London.
Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.
An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.
An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release on Monday it emerged that no explosive material had been found.
The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.
The suspects were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.

RAF Fairford incident 'clearly involves' foreign actor, US secretary of state says
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told Fox News last night that it was clear a “foreign actor” had been involved in the suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British base that houses American bombers that fly missions against Iran.
“I have to be careful, there are some things I cannot say on the air for a lot of different reasons,” he told Fox News’ Hannity programme.
“Suffice it to say, that what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened, in the UK over the weekend, is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor,” Rubio said, without providing evidence or giving further details.
“We are dealing with elements in the world and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally. We are always going to take that very seriously.”
Rubio said the UK authorities had been “very cooperative” in relation to the “serious incident” and have been “on top of it”.

The US president, Donald Trump, went further in his comments, telling reporters at the White House he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them,” the president said.
Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.”
The five suspects – all British nationals from London in their 20s - were arrested in Gloucestershire on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.
While the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged there was speculation over whether Iran was behind the incident, he insisted the force was considering “every possible angle”. The investigation is continuing and police are yet to establish a motive.

Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:48:29 UTC
18:48:29 KST

A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests.
More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British Transport Police (BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders.
A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive.
Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations. British Transport Police said that since the extension there had been three positive confirmed alerts of people who were subsequently confirmed to be complying with sexual harm prevention orders or other imposed court conditions.
When Transport for London announced its support for the extension of the trial, it said LFR technology “will target and identify people on police watchlists at key stations chosen for maximum impact” and would “specifically tackle violence against women and girls, whose travel behaviours are shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”.
Fraser Sampson, a former biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner for the UK, said the police needed to show that the use of the technology was proportionate. “There many variables and all need to align: the choice of location, times of day, make up of the watchlist and likelihood of people being present and many more.”
Sampson, who is now a non-executive director of Facewatch, a company that operates facial recognition systems in shops, added: “We know the technology works, but using it in supermarkets to deter shoplifters and prevent attacks on staff is very different from deploying it to catch people on a public transport network.
“Success in a shop means no such people coming in. Success for the police trying to catch people means people being caught. In that respect the trial doesn’t appear to have been very fruitful.
“Everything depends on the police watchlists; if you’re not on a watchlist, the live FRT cameras do not ‘see’ you and they don’t retain your image in the same way as CCTV cameras.
“However, they are processing special category personal data and the technology must be used in a way that is appropriate, proportionate and necessary. It’s for the police to show how any deployment meets those criteria and – as the ICO [information commissioner’s office] has recently reported – for their oversight boards to hold them firmly to account in doing so.”
More than half of police forces in England and Wales have now deployed LFR on British streets, according to an analysis by Liberty Investigates.
The Metropolitan police and London mayor’s office announced this summer that fixed LFR cameras would be installed in the capital’s West End. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has since confirmed the technology will be used on the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street.
A recent report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights, which called on the government to introduce a law to address the threat of artificial intelligence to human rights, identified the rollout of live facial recognition technology as a “particularly clear example of risk”.
Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Labour MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “Live facial recognition technologies are a serious invasion of our privacy. The government should be suspending their rollout until there are stronger safeguards in place, including a proper legal framework.”
A BTP spokesperson said it had launched the LFR pilot “to understand how the technology could most effectively support the identification of wanted offenders and individuals who may pose a risk to passengers and staff”.
They added: “During these deployments, officers have made a number of associated arrests, including for assault, theft, possession of an offensive weapon, breach of a criminal behaviour order and public order offences, as well as locating individuals wanted by the courts and other police forces. As these arrests did not result directly from an LFR alert, they are not included within LFR performance data.
“Throughout the pilot, we have continued to refine how the capability is deployed within the railway environment. This has included developments to deployment locations, operating procedures, equipment and watchlist construction.
“A particularly important point is that watchlist growth has been deliberate, controlled and aligned to BTP policy. We began with a more limited watchlist whilst ensuring data quality, governance and safeguarding arrangements were robust.”

Dale Vince plans London-wide news operation to take on ‘rightwing bias’ in the media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:48:16 UTC
18:48:16 KST

The green energy entrepreneur and Labour donor Dale Vince is planning to launch a London-wide news operation, as part of a “rescue” of one of the capital’s most highly regarded local newspapers.
Vince, who has vowed to take on what he sees as rightwing bias in the UK media, said he would invest “whatever it takes” to support the loss-making group behind the Camden New Journal (CNJ), Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra.
He told the Guardian he was already looking at expanding the Westminster edition to cover London-wide issues, in an attempt to serve a city in which a series of major newsrooms have closed or drastically shrunk over the past 20 years.
“We’re going to go forward together to put the CNJ on a better financial footing and take it digital – properly digital,” he said. “At the same time, [we will] get behind the Westminster edition and make that an edition for the wider London area.
“I think London is missing a local paper now, with the demise of a couple that have gone before. It’s quite a bold plan, that we might morph the Westminster edition.
“We might call it the north, south, east and Westminster edition, in a kind of nod to our intended larger audience.”
Vince’s rescue package for the titles, which has not been formally finalised, is one of several attempts being made to revitalise local journalism in London. Despite its 9m population, media outlets have struggled to support large London-focused newsrooms.
The Evening Standard, which has been published for almost 200 years, shut down its daily newspaper in 2024. It was replaced with a weekly edition renamed the London Standard, with a greater focus on arts and culture.
Other attempts to run daily freesheets failed. The London Paper, launched by Rupert Murdoch’s News International, now News UK, closed in 2009 after just three years. Its rival, London Lite, published by the owner of the Daily Mail, closed later that year.
Meanwhile, Metro, a national freesheet distributed in UK cities including London, is undergoing major structural changes to put it on a “sustainable footing”.
However, journalism focused on London has been boosted in recent years by the arrival of small, subscription-based operations.
Jim Waterson, a former Guardian journalist who founded the London Centric news site that now has more than 5,000 paying subscribers, said Vince had chosen to help a local group that had resisted “the disastrous choice in the 2010s to abandon quality for chasing clicks at all costs”.
However, he said the success of his own “back-to-basics local journalism” outlet was still “only enough money to support a tiny operation that’s still run from a kitchen table”.
“Vince has also realised that London is also one of the UK’s worst local news deserts,” Waterson said. “The challenge that we all face is how to get the funding to grow our audience without becoming financially unsustainable.”
While not large, the Camden New Journal group still employs 18 people, according to recent financial records. It spent a chunk of its cash reserves in the last year.
Vince said he was not supporting the Camden New Journal and its related titles “for business reasons”.
“I’m motivated by the impact of local journalism,” he said. “I’m motivated by the bias of media in our country more broadly – the rightwing bias – and trying to do something about that.”
Vince has already launched an online publication, Babelfish. He said he would consider writing comment pieces for the London titles, but would generally be a “hands-off” investor.
“Big picture-wise, I’ve got a view of the world and how things should be, and the Camden people already fit within that,” he said. “There’s no kind of culture clash and I write op-eds for all kinds of people already. I would absolutely write op-eds for the Camden [New Journal], but it wouldn’t be a requirement.”

US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Unknown

2026-09-29
09:45:51 UTC
18:45:51 KST

Breadcrumb
US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Lebanon has received negative signals from the United States over its efforts to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control, with Washington warning that Israel intends to continue its military operations in the south, The New Arab has learned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam received several messages while in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, including warnings from US officials that Israel intends to maintain the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington conveyed that Israel would continue its operations "as long as the Lebanese state does not take serious action to disarm Hezbollah", according to information obtained by TNA, and that it remains determined to destroy the group's military infrastructure.
US officials also told Salam that the steps taken by the Lebanese government so far were insufficient and that efforts to bring all weapons under state control must be accelerated.
According to the information obtained by TNA, Washington called for a firmer approach to the issue, warning that the situation could deteriorate further otherwise.
The warnings come as southern Lebanon faces near-daily Israeli escalation, with Israel stepping up its operations and insisting on maintaining the security zone it has established in the south.
Prospects for a solution are meanwhile receding, at least until Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Salam also received several messages of support, particularly from Arab and European countries, backing the government's decisions and Lebanon's demands for Israel to halt its attacks and withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory.
There was also support for the need to fill any security vacuum in southern Lebanon if the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) expires without renewal, with efforts expected to intensify in the coming period to find a solution to the crisis.
Hezbollah sets conditions for weapons talks
Attention is meanwhile turning to Hezbollah and whether the group could enter into a confrontation with Israel, particularly if Israeli military operations intensify.
Such a scenario remains unlikely in the near term, however, as Hezbollah is currently looking to developments between the US and Iran, with Tehran making Lebanon a key issue in its negotiations.
Hezbollah parliamentary sources told The New Arab that the group was "monitoring all developments, and its eyes will remain on the field. Iran remains committed to the Lebanon issue and will not abandon it, which is what should be relied upon rather than direct negotiations with the enemy".
They added that the Lebanese state should return to indirect negotiations with Israel and correct the course of the talks.
The sources said Hezbollah was open to discussing the issue of its weapons domestically and as part of a national defence strategy.
However, they said a complete halt to Israeli attacks and Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory must come first.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem on Sunday renewed his call for Lebanese authorities to end what he described as concessions and review the course of negotiations, calling for direct talks to be suspended in favour of indirect negotiations.
His comments came on the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah secretary-generals Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine.
"Let it be clear, Lebanon without resistance will disappear; the enemy wants all of Lebanon," Qassem said.
"Lebanon can only remain through its liberation and unity and the cooperation of its components. Whoever bets on retaining a part of Lebanon in exchange for abandoning the other part of the land or people is deluded."
Israel steps up attacks on southern Lebanon
Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks on several areas of southern Lebanon in recent hours, including the use of an Apache attack helicopter in a strike for the first time during the latest escalation.
The helicopter struck a commercial centre on the main road between the towns of Shoukine and Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces also carried out air strikes on Wadi Zibqin, Talouseh, Mais al-Jabal and the Al-Dabsh area, while artillery fire targeted Wadi Saluki, the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin.
Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire towards the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in the Azrael area, as well as Sarbin and the Al-Sadana area.
An explosion was also carried out by Israeli forces in Mais al-Jabal, while illumination flares were fired over Hadatha-Haris and Wadi Saluki.

Anthropic IPO filing warns AI may pose 'existential risks to humanity'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:44:13 UTC
18:44:13 KST

Anthropic has devoted almost a third of its IPO prospectus to risk factors, warning that its AI may pose "existential risks to humanity", while the filing also reveals a $42 billion (€36.9bn) net loss last year and a heavy reliance on just two customers.
Anthropic has told would-be shareholders that the technology it sells could threaten humanity itself.
The warning appears in a long-awaited initial public offering prospectus shared with a small group of partners, according to people familiar with the filing cited by the Financial Times.
The company behind the Claude chatbot dedicated almost a third of its lengthy S-1, the document companies file with the US Securities and Exchange Commission before listing, to risk factors.
These include the possibility that increasingly advanced AI models could manipulate, blackmail or behave in other unpredictable ways as Anthropic's own research has shown autonomous models sabotaging code, assisting fraud and manipulating information in controlled tests.
Such warnings complicate the task for investors trying to value a company whose listing, expected on the Nasdaq this autumn, is set to be the most highly valued IPO ever.
Anthropic has not publicly commented on the reports.
Two clients, a quarter of revenue
The filing also flags financial risks.
For instance, close to a quarter of Anthropic's revenue last year came from two customers, and many of its largest clients are not locked into long-term contracts.
Revenue jumped twelvefold to almost $4.6 billion (€4bn) in 2025, but operating expenses reached $12.65 billion (€11.1bn), more than half of it on computing and infrastructure, leaving an operating loss of more than $8 billion (€7bn).
Its net loss of about $42 billion (€36.9bn) included a roughly $34 billion (€29.8bn) accounting charge linked to financing that could eventually convert into shares, rather than money spent running the business.
Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion (€455.3bn) on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years. It had $20.28 billion (€17.8bn) in cash and short-term investments at the end of 2025.
Revenue reached $11.5 billion (€10.1bn) in the second quarter of 2026, and the company is on course for a second straight quarter of operating profit, albeit on an adjusted basis.
Backers expect Anthropic to list at a valuation above $2 trillion (€1.73tn), more than double the $965 billion (€848bn) set in its funding round in May.
As Euronews reported earlier this month, at their peak, pre-IPO contracts on the crypto platform Hyperliquid were already implying a valuation of roughly $2.36 trillion (€2.05tn).
Safety fears reach the White House
The prospectus lands amid a heated debate over AI risks.
Current and former Anthropic staff have warned that runaway AI could end humanity within a decade, and CEO Dario Amodei told the UN Security Council last week that AI was "the most important global security issue facing the world today."
Amodei has also led calls this month for "pacing the frontier" of AI development, backed by OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Yet, Anthropic released its Opus 5.5 model last week to counter OpenAI's momentum since the launch of GPT-6 Astra.
OpenAI revealed last week that its tools had hacked "dozens" of external sites, including government ones, and on Monday scrapped plans to release its newest model next month, citing safety concerns.
US President Donald Trump rejected Amodei's call to slow down, saying: "I'm for let's go and let's win," candidly describing the AI race as a competition between the US and China that America is leading and cannot afford to lose.
Amodei was left out of Thursday's White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, attended by Musk, Altman, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Apple's Tim Cook among other executives.
Trump then hosted him for a private dinner on Sunday night, their first one-on-one meeting, though the White House released no details about it.
The two sides have clashed since February, when Anthropic refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance which led the Pentagon to then classify the company as a supply chain risk, a decision a federal appeals court upheld last week.
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are due to meet AI executives on Tuesday.

2026-09-29

A Ukrainian unmanned ground vehicle amphibian delivered cargo to the front for the first time, covering more than 40 km by land and water
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Armed Forces' amphibious robot covered more than 40 km by land and water, delivering provisions and ammunition to the military. The system was further developed with the support of Brave1.
Military personnel from one of the separate mechanized brigades of the Armed Forces of Ukraine carried out a logistics mission for the first time using a Ukrainian amphibious unmanned ground robotic system. The robot covered more than 40 km by land and water, delivering provisions and ammunition to the troops’ positions. This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, writes UNN.
The amphibious UGRS covered more than 40 km by land and water, delivering provisions and ammunition to the positions
It is noted that bodies of water at the front are a real problem for military logistics. Rivers, canals, and marshy areas can complicate or completely block the route for a conventional UGRS. Air logistics is also not always the optimal solution.
An amphibious UGRS makes it possible to cover such a route using a single system. On land, the vehicle retains the high mobility of a ground-based UGRS, while within seconds it can switch to water and continue moving. In other words, one robot gains more capabilities to carry out missions across different terrain.
For this mission, the system was refined over several months in close cooperation with the military, taking into account real-world tasks, operational experience, and the characteristics of the frontline terrain. The Brave1 defense innovation cluster provided grant support for the system, helping bring the solution to practical application.

The drug exhibits stolen from the High Court in Suva, the capital of the Pacific island nation, amounted to nearly 40kg, media said.
Police began investigating after the Sept 15 discovery of the theft of seven out of 39 cocaine bars from an evidence room.
Forensic tests on the remaining drugs confirmed that exhibits had been tampered with, police said in a statement on Sept 29, adding that they would question a person of interest who was allegedly overseas.

Media said the cocaine was seized from Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman in 2019 and stored at the court as evidence while he appealed against his 2021 conviction and sentence.
Fiji police have said cases involving drugs such as methamphetamine and cocaine have surged since 2018.
In 2024, the United Nations said Fiji had emerged as a regional hub for drug trafficking in the Pacific.

Raytheon expands Sidewinder supplier base in U.S., Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:40:11 UTC
18:40:11 KST

The U.S. Navy is paying Raytheon up to $30.2 million to line up additional suppliers for key parts of the AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missile, including the cooling engine for its heat-seeking sensor and its warhead components.
The undefinitized contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers engineering work to qualify new manufacturing sources for several AIM-9X components. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it without competition, and the work is due to be finished in February 2030.
Qualifying a second source means testing and approving another factory to make a part that currently comes from only one supplier, so that production does not stop if that supplier falls behind or shuts down. The notice lists the parts involved: the cryoengine, which cools the missile’s infrared seeker so it can detect a target’s heat; connectors and wiring harnesses; sensor platform and warhead components; components of the optical target detector, which senses when the missile is close enough to its target to detonate; and parts of the inertial measurement unit, which tracks the missile’s movement in flight.
The work will be spread across the United States and Europe. About half, 51%, will take place at Raytheon’s missile plant in Tucson, Arizona. Another 19% is set for Schrobenhausen, Germany, 12% for Anaheim, California, and 8% for Heilbronn, Germany, with smaller shares in Camarillo, California; Delémont, Switzerland; Midland, Ontario; and Logan, Utah.
The modification is a cost-plus-incentive-fee arrangement, meaning the government covers Raytheon’s costs and pays a fee that depends on performance. Because it is undefinitized, work can begin before final prices and terms are agreed, up to a $30.2 million ceiling. The Navy committed $29.6 million in fiscal 2025 weapons procurement funds at the time of award.
The AIM-9X is the latest version of the Sidewinder, a short-range, heat-seeking missile carried by U.S. and allied fighter jets and also fired from the ground by the NASAMS air defense system. The U.S. Navy leads the program jointly with the U.S. Air Force, and more than 35 allied and partner nations use the missile.
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Raytheon a $1.1 billion contract for more than 1,900 AIM-9X Block II missiles, including 1,653 for U.S. inventories and 336 for foreign customers, with work running through September 2029. That followed another $1.1 billion AIM-9X award in June 2025, then the largest in the program’s history. Raytheon says it is raising AIM-9X production capacity to about 2,500 missiles a year.

Prior to hitting the road for a special tour of the UK, Europe and the US, Stevie Wonder releases four unheard songs from sessions of his seminal album ‘Songs In The Key Of Life’, which celebrates its 50th anniversary.
Legendary American singer-songwriter Stevie Wonder is preparing to return to the stage with a series of anniversary shows celebrating the 50 years of his seminal album ‘Songs In The Key Of Life’.
The special tour of the UK, Europe and the US will see Wonder perform the 1976 record in full during each show. It will kick off in Birmingham, UK, before heading to Paris, Oslo, Cologne, Amsterdam, Dublin and London. (Scroll down for the full tour dates.)
Routinely voted one of the greatest albums of all time, the double album features hit songs like ‘Sir Duke’, ‘As’, ‘Isn’t She Lovely’, ‘Another Star’ and ‘I Wish’, and earned Wonder his third Grammy Award for Album of the Year. It is a part of the National Recording Registry overseen by the US Library of Congress.
Now, to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the album, Wonder has released an EP of unvaulted tracks from the album’s extensive sessions.
Chosen by Wonder himself from the outtakes, the four unheard songs - ‘It’s Easier’, ‘My Life Story of Love’, ‘I Can See the Sun in Late December’, and ‘I’m Into Livin’’ - are out now as ‘Songs In The Key Of Life: The EP’.
“We’ve lived with Songs in the Key of Life for fifty years, but there’s still more to hear,” Wonder said in a press release. “We didn’t add these songs to the album, but they were part of what I was feeling and discovering as we made it. They bring me back to that time in my life, and now they get to become part of yours.”
All four songs are written and produced by Wonder, though ‘My Life Story of Love’ features a co-writing credit for former Supremes member Susaye Greene. The song ‘I’m Into Livin’’ also features background vocals from Shirley Brewer, Thelma Houston and Deniece Williams.
The original recording and mixing engineers, John Fischbach and Gary O Adante, recently mixed the tracks for release.
Wonder’s last studio album to date is 2005’s ‘A Time To Love’.

German retailer Metro loses control of Russian business after Putin decree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:37:41 UTC
18:37:41 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered that the assets of German retailer Metro AG be placed under temporary administration. The move comes amid escalating tensions between Germany and Russia over the Ukraine war.
German wholesaler and food retailer Metro AG lost operational control of its Russian subsidiary on Monday after Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the business under temporary administration. The decree put Metro Cash and Carry’s Russian operations under the management of UK Torg RUS temporarily.
The order, posted on a Russian government website on Monday, did not give a reason for the action. It follows similar moves against the Russian businesses of food company Nestlé and French retailer Auchan under a 2023 decree aimed at businesses associated with "unfriendly countries".
Temporary administration has also led to local owners taking over the Russian businesses of French dairy company Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg at knockdown prices.
Metro said it still formally owns its Russian subsidiary but no longer has operational control of it as the company is analysing the decree’s consequences, and informed that Torg RUS is owned by Johannes Tholey, CEO of Metro Russia.
Metro also said it had been reducing its ties to the Russian business since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Metro entered the Russian market in 2001 and it operated 91 wholesale stores in Russia, employing approximately 9,000 people there.
Russia remains a significant market for the German wholesaler.
During the first nine months of the 2025/26 financial year, Metro’s sales in Russia rose by 10.3% in euros to €2.14 billion, accounting for roughly 8.7% of Metro AG’s total group sales for the period.
Escalating tensions between Russia and Germany
The move comes amid a deepening diplomatic dispute between Berlin and Moscow.
Germany has concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and has closed a Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia responded by closing the German consulate in St Petersburg and denied the allegations.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met his German counterpart Johann Wadephul on Saturday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly but was dismissive afterwards, saying that Wadephul "simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia... you can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not."
Wadephul said the meeting had been necessary to raise Germany’s security concerns directly with Russia, but that he had sensed no seriousness from the Russian side, reiterating that the talks did not signal any change in Germany’s support for Ukraine.
"The Russians are raising the pressure on Germany in their hybrid war,” said Stefan Meister, a Russia expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
"It's being made clear that the Germans could lose even more companies and assets in Russia, in order to raise pressure on the German government from the German business community," Meister added.
He also explained that Russia sees Germany "as a key adversary since it is Ukraine's most important single supporter."
Some major Western businesses ceased operating in Russia and wrote off their businesses after 2022. Since then, the Kremlin has imposed burdensome conditions on the sale of local affiliates, requiring steep discounts, exit taxes and government approval.
Other companies have scaled back their operations, while some continue to do business as usual.

How America's AI boom is reshaping surveillance and power
The American AI data centre buildout is hiding the expansion of the national security state in plain sight.

What is Medicare for All, and how is it growing in US midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:34:29 UTC
18:34:29 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Medicare for All, and how is it a growing movement in US midterms?
Medicare for All is proposal for a national universal healthcare plan for US residents that would eliminate the need for private insurance and payments for doctors’ visits and procedures. Once a largely left-wing position, support for the plan is becoming increasingly mainstream amid rising healthcare costs.
It is one of the top policy platforms for progressive candidates running in the 2026 midterms. It affects the vast majority of Americans currently living under a system in which they can go bankrupt over one medical bill.
National public healthcare is often referred to as “single payer healthcare” with the idea being that the government would be the one entity paying the cost of healthcare.
What is Medicare?
Medicare is a healthcare plan that covers US seniors (both citizens and residents). Its purpose is to financially cover healthcare for those over 65. It was established in 1965 under then-US President Dwight Eisenhower to support seniors, who, at the time, were paying far more for healthcare than their younger counterparts.
Along with Social Security (in which Americans collect a pension after retirement), Medicare has long been one of the most popular government programmes in the US. This was confirmed by a 2023 YouGov poll, which found that among members of both major parties these two programmes were the most popular of all social welfare plans.
Why has Medicare for All become so important in US politics?
Americans pay more per capita for healthcare than anyone else in the world. Despite this, the country ranks low among developed nations in key metrics, such as life expectancy and overall health.
Over the past several years, with skyrocketing healthcare costs, the popularity of Medicare for All has surged.
A 2025 survey conducted by Data for Progress found that 65 percent of US voters (including 79 percent of Democrats, 71 percent of Independents and 49 percent of Republicans) support a Medicare for All system that would replace the current private for-profit insurance plans.
This survey was conducted prior to the 2026 rise in healthcare premiums, in which subsidies were removed and many enrollees saw a 60 percent increase in monthly dues. Rates are expected to spike again in 2027.
What would Medicare for All mean?
Medicare for All would mean the phased transition from private health coverage to a government-funded system similar to what exists in much of the rest of the world. The proposed US model has often been compared to that of Canada and Taiwan.
Who supports it?
Medicare for All has the support of at least 136 members of Congress – 19 in the Senate and 117 in the House of Representatives, all of them Democrats (except for Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats). They are co-sponsors of a bill that would require the government to provide health coverage.
The politician who has most actively advocated for it is Bernie Sanders, who had it as one of his main platforms in his 2016 and 2020 presidential runs. In the current midterm cycle, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, a doctor and a former public health director who wrote a book on Medicare for All, also has it as one of his main campaign platforms.
Who opposes it?
The main opponents of Medicare for all are health insurance companies and others who benefit from the current system. Perhaps surprisingly, given the plan’s popularity, Democratic House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries has been a vocal opponent of it.
What are the main obstacles to passing it?
At present, there are not enough votes in Congress to pass Medicare for All. At the same time, the healthcare industry remains the biggest lobby group in US politics, spending around $6.4 billion on lobbying between 1998 and 2025, according to Investopedia.

UK nearly triples blocked arms export licences to Israel as policy tightens over Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:30:49 UTC
18:30:49 KST

Britain has sharply expanded restrictions on military exports to Israel, suspending or refusing more than 80 licences for items that could be used by the IDF in Gaza, nearly three times the number affected when the policy was introduced in September 2024.
UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said more than 50 additional export applications had been refused since the initial suspension of around 30 licences, part of what he described as a tougher system for assessing exports to Israel.
The original September 2024 decision suspended roughly 30 of about 350 licences after the British government concluded there was a “clear risk” that certain military exports could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza. The affected equipment included components for military aircraft, drones, naval systems and targeting equipment.
Doughty said additional measures adopted this month had created what he called a “double lock” on approvals. Export applications must now be considered both under the existing international humanitarian law criteria and in light of Britain’s position on the legality of Israel’s presence in the Palestinian territories.
“We have suspended or refused over 80 licences now,” Doughty said, adding that he had personally reviewed each licence.
F-35 components remain largely exempt
Despite the broader restrictions, British components entering the international F-35 fighter jet supply chain remain largely exempt.
The UK government has maintained that stopping British-made parts from entering the global F-35 pool could undermine the wider program and have serious consequences for the security of Britain and its allies. Direct exports of F-35 components intended specifically for Israel remain suspended.
Doughty defended the continued supply of components through the international program, arguing that halting them could have serious implications for the broader European and allied security architecture.
Foreign Affairs Committee chair Emily Thornberry challenged that position, arguing that the issue was political rather than purely legal.
She suggested adopting an approach similar to the Dutch model, under which components entering the international supply chain could be marked as not intended for aircraft destined for Israel.
The initial suspension was introduced under then-Foreign Secretary David Lammy in September 2024. Lammy stressed at the time that the measure did not constitute an arms embargo and applied only to items assessed as potentially usable in military operations in Gaza.
The policy has since been tightened under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Miliband signals tougher line on Israel
The expanded export restrictions come as the Burnham government adopts a more confrontational policy toward the Israeli government.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband received strong applause at Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool after sharply criticizing the Netanyahu government’s policies and defending Britain’s decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Miliband accused Israel of war crimes in Gaza and said the British government had heard public anger over the conflict.
“We hear you. You were right,” he told delegates.
The tougher rhetoric and widening export restrictions mark a clear shift from the narrower 2024 policy, when Britain suspended around 30 licences while emphasizing that it was not imposing a general arms embargo on Israel.

Plastic Is Melting Onto Corals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Marine plastic pollution is rampant. That’s nothing new. Plastic waste has been found in a variety of marine ecosystems, including beaches, coral reefs, and even some of the ocean’s farthest depths. While a precise measurement is difficult, it’s estimated that several million metric tons of plastic lie on the seafloor.
Scientists have been recording marine animals entangled in or consuming plastic debris for over half a century, some even proposing the term “Plastocene” (the Plastic Age) to denote the geological epoch spanning from the 1950s onward. And now researchers have discovered a new way these substances are polluting the environment: Plastic is fusing with corals.
The discovery of this conglomerate—which researchers have dubbed “plasticoral”—was made during a survey of the beaches of the Ryukyu Islands in southern Japan. The scientists noticed small, brightly colored spots embedded in the white coral gravel. They collected samples from three beaches on the main island, Okinawa, and brought them to the lab where spectroscopic analysis revealed there were polymers derived from common household plastics.
Using micro-CT scans, the researchers determined that the polymers had melted into the microscopic pores in the fragments of coral skeleton, becoming so integrated that the two could no longer be separated.
This is also not the first time plastic has been found enmeshed with the natural world, though this phenomenon usually involves nonliving things like rocks. In 2019, another group of researchers found a thin layer of degraded plastic coating mussels and large algae in tide pools, which they called “plastiskin,” but this new study marks the first time plastic has been seen fused with corals.
And while coral rubble is no longer itself a living organism, even after being washed ashore, it often returns to sea later and plays an important role in coral reef ecosystems. It forms a stable foundation for new corals to settle on, and the irregular shapes make essential hiding places for small marine organisms to protect themselves from strong currents and predators.
How exactly the plasticorals may impact their living bretheren is unknown, though previous research has shown that some chemicals that can leach from common plastics inhibit coral reproduction. Other studies have found that plastic fragments can carry pathogens to corals.
Scientists are also not yet certain how the plastic is fusing with the corals. Though the temperatures of our oceans are ever increasing, they’re not quite hot enough yet to melt plastic. Ultraviolet radiation can also contribute, but the researchers consider beach bonfires to be the leading candidate.
Further investigation is needed to confirm this, but given plastic’s pervasiveness as a pollutant, it’s not unlikely that fires in even seemingly pristine areas are creating unintended fusions.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

New English homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:28:48 UTC
18:28:48 KST

The boss of Britain’s biggest insurer has said that homes being built now in England could become uninsurable in the future because they are sited in flood-risk areas.
Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said the flooding threat was “absolutely increasing”.
She told the BBC: “You’ve seen a very dry summer, and what happens if you then get heavy rain on very dry surfaces is you get more surface water flooding.”
She said 110,000 homes had been built in flood areas in the past 10 years, and if that continued, a further 115,000 new homes would be built in flood areas in the next decade. “That doesn’t seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built,” she said.
Blanc told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview podcast that England was “for sure” building properties that might become uninsurable in the future.
“If you think that there’s an inevitability of something happening, that’s not what insurance is, right? Insurance is a pool where you know there’s a risk that something happens for some people and not for others. When there is an inevitability, it makes it very difficult for it to be insured.”
She added: “It’s very well known where these flooding areas are. Let’s think very carefully about homes that are being built,” she told planners and housebuilders. “It’s dangerous.”
About 6.3m homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. It has said this could increase to about 8m, or one in four properties, by the mid-century as the climate crisis worsens.
If a property cannot get insurance cover or it is prohibitively expensive to insure because it is prone to frequent flooding, the homeowner would have to foot the bill, with knock-on effects on their ability to get a mortgage or sell the property. Some towns may have to be abandoned as climate breakdown makes many areas uninsurable, a Guardian investigation found last year.
Blanc said a lot could be done to mitigate damage, such as using bricks with self-closing air vents, having stainless steel kitchens instead of wooden furniture and creating plug points halfway up the wall rather than near the floor.
“You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood.”
According to Aviva’s research, more than a quarter (26%), or 101,657 new homes, have some risk of flooding now, and one in seven will be at medium to high risk of flooding by 2050.
After the very wet and stormy winter in the UK in 2023-24, the Met Office estimated that such winters had gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.
Blanc also called on the government to avoid policy “kite flying” before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
Aviva is a leading private pension provider, and speculation about changes to pensions led to a jump in withdrawals in the run-up to the budget in the last two years.
“Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can’t put it back in,” she said.
Blanc has come under criticism over her role as BP’s senior independent director in which she led the search for a new chair twice in a year, after the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold. She will stand down next year after five years on the board.
She said: “It’s been a tough gig, right? There’s no doubt about that, and there’s been a lot thrown at BP. But if I look at it today and the combination of a new chair, new CEO, I think that’s a good combination to take BP forward … it’s time for me to move away.”

On September 2, the IDF, Shin Bet (Israel Security Service), and various Palestinian militias captured Mu’in al-Arabid, one of Hamas’s top internal security officials.
The IDF and Shin Bet on Tuesday confirmed the overnight assassination of Hamas Northern Gaza Brigade Chief Izz al-Din al-Bik in Gaza City. Al-Bik had served in his current role since Ahmed Randur was assassinated by Israel on November 10, 2023.
This is the third assassination of a Hamas brigade chief since September 11; three of the five brigade commanders were killed during that period.
According to the joint statement, al-Bik was responsible for managing the activities of the brigade’s operatives, including issuing orders to carry out attacks on Israeli soldiers and civilians.
He also managed efforts to reconstitute the brigade’s capabilities, which had been heavily damaged over the last three years of war, said the IDF.
Defense Minister Israel Katz disclosed the assassination in a statement shortly before the official IDF and Shin Bet statement.
Prior, the IDF killed two of five Hamas brigade commanders
In mid-September, the IDF and Shin Bet killed Muhammad Yazouri in the Khan Yunis area. Yazouri served as commander of Hamas’s Khan Yunis Brigade.
He was appointed to the position after holding a series of roles in the brigade, including deputy commander of the Khan Yunis Brigade, and he replaced Rafa Salame.
Further, in mid-September, the IDF and Shin Bet also announced that they had struck Hamas Rafah Brigade commander Nayal Abu Obeid.
Abu Obeid replaced his predecessor, Mohammad Shabanah, who was killed by the IDF in May 2025.
Abu Obeid was a key figure among Hamas leaders, according to a statement from the IDF, previously the deputy commander of the Rafah Brigade and commander of the Tel al-Sultan and Yibna Battalions.

Malaysia begins sending back Rohingya refugees despite safety warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
