Murdered for their eyes: people with albinism living in terror in Madagascar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:59 UTC
18:00:59 KST

Not long after midnight in late May this year, three men barged through the door of the small room where Nicole Soalala lived with her family on the outskirts of Toliara, a coastal city in the south of Madagascar. Her husband got up to ask what they wanted, but they attacked him with a piece of wood and an axe.
Soalala, 32, grabbed her youngest child, Landricia – an 18-month-old girl with albinism – and hoisted her on to her back, holding her there with a piece of fabric she started to wrap around herself. Her eldest daughter, 15, hid under the table with her other two children, aged six and three.
As Soalala’s husband lay on the floor on the verge of losing consciousness, the attackers turned their attention to her. “I felt that I was the one they were coming for and I waited to die,” she says. “But then the one with the axe suddenly started trying to pull my child away from me.”
Soalala tugged on the fabric, pressing her daughter closer to her body. “Let the child go,” said the man. Soalala pulled tighter still. “Let the child go, or we will kill you,” he repeated. Losing patience, the men wrenched away the little girl and ran.
She chased after them, screaming for help and crying. “My heart hurt me so much that I couldn’t stand it and my legs gave up on me,” she says. She collapsed about 100 metres down the dirt road, outside the large faded red gates of a school.
Days later, Landricia’s decapitated body was discovered at the home of a witch-doctor. Her head was found wrapped in plastic bags in a suitcase at another property a couple of kilometres away from where she was taken.
Landricia is among 13 people with albinism who have been killed in the country this year, according to Albinos Madagascar, an organisation set up in 2022 to advocate for people with the condition. Every one of them was beheaded. All but three of the victims were children, ranging from nine months old to 14 years. According to the association, this is already the worst year on record for killings of people with albinism in Madagascar.
“The situation is very critical, very cruel.” says Fulgence Soja, the association’s president, who lives with albinism himself. “There are a lot of big problems facing us, and we feel really unsafe.”
Albinism is an inherited genetic condition that reduces the amount of melanin pigment formed in the skin, hair and eyes and occurs in all ethnic groups. It often leads to poor vision and heightens the risk of skin cancer.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the prevalence of albinism is the highest worldwide, affecting more than one in 4,000 people in some countries, according to the World Health Organization.
People living with the condition face severe threats, including ritual killings, rape and mutilation, in several African countries. These attacks are driven by harmful superstitions that their body parts bring wealth, political success and good luck.
In Madagascar, the eyes of a person with albinism are particularly sought after. Children are targeted because of beliefs suggesting their innocence will make any potion made from their body parts more powerful. They are also vulnerable and easier to kidnap.
Nobody will talk openly about what goes on, but everyone is aware. Witch-doctors the Guardian spoke to denied all knowledge of any beliefs surrounding people with albinism, or what they might be “used for”. They, and others, say these beliefs must come from “outside”.
This level of brutality against people with albinism is said to be a recent phenomenon in Madagascar. Soja remembers first hearing about a beheading of someone with albinism in 2017. Muluka-Anne Mitti-Drummond, the UN independent expert on albinism, started receiving reports of killings in Madagascar in 2021.
“We had recorded more than 28 cases of attacks between late 2020 and 2022; the majority were against children. I was very concerned,” she says. She visited the following year and compiled a report on what was happening.
Mitti-Drummond found that profiles of attackers varied, and included relatives of victims, community members, people who travelled from other regions, and dahalos (cattle raiders). “Most perpetrators are acting with the intent of selling body parts or exploiting a person with albinism for financial means,” she wrote. “In many cases, only the middleperson is caught, while the masterminds of the attacks remain unknown.”
Life-altering sums of money are paid to those willing to kill a child with albinism and procure their eyes. Often entire networks are involved, and violence is said to increase in the run-up to elections. Sources told the Guardian that, because of this and the expense, high-powered people, including senior politicians and business people, were probably ordering some of the killings.
Madagascar is one of the poorest nations on Earth with about 80% of its population living on less than $2.15 (£1.60) a day. Since it gained independence from France in 1958, the country has experienced bouts of political instability, disputed elections and violent coups. In October 2025, youth-led protests toppled president Andry Rajoelina, and Col Michael Randrianirina declared himself head of a transitional government for what he said would last 18 to 24 months.
The country is also among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis, with drought, floods and cyclones causing death, displacement, and damage to crops and infrastructure. A lean season and El Niño threaten to push the south into emergency conditions this year, with high levels of food insecurity and malnutrition.
Sabina Lauber, a senior human rights adviser to the UN in Madagascar, believes it is this that is driving people to target individuals with albinism. “Madagascar is one of the very few countries in the world where every development and wellbeing indicator has decreased over the last 10 years,” she says. “At the same time, the population has dramatically increased and so there is a level of desperation for survival. People are turning to harmful practices to address the problem.”
In the hours after Soalala’s daughter was taken, a phone and a flip-flop were found in the courtyard outside. They had been left behind by the attackers and were taken away by the police for investigation.
Soalala divided her time between searching for Landricia alone and with members of the police and her wider family and visiting her husband, Mario William Solovenin, in hospital. It was a few days before she remembered where she had seen one of the attackers before.
About three months earlier, she says she and Solovenin had taken Landricia to hospital to treat sunburn on her shoulders. On the way they met a man that Solovenin knew through his work as a rickshaw driver. That man later came by the house, which the family now believe was to scout out their home.
Soalala told this to the police, who went to arrest him. He gave up the names of his accomplices. Chantal Rasoavahininoro, Soalala’s cousin who also lives in Toliara and acted as an intermediary between authorities and the family, says the men were tortured to extract confessions and information as to where Landricia’s body was.
When Soalala was told her daughter had been beheaded, she was inconsolable, says Rasoavahininoro. “Her first question was, ‘Are the eyes there?’” she says. “She almost went mad, she lost her mind.”
Four months on, a team of lawyers representing the family is in the preliminary stages of putting a case together. According to one of the team, Arlette Rafanomadio, 18 people, including two women, have now been arrested and are being held in custody.
One is a Sri Lankan national involved in mining.
Madagascar has a wealth of natural resources, including gold, manganese and copper. The island produces at least 40% of the world’s sapphires, alongside rubies, emeralds and semi-precious quartz. Tohovery Razakamanana, a UN human rights officer, says a significant proportion of attacks against people with albinism have occurred in or near mining areas, particularly mines for precious stones and gold. He also notes that while these attacks used to be concentrated in certain areas of the south, widely seen to be poorer and with higher levels of food insecurity, they are now happening all over Madagascar.
“To get back to the very beginning,” he says, “it all started in the deep south. Then we observed some cases in the south-east, south-west, midwest, and then in the north. But rarely in the capital and surrounding districts.”
While data collection has been poor, making it difficult to determine the origins and extent of attacks against people with albinism, human rights organisations say the situation this year is particularly worrying because of the geographical spread and grisly nature of the killings. People in cities are now being targeted rather than just those in remote rural areas.
An atmosphere of terror now exists for people with albinism and their families. Odette, 20, lives in a city in northern Madagascar where it is hot year round. She doesn’t understand why she is a varira (the Malagasy word for someone with albinism), but she knows her eyesight is blurry and that she burns easily. She squints as she struggles to see, there are sores all over her arms and legs and her lips are cracked and swollen from the sun.
In February, her cousin Marcellin, 14, who also had albinism, was murdered. She remembers him as a cheerful and talkative boy, who used to come round asking for soap.
Marcellin was beheaded and his body left under a mango tree across the dirt track from the wooden property where he lived with his older sister and her family. His head has never been found.
When the Guardian visited, two young girls sat behind a table under the same mango tree selling vegetables. The tyre Marcellin was sitting on outside his front door when he was snatched is still there. According to Soja, four people linked to a local politician have been arrested.
Odette has a three-year-old son and struggles to make money; she earns about 3,000 ariary (50p) a day from working in the fields and doing odd jobs. She is not with the father of her child. When she told him she was pregnant he didn’t stick around. She says: “He told me, ‘I love the colour of your skin, but I’m not going to be with you, because you’re varira.’”
One evening about a month ago, she was at the home she rented with her son when she heard a group of men approach and bang on the door. She ran to her mother’s house. After that, she decided to move in with her wider family and now sleeps sharing a mattress with about a dozen people in a small mud hut with a straw roof overlooking a patch of water not far from the city centre.
“I am a varira like Marcellin, so I’m really scared,” she says. “The house is not a good one, it’s not secure. I worry that there aren’t enough people here and that if someone comes, they will murder me.”
About 90 miles (150km) west, nine-year-old Veroline and her younger brother play outside the mayor’s house in a village near a Unesco-recognised national park where tourists go to see lemurs and other wildlife.
Both children have albinism. Three members of the armed forces watch over them; one carries a shotgun, another wears a handgun at his side.
They are here, living under the mayor’s protection, because in May, their older brother, Rakotombelo, 14, was killed. Veroline was sleeping in the same room when some men crashed through the wooden door. It remains broken to this day. She has very few memories of that night, other than her aunt telling her to run. Her father, who lives in a nearby town, says she told him she hid under a cart parked outside, against the wall of the house. “Some people came and I found out they were enemies,” she says. “I saw them carrying my brother. I told them, ‘Why are you doing that? Is he a child you gave birth to that you can do that to him?’”
Her aunt, Rasoa, and her husband were held hostage by two men in the next room. “They carried knives and said ‘Don’t move, or we will kill you’,” says Rasoa. When they left, she screamed until neighbours came. It was then that she realised her nephew’s head had been cut off. His body had been left, and the wall was covered in blood. “What happened was scandalous,” she says. “I was so sad because he was like my child. Even now, I’m devastated that a child I raised was violated like that.”
While she was at Rakotombelo’s funeral a couple of days later, there was a secret ballot held among the villagers to determine who they suspected had committed the murder. Fourteen people were arrested and are being detained, according to Francois Xavier Zaranaina, the mayor. Rasoa’s husband is one of them. “We don’t have any proof, but all I can say is that some of them might have done it, some of them probably didn’t do it, but because of various rumours and conflicts, those people were arrested,” says Zaranaina.
He has heard the superstitions about the eyes of people with albinism and suspects that is why Rakotombelo, who he says was good at football, was killed. He is eager for Veroline and her brother to no longer be his responsibility, particularly as the killers may come back. “They are burdens,” he says.
The killings have become an issue of national concern. The president has deployed his personal guard to hunt down perpetrators, and the first lady has promised to open a centre in the south where people with albinism can seek refuge.
On 4 August, a video was posted on the president’s Facebook page showing the alleged perpetrators behind the murder of a child with albinism who were caught in a sting operation; among the accomplices were the child’s grandfather and police officers. Two days later, the president wrote in a post accompanied by photos: “Because I heard that there are still people threatening to kill this albino child and her mother, I have decided that the family will be brought up to [the capital] Antananarivo immediately, and I will personally take full responsibility for their lives!” The Guardian could not independently verify the information in the posts, or the videos.
UN experts and local advocates emphasise that addressing the crisis facing people with albinism in Madagascar requires collaboration. Soja, who is now advising the president on the issue, wants a national action plan that addresses security, education and health “so that we can live like everyone else”.
Before that, he says: “The priority is to stop [the killings] because any solution for people of albinism to be able to educate themselves and go to work, depends on that.”
Razakamanana at the UN says a lack of accurate data remains a stumbling block. He is urging the government to conduct a census to determine how many people with albinism there are in the country.
Much needs to be done in terms of raising awareness, he adds. “Even educated people in the capital are not aware [that albinism is a genetic condition]. We have to start with awareness-raising campaigns and education.”
Four months on from the murder of baby Landricia in Toliara, Soalala and her husband’s grief is still raw. They look broken, weary and like every last drop of joy has been drained from them. Tears form in Soalala’s eyes as she talks about what her daughter was like. Landricia had a reddish tint to her hair with chocolate-coloured eyes. “She took after her father, and was a calm and happy child,” she says.
Soalala still cries often and so does her eldest daughter. Her youngest remaining child, Patricia, who also has albinism, often asks where nanke (an affectionate Malagasy term for a younger sibling) is. “I tell her she is dead, I don’t want to lie. I also tell her I don’t want to talk about it,” says Soalala.
When Patricia was born, Soalala says people in the community warned her: “The child has albinism. Be careful, protect her because she might get stolen.” For that reason, Soalala doesn’t work and rarely goes out, preferring to keep her children hidden. The family relies on her husband’s daily income of about 6,000 ariary (£1) from driving a rickshaw.
The family lives in a constant state of anxiety and terror. As Patricia starts to cry and demands attention from her mother, Soalala says: “I can’t sleep at night because I’m so scared and anxious. The evil people might still be seeking this child.”

U.S. Air Force pays $64 million for secretive balloon project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Aerostar a $64.4 million sole-source contract for Swamp Gas, a prototype for an urgent high-altitude balloon need.
- The contract runs through March 2028, and the balloon's mission, users and payloads have not been disclosed.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded balloon maker Aerostar a $64.4 million contract to quickly build a prototype for an urgent high-altitude balloon requirement under a project called Swamp Gas.
The contract covers development of a “minimum viable product” prototype, meaning an early working version with just enough capability to be tested and used, to support what the Pentagon called a “High-Altitude Balloon Operational Urgency.” Operational urgency is the term the military uses for a need from the field that has to be met faster than normal acquisition allows.
The notice does not say what the balloon is meant to do, which U.S. military command or unit asked for it, what it will carry or where it could be used. Work will be done in Arlington, Virginia, and is scheduled to finish by March 23, 2028.
Aerostar Technical Solutions received the contract without competition. Nearly all of the money was committed at once: $57.7 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds and $6.3 million in fiscal 2026 funds, about $64 million of the $64.4 million total. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is managing the contract.
The project name has an unusual history. In 1966, U.S. Air Force consultant J. Allen Hynek suggested that “swamp gas” could explain a wave of UFO sightings in Michigan, an explanation that became a lasting punchline in the UFO world. The Air Force did not say why it chose the name.
Aerostar builds stratospheric balloons that fly far above commercial airliners. Its larger Thunderhead balloon operates between about 16,800 and 22,900 m (55,000 and 75,000 feet), can stay aloft for 60 days or more and can carry up to about 90 kg (200 pounds) of equipment, according to the company. It also makes a smaller balloon, Lightning, designed to carry a single payload and be launched by a small team without a runway.
The company has worked with the Pentagon on balloons for years. In 2021, the Defense Innovation Unit hired Aerostar to demonstrate how stratospheric balloons could carry communications relays and sensors for U.S. forces. More recently, Aerostar has paired its balloons with the solar-powered Apollo-R drone built by Icarus, with the balloon lifting the drone into the stratosphere before it flies on its own. Aerostar executive Russ Van Der Werff told The War Zone in July that its balloons carry radio links with ranges beyond 160 km (100 miles) and that a Thunderhead could act as a “mothership” for several drones.
The U.S. Army has tested balloon-carried drones in at least three exercises this year, most recently launching micro high-altitude balloons, one carrying an Apollo-R, on Japan’s Hokkaido island on Sept. 18 during Exercise Orient Shield 26. Earlier launches took place off Morocco during African Lion 26 and on Guam during Valiant Shield 2026.
High-altitude balloons drew wide public attention in February 2023, when a U.S. Air Force F-22 shot down a Chinese balloon off South Carolina after it drifted across the United States. Supporters of the technology argue that balloons are cheaper than satellites and aircraft such as the Global Hawk and can linger over an area for weeks.

Borrowers again 'hit over the head' to bring inflation down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:46 UTC
18:00:46 KST

analysis
Australia's rising interest rates are not just down to government spending
Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?
If you listen only to the opposition, some economic commentators, and sections of the press, it's entirely down to government financial mismanagement at the federal and state levels.
If, instead, you choose to listen to the person most responsible for your mortgage rate, it's a bit of everything all at once.
"The bottom line is that there are a number of pressures all bearing down on inflation at the moment," RBA governor Michele Bullock told reporters following the meeting where the bank's board raised its benchmark rate to 4.6 per cent.
The most serious energy supply shock in 50 years has collided with the biggest technology investment boom on record, pushing up the cost of imported fuel and tech equipment, at the same time as Australia was at the tail end of a housing boom and consumer spending spree.
Speaking specifically about the energy shock, Ms Bullock (and the rest of the board in its post-meeting statement) emphasised the role the lingering, and worsening, conflict has played in stoking inflation.
"The longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases,"
"Now, will they be able to? If they're in industries, for example, where there's excess demand, they might be able to pass it on."
This is not the pandemic version of excess demand, where ultra-low rates and mammoth stimulus payments to households and businesses sent the economy hurtling down a supply-constrained, pothole-strewn back road at 100 kilometres an hour.
This is the economic equivalent of not noticing the speed limit has changed and doing 60 in a roadwork zone.
In other words, the current "excess demand" isn't feeling very excess for most households, even though they're the ones (if they have a mortgage) being asked to pay the penalty.
In the more wonky language of the post-meeting statement, the RBA board explained:
"Growth in aggregate demand needs to remain subdued for a period to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target."
In plain English, we need you, mortgage borrowers, to enjoy a lower standard of living so that the economy has capacity to build lots of data centres and pay for more expensive fuel imports while inflation still comes down.
As independent economist Chris Richardson told The Business last night:
"Inflation is just too much money chasing too little stuff.
"But no Reserve Bank, no government can wave a magic wand and make Australia produce more stuff overnight.
"So the question becomes, who gets less money to spend? Who gets hit over the head? We have a system that uses interest rates to to basically hit borrowers over the head."
Loading...
So is the government off the hook?
Not entirely. While it has been keen to talk up the effect of the Middle East crisis, Michele Bullock said that was not the sole driver of Australia's inflation woes.
"This isn't all about the Middle East conflict," she told reporters.
"It is making things much worse, but we did start from a position of excess demand anyway, and that's why we started raising interest rates even before the conflict started."
Loading...
Her response is still well short of the critique launched by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.
"The current interest rates are a result of Labor's actions, let's be clear,"
"And we know that this is a government that is spending too much."
A criticism that drew a sharp rebuke from Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
"I delivered the first surplus, in fact the first two surpluses, for a decade and a half," he fired back at reporters questioning his fiscal credentials.
"Average real spending growth has been less than half our predecessors and less than it was before COVID."
When you look at international comparisons, it's hard to argue that Australia has the second-highest central bank interest rate among advanced economies because of extreme fiscal indiscipline.
As this OECD chart shows, when it comes to deficit spending, which is what matters for the net amount of demand the government is injecting into the economy, Australia is broadly around the middle of the pack, and a long way behind the budget train wreck that is the US.
If the government's deficit is part of the problem, Angus Taylor's solution of "axing Labor's toxic taxes" in the absence of concrete plans to slash government services or payments to make up for the lost revenue, and then some, is hardly a fiscally responsible alternative.
As Richardson noted in an AFR column earlier this year, despite the argy-bargy between Australia's politicians over modest tax rises here and spending restraint there, Canberra is fiddling while the nation's finances are in a slow burn.
"If inflation is too much money chasing too little stuff and governments give us extra money — and they did a lot of that, state and federal in recent years — they become part of the problem and make the Reserve Bank's life harder," Richardson observed.
Loading
Is there another way to lower inflation?
Yes, but the ball is firmly in the government's court.
When asked by The Australian's Matthew Cranston whether adjusting the super guarantee to take some money out of people's pay but leave it in their future retirement nest egg might be a more "nuanced" way to tackle inflation, Bullock declined to comment, saying, "That's not at all within our gift."
Preliminary research undertaken by the progressive Centre for Policy Development think tank suggests that temporarily increasing the super guarantee by 0.5 per cent might take about $2 billion per quarter out of the economy, similar to the effect of a 0.25 percentage point rate hike.
If you want government spending restraint, another option is to index administered prices to the midpoint of the RBA's target band, rather than the consumer price index.
The CPD's economists, led by Warwick Smith, found administered prices accounted for 7.2 per cent of the 26.8 per cent cumulative inflation between 2020-2026.
"This bakes cost-push shocks (such as oil spikes) into statutory prices a year later, feeding a price spiral, inspiring extra wage claims and extending the duration of inflation episodes," they argued.
Limiting those regulated price increases would be incredibly painful for the public and corporate operators in those industries as they would be unable to offset their input cost increases, but it would be an effective way to help short-circuit inflation.
The reality is, there is no painless way to lower inflation, especially when it's largely imported and overseas corporates and governments are the main profiteers
"We get to pick our poison, but we can't avoid the fact that it is poison to bring inflation down," Richardson said.
The difference is that we could force more people to take the poison rather than dosing up one particular section of the population so much it almost kills them.

Italy: Meloni government extends fuel decree, excise duty cuts to 1 May
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:46 UTC
18:00:46 KST

"It will cost 500 million euros," Economy Minister Giorgetti announced after Friday morning's cabinet meeting. The 25-cent discount due to end on 7 April, with tax credits extended to agricultural firms.
El Consejo de Ministros ha dado luz verde al nuevo decreto ley sobre carburantes, que prorroga el recorte de los impuestos especiales hasta el 1 de mayo. Así lo ha anunciado este viernes por la mañana, al término del Consejo de Ministros, el ministro de Economía italiano, Giancarlo Giorgetti.
La primera medida, aprobada el 18 de marzo, vencía el 7 de abril.
En rueda de prensa, Giorgetti ha anunciado también "una intervención específica para las explotaciones agrícolas", a las que se extiende el crédito fiscal del 20%, ya adoptado para la pesca.
Las novedades afectan también a las exportaciones y en particular a Simest, la sociedad del Grupo CDP dedicada a la internacionalización de las empresas italianas.
"El coste de esta medida, ha añadido Giorgetti, es de alrededor de 500 millones de euros. De ellos, 200 millones cuentan con autocobertura que deriva del incremento de la recaudación del IVA, mientras que 300 millones son recursos que se han recuperado sustancialmente de las partidas ETS CO2 que aún no se habían utilizado, teniendo cuidado de no tocar las que se habían destinado originalmente al alivio de los grandes consumidores de energía".
En cuanto a las preocupaciones por la prolongación de la guerra en Oriente Medio, el ministro ha dicho que, si la situación no cambia, la derogación de la Unión Europea (UE) sobre los límites de déficit y el umbral del 3% "será inevitable". Italia estaba cerca de volver a situar el déficit por debajo del 3% del PIB y de salir del procedimiento de la UE, con el beneficio de disponer de más flexibilidad en las restricciones de gasto.
Qué prevé el decreto sobre carburantes
La medida aprobada este viernes prorroga el descuento en los surtidores introducido por el Gobierno el 18 de marzo. Los italianos ya pagan 25 céntimos menos por litro de diésel y gasolina, mientras que la rebaja es de 12 céntimos en el repostaje de GLP. La primera fase ha costado unos 528 millones de euros.
El decreto incluye también un crédito fiscal del 28% sobre las compras de gasóleo a favor de los transportistas por carretera y de los pescadores.
Desde la entrada en vigor de la medida, los precios han seguido subiendo, en línea con la tendencia al alza del precio del petróleo, mientras las tensiones y los enfrentamientos en Oriente Medio entre Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán no parecen remitir, y sigue bloqueada la partida en el crucial estrecho de Ormuz, por donde transita alrededor del 20% del petróleo mundial.
Según el seguimiento del Ministerio de Medio Ambiente, durante la semana pasada los precios medios han situado la gasolina en 1,733 euros por litro y el gasóleo en 2,032 euros. En comparación con el periodo anterior al ataque de Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán, se trata de 6 céntimos más por litro para la gasolina sin plomo y de 31 céntimos adicionales para el gasóleo.
Codacons: "La prórroga no basta, el descuento debía haberse aumentado"
"La prórroga del recorte de las accisas decidida hoy por el Gobierno no es suficiente para devolver los precios de los carburantes a niveles aceptables". Así lo afirma Codacons.
"A causa de las continuas subidas en los surtidores, el precio del gasóleo, y pese a la reducción de las accisas dispuesta por el Gobierno el pasado 18 de marzo, ha vuelto a los niveles anteriores a la medida fiscal y, a día de hoy, supera los 2,1 euros por litro en nada menos que 9 regiones italianas", explica la asociación de defensa de los consumidores.
Los precios más altos se registran en Bolzano, donde el diésel en autoservicio cuesta 2,134 euros por litro, seguida de Calabria (2,116 euros/litro), Friuli Venezia Giulia (2,113 euros por litro), Liguria y Lombardía (2,108 euros/litro), Apulia y Valle de Aosta (2,104 euros/litro), Basilicata (2,102 euros/litro) y Piamonte (2,100 euros/litro).
En las autopistas, el gasóleo cuesta hoy 2,137 euros por litro y la gasolina 1,822 euros por litro, señala Codacons, según la cual "el efecto del descuento sobre las accisas dispuesto por el Gobierno ha quedado totalmente anulado por las subidas en los surtidores. Por este motivo esperábamos hoy del Consejo de Ministros no solo una prórroga del recorte de las accisas, sino un refuerzo del descuento fiscal para devolver los precios del gasóleo a niveles aceptables", concluye.

EU’s net payers insist on ‘several hundred billion euros’ in budget cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:58:03 UTC
17:58:03 KST

The European Commission wants to create new powers to raise revenue directly through bloc-wide taxes, with e-cigarettes, vapes and cryptocurrency transactions all being considered. | Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — A coalition of wealthy EU nations is demanding that the next long-term budget be dramatically scaled back as diplomats and officials try to reach a deal by year-end.
In a letter seen by POLITICO, the leaders of Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Denmark, Sweden and Finland call for the next draft of the budget to be "reduced by several hundred billion euros" when it is presented by Ireland, which holds the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU.
The next seven-year multi-annual financial framework, due to take effect in 2028, governs spending on everything from agriculture subsidies to defense schemes, infrastructure investments and payments to poorer regions. The European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion.
Advertisement
However, many net contributors — those who pay in more than they get out — want their bills cut. Others, including those who stand to gain most from the funding, want to see spending increased.
"Our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all Member States’ contributions. While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden," the letter reads. A 60% nominal increase in the size of the budget compared to the current one, they argue, is "simply not realistic."
In a bid to lessen the financial pressure on national capitals, the Commission wants to create new powers to raise revenue directly through bloc-wide taxes (known as own resources), with e-cigarettes, vapes and cryptocurrency transactions all being considered. That, however, has not satisfied more frugal nations.
"The EU budget is ultimately paid for by European citizens. That remains true whatever financing mechanism or own resources we invent," the letter cautions.
The Irish presidency is due to present a new negobox — a detailed breakdown of the proposed budget with fresh figures — in the coming days. Leaders will then hold talks over its content at a two-day summit in Brussels from Oct. 15.
Negotiators are eager to get a deal by the end of the year to ensure the budget is in place when the current one expires, and to prevent discussions being roiled by national elections in France, Poland and other countries.
Advertisement
European Council President António Costa has been publicly optimistic about the prospect of an agreement. However, an internal German diplomatic cable obtained by POLITICO warned ministers and officials that “no potential areas for compromise were apparent” between the two sides when they met for negotiations earlier this month.
“Entrenched positions” from both frugal countries and those that want higher spending have yielded “no surprises,” the cable stated — adding that Ireland is now pleading with envoys to start compromising.

Gaza’s child amputees find hope and support at Al-Bait Village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:57:59 UTC
17:57:59 KST

Breadcrumb
From limb loss to rehabilitation: Inside Al-Bait Village, where Gaza's child amputees are learning to live again
Upon arriving at Al-Bait, the first village in Deir al Balah in central Gaza, providing education, healthcare and rehabilitation to orphaned children and children who have lost limbs, I expected to see children whose lives had been shattered by the devastation caused by Israel's ongoing genocidal war.
Instead, what stood out was the effort being made to give the children back something they had lost even before their limbs: the feeling of simply being children.
That sense of normality showed up in the ordinary things around the village: children sitting together for meals, drawings covering the walls, and teachers welcoming them as they arrived for the day, making the place feel less like a centre for children affected by the war and more like a new home.
This feeling of home is reflected in the name Al-Bait, which translates to 'the house' in English, and the idea for such a place came from an experience Abu Majed, the founder, had several months before the village opened.
In July 2025, while Gaza was experiencing one of the most difficult stages of the war and famine, Abu Majed left his home looking for food for his starving family.
Markets were empty and, after losing hope of finding anything, he headed towards an aid distribution point, hoping to find something among those returning from there.
On that journey, Abu Majed saw scenes that would later lead him to create Al-Bait Village.
While the sounds of bombing filled the area, he saw a mother trying to protect her child amid the fear and chaos and heard her saying, "I lost your father. Who do I have left if you leave me too?"
On his way back, he also saw two children who had lost limbs waiting for one of their relatives to return from an aid distribution point.
The scenes stayed with him after he returned home, and he began thinking about what he could do for children whose lives had changed in a single moment.
The project began to take shape in November 2025, with the village welcoming its first children at the beginning of 2026.
With limited funding and resources to begin with, a group of volunteers worked to transform a rented building into a suitable space for children, initially aiming to support around 130 children.
As more children began coming to the village, that number grew to around 240 children aged four to 14.
A new sense of routine
The daily routine at Al-Bait is designed around giving the children a sense of structure.
Every morning, a village bus picks them up and brings them to the centre, where teachers welcome them at the door before their day begins with education and skill-building activities.
Their time there isn't limited to books and lessons; some days are spent making wooden models, while others involve dabke, singing, and activities related to technology and artificial intelligence.
That routine also includes medical and psychological support, as the village provides healthcare and regular medical check-ups alongside rehabilitation for children who have lost limbs.
Every week, a psychologist meets with the children individually, as workers say not all the effects of the war show up in their bodies.
Some of what they carry shows up as fear, silence, or difficulty returning to daily life after experiences that have changed everything.
The children's physical and emotional needs can also affect how they adjust to the village itself.
Workers say some children arrived suffering from malnutrition and psychological trauma, while during their first days others did not want to study or stay at the village.
After months of displacement and fear, returning to any form of normal life could feel unfamiliar, but over time the place became part of their lives.
For some children, leaving the village has also been difficult because of the routine and community they found there.
One child who had returned to northern Gaza cried upon learning he would no longer be able to return to Al-Bait Village, so the team later arranged monthly transportation for him to continue attending.
For children who have lost limbs, however, the support they receive at the village is only one part of the much longer process of adjusting to life after their injuries.
Life without a limb
The loss of limbs among children has become one of the most devastating consequences of the war in Gaza, with thousands reported to have lost one or more limbs since Israel began its attacks on the Gaza Strip.
For them, the injury does not end at the moment of amputation, as the lack of suitable prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation programmes can affect their movement, independence and ability to return to the lives they had before.
The experiences of people who have lost limbs came into renewed focus in September 2026 after the controversy surrounding Adidas' campaign featuring an amputee Israeli veteran.
The campaign prompted criticism and calls for a boycott, while activists drew attention to people who have lost limbs in Gaza, and Adidas later apologised for the campaign.
But behind the debate around the advert are the stories of children facing a different reality: losing a limb, waiting for a prosthetic and going through a long process of rehabilitation to regain some independence.
For the children at Al-Bait Village, those difficulties show up in the details of their everyday lives, with each child experiencing how their injury has changed what they can do.
Mahmoud, a 10-year-old boy, was inside his home while his mother was preparing food when they were hit. He says his sister was killed before she could eat, while his own leg was amputated up to his hip.
"I was standing inside the home while mama was preparing food. Suddenly, we were hit. Even my sister was killed before she could eat. I was injured, and my leg was amputated up to my hip," he tells The New Arab.
Before his injury, Mahmoud loved playing, especially football, and imagined himself growing up like his older brother, going to the gym and practising sports.
Now, he says the hardest thing is going outside and moving around like other children, which has also changed ordinary parts of his life, such as buying shoes.
"The hardest thing for me is going outside and moving like the other children," he says. "I buy boots, but I only wear one of them."
For Mahmoud, the solution he wants is a prosthetic limb, which he sees as a way of regaining some of the movement he has lost.
"I want to have a prosthetic limb," he adds.
Abdul Rahman, 12, has already received one. Before his injury, much of his life revolved around playing outside and riding his bicycle, and he was sitting outside his home when he got off his bike to help a neighbour charge a battery.
Moments later, the bombing happened, leaving him injured and without his leg.
The injury affected more than just Abdul Rahman's ability to move; he says he became embarrassed about going outside and spent most of his time on his phone.
Later, receiving a prosthetic limb helped him regain some independence and made it easier to move around.
"I was embarrassed to go outside and move around. I spent all my time on my phone," he says. "Since I got the prosthetic limb, I have been able to move better."
Abdul Rahman adds that he dreams of having an advanced electronic prosthetic limb, but his priorities shift as he talks about the other children at Al-Bait Village who are still waiting for prosthetics.
Rather than focusing on what he wants for himself, he says he wants the other children to have the same opportunity to move more independently.
"I don't want an electronic prosthetic limb anymore. I just want all my friends here to have prosthetic limbs too," he explains.
The long road to independence
Mohammed Musleh, a child from northern Gaza who was displaced to Deir al Balah, is also still adjusting to the changes caused by his injury.
His father had gone to an aid distribution point in the Al Nabulsi area during the famine, and after his father was delayed, Mohammed and his brother went looking for him before they were hit by shelling.
Before the injury, Mohammed says he was able to run, carry water jerrycans and do whatever he wanted, but he now needs help with many parts of his daily life even though he has received a prosthetic limb.
"I used to run, do whatever I wanted, and carry water jerrycans," he says. "Now I feel trapped."
Mohammed says the prosthetic limb has helped him, but only partly restored the independence he had before his injury.
"The prosthetic limb helped me by about 50%," he continues.
His experience reflects a wider problem facing the children at Al-Bait Village, because receiving a prosthetic limb is not necessarily the end of the process.
Children still need rehabilitation and time to learn how to use their prosthetics, while access to suitable limbs and the equipment needed to support their recovery remains a major challenge.
Al-Bait Village continues to support children who already have prosthetics and help others whenever resources become available, but the need remains much greater than what the village can provide on its own.
For children still waiting, losing a limb can affect ordinary parts of life, from moving around outside and playing with friends to doing things as simple as putting on a pair of shoes.
That is why the work at Al-Bait goes beyond rehabilitation. The village is also trying to provide children with a place to learn, eat together, participate in activities, and spend time with others who have experienced similar things, while supporting them through the emotional and physical effects of the ongoing genocide.
Months after Abu Majed first saw children who had lost their limbs while searching for food for his own family, he now stands among hundreds of children inside the village that grew out of that experience.
The shortage of prosthetic limbs and medical equipment continues to limit the children's ability to fully rebuild their lives, but Al-Bait Village is trying to give them somewhere to continue with their education, receive support and experience parts of childhood that the war has taken away from them.
Hassan Herzallah is a Gaza-based translator, writer and storyteller. He is in his third year studying English translation at the Islamic University of Gaza and continues his education online after the university was bombed. He contributes to Mondoweiss, Palestine Chronicle, The Massachusetts Review and other international outlets, documenting life under siege and displacement

Gokhan Ergocun
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Germany's general public debt rose 1% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter of 2026, driven by higher borrowing in special federal funds.
 
The country's general public budget owed the non-public sector €2.75 trillion ($3.12 trillion) at the end of the second quarter of 2026.
 
Preliminary data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed that public debt increased by 1%, or €26.3 billion, compared to the first quarter of the year.
The general public budget includes the federal government, states, municipalities and social security, along with all extra budgets, while the non-public sector comprises credit institutions and private companies.
Federal debt grew by 1.1%, or €20.5 billion, from the previous quarter to reach €1.9 trillion.
 
Two special funds drove this increase, just as they did in the previous quarter.
The Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality fund increased its debt by 39.1%, or €13.8 billion, to €48.9 billion.
The Bundeswehr special fund expanded its debt by 8.8%, or €4.2 billion, to €51.6 billion.
State governments held €646.2 billion in debt at the end of the second quarter, marking a 0.5%, or €2.9 billion, increase from the previous quarter.

North Korean landmine blasts in DMZ a 'violation of armistice,' Seoul says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:56:28 UTC
17:56:28 KST

The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world's most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
The blasts that wounded three South Korean soldiers last week were apparently caused by North Korean mines, Seoul said on Tuesday, adding it was an armistice violation that would prompt "corresponding measures."
One troop lost a foot due to the explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world's most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul's comments came a day after his ministry said North Korean mines were "highly suspected" of causing the two explosions last week.
"This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures," he told a parliamentary hearing, when asked whether the military had tentatively concluded that the mine was North Korean.
Kang said South Korean forces were in the DMZ to clear the area in advance of an operation with the UN Command to assess terrain changes caused by North Korean forces south of the Military Demarcation Line, which marks the nations' effective border.
The mine detectors used by the officials were the "latest models," the minister said, but detection efforts were hampered by dense vegetation in the area, noting that "clearing all the vegetation as they advanced was difficult."
"Our current assessment is that the mines may not have been detected because the detectors were being operated too far above the ground," he said.
At the hearing, Yang Jin-hyeok of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told lawmakers that a site investigation earlier on Tuesday discovered an unexploded North Korean plastic anti-personnel mine.
Kang told lawmakers the military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages", without giving details.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in a truce, not a peace treaty.
'Principal enemy'
Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, said on Monday that two landmines exploded during the 21 September incident and that a third, unexploded mine was found while soldiers were withdrawing after the blast.
"Taking into account the crater and the pattern of the flames from the explosion, the extent of the injuries sustained by the service members...we assess that North Korean landmines are highly suspected to have caused the blast," Kwon said at the time.
Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country's "principal enemy," Pyongyang's military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.
In a 2015 landmine incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.
Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the Military Demarcation Line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.
The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts along the border.

US, China cooperate on global AI governance despite intensifying competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:56:16 UTC
17:56:16 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The intensifying competition between the US and China in artificial intelligence (AI) continues alongside efforts to cooperate on governance rules, monitor AI-powered cyberattacks, and prevent frontier models from being controlled by non-state actors.
Two distinct approaches to global AI governance are emerging from the US and China, while a third approach is coming from the UN, according to a recent report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The number of partner countries in the US-led Silica Initiative, focusing on AI and semiconductor supply chains, reached 24 in June, while, on the other side, some 29 countries joined the rival Chinese-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) as founding members, the report published on Sept. 21 showed.
Pax Silica was made up of participants primarily from high-income economies and the US’ security partners in Europe, the Indo-Pacific, the Middle East, and Latin America. WAICO members are, in contrast, from low- and middle-income countries, with Kazakhstan being the only country participating in both initiatives.
The key AI agenda items between the US and China mostly focus on cooperation in tracking AI-powered cyberattacks, China’s access to advanced American models, Washington’s restrictions on open-source Chinese models, and preventing state-of-the-art frontier AI models from falling into the hands of non-state actors.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last week, talks between Xi and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, focused on developing AI in a human-centered and controllable way, as well as potential risks.
The CSIS report stated that the dialogue between the two parties could focus on developing common definitions to serve as a foundation for future discussion, such as determining which systems can be classified as frontier models.
One of the key elements of technological competition between the two countries is access to high-performance chips used in developing models.
US export controls on advanced technologies make it difficult for Chinese AI labs to access such chips and other computing resources, while China is moving toward developing its own semiconductor and AI capabilities.
The report highlighted that there is still no established mechanism for the parties to verify model security compliance, which stands in the way of potential AI security regulations.
 
US-China issues ‘no longer limited to trade deficits or tariffs’
 
Arzu Al, a political economy professor at Marmara University, told Anadolu that the meeting between Xi and Trump in Washington should be regarded as a strategic balancing act to manage the costs of competition, noting that the core issue between the two nations is no longer limited to trade deficits or tariffs.
“AI, advanced semiconductors, data infrastructure, energy capacity, and critical minerals became integral parts of economic power, national security, and foreign policy capabilities,” she said.
“Xi emphasized that AI must remain under human control and that its risks and benefits should be addressed together, while Trump supported the continued dialogue and cooperation in the area – this by no means constitutes the end of their technological competition, but in fact, it shows that the competition is intensifying in some areas while other areas remain open to controlled cooperation,” she added.
Al stated that the structure we’re seeing today should not be explained through the lens of classic Cold War bloc formation between the countries, but through a “controlled techno bloc formation.”
While the US and China have yet to fully sever their economic ties, the two countries also do not want strategic interdependencies to limit their potential.
“What is decisive in the technopolitical order is not so much the interdependence but rather the extent to which the interdependence is asymmetrical and whether it can be weaponized to pressure one side,” she said.
Al noted that Taiwan coming up during the meeting showed that structural disagreements between the US and China on security matters persist.
“Maintaining serious competition in security and technology while cooperating on AI at the same time is not a contradiction – it is precisely the nature of the current relationship between the two countries,” she said.
“This is also precisely where the real significance of this meeting lies, as the competition between Washington and Beijing is not mutually exclusive, and both competition and cooperation will exist simultaneously in this new era – the struggle to grow technological capacity and access critical inputs will continue to be one of the fundamental axes of US-China relations,” she added.

Google appeals EU data-sharing order, warns of 'irreversible harm'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:52:18 UTC
17:52:18 KST

Google argues that Android is already open to other services and that the search data requirements lack adequate safeguards, user knowledge and consent.
Google said on Tuesday it had appealed EU measures announced in July requiring it to share data with rival search engines and give competing AI services greater access to Android, warning that the measures could put users’ privacy at risk.
The company filed its appeal with the EU’s General Court in Luxembourg.
“We’re appealing decisions that will force us to share people’s private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken vital security protections on Android,” said Oliver Bethell, Google’s senior director for competition.
The European Commission said Google must begin sharing search data from January 2027 to “rebalance the playing field” for rival search engines.
Changes to Android are also due next year. The Commission said the changes would give competing AI assistants access to features available to Google’s own services, such as Gemini, allowing users to activate a rival assistant by voice or ask it to carry out tasks in other apps.
Google argues that Android is already open to other services and that the search data requirements lack adequate safeguards, user knowledge and consent.
“People use Search for their most personal questions — from medical worries to close relationships — and mandating we share these personal queries without adequate safeguards would cause irreversible harm to user privacy,” Bethell said.
However, the Commission said when it announced the measures in July that they include protections for users’ privacy and device security.
It said search data would be anonymised before being shared and Google could assess whether a recipient posed serious security or data protection risks.
The appeal is the latest clash between Google and Brussels under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which sets rules for large tech companies that dominate key digital markets.
In a separate case in July, the Commission fined Google €890 million for favouring its own services in search results and restricting app developers from directing customers to other ways of buying their products.

No, he hasn't suddenly become a fashion icon overnight: these pictures are actually AI-generated, and Italians are sharing them over a controversial statement he made about women.
To understand the joke, we need to go back to something Tajani, leader of the centre-right Forza Italia party, said at a political event near Rome on 18 September.
He was responding to a question about why voters should choose an established party, such as Forza Italia, rather than a newer and more eye-catching rival, such as National Future, the far-right party led by MEP Roberto Vannacci.
Tajani compared a voter's choice of party with the advice he might give his son on what type of woman to marry.
In his analogy, he contrasted an attractive but potentially unfaithful woman with one who was less conspicuous but more dependable.
He then suggested the more "serious" woman might wear a longer skirt.
"Even if the polls say they prefer the [flashier girl], or the serious girl who maybe has a longer skirt than the other one, or it could be a muscular playboy versus the one who wears a tie to the office a little more often," Tajani said to the audience at the ITACA event. "I always recommend choosing the reliable one, and the centre-right is reliable."
The comment has gone viral on social media, where users have turned Tajani into a meme, commenting that the length of a woman's skirt says nothing about her loyalty.
Politicians and priests weigh in
The remarks have also prompted criticism from Italy's opposition politicians.
Former Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi, leader of the centrist Italia Viva party, shared two of the pictures, saying that Tajani was "more of a meme than a minister."
Elsewhere, senators from several opposition parties posted pictures of themselves in skirts as a protest. One participant described the demonstration as being about women’s freedom to dress without men judging them.
"This is a gesture of freedom to say that we are free to dress as we want," said Raffaella Paita, also from Italia Viva, who spearheaded the protest. "We believe that women's freedom is measured by every gesture of freedom, including the length of a skirt or any other gesture women choose to make without being judged by men."
The controversy also drew a response from the Catholic Church: Giuseppe Baturi, secretary-general of the Italian Bishops' Conference, said that women must be treated with respect.
"Every word, every glance at women must be filled with respect and admiration," he told journalists in a press conference. "For us Christians, the first place where the Word became flesh was a woman's womb."
"For those of faith, this forever affects how they look at women," he added. "Respect is needed, especially towards women, to the extent that they can be the object of superficial glances."
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the comment "came out badly", adding that she would not "blow it out of proportion."
As for Tajani himself, he has since apologised, saying he never intended to offend women.

Ugandan kingdom enthrones ex-TV anchor after succession fight
FORT PORTAL, Uganda, Sept 29 - A former television news anchor was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom on Tuesday, becoming the 13th monarch of the Batooro people in a ritual-laden coronation that ended a succession dispute.
Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeded King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, whose death last month from cancer at age 34 triggered a feud, with his mother saying a previously undisclosed son was entitled to the throne.
Uganda is a constitutional republic governed by an elected president, but four pre-colonial kingdoms remain as influential symbols of identity and heritage despite not having any political power.
A 21-member committee from the royal Babiito clan selected Kijanangoma, 56, who is Oyo Nyimba's cousin.
A source with knowledge of the succession dispute told Reuters that Uganda's central government pushed through that decision over the mother's objections.
Kijanangoma took the new royal name Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I in a traditional ceremony that included the slaughter of a bull and sprinkling of a hen's blood in Tooro's capital Fort Portal.
Nyabongo I walked to Karuziika Palace between midnight and 3 a.m. before taking part in a mock battle for the crown.
At Karuziika, young men dressed in tunics, orange shawls and skins held sticks and spears, some prostrating before the king.
Traditional dancers and drummers, some wearing calabashes, entertained guests who included President Yoweri Museveni.
Earlier, Charles Kayondo Kamurasi, the Omusuuga or head of the Babiito clan who had been wielding power since Oyo Nyimba's death, handed over authority to the new king in a church service at St. John's cathedral.
"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," Nyabongo I said in his maiden speech, pledging to rally his subjects to protect the environment.
TODDLER KING
Oyo Nyimba died in the US on August 27 while receiving treatment for angiosarcoma, an aggressive cancer.
He drew global attention in 1995 when enthroned at age 3 after the death of his father, with images of the toddler king in royal robes and a crown prompting widespread fascination.
Former colleagues of Nyabongo I at the state broadcaster UBC where he worked as a news anchor and editor, describe him as humble and down to earth.
"Everyone in Fort Portal is happy because of this new king. We are preparing. Women are ironing their masuka. Men are ironing their kanzus," said Tooro resident Elizabeth Kengonze in the run-up, referring to traditional clothes.
"People are practicing how they will sing Amakondere (praise music). We are very happy and grateful because Tooro, as a culture, is being promoted and the young ones are now knowing and learning how the Tooro culture was."
The coronation took place despite objections from Oyo Nyimba's mother, Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale. They say the late king left behind a young son and a will naming him as heir.
Oyo Nyimba was not married and was not publicly known to have children. The kingdom's prime minister first mentioned a child in a statement announcing his death.
Kamurasi said the clan knew of no child and had followed Tooro's customs in choosing a successor.
"The child they are claiming to be there is not known," he told media last week. REUTERS

African leaders to gather in Egypt for ambitious business summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:44:32 UTC
17:44:32 KST

Breadcrumb
African leaders to gather in Cairo for ambitious business summit as Egypt eyes expansion
African leaders will meet in Egypt on Friday for a business summit that Cairo hopes will bolster its clout across the continent.
The inaugural three-day Alamein Africa Forum is part of Egypt's push to reassert itself in a continent where China and Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, have emerged as major players.
After long focusing on the Middle East and the Mediterranean, Egypt is keen to rebuild its influence within Africa.
It has also sought to rally backing in its long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), which it sees as a threat to its vital share of Nile waters.
Friday's forum is expected to bring together more than 20 heads of state and government representatives in the Mediterranean city of Alamein, alongside business leaders, bankers and development institutions.
"This is an African platform," Egypt's deputy foreign minister for African affairs Mohamed Abu Bakr Saleh told AFP. "A country in East Africa should be able to sign an agreement with a country in West, North or southern Africa through this platform."
Saleh said the forum would become a biennial event under an African Union mandate, focusing on infrastructure, trade, agriculture, healthcare, mining, technology and renewable energy.
Officials estimate Egyptian investments across Africa at around $14 billion. Among Egypt's flagship ventures is Tanzania's $3 billion Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, built by a consortium led by Egyptian companies.
'Vast resources'
Yet trade within Africa remains limited, totalling just $192 billion in 2023 and only accounting for around 15 percent of the continent's total trade, compared with more than 55 percent in Asia and over 70 percent in Europe.
Africa also attracted about $70 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, a fraction of the roughly $1.6 trillion invested globally, according to the UN.
"Africa possesses vast resources, but they are still not being exploited to the level we would like to see," Saleh said.
The gathering also takes place against the backdrop of an unresolved dispute between Egypt and Ethiopia over the $5 billion GERD, Africa's largest hydroelectric project.
Ethiopia says the dam, inaugurated last year, is vital for economic growth, while Egypt says it could threaten Nile water supplies without a binding operating agreement.
More than a decade of negotiations have failed to yield a settlement.
"Our position on Egypt's water security has not changed and will not change," Saleh said. "It is an existential issue for Egypt."

Learning from the front line: Estonian defence sector bets on cheap, smart and flexible military drone systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:43:32 UTC
17:43:32 KST

Estonia is betting on cheap, resilient and locally built drones to deter a much larger neighbour. Euronews Next saw the technology in action and heard how lessons from Ukraine are helping shape it.
Estonia, the Russia-bordering NATO member, has a relatively small army — but as one of the world's digital leaders, it is looking to make up for that with technology.
Its defence industry is now building a wide range of cutting-edge military equipment, battle-tested in Ukraine and ready to scale up: low-cost, jamming-resistant drones, portable launch systems and sensors that spot threats in the sky.
Euronews Next was invited to an undisclosed location near Tallinn to see a demonstration of these Estonian-made systems.
KrattWorks showed how a single operator can now control a swarm of drones, each capable of carrying deadly explosives, at the same time. The company's core idea is to make each soldier count for more.
"The Estonian army is about 40,000 strong, but the adversary is quite a lot bigger. So we need to multiply our soldier [count]," Karmo Saar, Head of Sales at KrattWorks, told Euronews Next.
In Ukraine, he explained, one operator can already control seven of their drones.
The machines can also fly without a constant link to their operator. "The systems we develop in Estonia are fully autonomous," Saar said. "If they are being jammed and the connection is lost, they have all the computing power on board and they finish the mission themselves."
Estonia's defence industry is almost entirely private. Many firms supply Ukraine — while improving their products based on feedback from the battlefield.
Threod Systems, which makes surveillance drones, says that feedback has improved its designs.
"If you lose the GPS, what will the aircraft do? Previously it mostly crashed somewhere," Margus Allas, Test Engineer at Threod Systems, told Euronews Next.
"Nowadays, our product is that safe that it comes home — you can take it over and land safely. So that was a key feature that came from Ukraine."
Allas said Ukrainian users also pushed the company to test in harsher conditions. "In real life we want to use the aircraft in bad weather," he told Euronews Next.
Some operators are exhausted and have gone days without sleep, he added, so the software has to be simple to use.
Cheap, local and scalable
That experience has pushed Estonian firms towards flexible, lightweight and affordable solutions.
One example is a pneumatic drone catapult, also produced by Threod and widely used in Ukraine. The "Cata B" can be set up in minutes and needs only diesel fuel to launch drones.
Detection matters as much as the drones themselves. Rantelon, a radio-frequency technology company, showed a passive drone detector.
It emits no signals and only listens, so an enemy cannot easily locate it. "The advantage of being passive is that your enemy can't tell where your systems are," Kaspar Põder, Sales Project Manager at Rantelon, told Euronews Next.
The device can track several drones at once, across different radio bands, and covers military as well as civilian models.
Põder said uses range from border protection to critical infrastructure and large public events. "Drones are here to stay, and the market is growing," he told Euronews Next.
Electric Wings Group showed a 10-inch FPV drone designed to carry a munition to its target. The drone uses radio frequencies and is "not jamming proof," Jordan Vähesoo, Sales Manager at Electric Wings Group, told Euronews Next.
But jammers are expensive and not everywhere, he said: "If one [drone] breaks down or gets jammed, you just open a new one from the box and you go again."
The company can produce about 10,000 units a year now and says it can scale up from there.
The frames, propellers and motors are made in Estonia, and the batteries are assembled there. "I think it's important that every country has its own manufacturer. A lot of components right now are still coming through China," Vähesoo told Euronews Next.
Chinese parts are cheaper, he said, but European tenders increasingly ask for European electronics. "I would like to see that switch," he added.
The state is backing the push. Estonia wants to become a global hub for testing and building drones. The government aims to triple defence industry revenue to €1 billion between 2023 and 2030.
An adapting army
The armed forces are changing too. Hugo Urbla, Director of Operations at the Estonian Defence Forces' Force Transformation Command, told Euronews Next that Ukraine has shown how cheaply damage can now be done.
"A bang has become cheaper, because it costs [just] a few euros to fly something now," he said.
The Force Transformation Command organises cooperation between the armed forces, industry, research institutions and international partners.
"Things that are produced by Estonian companies, be it for dual use or for only military purposes, are being actively tested by the Defence Forces on major exercises but also on a day-to-day basis," Urbla said.
"This does not mean that these systems are off-the-shelf ready. A technological system will always need direct feedback from soldiers who are using it. Only this way can the system actually become one that is worth something to a soldier."
But drones will not replace conventional forces, he added.
"The armour and manoeuvre units will have a place in the next war," Urbla told Euronews Next. "We know what the current war looks like, but we do not know what the next war will look like."

“Humanitarian and relief conditions in the Gaza Strip had become dangerous and catastrophic, exposing hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians to deadly consequences,” the office said in a statement.
It dismissed Israeli claims that ample supplies had been allowed into Gaza as “misleading.”
“Israel permitted only 35% of the agreed number of trucks carrying humanitarian and relief aid and reconstruction materials to enter the enclave,” the office said. “Only 72,826 trucks were allowed to enter out of 210,600 humanitarian and relief trucks and trucks carrying reconstruction materials that were supposed to enter under the agreement.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Ambassador to Paraguay Lee Yueh-jung (李岳融) said bilateral cooperation has benefited education, health care, trade, and economic development, La Nacion reported Tuesday.
In an op-ed published by La Nacion, Lee said the partnership will mark its 70th anniversary next year. He said cooperation has covered agriculture, aquaculture, support for small businesses, and microloans for women entrepreneurs.
Taiwan has also helped finance social housing and major infrastructure projects, including the Tres Bocas tunnel, Lee said. He highlighted education and health care as particularly important areas of cooperation.
The government has offered scholarships to Paraguayan students since 1991, with more than 900 pursuing undergraduate or graduate degrees in Taiwan. It also provides professional training in fields including medicine, nursing, engineering, cybersecurity, hairdressing, and culinary arts.
The two countries jointly established the Taiwan-Paraguay Polytechnic University to train engineers. The university has more than 300 graduates and plans to launch a master’s program and move to its permanent campus next year.
In health care, Taiwan has worked with Paraguay to introduce a digital information system at public health facilities. More than 1,300 facilities use the system, which has recorded over 61 million patient visits.
The system provides digital medical records and helps manage medicines, supplies, and staff. Lee said it also gives authorities real-time data to support health care decisions.
Trade between the two countries has also grown. Taiwan is the largest buyer of Paraguayan pork, a major buyer of its beef, and recently opened its market to Paraguayan poultry.
Lee said diversifying export markets has become increasingly important as trade tensions and economic pressure disrupt global supply chains. He encouraged Paraguayan businesses to build closer ties with Taiwanese companies and universities and explore opportunities for investment and cooperation.
Lee was also scheduled to attend the first Paraguay-Taiwan international forum at the Catholic University of Asuncion on Tuesday. The event was set to focus on Taiwan’s role in democracy, its geopolitical challenges, and its significance to Paraguay and Latin America.

Taiwan reports 12.3% drop in road deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:16 UTC
17:39:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan recorded 1,569 road deaths from January through July, down 12.3% from the same period in the government’s 2023 baseline year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said Tuesday in a press release.
The ministry said all major road safety indicators had improved from the baseline, although elderly road deaths remained a concern. Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌), director-general of the Department of Railways, Highways, and Road Safety, said motorcycle fatalities fell by 206, or 18.1%, while pedestrian deaths declined by 18, or 9%, and deaths involving drunk driving fell by 82, or 54.3%, per CNA.
Compared with the same period last year, however, deaths among people aged 65 and older increased by 33, or about 5%, to 697. Wu said the increase was concentrated in Taoyuan, Taichung, and Hualien County.
Motorcycle crashes accounted for about half of the elderly deaths in those three localities, with many occurring when riders turned left at intersections. Pedestrian incidents accounted for about 20%, with many occurring while people were crossing roads.
The ministry designated 2023 as its baseline year because that marked the beginning of a four-year road safety improvement plan. Compared with the 2023 baseline, elderly road deaths fell by 22, or 3.1%.
Wu warned that data from previous years showed elderly road deaths tended to increase during the fourth quarter. He attributed the trend to larger temperature differences between day and night, shorter daylight hours in autumn and winter, and age-related declines in physical function.
Wu urged older people to take extra care when traveling early in the morning or at night and to wear brightly colored clothing or reflective accessories to make themselves more visible.
The ministry expanded its definition of drug-impaired driving incidents in July. Previously, the statistics counted only cases in which the party considered primarily responsible was impaired. They now also include cases in which another party was impaired and committed a traffic violation.
From January through June, 23 deaths were recorded in incidents involving drug-impaired driving, followed by seven in July alone. Officials said the revised definition was intended to present a more complete picture of such incidents and help police assess enforcement measures.
