====================================================================================================

Europe’s most troubled companies: Who’s hit hardest by high interest rates?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:14:27 UTC
15:14:27 KST

From Legoland's owner to Lipton tea and Aston Martin, Europe's lowest-rated borrowers face a looming refinancing wall as interest rates rise again.
Borrowing money is getting more expensive again.
For most European companies, that is uncomfortable but manageable. For businesses already heavily indebted, it can become a much bigger problem.
Some of the names caught in the squeeze are surprisingly familiar.
They include the company behind Legoland and Madame Tussauds, the owner of Lipton tea, one of Europe's largest residential property managers and the telecoms empire built by billionaire Patrick Drahi.
Then there is Aston Martin, the British maker of James Bond's car.
Many borrowed heavily when interest rates were close to zero.
All sit in, or close to, the CCC area of the credit-rating scale, among the lowest ratings before default.
Now some of that debt is approaching maturity, just as borrowing costs are rising again.
And investors are demanding very high returns to lend them money.
The ECB hiked again: That's raising the pressure on Europe's weakest borrowers
After cutting rates through 2025, the European Central Bank has reversed course.
It raised its deposit rate in June, its first hike in nearly three years, as the war involving Iran pushed energy prices and inflation higher.
It followed with a second increase this month, taking the rate to 2.5%.
The US Federal Reserve has done the same, lifting its rate to a range of 3.75% to 4% in September.
For a healthy company, a small rate rise hardly matters.
For a company already struggling with debt, it can be the difference between getting a new loan and not getting one.
"Higher for longer is a slow squeeze for low-quality credit," Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, said in a note published on Friday.
In other words, the longer rates stay high, the harder life gets for the weakest borrowers.
Slok added that rate rises are "working with a lag and working unevenly": they take time to be felt, and they don't hit everyone equally.
The squeeze can take years to appear because companies do not refinance all their debt at once.
But every maturity brings another test.
A refinancing wall looms
S&P Global Ratings highlighted the 10 largest CCC-rated borrowers held by European collateralised loan obligations, or CLOs, in a report published on 31 July.
The name sounds complicated. The structure is not.
CLO managers essentially buy hundreds of corporate loans and bundle them into portfolios, which are then financed by investors.
S&P found that European CLOs held €5.3 billion of loans to CCC-rated companies maturing in 2028 at the end of June.
That was up sharply from €3.5 billion at the end of 2025.
Six of the 10 largest CCC borrowers identified by S&P face debt maturities in 2027 or 2028.
Here is where the pressure is greatest.
Europe's 10 most troubled borrowers
10. Colisée
France's Colisée operates nursing and elderly-care homes in several European countries.
It shows what happens when a debt burden becomes too large.
A Paris court approved its restructuring plan in April. Lenders swapped part of their loans for ownership of the company, and most of its remaining debt was pushed out to 2031.
S&P treated the deal as a default, then upgraded Colisée to CCC+ in May.
That is why its senior debt was yielding only around 5% in S&P's July snapshot. The pain has already been taken.
9. Stow Group
Belgium's Stow Group makes warehouse storage systems and automated logistics equipment.
If an Amazon-style warehouse needs racks, shelving or automated storage, Stow operates in that world.
Blackstone is its majority shareholder.
S&P rates it CCC+ with a stable outlook, and European CLOs held €364 million of its loans.
Its next maturity comes in September 2028. Its senior debt yielded around 9% in S&P's July data.
8. Merlin Entertainments
Merlin owns some of Europe's best-known attractions, including Legoland parks, Madame Tussauds, Sea Life aquariums and the London Eye.
It is controlled by KIRKBI, the Lego family's investment company, alongside Blackstone and Canadian pension fund CPP Investments.
European CLOs held €583 million of its loans. S&P's July snapshot showed its senior debt yielding around 12% to 13%.
Since then, investors have become calmer.
In early September, Merlin secured new financing to deal with debt due in 2027. Its 4.5% euro bond maturing in November 2027 jumped from around 95 cents on the euro to about 98 cents, implying a yield of roughly 6% to 7%.
The bond market is saying Merlin remains highly indebted, but its immediate refinancing risk has eased.
7. Solera
US-based Solera makes software used throughout the motor industry, although its loans are widely held by European funds.
Car insurers use its technology to estimate accident damage, repair shops use it to manage claims and vehicle businesses use its data platforms.
Vista Equity Partners owns the company. S&P rates Solera CCC+, and European CLOs held around €515 million of its debt.
Its next major maturity is in March 2028. S&P's July snapshot showed its senior debt yielding roughly 11% to 14%.
6. AD Education
AD Education runs private colleges and specialist schools, particularly in design, communication and digital skills.
The French group is majority-owned by private equity firm Ardian.
Its problems are partly operational. S&P downgraded the company to CCC+ in May as profitability came under pressure.
European CLOs held €343 million of its loans. Its debt does not fall due until May 2031, but its senior debt was yielding about 15% in July.
5. Pharmanovia
British-based Pharmanovia sells established and specialist medicines around the world.
Private equity firm Triton Partners is its majority owner. S&P cut the company to CCC+ in January, describing its capital structure as unsustainable.
European CLOs held €485 million of its loans.
Its nearest maturity is further away, in August 2029. But investors are not relaxed: its senior debt was yielding around 17% in July.
4. Lipton Teas and Infusions
Lipton Teas and Infusions owns some of the world's best-known tea brands, including Lipton, PG Tips, Pukka, T2 and Tazo.
CVC Capital Partners agreed to buy the business from Unilever for €4.5 billion in 2021, and the deal was completed in 2022.
There is nothing inherently risky about selling tea. The risk sits in the financing structure.
S&P rates its parent, Cuppa Bidco, CCC+ with a negative outlook and flags "significant" downside pressure. CLOs held €330 million of its loans.
Its next major maturity is in June 2029. In July, its senior debt was yielding more than 20%.
3. Emeria
Paris-based Emeria, formerly Foncia Groupe, manages residential properties and apartment buildings across Europe. It still uses the Foncia brand in France.
It has built up a heavily leveraged balance sheet under owners Partners Group and TA Associates.
S&P cut it to CCC+ in June, citing persistently high leverage and refinancing risk, and flags "significant" downside pressure.
European CLOs held around €1.1 billion of its loans, the largest amount on the list. Its next significant maturity arrives in September 2027.
S&P's July snapshot put its senior debt yield at around 17%.
The bond market has since painted an even starker picture.
An Emeria euro bond paying 3.375% and maturing in March 2028 traded at around 74 cents on the euro on 11 September. By 28 September, it had slipped to around 71 cents, implying a yield of about 29%.
2. Arxada
Arxada is a Swiss speciality chemicals company headquartered in Basel.
Its products are used in areas ranging from paints and coatings to hygiene, personal care and wood protection.
Private equity firms Bain Capital and Cinven own the business.
S&P cut it to CCC with a negative outlook in June and flags "high" downside pressure.
Arxada's problem has already reached the negotiating table.
In May, it agreed a deal with lenders under which its owners would inject CHF 200 million (€211.40 mn) of new money and most of its debt would be extended by about three years, to 2031 and 2032. An English court approved the plan on 15 September.
That buys time. It does not reduce the debt.
European CLOs held €748 million of its loans. Its 4.75% dollar bond, which now matures in 2031 instead of 2028, was quoted at around 87 cents on the dollar in late September.
1. Altice International
Altice International sits within Patrick Drahi's heavily indebted telecoms empire.
It controls Portuguese telecoms operator MEO and Israeli cable company HOT.
S&P rates it CCC with a negative outlook and flags "high" downside pressure. CLOs hold €525 million of its loans, and its next maturity arrives in February 2027, the soonest on the list.
It also has the weakest recovery prospects in the group. S&P estimates first-lien lenders would get back only about 35% in a default.
In July, its senior debt was already yielding more than 35%.
More recent bond prices are even more striking.
An Altice Financing bond paying 3% and maturing in January 2028 was quoted at around 56 cents on the euro on 28 September, implying a yield of more than 60%.
At those levels, investors are no longer simply asking how much interest Altice will pay.
They are asking how much they might recover if the capital structure has to be changed.
And then there is Aston Martin
Among publicly traded companies, Aston Martin Lagonda Global Holdings offers perhaps the most visible example of Europe's debt squeeze.
The British luxury carmaker is behind the DB12, Vanquish and Vantage, and its brand is famously associated with James Bond.
Its business is improving in some respects.
First-half revenue jumped 38% to £629 million (€733mn) in 2026.
But Aston Martin still lost £154.2 million (€179.7mn) before tax, while net debt stood at about £1.54 billion.
In July, it raised £550 million (€641mn) of new debt.
The price shows how expensive new financing has become.
The financing carries interest of 6.75 percentage points above SONIA, the benchmark sterling overnight rate, and matures in 2031.
Because those new lenders received stronger claims over assets, S&P subsequently cut Aston Martin's existing secured notes to CCC and changed the company's outlook to negative.
The secondary bond market looks even harsher.
Aston Martin’s 10% dollar bond due in March 2029 was quoted at only around 57 cents on the dollar on 28 September. That implies a yield to maturity of about 37%.
The bond market is showing no mercy to James Bond’s carmaker.
Europe does not have a corporate debt crisis
There is one important caveat.
These companies are the weakest tail of Europe's credit market. They are not the typical European business.
CCC-rated bonds make up just 4.3% of the European high-yield market, according to David Fancourt of M&G Investments, writing on the firm's Bond Vigilantes blog in August.
The CCC index offered investors 13.06 percentage points of extra yield over government bonds.
The average is pulled up by a small group of companies already in serious trouble, whose bonds trade on what lenders expect to recover in a restructuring.
The same pattern shows up across the wider market. The typical European high-yield bond is priced near its most expensive level in five years.
In other words, healthy companies can still borrow on reasonable terms.
At the other end, bonds issued by Emeria, Aston Martin and Altice now trade at yields between roughly 30% and more than 60%.
Higher interest rates are not crushing corporate Europe uniformly.
They are exposing the companies that borrowed the most when money was cheap, one refinancing deadline at a time.

Google appeals against EU order to share data, open Android to AI rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:13:10 UTC
15:13:10 KST

Google said on Sept. 29 that it has appealed an EU decision requiring it to share data with other search engines and open up its Android system to rival AI services, citing privacy concerns.
Brussels had issued the order in July under the European Union's flagship Digital Markets Act (DMA), which forces the world's biggest tech firms to open to competition in a bid to give users more choice.
"We're appealing decisions that will force us to share people's private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken vital security protections on Android," said Oliver Bethell, Google's senior director for competition.
In July the European Commission said Google must start sharing search data from January 2027 to "rebalance the playing field."
Changes to Android should kick in in July next year and Brussels said it hoped they would lead to the emergence of alternatives to Google's AI services, such as Gemini.
But Google countered that Android is already open and interoperable and the EU decision forced it to hand over private search data to other firms without adequate anonymisation, user knowledge, or consent.
"People use Search for their most personal questions - from medical worries to close relationships - and mandating we share these personal queries without adequate safeguards would cause irreversible harm to user privacy," said Bethell.
The appeal was filed with the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union.

Taiwan Air Force to order additional 35 mm rounds as drone threat grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:08:56 UTC
15:08:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force plans to purchase Advanced Hit Efficiency and Destruction (AHEAD) rounds and high-explosive tracer rounds for its 35 mm anti-aircraft guns beginning next year.
The Air Force has allocated NT$1.680 billion (US$52.76 million) for the AHEAD procurement program, which will begin next year and last for two years, Liberty Times reported. It has set aside NT$4.032 billion from 2027 to 2031 for the high-explosive tracer round procurement program.
Rather than relying on a conventional projectile to strike a target directly, an AHEAD round detonates about 40 to 60 meters in front of the target, releasing 152 tungsten sub-projectiles to create a dense cloud that can destroy incoming threats, per Liberty Times.
The Air Force already uses both types of 35 mm ammunition in its existing anti-aircraft guns, which are primarily deployed at Air Force bases and other key facilities. The guns are paired with Skyguard radar systems to provide low-altitude air defense against cruise missiles, anti-radiation missiles, fixed-wing aircraft, and helicopters, with an effective range of about 4 kilometers.
The Air Force previously considered replacing the guns, which have been in service for over 40 years. However, the widespread use of low-cost drones in the war in Ukraine has renewed interest in AHEAD rounds, according to Liberty Times.
The Air Force signed an NT$1.64 billion contract with Germany’s Rheinmetall for training ammunition earlier this month, with deliveries expected to be completed by the end of June 2028.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC is reportedly considering Texas for a second US chipmaking hub, with investment potentially exceeding the NT$8.42 trillion (US$265 billion) planned for its Arizona operations.

US customers accounted for approximately 75.64% of TSMC’s revenue in the first half of 2026, according to UDN, making proximity to the US market and reduced exposure to potential tariffs important considerations.

The report also cited US President Donald Trump’s warnings that chipmakers could face tariffs of up to 200% if they do not move manufacturing to the US.
North Texas, known as “Silicon Prairie,” has an established semiconductor manufacturing base, silicon wafer supply chain, optical communications industry, and defense sector. Companies including Texas Instruments, Coherent, Samsung, and Tesla have operations in the region, potentially creating an industrial cluster around a new TSMC campus and supporting Washington’s efforts to localize semiconductor supply chains.
Texas could also offer advantages over Arizona, where TSMC faces challenges related to water, electricity, and labor availability. Industry sources cited by UDN said Texas has a larger available workforce, lower taxes, and a stable power supply.
Supply-chain sources said they believed the site evaluation was nearing its final stages, though TSMC’s board had not made a final decision.

Among the government's priorities for the session are legislation related to its new population strategy, the proposed SME Transformation and Upgrading Development Act, and amendments to the National Sports Act. The Cabinet has identified about 40 priority bills for the new session, including measures related to family support, business transformation, and social welfare, per a Cabinet press release.

The Taipei District Prosecutors Office said a suspect surnamed Liu (劉) received instructions from the unidentified person and recruited another man, surnamed Kuo (郭), to carry out the attack, per Liberty Times.
The two men were charged with offenses including intimidation and property damage. Kuo allegedly divided a mixture of white paint and feces among four bags and threw their contents at the club, damaging its windows, walls, and floors.
Liu paid Kuo NT$50,000 (US$1,500) in Taoyuan early the following morning, prosecutors said. Investigators were still examining whether other suspects were involved, Liberty Times reported.
Prosecutors asked the court to sentence Liu to 22 months in prison and Kuo to 20 months, per CNA. Commenting on the indictments, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) said treating the case primarily as property damage was too lenient, Liberty Times reported.
Liang said he hoped the public would support amendments to the National Security Act and Anti-Infiltration Act addressing similar cases of transnational repression.

US forces exit Iraq after two decades, leaving opening for Iran

US forces exit Iraq after two decades, leaving opening for Iran
- US forces will fully withdraw from Iraq by Sept 30, ending a two-decade presence marked by 4,500 American deaths and shifting power dynamics in the region.
- Iran and its allied militias view the US exit as a strategic victory, expecting increased influence over Iraq's security and politics.
- Concerns rise over a security vacuum that may empower Iran-backed groups and allow Islamic State sleeper cells to regroup and launch attacks.
AI generated
BAGHDAD – US forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Sept 30, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.
Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal – agreed in 2024 under then President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran – could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other US enemies, including ISIS, to stage a comeback.
“Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition’s departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a counterweight to Tehran’s influence in Iraq,” said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specialising in studying armed Shi’ite groups aligned with Iran.
He predicted that the pro-Iranian militia groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also “seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making”.
Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the US withdrawal as “a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project”.
“On Sept 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country,” he told Reuters.
“Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people.”
Not ready
While the eventual departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature.
“We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time,” Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, told Reuters.
“All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the (US-led coalition) leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear.”
American forces invaded Iraq as part of Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003 to topple Sunni Muslim dictator Saddam Hussein, and went on to occupy the country, install a Shi’ite-led government and fight a years-long counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011.
They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group ISIS in a major war from 2014 to 2017.
Around twice as many Americans died in Operation Iraqi Freedom as in the much longer parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt US withdrawal in 2021.
In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the US and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield.
The US killed a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike near Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran’s allies repeatedly fired on US bases, sometimes drawing reprisals.
In the 2026 war against Iran, seven of the 18 US service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Victory for Iran’s axis
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region.
“Lasting security will prevail in Iraq” once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran’s Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Sept 28.
Iran “welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it”, he told Iran’s parliamentary news service.
“Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops.”
Washington has accused Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline earlier in September.
The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence.
New life for ISIS?
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to ISIS fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former US military base.
A lack of US intelligence, logistical support and drones will give ISIS a chance to regroup, said Kurdish commander Sirwan Barzani.
“For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by (ISIS) sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September,” he said.
“This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale” of the fighters.
Iraqi security forces said a suspected ISIS cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout.
The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials.
ISIS “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks”, said Colonel Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk. REUTERS

Ancient olive economy leaves female imprint in Antalya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:07:34 UTC
15:07:34 KST

Excavations reveal an important olive oil production center containing dozens of workshops.
Lyrboton Kome, an ancient settlement in Antalya that was a major olive oil production center during the Roman period, is shedding light on not only the region’s ancient olive economy but also the prominent role women played in economic life. Arete, a priestess of Demeter, used her own money to have an olive oil tower built and established a foundation whose provisions protected olive trees and supported religious festivals.
Located in Antalya’s Kepez district, Lyrboton Kome was the subject of the first comprehensive excavations and research beginning in 2016 under the leadership of the Antalya Museum Directorate.Excavations led for four years by Nevzat Çevik, a professor at Akdeniz University’s Department of Archaeology, revealed an important olive oil production center containing dozens of workshops.
The ancient settlement, which was affiliated with Perge, has provided evidence not only of large-scale olive oil production but also of women’s significant role in economic and social life. Arete’s decision to finance the construction of an olive oil tower and establish a foundation with her own wealth is among the clearest examples of women’s economic influence at the site.
Çevik said Lyrboton Kome was essentially an olive-producing farm in antiquity.
“Another name for Lyrboton Kome was Elaibaris. ‘Elaia’ means olive and ‘baris’ means farm. So the name actually means ‘olive farm,’” he said. “Although this was not a large urban settlement but a village, its most important feature was that it was one of the largest olive oil production centers you could see. Dozens of workshops and mechanisms indicating large-scale production show that very large quantities of olive oil were produced here.”
Antalya and its surroundings were an important export center in antiquity, particularly during the Roman period, Çevik said, adding that the region generated substantial revenues from olive oil production.
“So much income was generated that monumental buildings in Perge and many structures along its main street were built with money earned from this production,” he said.
Çevik said some structures in Perge were financed by the economic wealth generated by the olive production center.
“Lyrboton Kome belonged to the maternal family of the brothers Demetrios and Apollonios, who commissioned buildings in Perge. One of the family’s grandmothers was named Arete, a name meaning virtue or excellence,” he said. “After Arete, her sons and grandchildren continued producing olive oil here and made enormous amounts of money. Then Kille came into the picture, and she was also a woman. So we see that women had a very strong place in the history of this settlement.”
Women played active role
Women played active roles in both production and administration during the period, Çevik said.
“Arete was an important woman in the family. Later came her granddaughter Kille, also a woman. And this was not an independent foreign settlement separate from Perge; it was Perge’s village,” he said.
“Perge also had Plancia Magna, the daughter of an important Roman family, who was an extremely influential woman in the city’s administration. So we see women taking active roles. Moreover, where women were present, strong economic activity and solid, productive enterprises also emerged.”
Lyrboton Kome contains numerous documents relating to the ancient practice of establishing foundations, Çevik said.
“Arete had the olive oil tower, bearing inscriptions, built with her own money. Her son, granddaughter and other family members continued this tradition,” he said.
An inscription on the monument established rules intended to remain in force indefinitely, he added.
“It says that these trees can never be cut down, sold or used for another purpose. It is as if they wrote on the wall a law explaining how this place should be protected, almost as a message to us today.”
Çevik said the relationship between urban centers and rural production was crucial to the ancient economy.“Cities do not produce; they largely consume and spend. The countryside produces the city’s wealth. Perge’s economic power was actually supported by rural production centers such as Lyrboton Kome.”
The economic importance of olive oil production was also reflected in religious and social life, Çevik said.
He noted that the site’s foundation provisions required annual festivities in honor of Apollo on the 20th day of the first month, financed by revenue from olive oil production.
“The entire village population was to be properly hosted, entertained and fed during these festivities. In other words, the Apollo festivals were organized with income from olive oil production,” he said.
Archaeologists have also uncovered an area dedicated to Apollo at the site, Çevik added.
He said Arete dedicated the tower to Artemis of Perge after having it constructed, adding that Turks arrived in the region in later periods but did not settle at the site immediately.

Radio amateurs broadcast Karahantepe to the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:07:23 UTC
15:07:23 KST

The event aims to bring international attention to Karahantepe. (AA Photo)
Amateur radio operators in the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa promoted Karahantepe, a major Neolithic archaeological site, to a global audience by setting up a dedicated station and antennas on location.
As part of an initiative to promote Türkiye’s historical heritage, members of the Turkish Radio Amateur Association (TRAC) secured permits to broadcast directly from the active excavation site at Karahantepe.
The team installed radio equipment in a dedicated room at the Karahantepe Visitor Center and erected high-reaching antennas outdoors.
Using the special call sign “TC8KHT” assigned for the event, amateur radio operators established contacts with stations in different parts of the world and provided information about Karahantepe.
Speaking to state-run Anadolu Agency, TRAC Deputy Chairman Hüdaverdi Güneş said that the year-in-the-making event aimed to bring international attention to Karahantepe.
Expressing pride in launching the initiative from Şanlıurfa, Güneş noted that modern radio gear enabled them to reach nearly 1,000 stations across 40 countries during the three-day broadcast.
Güneş said that operators shared historical overviews of Karahantepe during transmissions and directed contacts to official websites for more detail. Several international listeners were already familiar with the site, including a German operator who had followed television reports about the upcoming broadcast and local history.
İbrahim Halil Seysenbek, head of TRAC’s Şanlıurfa branch, praised the 11-member team from across Türkiye who spent three days transmitting via a 20-meter antenna under the special call sign “TC8KHT.”
Highlighting the project’s purpose, Seysenbek stated. “We are telling the whole world, or all the stations we reach and address in our calls, that Karahantepe is the zero point of history.”

Freshly baked simit and traditional turnip juice are displayed at an Adana food festival stall.
Türkiye’s southern city of Adana is aiming to attract more than 1 million visitors to the 10th International Adana Taste Festival, which will take place from Oct. 9 to 11 at Merkez Park, Governor Mustafa Yavuz said.
The festival welcomed around 800,000 visitors in 2024. Organizers expect attendance to surpass the one-million mark this year as the event marks its 10th anniversary with an expanded international program.
Speaking about preparations, Yavuz said planning has been underway for months through consultations with industry representatives, municipalities, chambers of commerce and commodity exchanges. He noted that the festival, launched in 2017 as a local event, has evolved into an internationally recognized gathering after hosting participants from 12 countries in 2019.
The three-day event will bring together Turkish and foreign chefs, with flavors from countries including India, Mexico and Egypt. The central Anatolian province of Kayseri and the southwestern province of Muğla will participate as guest regions, showcasing their local cuisines.
Yavuz described the festival as a form of “gastro-diplomacy,” saying it promotes Adana’s history, culture, agricultural products and culinary traditions to international audiences.
Known internationally for its spicy kebab dishes, Adana plans to broaden the festival’s culinary focus this year by highlighting desserts, street food and seafood, an area less commonly associated with the city.
The program will include concerts, cooking competitions, harvest tours and workshops. Authorities expect the festival to generate significant economic activity not only in Adana, a city of around 2.3 million people, but also in neighboring provinces, where accommodation facilities are expected to see high occupancy rates during the event.
Organizers are also placing a strong emphasis on sustainability. The 2026 festival will be held under a zero-waste theme, with biodegradable and recyclable products replacing conventional packaging materials, plastic bags and straws. Officials said waste management and environmentally friendly practices would be integrated throughout the event.

Trade Minister Ömer Bolat discussed the potential impact of the European Union’s proposed “Made in EU” approach on Turkish industry during meetings with senior EU officials in Brussels.
Bolat told Anadolu Agency that he met with Stephane Sejourne, the European Commission’s executive vice president for industrial strategy; Marta Kos, commissioner for enlargement, and deputy leaders of the liberal group in the European Parliament.
Discussions focused on the EU’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act and its “Made in EU” initiative, he added.
The minister said the proposed measures could have significant implications for foreign trade and investment, adding that Türkiye has been regularly conveying its position, expectations and assessments of the possible effects to EU institutions and member states.
He noted that when the issue first emerged on the EU agenda about a year ago, proposals were largely focused on protecting European industry and paid limited attention to their impact on external trade relations.
However, he said the European Commission’s proposal published on March 4 included Türkiye and the EU-Türkiye Customs Union within the scope of the “Made in EU” framework.
He added that restrictive provisions remained in the annexes of the proposal, particularly for the automotive sector, and said Türkiye had communicated its concerns to European Commission officials, members of the European Parliament and ministers from EU member states.
Bolat noted that the Türkiye-EU Business Summit and the third High-Level Trade Dialogue meeting will be held in Brussels in two weeks.
Following the meeting with Kos, Bolat said in a post on X that the EU’s new industrial, competition and trade policies, particularly the Industrial Acceleration Act, should be compatible with the functioning of the Customs Union.
He said both sides agreed to work on a concrete and positive trade agenda, identifying public procurement, technical regulations and connectivity as priority areas for deeper cooperation.

Oil prices rise as bond sell-off hits global markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:03:49 UTC
15:03:49 KST

Oil prices climbed further on Tuesday as uncertainty over US-Iran talks fuelled inflation fears. Government bond yields rose to multi-year highs, putting pressure on stocks.
International crude oil prices climbed further on Tuesday morning amid uncertainty over US-Iran talks, as hopes of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway crucial to oil shipments, faded.
Hopes that Middle East tensions would ease were dashed at the weekend when Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day truce.
Mediators are working with the US and Iran on a deal to end the fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, officials told the Associated Press. The disruption to shipping through the waterway has affected global trade and added to inflation.
Iran has proposed reopening the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports and eases sanctions, among other conditions. Washington says any deal must also address Iran’s nuclear programme. Officials said the two sides disagree over the timing of concessions and who should act first.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, gained nearly 2% and traded above $107 a barrel early Tuesday, well above its price of roughly $72 a barrel in late February before the Iran war.
US West Texas Intermediate crude rose 1.8% to more than $94 a barrel.
High oil prices have renewed inflation concerns and expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next month. Government bond prices have fallen as a result, pushing yields to multi-year highs.
The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose above 5.27% on Monday, its highest level in 19 years, following a rise of nearly half a percentage point through September. Yields rise when bond prices fall, and this month’s sell-off is the heaviest in two years.
The US two-year yield has risen even further, climbing by more than 0.57 percentage points this month to nearly 5%. In Europe, Germany’s benchmark 10-year bond yield reached 3.62%, its highest level since June 2009.
Government bond yields help set borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to company loans. As yields rise, governments, businesses and households face higher costs, while stocks can become less attractive to investors.
In Japan, a 40-year government bond auction drew its strongest demand since 2020 as relatively high yields attracted investors, according to Bloomberg.
Stock markets also struggled after all three main Wall Street indexes fell on Monday.
In Europe, Tuesday's open showed a mixed reaction.
The Euro Stoxx 50 was flat in early trading while the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded 0.2% higher.
The UK's FTSE 100, Italy’s FTSE MIB, Spain's IBEX 35 and the Netherlands' AEX all traded between 0.1% and 0.2% higher than their Monday close.
However, France's CAC 40 and Germany's DAX 30 both dropped about 0.5%.
Over in Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 1.3%, South Korea’s Kospi declined 0.9% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 0.6%. Hong Kong-traded shares of Shein fell 11.7% after the online retailer reported a 67% fall in quarterly adjusted net profit from a year earlier.
The Shanghai Composite was little changed following a report from China’s official Xinhua News Agency late Monday that its State Council had discussed ways to make economic policies more effective.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was down more than 0.1% by early morning in Europe.
Australia’s central bank raised its key interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6% on Tuesday, a 15-year high, as rising oil prices fuelled inflation. The Reserve Bank said higher fuel costs were pushing up prices across the economy, while growth and inflation had been stronger than expected.
The US dollar edged up to 157.42 Japanese yen from 157.39 yen. The euro fell to $1.1362 from $1.1371.
Gold remained near $4,160 after steep losses on Monday, as expectations of further rate rises weighed on the metal, which pays no interest.
Investors are also awaiting key US inflation and jobs data this week that could influence the Fed’s next decision. Markets are pricing in another rate rise at the end of October.

Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026: Watch live from Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

The Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels brought together political leaders, policymakers and industry experts to debate the biggest issues shaping the future of travel.
Europe’s travel industry was in the spotlight today at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 at the Albert Hall in Brussels.
Throughout the day, Euronews was live from the Belgian capital with interviews, panels and debates exploring how tourism is responding to a year marked by geopolitical disruption, airspace closures and extreme weather.
Below are the updates and highlights from the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels
Michelin Guide offers curation of human-centred hotel stays amid digital algorithms noise
The Michelin Guide’s expanded role beyond restaurants is helping travellers sort through digital noise with a human-centred curation of stays that doesn’t rely solely on new technologies.
At the closing panel of the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Marie-France Perrel, Head of Business Development, Hotels at Michelin Guide, said the hotel selection for the Michelin Keys “is based on real humans travelling the world deciding whether or not a property should be a part of the collection based on the five criteria”.
Amid algorithms and endless digital reviews at play, Perrel said that the role of hotel guide is “essential” amid all the online chatter.
Hotels can receive one, two or three keys based on their quality and consistency, architecture and interior design, personality and character, value for money, as well as what the property adds to its locale.
She also highlighted a growing trend of food and travel being seen as one experience. Data from the Michelin Guide found that in 2026, users looking to book a hotel also searched for dining spots nearby.
Perrel also highlighted the changes in luxury travel trends, with a shift towards travellers seeking a sense of place and properties that offer a connection to their surroundings. Luxury travel is now an “ecosystem,” she said, adding that it’s also a “broad spectrum,” with the Guide also offering insights into the wide world of hospitality.
Direct links to Europe and easier visa set to boost Central Asian and European travel
Kyrgyzstan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Belgium has revealed that the Central Asian country is planning direct air links to Europe, with routes potentially launching as early as 2027.
Aidit Erkin, Kyrgyzstan’s envoy, said that transport connectivity is an “extremely important” priority, alongside strengthening cooperation and partnerships with Europe. Currently, travellers in Kyrgyzstan connect to Europe with Turkish Airlines-operated flights via Istanbul.
However, now that all Kyrgyzstan-certified carriers have been removed from the EU’s Air Safety List in June, Erkin announced during the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 that work is underway for “direct flights from Kyrgyzstan to Europe”, with routes on the horizon to launch next year.
Joining Erkin on the panel was Florian Sengstschmid, Chief Executive Officer of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board. He highlighted a growing demand for travel between Azerbaijan and Europe, saying that policymakers should consider ways to facilitate that demand.
Sengstschmid pointed to visas as a “bottleneck” in Central Asian-European connectivity. Meanwhile, Erkin added that the Kyrgyz President is promoting a common “Silk Road visa” that would unlock access to all Central Asian countries for travellers with a single visa.
EXPO 2027 Belgrade poised as tourism catalyst for Belgrade and Western Balkans
Amid preparations for Expo 2027, Dušan Borovčanin, advisor at EXPO 2027 Belgrade, sees the event as a catalyst for tourism and development for Serbia’s capital and beyond, across the wider Western Balkans. Belgrade won the right to host over competing proposals like Spain, the US, Argentina and Thailand.
Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Borovčanin highlighted that Belgrade’s hosting of the event marks the first time it's being hosted in the region. As well as instilling a sense of “national pride” for Serbians, Borovčanin added that Expo 2027 will be an opportunity to showcase the country’s development over the past 20 years.
“We want this to be a catalyst for the further development of our region in economic terms,” he said. “But also in terms of the national branding and national pride, and I think that is the reason why countries are also signing up and participating.”
He added that 141 official participants are confirmed, and that there is a need “to shed light on the entire region”.
Dubrovnik is open to everyone – but under certain circumstances
Mayor of Dubrovnik Mato Franković has highlighted the success of his city in being able to find a “new balance” between welcoming large tourist numbers and protecting the quality of life for residents and the local charm.
During his one-to-one discussion in Brussels, he revealed that when he took office as mayor in 2017, Dubrovnik was written off as a city that was dying amid the sheer strain of tourist influxes. In response, Dubrovnik launched the "Respect the City" initiative to tackle unsustainable cruise ship arrivals, as well as manage day and overnight visitor flows.
While taking into account that the regulations may have taken a toll on the "magic" of visiting his native Dubrovnik, he argued that it has ultimately been for the better, preventing visitors from long queues and busy crowds, especially in the city's Old Town.
Despite the measure, Franković highlighted that the city received 35% more guests compared to 2017, but emphasised that the distribution of visitor numbers throughout the day is “crucial”. He added that Dubrovnik is “a world city, it's a historical world site, and it should be open for everyone. But, under certain circumstances”.
‘We have to put our money where our mouth is’
Members of the European Parliament must work to ensure that under-the-radar destinations are able to grow their tourism sectors, while hotspots need "room to breathe”, according to Daniel Attard MEP, S&D.
Speaking during the panel “Managing visitor flows and shaping tomorrow’s destinations”, he said that there is no use in encouraging travellers to venture beyond the beaten path, especially if there are no means to be able to connect them to those destinations.
As such, “we have to put the money where our mouth is at the European level”, he said, adding that “we have to create better connections, invest in new connections”, as well as bolster aviation services.
Attard was joined by Ourania Georgoutsakou, Managing Director of Airlines for Europe (A4E), who added that air connectivity is equally as important. She also noted that the trend over the past few years has seen the shoulder season extend and steadily grow by upwards of 30%.
“People are choosing to go longer and that kind of collaboration with the local hospitality sector, with the authorities, allows an offering of an extended season, which is an important way of going forward,” she said.
While when it comes to destinations experimenting with tourist taxes to manage demand, Marta Machado, Deputy Director General of HOTREC - Hotels, Restaurants, Bars & Cafés in Europe, highlighted the need for better data, especially on the continent's short-term holiday homes to enact better decisions "on the management of the completion capacity of the visitor flows".
Edi Rama speaks exclusively to Euronews
Speaking exclusively to Maria Tadeo at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama explained that his country is making significant leaps and strides in the tourism world.
He explained that Albania used to be the “most isolated country in Europe and the North Korea of Europe” and that, after it had emerged, it was “confronted with very, very disturbing stereotypes”.
Rama added that the country plans to target the world in terms of tourism. He admitted that the country’s infrastructure is somewhat lacking, but that it’s improving significantly.
He claimed that it has an airport that is “the fastest growing airport of Europe”, and there are plans in place to open a new airport in Vlorë, and another seasonal hub in the country’s south.
“We have a fourth up in the mountains, but it’s not yet working as we wish,” he added.
‘The South Caucasus is completely underrated’: Azerbaijan calls for more visitors
Azerbaijan is looking to expand its tourism offer beyond Baku, with the country’s tourism chief highlighting its natural diversity, cultural heritage and growing connectivity as it seeks to attract more international visitors.
Speaking to moderator Jane Witherspoon, Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said the wider South Caucasus region remains largely overlooked by international travellers.
“The South Caucasus is completely underrated,” he said, adding that Azerbaijan had “much more to come and much more to offer”.
He urged visitors to venture beyond the capital and explore the country’s Silk Road heritage, ancient villages, UNESCO sites and mountain landscapes.
“It really is to travel beyond Baku, to travel along the Silk Road through side valleys, ancient heritage villages, UNESCO World Heritage sites,” he said.
Azerbaijan is also working to improve international connectivity, with Brussels set to gain four weekly flights to Baku from May 2027.
Schmid said tourism development should also benefit local communities, pointing to villages where investment had helped create businesses and revive traditional crafts.
But he said growth should not simply be measured by visitor numbers.
“Is it all about the numbers? No, it’s not all about the numbers,” Sengstschmid said.
“It’s about how you really increase the length of stay. How do you make people enjoy more of the country during their journey?”
His ambition, he added, was for “a few more travellers, but a higher impact”.
Romania invites travellers to explore beyond Bucharest
Dan-Adrian Pop, Romania’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of Economy, Digitalisation, Entrepreneurship and Tourism, spoke to moderator Evi Kiorri about one of the most exciting emerging destinations in Europe.
Despite Romania’s proximity to Ukraine and the ongoing conflict, Pop urged visitors to come and see the nation for themselves.
“Overall, I would say that we are safe as any other European country. The whole country is very well protected, and from internal security for the citizens and for the travellers, I think we are one of the safest countries in Europe,” he said.
Bucharest as a destination has long been popular with European travellers, but Pop explained that Romania has so much more to offer than just the charms of its capital.
“We focus very much on rural tourism, spa tourism, and adventure and active tourism,” he said.
“They have a lot of options to be out in nature and close to the citizens, to the people who live there, who know the places, and who guide them through this experience.”
He also praised the vast amount of walking routes in the country, some “1,000 kilometres from north to south, through the Carpathian Mountains”.
While he admitted that infrastructure is lacking in some places, and the summer season isn’t as long as in other European nations, there’s still plenty to experience thanks, in part, to the country’s citizens.
“The people of Romania are one of our most valuable promoters, and they know the destinations, the local destinations that would fit for their friends. They are the first ones to invite their friends all over the world to Romania,” Pop said.
Cruise industry targeting younger travellers and greener future
Gianni Onorato, CEO of MSC Cruises, speaking to Hannah Brown as part of The Big Question, has said the sector is attracting a younger generation of travellers, while diversification and new technology could help it tackle concerns around overtourism and environmental impact.
The cruise executive also said the profile of passengers had changed significantly during his 40 years in the industry.
“While now there is a much younger demographic. The average age is 35 to 54. A lot of families, a lot of young people, and this is very good because this can ensure the future of this industry,” he said.
He also pushed back against the perception that cruise passengers simply arrive in a destination, spend little money and leave again, pointing to the industry's wider economic contribution.
“Cruises contribute to the European economy by €65 billion a year and with 445,000 permanent jobs,” he said.
He argued that cruise operators could also help spread tourism beyond Europe's busiest destinations by working with local authorities and promoting lesser-known ports.
“We are looking very much to diversify our destinations,” he said, highlighting the Greek island of Syros, close to the more famous Santorini and Mykonos.
“Syros is becoming more and more on the map of tourism, and we are very happy about it because it is also helping to respond to the [overtourism problem],” he added.
The executive also pointed to the potential for cruises to support tourism outside the traditional summer season, noting that ships can move between destinations as weather conditions change.
On sustainability, he said the industry was making progress but still had work to do. He said MSC had reduced its emissions by almost 42 per cent against its 2008 baseline, putting it “almost five years ahead of the checkpoint for 2030”.
But he said the availability of cleaner fuels remained a major challenge.
“The target is there. There is only one issue: the fuel availability. So that needs to be produced at large scale,” he said.
Looking ahead, he predicted that cruise holidays would continue to attract new audiences, including solo travellers and multigenerational families.
“More and more we will have a younger audience. By the way, we will have new segments: solo travellers. It’s a new segment, very important,” he said.
Onorato also suggested the industry could increasingly move away from measuring success simply by passenger numbers.
“I believe tourism in general will be much less measured on the quantity, on the volumes, but much more on the quality of the emotions that we are able to give to the travellers and also the quality of the contribution, not only economically, that we can give to the locals and local community,” he said.
Sustainability in focus
Sustainability, affordability and accessibility can work together, but tourism needs to balance environmental, social and economic considerations, panellists told the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit.
Speaking to moderator Mike Starling, Andreea Stăjcu, Deputy Head of Unit, Head of Tourism Sector, DG MOVE at the European Commission, said travellers themselves were increasingly demanding more sustainable options.
“The travellers really want to travel in a sustainable way,” she said, pointing to cycling and night trains as examples.
MEP and former Croatian tourism minister Nikolina Brnjac said sustainability could not be reduced to environmental measures alone.
“It is achievable, but only if we approach it in three pillars: social, environmental and economical,” she said, adding that better rail and public transport connections were needed to reach rural and peripheral areas.
Managing visitor numbers was another key theme. “We must not be afraid of the numbers,” Brnjac said.
“It’s bad management of the tourist flows.”
István Ujhelyi, former MEP and UN Tourism official, similarly stressed that tourism growth cannot simply be stopped.
“You can’t stop this growing,” he said, noting that international tourist numbers had risen from 25 million in 1950 to more than 1.5 billion last year.
Sven Wiltink of Radisson Hotel Group said sustainability needed to become part of the industry’s core business, rather than an optional extra.
“Sustainability is not a bolt-on element,” he said.
Central Europe as 'one destination'
Olivér Csendes, President, Hungarian Tourism Agency and Sandrine Buffenoir, Director, Netherlands, Belgium & Luxembourg, Atout France, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to talk about looking at Central Europe as one destination and the inextricable link between nature and tourism.
Oliver Cndish, representing the Hungarian Tourism Agency, said tourism should be used to promote Central Europe as a single, interconnected destination rather than being constrained by national borders.
“I would love to see more international collaborations where we position the way we live and our regions, basically as one destination,” he said.
“We don’t have to limit our thinking and the creation of experience spaces to national borders,” he added.
Cndish pointed to the relatively short distances between European countries as an opportunity to create multi-country experiences - part of the popular “trip-maxxing” trend, which has gained traction this year especially.
“If you look at it from the US or Asian perspective, the distances are very small in Europe. You can travel 100 kilometres, and you have already touched two or three Central European capitals,” he said.
He also highlighted the Danube as an example of an attraction that could be promoted across borders.
“We have treasures like the Danube, that’s found in a lot of countries in Europe, and has always been a connection, connecting cultures,” he said. “So why not use this as an active part of the experience that people will have, enriching their lives and the way they see and experience Europe.”
Cndish also praised cooperation within the EU, saying: “I believe Europe is doing an amazing job collaborating.”
He pointed to the European data space for tourism as one example, saying it could help countries work together on issues including visitor flows and extreme weather.
“Think about all the discussions we had about visitor flow, protecting visitors, warning them in case there is a danger, whether it’s wildfire, whether it’s whatever different extreme weather conditions. This is only possible if we have the right data at the right places,” he said.
He also stressed the importance of protecting the natural environment, saying: “There is no tourism without nature.”
“Tourism needs to be a force for good and needs to also support the resilience of the living areas,” he added.
Atout France’s Benelux director Sandrine Buffeno also highlighted tourism’s role in bringing Europeans together.
“Tourism is a key aspect of connection between all European people. It’s a key factor in knowing each other better, in working together better, living with each other,” she said.
“It’s a classroom to learn about each other,” she added.
'Climate change the biggest threat to tourism'
Eduardo Santander, the CEO of the European Travel Commission, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to speak about the impact of the threat of climate change on global tourism and the role of Europe as a destination.
The CEO explained that “climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now, by far.”
He was speaking following a summer of record heat and related travel chaos across the continent.
“We see that trains cannot run sometimes because the rails are expanded because of the heat. We saw this at the cruise lines on the European rivers - they couldn’t run because it was too dry,” Santander said.
“We have to prepare for that in a much more coordinated and comprehensive way,” he added.
“We see resilience becoming one of the engines of European tourism. We have to become even more resilient to whatever is next.”
Santander explained that, due to the impact of climate change, travel and tourism is getting less affordable.
“Travelling is becoming much more expensive, and you all have travelled this summer, I guess, and you notice it in your pockets.”
He also spoke about the trend for “coolcations”, which have gained plenty of traction this year, especially: “We see a lot of people from southern European destinations looking for what we call ‘cool locations’ — places that are cooler in summer and where you can enjoy the weather in a more predictable way.”
Santander also emphasised the economic importance of tourism, which makes up some 10% of the European economy, a figure that rises to between 15% and 20% of some nation’s GDP.
He also sang the praises of Europe as a tourism destination.
“Europe is becoming the playground, some people call it. It’s becoming a museum, an attraction park,” he said, asking, “what’s wrong with that?”
“An attraction park or a museum is a perfect place to be. Normally it’s well organised, well managed, they have a nice restaurant, they have clean toilets, so there’s nothing wrong.”
US Global Entry for Belgians by end of 2026?
Bill White, the Ambassador of the United States of America to the Kingdom of Belgium, sat down with summit host Jane Witherspoon to speak about the special relationship between the two nations.
While the Ambassador praised Belgium for having so much more to offer than “waffles, chocolate and beer”, he did criticise the lines at the airport in Brussels, saying they “suck”.
“They’re really bad. One of the things we have to do in our transatlantic alliance and relationship is to recognise that if we want people to come to Belgium, we have to fix this problem. It must get better immediately,” he added.
Nevertheless, White announced that he has received approval from President Donald Trump to allow Belgian citizens to apply for the US Global Entry programme, which is designed to speed up entry at US airports. Global Entry is a DHS programme for pre-approved international travellers.
In practical terms, he explained, that means: “you’ll register, you pay your fee, get vetted, and then you fly to the United States, and you look at the kiosk at JFK or wherever it is, you smile, don’t smile, you get ‘whoop!’ right through, and then you go get your bags and spend money”.
He urged Belgian citizens to “write to your congressman or your parliament person, let’s go, get the paperwork done, because when you travel, it’ll be seamless. One, two, three.”

Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief, prevent blood clots and tackle high blood pressure.
Dozens of NHS trusts in England have encountered scarcities of aspirin, the painkiller co-codamol – a combination of paracetamol and codeine – and ramipril, a blood pressure tablet.
Nine trusts have had problems getting enough supplies of two of those three common medications, while one – Kent community health NHS trust – ran short of all three.
The shortages underline how precarious the health service’s supply chains for basic medicines have become in recent years as a result of trade disputes, global conflict and manufacturing problems.
Pharmacists have said supply problems have become a “national crisis” and in some cases have left patients unable to access their usual medications for weeks at a time.
Hospitals’ drug supply problems have emerged in freedom of information requests by Dr Rodolfo Catena, an expert in global health supplies at University College London, about stock levels of the three drugs. Sixty of the 184 trusts from which he sought figures responded.
The most widespread shortage involved aspirin, which is used to reduce pain and the risk of blood clots. Twenty-six (62%) of the 42 trusts that responded about it had experienced disruption to their supplies between last December and March this year.
Thirteen (31%) of the 42 trusts that replied on co-codamol had run short of that drug, which helps relieve muscle pain, period pain and toothache. York and Scarborough NHS trust’s supplies had been disrupted since May 2025, and Royal Wolverhampton NHS trust had trouble getting enough co-codamol for the 10 months between October 2025 and August this year.
Seven (16%) of the 43 trusts that answered Catena’s question about ramipril had been unable to get as much of it as they needed. More than a third of adults in England are thought to have dangerously high blood pressure, which heightens the risk of a heart attack or stroke, but 59% are unaware they have it, research showed last week.
Frimley Health NHS trust, which cares for people in Surrey, Berkshire and Buckinghamshire, resorted to paying higher prices for ramipril to ensure uninterrupted supply of it, rather than risk supply problems that would affect patients, Catena found.
His findings tally with National Pharmacy Association analysis. It has found that although shortages in recent years have mainly been of specialist drugs, for example to treat ADHD and epilepsy, supply problems now often involve generic medicines, which are much cheaper to produce.
Catena, an associate professor in operations and supply chain management in UCL’s Global Business School for Health, believes the shortages he found show that NHS England is wrong to classify drug scarcities in its operational risk register as only a “medium” risk to the provision of care.
NHS England has given drug shortages a score of 16 out of 25 on its risk assessment scale. But the widespread nature of shortages makes it unlikely that it will be able to fulfil its ambition to reduce that score to nine by next month, Catena added.
Improving supply chain resilience is also a key priority for the Department of Health and Social Care. Catena called on it to change the current system whereby only drug companies are obliged to warn it about any impending shortages. He said NHS trusts should be put under the same obligation so that service bosses were more aware of disruption to drug supplies and could act to minimise them.
Almost all (92%) of the trusts that responded said they had no contingency plan to tackle supply problems and 82% said they had not reported the scarcities they were facing to NHS England.
A spokesperson for the Society for Acute Medicine, which represents hospital doctors, said: “Medicine shortages can disrupt treatment and create additional pressure for clinical and pharmacy teams. The key is ensuring resilient supply chains, timely communication and access to suitable alternatives so patient care is not delayed.”
A health department spokesperson said: “We regularly speak to NHS trusts and national clinical leads about medicine availability and are aware that ramipril is in limited supply, which is why we issued serious shortage protocols so patients in the UK can still get the medication they need. We are working closely with relevant suppliers to resolve this and issues with co-codamol and aspirin to ensure continuity of supply.
“The vast majority of the UK’s licensed medicines are in good supply, and we have robust measures in place to mitigate disruption for patients. This government is investing in the UK medicine manufacturing industry to manage supply disruptions where they occur.”

UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

The world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, a United Nations report has warned.
More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority.
The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments.
Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.”
Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods.
Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources.
“This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states.
It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year.
Qu Dongyu, the FAO director general, said the report “makes clear that forest and landscape restoration is more than an environmental priority – it is a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development”.
He said: “The window for action is narrowing, and delayed or poorly designed restoration will increase long-term costs, exacerbate inequalities and risk locking landscapes into unsustainable trajectories. Given the continued loss and degradation of forest ecosystems, as well as growing global demand for land-based products and services, there is an urgent need to scale up effective restoration.”

====================================================================================================

Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:00:55 UTC
15:00:55 KST

Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.
The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.
Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since the M2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIY iMac.
The machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.
It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.
The mini runs the latest macOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design that was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.
Siri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.
Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.
Specifications
- 
  Processor: Apple M6
- 
  RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB
- 
  Storage: 256, 512GB, 1 or 2TB SSD
- 
  Operating system: macOS 27 Golden Gate
- 
  Ports back: 3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb Ethernet
- 
  Ports front: 2x USB-C (USB3), headphones
- 
  Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread
- 
  Dimensions: 127 x 127 x 50mm
- 
  Weight: 670g
Serious M6 speed
The Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.
For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.
The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.
Sustainability
The Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
Price
The Mac mini M6 costs from £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
For comparison, the A18 Pro MacBook Neo costs from £699, the M5 MacBook Air starts at £1,299, the M4 iMac starts at £1,499 and the Mac Studio costs from £2,499.
Verdict
The Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.
The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.
The only downside is the RAMageddon-linked price hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.
 Pros: very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.
