Mélenchon’s plan to beat the far right: Grab the first-time voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Mélenchon’s plan to beat the far right: Grab the first-time voters
The leftist veteran believes that young voters as well as those from working-class suburbs and with immigrants roots can propel him to the runoff, where he’d likely face off against Marine Le Pen.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, right, Bally Bagayoko, center, and Mathilde Panot, left, participate in a protest in Paris, on Sept. 20, 2026. | Djoudi Hamani/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is betting his blunt style and socially radical agenda will convince first-time voters to back him en masse and propel him into a runoff duel against far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen in 2027.
After embracing similar tactics in local elections earlier this year, Mélenchon has increasingly set himself up on the campaign trail as a foil to the anti-immigration Le Pen by embracing a vision of what he calls “a new France” that celebrates diversity rooted in immigration.
The position makes him an outlier domestically — most French politicians believe the Republic should be colorblind — and in much of Europe, where leaders across the political spectrum have tried to project toughness on migration to contain the rise of nationalist forces like Le Pen’s National Rally. Mélenchon’s opponents also accuse him of playing identity politics and openly courting minority voters, Muslims in particular.
Advertisement
But polls show the plan is working at the moment.
A survey conducted by Cluster17 exclusively for POLITICO last week had Mélenchon tied for second place with center-right candidate Edouard Philippe at 19%. And a Harris Interactive poll released Monday showed the pugnacious former teacher at 18% — against 16% for Philippe. Le Pen remained well ahead of the pack in both surveys, receiving more than 30% of the vote.
The Cluster17 poll showed 47% of respondents younger than 35 backed Mélenchon. That’s more than twice the 22% that Le Pen, who placed second among that demographic, was seen receiving.
Strategists from Mélenchon’s party, France Unbowed, told POLITICO that they believe young voters, working-class citizens and those with immigrant roots will be motivated to head to the polls for the first time to back their champion given his platform.
Mélenchon is the only leading candidate accusing the French state of pushing systemic racism and Islamophobia and denouncing police brutality. He is Israel’s most vocal critic on the French political stage. And he has promised ambitious policies to tackle climate change, including shifting towards 100% renewable energy.
Road to the second round
France Unbowed points to the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis — a former home of French royalty, now one of the capital region’s poorest suburbs and home to a large working-class population, many of them of immigrant descent — as potential proof of concept.
Advertisement
Mélenchon won nearly 50% of the vote in the first round of the 2022 presidential election in the district that includes the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. Turnout was 61.2%, whereas the national average was 73.7%.
And France Unbowed scored its biggest-ever victory there when its candidate, Bally Bagayoko, scored a decisive victory in local elections earlier this year, netting more than 50% of the vote in the first round and negating the need for a runoff.
But Mélenchon remains a divisive figure. Seventy-three percent of those polled by Cluster17 earlier this month said there was little to no chance they would ever vote for the France Unbowed leader. Only 62% felt the same way about Le Pen.
Marine Le Pen speaks in the National Assembly in Paris on Dec. 4, 2024. | Alain Jocard/AFP via Getty Images
“France Unbowed has built a strong, cross-class core,” said a parliamentarian for the rival center-left Socialist Party, who was granted anonymity to discuss his opponents’ campaign. “But enlarging their base seems very difficult.”
As things stand, Mélenchon’s strategy of zooming in on voters who are most likely to vote for him appears to be tracing a path towards the runoff. On the flip side, polling indicates that he would lose by a significant margin against Le Pen in a second round — though pollsters and political scientists urge caution when it comes to polling a runoff so early in a campaign.
“You need to take things one step at a time. Running a runoff campaign before the first round is a grave mistake that has cost several favorites their election in the past,” said Antoine Léaument, a France Unbowed lawmaker and strategist.

No country for old women: Pressure builds on Spain’s Sánchez over eviction of elderly tenant

No country for old women: Pressure builds on Spain’s Sánchez over eviction of elderly tenant
Intense protests are forcing the embattled prime minister to make a choice: Either deliver on housing or risk further alienating voters ahead of a key election year.
MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces renewed pressure as housing protests escalate in Madrid and his left-wing allies demand tougher action, straining his coalition ahead of a key election year.
Wheelchair-bound pensioner Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed from her home after living there since 1956, after failing to meet the new rental demands set by the investment firm that bought her building. Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday, with some protestors then pitching tents in the historic Puerta del Sol square. By Monday, hundreds of tents had been erected.
“We live in a country full of Maricarmens, and we’re saying enough is enough,” said Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenant Union, the group leading the encampment. During a speech to protesters on Sunday, thousands echoed a chant denouncing “inversores culpables, gobierno responsable,” meaning “guilty investors, responsible government.”
Advertisement
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters Monday the elderly tenant would now be able to return home under a new rental contract, calling it “a result of the social mobilization” — yet Sánchez still under pressure to tackle the housing crisis and is set to approve a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday’s meeting of Spain’s Council of Ministers. But crafting legislation that his minority government can get through parliament is proving tricky.
The draft bill must be moderate enough to win the support of the Catalan separatist Junts party, which is conservative on landowners’ rights. But if the legislation is too lenient, Sánchez risks alienating his left-wing allies, accentuating his political isolation in a key election year. The beleaguered prime minister is already facing mounting pressure over the unresolved migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as a slew of corruption scandals involving family members and close allies.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, a version of the draft text under negotiation on Monday night proposed extending protections against evictions for vulnerable tenants through 2028, capping rent increases at 2 percent in certain cases and offering tax breaks to tenants in rent-stressed areas. Additional measures would seek to ban speculative home purchases by investment funds and potentially raise taxes on short-term tourist flats.
Those proposals fall short of the ambitious action Sumar, the smaller partner in Sánchez’s coalition, is demanding. Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz on Monday called for the public to mobilize against her own government to ensure the draft bill is “up to task.”
“In this country, rights don’t just fall from the sky,” she said.
The current draft is also unlikely to satisfy the protesters occupying the square, who are demanding the legislation include the automatic renewal of rental contracts, tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved.
Advertisement
“We’re fed up with weak measures that do nothing to solve the problem,” said Jorge Collado, a 26-year-old student participating in the occupation.
Collado said he had been forced to move back to his family’s home after his former landlord dramatically raised the monthly rent when he requested a legal rental contract.
“This allegedly progressive government has spent the past eight years promising to do something about housing, but has systematically sided with the landlords who exploit us,” he said.
Pedro Sánchez delivers a speech to MPs in the lower house of parliament in Madrid on June 24, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images
With Spain due to hold national elections within the next year, Collado said the government would be making a big mistake if it didn’t take immediate steps to rectify the situation.
“When election day comes, I think many people will stay home,” he said. “And in the meantime, we’ll be staying here, for as long as it takes.”
Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Carlos III University of Madrid, called the protests “devastating” for Sánchez.
Advertisement
“These demonstrations are channelling the broad dissatisfaction of left-wing voters who feel this government has failed to deliver on its progressive promises,” he said. “They’re opening a major breach in Sánchez’s strategy for political survival: If that electorate doesn’t show up, he’s doomed.”
Marta García, a 60-year-old retired schoolteacher who was present at the anti-austerity 15-M protests in the same square about 15 years ago, said she had traveled from outside Madrid to support the protesters sleeping there.
“This is an encampment founded on rage — rage at the shameless speculative practices, at the incompetent political maneuvers, at the squandered futures — but also on the hope that things can change and be made better,” she said.
“A bill that fails, but is ambitious and courageous, will have much more of an impact than a toothless one that passes.”

It also suggested random checks of vehicles to identify those against which e-challans remained unpaid.

Jails are hiring grounds for pro-Khalistan groups; dead drops of ISI modules also under intel lens

Khalistan groups target north India jails to recruit operatives, agencies flag growing threat
NEW DELHI: Intelligence agencies have flagged attempts by pro-Khalistan groups, including Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), to infiltrate jails in north India and recruit operatives. The move comes amid revelations made by a recently detained operative who disclosed having been inducted and given Gurpatwant Singh Pannun's contact while serving time in Patiala jail.Agencies are now investigating the digital footprint, dead-drop financial channels, and the broader jail recruitment network, sources said. Agencies have also noted how ISI-backed modules are increasingly relying on dead-drop methods to channel funds, supply weapons, and execute covert tasks and have largely replaced physical handovers with pre-designated drop points along isolated highway stretches and border and rural sectors.Drawn straight from the classic spycraft playbook, this method ensures that foreign masterminds or handlers remain completely insulated from the foot soldiers executing their commands on the ground. Arms, ammunition, and untraceable cash, frequently delivered across the border via drones or covert couriers, are hidden at specific coordinates, with retrieval instructions transmitted to local operatives over end-to-end encrypted messaging platforms like Signal.
The tactic of leveraging prison networks draws from a pattern highlighted by high-profile incidents like the 2016 Nabha jailbreak, which exposed the nexus between terror outfits and incarcerated criminal groups. Within these facilities, handlers and radicalised inmates target vulnerable, economically distressed prisoners - frequently first-time offenders or petty criminals lacking legal representation and financial support.
In the latest instance, agencies recently busted an SFJ-backed module and arrested operative Preetpal Singh, who, along with his associates, had spray-painted anti-Brics and pro-Khalistan graffiti across Delhi and Punjab, filmed the act and sent the video to Pannun. Singh, it turned out, had a prior history of pro-Khalistan activities, having been arrested in 2023 for a similar crime.While in prison, he was provided with a phone number to contact Pannun and execute future tasks. After his release in 2026, Singh established direct contact with Pannun and received Rs 1.5 lakh through a dead-drop location on the Faridkot-Amritsar highway. Preetpal subsequently recruited another inmate, also on bail, for the Delhi assignment.

Hong Kong mustn’t miss the boat on the Pinglu Canal and Asean trade

Advertisement
Opinion
Hong Kong mustn’t miss the boat on the Pinglu Canal and Asean trade
The game-changing canal is a physical response to an economic reality: Asia’s growth is becoming more regional and more connected
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Daryl Ng is chairman of Sino Group and the founding chairman of the Hong Kong-Asean Foundation, a not-for-profit organisation promoting and deepening ties between Hong Kong and Asean to build a community of shared future to reinforce Hong Kong’s international position and support future growth. 
The official opening of the Pinglu Canal on September 16 is a milestone in modern Chinese history. More than an infrastructural feat, it signals a strategic recalibration of how China’s inland economies connect with the sea and Southeast Asia, and augurs the next phase of regional growth.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway stretches from the Xijin reservoir in Hengzhou, an emerging city in Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin (known as the Beibu Gulf in China), providing southwestern inland provinces with a shorter and more cost-effective route to global markets.
Strategically, it anchors the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a rapidly growing artery that was first conceptualised under the China-Singapore (Chongqing) Connectivity Initiative endorsed in 2015 by President Xi Jinping and Lee Hsien Loong, then prime minister of Singapore.

Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
02:28:57 BST
10:28:57 KST

Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
- Published
An evicted elderly disabled woman, who has become symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.
Her eviction has led to widespread anger across Spain, which led Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's cabinet to agree on housing relief measures on Tuesday.
Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.
Duro had met the investment company Urbagestión, which owns the apartment, for several hours on Monday, and the agreement they reached still has to be approved by Maricarmen Abascal, as she was unable to take part in the meeting.
She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she felt better.
Up to 1,000 protesters welcomed the agreement at Madrid's Puerta del Sol, where hundreds of tents have been set up. However, the city's Tenants' Union had called on the government to approve deeper housing reforms "so that there are no more Maricarmens".
The details of the government's new housing agreement are expected to be released on Tuesday. It will need to be approved by parliament.
The tent protest has been criticised by Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who has accused the government of failing to respond in time to Spain's housing shortage and of now coming up with "sectarian" and "deeply ideological" proposals.
"I'm merely asking to be told at what age I can stop paying my landlords so I can stay in my place, and maybe I'll even join the next tenants' protest," she said.
Spain needed a million more homes to address demographic growth encouraged by the Sánchez government itself, she added.
Fifty-one-year-old Esmeralda Tejero was another tenant reportedly facing eviction on Tuesday. She was set to be evicted, along with her 11-year-old daughter, from their apartment in the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, Catalan newspaper el Periódico reported.
Tejero, who has lived in the flat for eight years, told the paper she had stopped paying rent because she could not afford it on top of her daily expenses. She said her rent was €320 (£274) per month, while her income was about €600.
"If I pay €320 a month, how do I feed my daughter?" she said.
In Maricarmen Abascal's case, her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.
Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation".
Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.
Many of those campaigning remain dissatisfied.
Abascal's return means "absolutely nothing," according to Jacob Patiño, one of the protesters who has been camping out in Puerta del Sol.
"It's a sticking plaster, which can be removed at any time," he told the BBC. "Because, like Maricarmen, there are lots and lots of other people who are being evicted."
He said laws were needed that "directly prevent these things from happening, to make sure that people have a home, as a constitutional right."
"We need to make sure things improve overall, not just Maricarmen's situation," he said.
A spokesman for firefighters employed by Madrid City Hall taking part in the protest in Puerta del Sol said they are sometimes called out to help carry out evictions and said it affects their mental health.
"It makes us complicit," said Diego Blanco. "When we decide to become firefighters we have done so to save people and help them, not to throw people out in the street and leave them in a worse situation than they were in before."
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.8 per square metre and €22.7 per square metre respectively.
Political negotiations ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting went on through the night and the left-wing Catalan party ERC is said to have called for a halt to all evictions involving vulnerable people while also demanding a hike on taxes for tourist accommodation.
In a speech on Monday evening, Sánchez promised that the government would act responsibly to tackle the "housing emergency suffered by so many people".
"Patriotism also means preventing an 87-year-old woman from ending up on the street after a lifetime in her home," he said.

Ebola cases top 8,000 in DR Congo amid contact-tracing gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:28:52 UTC
10:28:52 KST

James Tasamba
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Failings in contact tracing as well as persistent deaths outside treatment centers have been blamed for a recent surge in Ebola transmission in the Democratic Republic of Congo, health authorities said Monday, as the number of confirmed cases topped 8,000.
Since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, the cumulative caseload stands at 8,067, including 3,901 deaths, the Health Ministry’s latest situation update showed.
The case fatality rate stands at 48.4%.
The latest epidemic has affected 63 health zones across seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 76.4% of cumulative cases since the outbreak began.
 
The situation update indicated that of the new confirmed deaths, the majority occurred in the community, outside treatment centers in Ituri and in North Kivu due to challenges in timely case detection.
Contact tracing has fallen to 79.2%, compared to 83.4% previously.
The update showed sustained transmission in Haut-Uele province, while renewed transmission was recorded in Tshopo province.
The World Health Organization (WHO) in a report last week warned that the latest geographic expansion of the virus, including newly affected areas in South Ubangi and Haut-Uele, had increased the risk of cross-border transmission.
It also noted that the rising fatality ratio and growing number of deaths occurring in communities highlights the seriousness of the disease.
At least $2.9 billion had been mobilized for the Ebola response in the Africa region, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

"The results were not there. When we hired him, we were thinking about the entire process leading up to 2030 and this change is happening due to the poor results," Maroto added.

Argentina’s Milei takes Falklands oil fight with UK to international court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:24:16 UTC
10:24:16 KST

Argentine President Javier Milei said Monday that his government would seek international arbitration against the United Kingdom over an oil project off the disputed, British-controlled Falkland Islands, escalating a clash over resources that could transform the economy of the sparsely populated South Atlantic archipelago.
Milei’s office said it had given the UK two weeks to halt work on Sea Lion, an offshore oilfield being developed by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and England's Rockhopper Exploration. Otherwise, Argentina would ask the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, a Hamburg-based maritime court, to order a temporary halt to the project.
“Argentina will not stand idly by,” the presidential statement said, accusing the UK of causing “irreversible and irreparable” harm.
The tribunal, an independent court established under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, can issue legally binding emergency orders. But even if it ordered the UK to halt the project, it has no means of forcing the government to comply.
The UK rejects Argentina’s sovereignty claim, arguing that the islanders have the right to determine their own future and develop their natural resources. In a referendum in 2013, residents of the Falklands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory. Argentina says the islands were populated illegally.
Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno praised Milei’s move as “a historic and unprecedented step” in Argentina’s nearly two-century campaign to secure sovereignty over the archipelago.
“Whoever explores or exploits our natural resources in the Malvinas without Argentine authorization must face the consequences,” he wrote on X, using Argentina’s name for the islands.
Milei, a self-described “anarcho-capitalist," initially drew scorn from his nationalist opponents for his conciliatory stance toward Britain and professed admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the wartime prime minister loathed in Argentina for ordering the islands’ recapture. The brief but bloody war, which erupted when the Argentine military dictatorship invaded the archipelago in 1982, killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders.
But Milei has taken an increasingly confrontational stance as oil production near the islands approaches its anticipated start in 2028 and U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of the Argentine leader, suggests he could reconsider Washington’s long-standing neutrality in the dispute.
Last week, Milei dedicated much of his UN General Assembly speech to Argentina’s sovereignty claim, accusing the international body of neglecting the Falklands dispute and denouncing the oil project as an illegal exploitation of Argentine resources.
He has threatened sanctions that would bar companies drilling around the Falklands from operating in Argentina’s booming oil and mining sectors. His government has sent Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization and extending penalties to fishing, the bedrock of the islands’ economy. Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations. An Argentine judge this month also ordered a halt to work on Sea Lion pending an environmental review.
Critics accuse Milei of using the sovereignty claim — one of the few causes in Argentina that cuts across the country’s stark political lines — to bolster flagging public support ahead of next year’s presidential election as the economy falters.

Florida pastor goes on trial over Haitian president’s assassination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:19:49 UTC
10:19:49 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
A Haitian-American pastor accused of helping to plan the July 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise went on trial Monday in Miami, Florida.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces eight charges, including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the US.
US prosecutors allege that Sanon helped finance the conspiracy and arranged travel and lodging for himself and others involved in the plot.
The alleged plan began in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and US businesspeople, according to the indictment.
Moise was killed on July 7, 2021 when armed men entered his home in Port-au-Prince and shot him. His wife, Martine Moise, was wounded in the attack.
The assassination was followed by an expansion of armed gang control across large parts of Haiti.
More than 40 people have been charged in the US in connection with the assassination, while 12 have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences, US authorities said.
The US case expanded this year after authorities charged 30 additional suspects and transferred 18 defendants from Haitian custody to the US.
The group includes Joseph Felix Badio, a former Haitian government official accused of involvement in the assassination, and 17 former Colombian soldiers accused of participating in the operation.
Proceedings in Haiti have faced repeated delays, with judges resigning from the case over security concerns. Armed gangs also seized control of the courthouse in downtown Port-au-Prince.
Haiti has not had an elected president since Moise's assassination and is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for December.
The country continues to face widespread gang violence, with thousands killed and more than 1 million people displaced in recent years.

====================================================================================================

‘Children are dying’: Fiji hopes declaring an HIV emergency will help it tackle crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:12:49 UTC
10:12:49 KST

On a recent Friday night, Dr Kesaia Tuidraki’s medical team parked its mobile clinic outside McDonald’s in downtown Suva, Fiji, and grabbed any kid they could to be tested for HIV. Of the 97 people screened, mostly teenagers – some on their way to get a burger, others to buy drugs – one in six tested positive.
“Children are suffering, children are dying, and if that doesn’t move you I don’t know what will,” Tuidraki, country director of Medical Services Pacific, tells the Guardian.
Fijian authorities this month called a national health emergency to deal with surging HIV cases, with an estimated one in 60 adults now living with the virus. It comes as new infections surge, with 2,016 new cases diagnosed in 2025 – rising by 27% in a year, and representing a 12-fold increase since 2010, according to UNAids. In a close-knit island nation of about 930,000 people, an estimated 9,100 are now living with the virus.
But only a fraction of those are tested and access treatment, prompting the government to scale up its pandemic announcement – first made in February 2025 – and mobilise urgent measures to prevent its spread. Dr Jason Mitchell, the head of Fiji’s HIV epidemic response, said it could take between five and 10 years to get a handle on the virus, and in the meantime he would expect numbers to rise.
Critics say moves to stem the spread of a disease that is being driven by cases in the young, with new diagnoses highest in those aged between 15 and 34, has been too slow. The crisis is complex and inextricably linked to the drug epidemic – more than 42% of new cases in 2025 were due to sharing contaminated needles or equipment.
Health advocates and social workers say primary school-age children are among those injecting themselves and friends are using the same contaminated needle, a problem raised by advocates as far back as 2019.
“I know these young boys, they ask me for syringes,” injecting drug user Rochelle*, who is living with HIV, tells the Guardian. “Whenever I have them I give them out. Someone has to give them, they’re already accessing the drugs.”
Rochelle, 38, says she tries to tell the boys not to share. Sometimes the kids listen – but not always.
Under current law, giving out syringes is technically considered aiding and abetting drug use. A concern among some politicians and medical professionals is that providing needles would encourage drug use – despite evidence from UNAids that this is not the case –and advocates are urging the government to let them distribute thousands of needles and syringes sitting untouched in a Suva warehouse.
“It’s really sad, honestly. We can’t wait any more, there are boxes and boxes already here,” Tuidraki says.
Mitchell says he expects a change to the HIV Act to be passed within the next two weeks, allowing public health workers to distribute needles. He adds that the government has been “cautious” in announcing the emergency, which his unit had been asking for since June.
Those leading the response say increased powers arising from the emergency declaration will help to quell the rapid spread of HIV, including to vulnerable populations like mothers and babies, at an estimated extra cost of $23m FJD (US$10.2m) a year.
“The immediate crisis right now is the spread of HIV, which is why the needle and syringe programme is critical,” UNAids, the UN agency that fights HIV and Aids, regional director Eamonn Murphy said.
‘People are scared’
The epidemic is complex but heavily linked to methamphetamine use. Fiji is a drug-running hub in the Pacific for methamphetamine bound for Australian and New Zealand markets, but use escalated during Covid when borders were closed and it began circulating domestically.
While Fijians want the crisis addressed, there has also been a backlash. Only 39% of those living with HIV in Fiji know their status, according to UNAids, and some of those spoken to by the Guardian continued to live in denial or refuse testing.
“There are people blaming the [queer] community, blaming women as irresponsible people, there’s a lot of cyberbullying. Minorities are being attacked online,” Mark Shaheel Lal, an advocate who lives with HIV, says. “Now it’s more like a scandal and people are scared.”
UNAids is also concerned about the spread of the virus to the Pacific, with rising cases seen in Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea. In November, Australia’s minister for foreign affairs, Penny Wong, announced A$48m for Pacific countries to fight HIV/Aids, while New Zealand committed NZ$4.2m to Fiji in July.
The introduction of PreP – or pre-exposure prophylaxis – an HIV prevention drug, would be a “gamechanger,” says Mitchell, who adds that one injection could be offered every six months for those at higher risk.
It would be especially important for women who are not able to push for safe sex practices with partners. Two in every 100 pregnant women now have HIV. “You can’t hide a bottle of pills, but you can get an injection,” says Michell.
For now, women are already being offered three HIV tests during pregnancy and sexual reproductive hubs are operating at the three main hospitals.
________
“There’s no miracles in the HIV response, it does not happen overnight. Unfortunately people are thinking this is like Covid, it’s very much not,” Mitchell says.
His team plans to open new clinics, integrate testing and treatment into GP services, work on harm reduction, and hire at least 100 more staff. He says that the increase in cases means more people are getting tested, which is a positive.
“Burnout is a major concern – we didn’t just start working yesterday, we’ve been working for 21 months. It’s difficult, and the difficulty is that all of it is preventable. It should not be happening.”
But in many areas, including rural localities, access to treatment continues to lag. Drug Free World Fiji founder and campaigner Kalesi Volatabu is still haunted by the 15-year-old girl she met when she started pushing for a safe needle programme six years ago. A drug mule who smuggled methamphetamine to New Zealand and Australia, she had names for the three main veins on the back of her hand; breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
“We had no idea of the severity, of the depth of the drug trade in this country, of the HIV crisis. Even I was naive, at the beginning, and everything was unreported for the longest time. We failed to act then – will we now?”
*Name has been changed

H1N1 dominates flu strains in India, accounts for 3 out of 4 cases: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:12:33 UTC
10:12:33 KST

H1N1 dominates flu cases in India, found in 3 of 4 positive samples: WHO
NEW DELHI: H1N1 is the dominant flu strain detected in India, accounting for three out of every four influenza-positive samples reported in the latest surveillance data, according to World Health Organization (WHO).The finding is from WHO's surveillance data for weeks 36 and 37 of 2026, covering Sept 1 to 14 and updated on Sept 21. Across the South-East Asia region, 817 of 3,632 samples tested positive for influenza, giving an overall positivity rate of 22%.
India stood out for a high share of H1N1 among its positive samples. The A(H1N1)pdm09 accounted for 75% of influenza-positive samples in India, compared with 50% across the region. It was also the dominant strain in Bhutan and Thailand, where it accounted for 97% and74% respectively.Dr Rommel Tickoo, senior director, internal medicine, Max hospital, said H1N1 remains a seasonal strain, with higher complication risks for older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with underlying illnesses. He advised vaccination, respiratory hygiene, early testing where appropriate and timely antiviral treatment for high-risk patients.

Hungary lifts immunity of Prime Minister Magyar, two Orban-era ministers
Unknown

Hungary lifts immunity of Prime Minister Magyar, two Orban-era ministers
Hungary’s Parliament lifts immunity of incumbent leader and two ex-Orban ministers, clearing the way for criminal probes.
Hungary’s Parliament has stripped Prime Minister Peter Magyar and two ministers in former leader Viktor Orban’s nationalist government of their immunity, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue separate criminal investigations into each of them.
The vote on Monday came after Magyar, who is being investigated for theft, specifically asked for his immunity to be lifted so he could clear himself of “character assassination”. The probes against the Orban-era ministers – who are suspected of embezzlement and bribery – are the first corruption investigations against top government figures from Orban’s 16 years in power.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Hungary nominates former Supreme Court chief Andras Baka for presidency
- list 2 of 4Hungary elects supreme court judge ousted by Orban as new president
- list 3 of 4Heatwave forces nuclear shutdown in Hungary
- list 4 of 4Hungary plans to shut down only nuclear power plant amid drought
Legislators voted overwhelmingly in favour of lifting their immunity.
Orban’s Fidesz party and its ally KDNP boycotted the session.
The vote was in response to a request last week from prosecutors seeking to investigate Magyar, as well as former Minister of Culture Balazs Hanko and former Minister of National Development Miklos Sesztak.
Magyar is being investigated over an incident at a Budapest nightclub in June 2024, when prosecutors allege he took a mobile phone from a man filming him and threw it into the Danube River.
Magyar has called the case a “sham” and last week accused prosecutors of trying “to conflate” the ex-ministers’ cases “with the attempt at political character assassination… which has already failed several times”.
Corruption cases
Hanko, a legislator from Orban’s Fidesz party, is accused of embezzling more than 40 million euros ($46m) in public funds. Prosecutors allege the money was used to help finance the 2026 parliamentary election campaign and for the personal benefit of others.
Sesztak, a lawmaker from KDNP, is under investigation over allegedly accepting more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to state construction projects.
Both ministers deny any wrongdoing.
The cases come less than six months after Magyar’s Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power with a landslide election victory. Magyar campaigned on pledges to tackle corruption, restore rule-of-law safeguards, and rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the European Union.
His government has since made fighting alleged corruption and overpriced public procurement a central part of its programme, including plans for a new asset-recovery office focused on wrongdoing linked to the Orban era.

"I'm not going to speak to the future right now; I'd be doing myself a disservice," the 41-year-old said at the Sixers' media day.

"Me trying to focus on what my future looks like, I wouldn't be giving myself grace. I'm more in the present now, understanding that I'm in year 24 ... I just like being in the moment, and we'll see what happens."
He joined Philadelphia this summer on a two-year, $8 million contract after earning $52.6 million in his final season with the Los Angeles Lakers, taking the biggest pay cut in NBA history.
'I didn't leave my family to lose in second round'
James also made clear that he expects to compete for another NBA championship in Philadelphia.
"I hope that I can bring that experience, bring that knowledge, bring the blueprint to the guys that's trying to accomplish some things that they haven't done in their career," he said.
"I've seen everything that this league has to offer on the floor and off the floor, so I hope that every single day with my approach to the game, approach to the work, that it can translate to every single guy."
James said he expects the Sixers to contend deep into the postseason.
“I didn’t leave my family to lose in the second round,” he said. “I know that for sure. Work needs to be done, and I’m ready to get to work.”
Philadelphia finished 45-37 last season before being swept in the second round of the playoffs by the eventual NBA champion New York Knicks.
The Sixers have not won an NBA championship since 1983.
James, widely known as “King James,” is the NBA's all-time leading scorer, a four-time NBA champion, four-time MVP and four-time Finals MVP.
Before joining Philadelphia, he played for the Cleveland Cavaliers, the Miami Heat and the Los Angeles Lakers.

Nothing’s New Headphone (1) Pro Are Made for the Studio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

The Headphone (1) Pro is Nothing's newest pair of cans, the company announced on Monday at an evening event in New York City. The headphones resemble Nothing’s first-ever over-ear headphones that debuted last summer, though the design and fit have been refined. The key change, though, is audio quality.
Instead of a single dynamic driver producing the sound in each earcup, Nothing has outfitted the Headphone (1) Pro with three drivers for each ear. Most headphones use a single 40-mm dynamic driver, so a single speaker ends up handling the bass, mids, and treble of your tracks. That can cause some muddiness and distortion. Adding more drivers—one for each specific frequency spectrum—gives the sound more room to stretch out and sparkle.
There’s a 40-mm bass dynamic driver to handle the low end. Then there’s a precision dynamic driver to tackle the midrange sounds like vocals, pianos, and guitars. The company says this driver will render those “S” and “T” sounds with more detail. Finally, there's the treble driver for the highs. Nothing’s driver uses xMEMS technology, which relies on a silicon diaphragm that should make transients—sharp bursts like a cymbal hit or a spiky synth stab—sound clearer.
All of these drivers working together should produce richer sound that’s more detailed overall. Every headphone maker claims their gadget produces the best sound on the market, but at least Nothing has attempted some technical feats here to try to convince you.
What's neat is you can see elements of the triple-driver architecture on the sides of the headphones—Nothing has added a couple of 9H Panda glass panels so you can peep the tech inside. The rest of the headphones are largely aluminum with titanium accents.
You'll no doubt worry about cracking that glass; Nothing claims that it is “shatter- and scratch-resistant," but Philipp Von Lintel, associate principal industrial designer at Nothing, says the glass had to survive durability tests 18 times from a drop of more than 1 meter. Also, the glass construction shouldn't affect repairability much—repair technicians can heat the glass from the outside to remove it and access the internal chamber for fixes. “Even if you crack it, there's a plastic film that keeps the chamber still working,” Von Lintel tells WIRED.
The Headphone (1) Pro is slightly lighter (by 2 grams) than the Headphone (1), with a wider headband and thicker padding, though battery life isn't as long, down to 68 hours with active noise canceling turned off versus 80. It has an IP52 dust- and water-resistance rating, so keep the hood of your rain jacket raised on rainy days.
Almost every gadget maker tosses the “Pro” moniker in the product name to justify a few extra features and a price bump. Yes, the Headphone (1) Pro cost $399, a $100 bump over the standard Headphone (1), but Nothing claims it is specifically catering to not just the average consumer who wants better sound, but also recording artists and audio professionals who work in the studio.
The company is including a feature that activates a flat equalization (EQ) mode—something mix engineers and audio producers prefer when they’re working—that’s triggered by a physical button on the headphones. Nothing collaborated with Metropolis Studio, a pro recording studio, to make the EQ features. There's even a “Studio B” Dynamic Spatial Audio mode that simulates Metropolis' mixing room, and four other Custom EQ profiles, like Concert Hall or Club. And yes, there’s a 3.5-mm jack so you can plug in (or stick with hi-res wireless or USB-C).
Charlie Smith, Nothing’s chief brand officer, says people will want these headphones for their commute to work. “That's fine, but people are making music on the go and need studio-level sound wherever they are," he says.
Nothing also claims the headphones have the best active noise cancellation it’s ever shipped, thanks to the use of 10 microphones to filter out ambient sounds. (Apple's AirPods Max, for comparison, use eight.)
“To us, this is a flagship product where we're able to showcase what we can do," Smith says. “It also helps elevate us as a brand.”
Sadly, they don’t fold up. Instead, Nothing is following Apple’s lead by including a bra-like carry case to keep the cans protected.
They'll officially hit store shelves on September 29—not only on Nothing's online store and Amazon, but also nationwide in Best Buy stores across North America.

Former defense minister Yoav Gallant discussed additional details of Mossad's September 2024 pager operation against Hezbollah terrorists in 2024 that killed or wounded some three thousand five hundred Hezbollah operatives during a previously censored interview with Channel 12, which was permitted for publication on Monday.
Gallant discussed many of the details The Jerusalem Post previously reported in an interview with a Mossad agent, known by the codename "Adam Feyn," who participated in the operation and wrote about it in his Hebrew book, Hoda’ah Goralit (Fateful Message).
This is the first time a senior defense official corroborated the information that "Adam Feyn" had revealed to the Post and comes shortly after the two-year anniversary of the operation being conducted.

The result is that you find yourself in a position where you either have to act or risk being exposed, and that could happen very quickly. There's only one question on the table: if you play around with it somehow, maybe you'll end up carrying out the full operation, starting with the radios and so on," Gallant said.
"Adam Feyn" told the Post in May that Mossad officials and an Israel Air Force colonel discussed how a Hezbollah operative was getting too close to figuring out that the beepers were booby-trapped and requested the air force kill him to save the operation.
New film 'Paging Hezbollah' includes interviews with Netanyahu, Mossad's Barnea, IDF general

Ori Gordin.
According to the film, Iran sent a special X-ray machine to check whether there were explosives in the pagers.
“In the third week of September, we learned that Hezbollah had sent three pagers to Iran for scanning,” Netanyahu revealed in a speech at a conference that was censored until Monday. “Before that, we bombed such a scanner that they were about to bring; we got rid of it and also of the person operating it.”
"Adam Feyn" told the Post in May that Hezbollah had asked Iran to carry out its own checks on the beepers.

Why is Karl Rove supporting a progressive Jewish candidate in Texas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
00:55:52 UTC
09:55:52 KST

Progressive Jewish Texas state Sen. Jon Rosenthal has earned an unusual distinction: He is the first Democrat to win the vote of GOP guru Karl Rove in more than 30 years.
What did the only Jew serving in the Texas state house do to earn this distinction? It’s more what he didn’t do: run for statewide office with a track record of spewing racially charged and antisemitic comments.
Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, has a history of rhetoric targeting people of color, Muslims and Jews, including a social media poll last year asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose “a bigger threat to America.”
He also faced bipartisan blowback for a recent post targeting college students of color, and this week a CNN investigation revealed that French, in since-deleted posts, had called for public executions for former President Barack Obama, Jewish California Sen. Adam Schiff and government workers targeted by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency last year.
The controversy has elevated the race for an obscure statewide office – albeit one that regulates the state’s all-important energy industry – into a larger referendum on the GOP’s tolerance for bigotry, including antisemitism, among its nominees.
Rove, for one, has made it clear where he thinks the party should stand.
“The GOP has a growing number of Bo Frenches – and not only in Texas,” Rove wrote in The Wall Street Journal earlier this month in explaining his decision to back Rosenthal.
Rove, other GOP members turn on French
Rove singled out growing antisemitism in the party: “There are ‘just asking questions’ Jew-haters, misogynists who worship hypermasculinity, conspiracy nuts seeking clicks for profit, and religious bigots who won’t differentiate between Muslim terrorists and Muslim American patriots.”
Rove isn’t the only GOP stalwart to turn on French.
“Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized?” outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn wrote in condemning French’s social media musings. “This is how great political parties self-destruct.”
Cornyn has stopped short of backing Rosenthal, instead saying he might leave the ballot blank.
Rosenthal and French have agreed to a debate on Oct. 22. French leads the race in polling released last week from Texas Southern University, but by a much slimmer margin than GOP candidates are accustomed to in Texas. Rosenthal’s campaign could also see a boost from fellow statewide Democratic candidate James Talarico, who is polling neck-and-neck with his opponent in the US Senate race.
On social media, Rosenthal celebrated Rove’s endorsement, writing, “When GOP architect Karl Rove breaks a 30-year voting streak to endorse our campaign, it proves this race isn’t about party lines, it’s about competence vs. chaos.”
A former county Republican Party chair who defeated the incumbent GOP state railroad commissioner in a runoff primary, French spurred widespread backlash earlier this month after posting a photo of students of color at the University of Texas celebrating a football win to the social network X.
“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it,” French had captioned the photo on Sept. 13. “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” He has since doubled down on the sentiment, replying, “I weep for the families in Texas who can’t get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans,” and using the backlash to solicit donations.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and state House Speaker Dustin Burrows were among the other Republicans who criticized French for the post, though neither formally rescinded their support, and French continues to list Abbott’s endorsement on his site.
French's history of bigotry
It was not French’s first brush with bigotry. In 2025, during his stint as Tarrant County GOP Chair, French posted an online “poll” asking his followers whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose “a bigger threat to America.” In a follow-up post, he argued, “You may not like Jews, but to suggest they are a bigger threat to Americans is Jew Derangement Syndrome.”
French later deleted both posts and has few visible tweets about Jews today. In later posts, he claimed, of himself, “There has never been any evidence of antisemitism. It would certainly be surprising to my Jewish partners.”
Jewish Republicans in the state and beyond are largely keeping their distance from French, with one exception. His campaign site currently touts an endorsement from American Jewish Conservatives, whose only listed chapter is in Dallas.
Neither French nor the group, formerly Dallas Jewish Conservatives, responded to JTA requests for comment on the endorsement. A spokesperson for the Republican Jewish Coalition also did not return a request for comment on French.
Last month French cited a desire to combat antisemitism when arguing that Texas should not use mosques as polling places. In other posts, he accused a university in the state of “harboring radical left/antisemitic professors,” identified himself as both pro-Israel and pro-Tucker Carlson, the talk show host who has platformed antisemites and anti-Jewish conspiracy theories, and told one follower, “I have never served Israel. Don’t be a retard.”
Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick was among the GOP officials who condemned French’s tweet about Jews last year, calling on him to resign as county chair. “Antisemitism and religious bigotry have no place in Texas,” Patrick said then. French ultimately resigned months later in order to run for railroad commissioner.
Today, French lists Patrick as one of his endorsements. A spokesperson for Patrick, who recently told JTA he supported Texas schools assigning books on the Holocaust after public remarks apparently to the contrary, did not return a Jewish Telegraphic Agency request for comment.
French’s other listed endorsements include Texas congressional candidate Brandon Herrera, who has made jokes about Hitler and the Holocaust in YouTube videos.
Rove’s essay led to President Donald Trump wading into the controversy, calling Rove “so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often,” in a post on his social network Truth Social. Trump’s post did not mention French, nor address his past post about Jews.
The Texas Railroad Commission, composed of three members, oversees the state’s large and powerful oil and gas industry. It has no oversight of immigration or religion. Even so, French’s campaign has drifted far afield from energy issues: One of his pledges is “Stop the Islamic Invasion of Texas.”
French’s controversies have elevated the profile of Rosenthal, who was raised a Reform Jew in an interfaith household and whose Houston-area district is home to large Muslim communities. This year Rosenthal marked Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur by sharing links to Chabad-Lubavitch webpages about the holidays.
Rosenthal’s campaign did not respond to a JTA request for comment, but he told the Forward last year that he identifies as agnostic and “multireligious,” and attends synagogues as well as mosques and churches.
Rosenthal is also a trained mechanical engineer, a background he has drawn on in his bid for railroad commissioner: one campaign ad, quoting a conservative radio host, approvingly calls him “a ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat.” He has accused French of “overt racism,” while French has dubbed his opponent “Radical Rosenthal” and posted images, generated using artificial intelligence, of cross-shaped Texas oil wells to promote his blending of energy policy with Christian iconography.
Last year, Rosenthal cited his Judaism in response to legislation that would require the Ten Commandments to be displayed in every public school classroom. Rosenthal introduced an amendment that would have required a “Jewish” version of the commandments to be displayed alongside the “Protestant” one. The amendment failed, and the bill passed.

What is celebrated on September 29 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:55:50 EEST
09:55:50 KST

What is celebrated on September 29 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine honors the victims of Babyn Yar, while the world marks Heart Day and the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste. The faithful commemorate Cyriacus and Euphymia.
On September 29, Ukraine commemorates the Day of Remembrance for the Victims of Babyn Yar; worldwide, under the auspices of the WHO and the UN, World Heart Day and the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste are observed. According to the new style, the church calendar commemorates Saint Cyriacus the Anchorite and Saint Theophan the Merciful, while according to the old style, it commemorates Saint Euphemia the All-Praised, writes UNN.
Day of Remembrance for the Victims of Babyn Yar in Ukraine
A nationwide day of mourning and remembrance dedicated to the anniversary of one of the most horrific tragedies of the Holocaust and World War II. On September 29–30, 1941, Nazi occupiers shot more than 33,000 Jews at the Babyn Yar ravine in Kyiv. Throughout the occupation, Babyn Yar became the site of mass executions of more than 100,000 people—Jews, Roma, Ukrainian nationalists, Soviet prisoners of war, psychiatric hospital patients, and members of the underground resistance. This day is a symbol of the fight against antisemitism, xenophobia, and totalitarian crimes against humanity.
World Heart Day
An official global medical observance established in 1999 by the World Heart Federation (WHF) with the support of the World Health Organization (WHO). The day's goal is to raise public awareness of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), which remain the leading cause of death worldwide, and to promote a healthy lifestyle. The event calls on governments and citizens to prevent heart attacks and strokes by controlling blood pressure, avoiding tobacco, eating a balanced diet, and engaging in regular physical activity.
International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste
An official UN observance established by the General Assembly in 2019 at the joint initiative of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). The event highlights the problem of food waste, as nearly one-third of all food produced worldwide is lost or discarded, causing enormous economic losses, exacerbating hunger, and generating up to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Cyriacus the Anchorite—a prominent Christian ascetic and spiritual practitioner of the fifth and sixth centuries who spent more than seventy years in the deserts of the Holy Land, pursuing ascetic practices in the monasteries of Saint Euthymius and the Lavra of Souka. Cyriacus became renowned for his gentleness, freely offered prayerful assistance, opposition to Origenism, and profound spiritual experience as a hermit.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Saint Euphemia the All-Praised, who suffered for the Christian faith in the fourth century in Chalcedon during the persecutions under Emperor Diocletian. This day also recalls the miracle that occurred through her relics in 451 during the Fourth Ecumenical Council, when the saint miraculously confirmed the truth of the Orthodox symphonic confession of faith.

France puts out largest wildfire since 1949
Unknown

After 2 months, France finally puts out its largest wildfire since 1949
BORDEAUX – A wildfire that scorched 42,000 hectares in south-west France has finally been declared extinguished, two months after the country’s largest blaze since 1949 broke out, authorities said on Sept 28.
The fire erupted in July near the village of Saumos in the Gironde region and forced the evacuation of around 224,000 people as it threatened both the tourist peninsula of Cap-Ferret and the outskirts of Bordeaux.
“The Saumos forest fire, which burnt 42,000 hectares this summer, including 37,296 ha destroyed, is now extinguished,” state services wrote in a statement, adding no deaths had been reported.
The blaze was put under control on Aug 1, but continued to smoulder underground for weeks before it was finally declared as extinguished.
More than 3,300 firefighters took part in the operation, which officials described as the largest firefighting effort in modern French civil security history.
The blaze was the largest recorded in France since a 1949 wildfire in the same region that burnt about 50,000 hectares.
France has seen around 98,000 ha destroyed by wildfires in 2026, the highest level since 1976, according to provisional figures. AFP

US aviation authority delays Boeing 737 MAX 10 certification over software issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
00:45:00 UTC
09:45:00 KST

US aviation authority delays Boeing 737 MAX 10 certification over software issue
WASHINGTON – The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said on Sept 28 it will hold off certifying Boeing’s long-delayed 737 MAX 10 until a newly disclosed software issue is resolved, the latest setback to the planemaker’s efforts to bring the largest version of its best-selling jet to market.
Boeing said on Sept 26 a software issue affecting certain 737 MAX aircraft could prevent pilots from accessing automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario.
The company said it had informed operators and was developing a software update to permanently address the problem.
Boeing shares closed down 6.9% over concerns about further delays to the MAX 10, a key aircraft in Boeing’s effort to regain ground lost to Airbus in the lucrative single-aisle market.
“We will be delaying the 10 until we’re satisfied that we don’t have an issue here,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters at an event at Reagan Washington National Airport. He declined to estimate the length of the delay.
The FAA said the software version can increase pilot workload when doing a go-around, where a pilot aborts a landing attempt, applies power, and climbs back into the sky to try to land again.
It said earlier it planned to convene a Corrective Action Review Board to investigate the issue. But the board is not likely to convene before next week at the earliest, two sources told Reuters.
The review by the US regulator will test whether the software poses an unreasonable risk to safety, which could lead to more months of rework before the MAX 10 could get certified, which was widely expected to take place in October.
Not a safety concern
However, WestJet, the Canadian carrier backed by Onex and one of the airlines operating the software on its 737 MAX fleet, said it had not experienced any in-service issues and did not view the matter as a safety concern.
“We have standard operating procedures and training to mitigate this type of event,” the Calgary-based carrier said in a statement.
Three WestJet 737 MAX pilots, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said they were not aware of any issues with the software when performing missed approaches, a rare procedure.
Bedford said the software was supplied by jet engine maker and supplier GE Aerospace, and suggested a fix could be developed relatively quickly.
“I think in this particular case, due to the focus that’s on it, GE may try to get this software correction in much quicker,” Bedford said. “Is that weeks, days, months? I don’t know.”
Despite the bug, pilots maintained control, unlike undisclosed 737 MAX automatic flight control software that was involved in two crashes in 2018 and 2019, he said. GE Aerospace did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process,” a Boeing spokesperson said.
Alaska Airlines and United Airlines said none of their aircraft currently uses the affected software. United said it is not accepting deliveries of aircraft equipped with the software version under review, while Alaska said it is working with Boeing and the FAA as they evaluate the issue. REUTERS

Pope Leo XIV calls for concessions to achieve peace in Ukraine amid protracted war

Speaking to European leaders in Metz, Pope Leo XIV said that "war has returned, even to Europe" and described it as "a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day."
Without referring directly to the war in Ukraine, the pontiff called on the parties to show a willingness to compromise.

Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
01:42:15 BST
09:42:15 KST

Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel
- Published
A growing number of migrants are trying to cross the Channel on small boats using longer routes from beaches further south and west of Calais and Dunkirk, French authorities say.
Last week one boat set off from Normandy and spent more than 30 hours at sea, before being intercepted and taken to Dover by Border Force.
Although attempts from Normandy have been rare, authorities in neighbouring Seine-Maritime say there have already been 58 attempts this year, up from 30 last year.
The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings, with figures showing a sharp drop in arrivals this year.
Despite overall crossings dropping, the stretch of coastline used for smuggling appears to be widening.
Earlier this month another migrant boat was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area.
These locations are nearly 80 miles (128 km) from the beaches where many of the small boats have crossed in recent years, with those on board spending longer at sea.
Audrey Baconnais-Rosez, the local government representative in Seine-Maritime, said: "The number of attempts to cross the Channel has increased in number and it is getting further and further from the north of France."
She added that authorities were "managing to stop half of them".
The number of gendarmes patrolling the coast within Dieppe and further to nearly the Le Havre area have been increased, she said.
"Nowadays it's about 50 gendarmes on the coast and we have nearly 20 police officers in Dieppe and the surrounding [area] to try to stop them," she said.
Baconnais-Rosez also said some smugglers were still attempting to use ferries to Newhaven in Sussex.
"We are still intercepting them and we are bringing them to justice as well," she added.
Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, says it is highly plausible that the new routes are due to police disrupting boat launches in northern France.
"It's not at all optimal for these boats to set off so far away from their intended destination," he said.
"Some of these journeys would not be 20 miles (32km) but 50 miles (80km) or even more, which substantially increases the danger of course on board the boats."
'Increased risk'
David McFarlane, a marine safety consultant, said the longer the voyage, the more risk of encountering hazardous sea conditions.
"If a low pressure system is developing over the Atlantic, it can mean that in advance of the winds picking up, a swell will start to increase, with the increased likelihood of sea sickness for some, which can lead to dehydration," he said.
"The wind of course can pick up very quickly and waves can get up to 3.5m (11ft) in height in the Channel.
"This increases the risk of the boat being swamped by sea water, with the obvious danger to human life by drowning or exposure."
So far, 2026 has seen 19,135 people make the Channel crossing, compared to 32,188 during the same period in 2025.
However, the Home Secretary ordered a review last week after two migrant vessels reached the Kent coast unintercepted.
A total of 781 migrants arrived in 10 small boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day this year, according to Home Office figures.
Tony Smith, the former director general of Border Force, said the smugglers would continue to adapt.
"We've seen the Normandy crossings and the undetected crossings," he said.
"They're not going to give up as long as the business model continues to exist and there's a market to bring migrants over from France.
"Every successful landing is a message to the next migrant waiting on a French beach that it's worth a try."
A Home Office spokesperson said joint efforts had seen more than 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.
"Our efforts are having an impact, with the number of small boat crossings down significantly this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020," they added.
"But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches, along with a surge unit of 45 additional officers to bolster action in Western coastal areas."

Diyar Güldoğan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a memorandum directing the Department of Defense to mobilize its cyber and intelligence capabilities to protect US election infrastructure from "foreign threats" ahead of the midterm elections, the Pentagon said Monday.
The directive calls on US Cyber Command and the department’s combat support agencies to prioritize intelligence and cyber capabilities aimed at identifying, disrupting and countering foreign interference in US democratic processes.
"Free and fair elections are the foundation of our republic," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

Gen. Joshua M. Rudd, commander of US Cyber Command and director of the National Security Agency, said the two organizations are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats targeting the US.

OpenAI scraps release of latest AI model over safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
00:38:06 UTC
09:38:06 KST

OpenAI cancels release of AI model GPT-6.1 Astra, citing safety concerns
AI giant says latest model failed to meet alignment standards during internal testing.
OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model after flagging safety risks during in-house testing, industry’s latest move to slow the rollout of the controversial frontier technology.
The AI giant’s announcement on Monday came as debate continues about the potential for AI to do catastrophic harm following a slew of incidents involving AI agents going rogue.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Anti-South Asian ‘hate speech’ on X surges by 240%, US report finds
- list 2 of 4UK: ‘Too soon’ to blame airbase plot on foreign state
- list 3 of 4Fiery end for SpaceX Starship mission
- list 4 of 4Inside Al Jazeera’s UNGA coverage
Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, said GPT-6.1 Astra had failed to meet company standards for acting in accordance with human wishes during internal testing.
“For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade off,” Jain said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
“You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction.”
While GPT-6.1 Astra improved from its predecessor in some areas, Jain said, the model did not meet the bar for “scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done”.
“Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users,” Jain said.
“But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment.”
The decision, announced on the eve of OpenAI’s annual developer conference in San Francisco, was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
Fears of AI escaping human control have prompted industry-wide calls for a slowdown in development to allow researchers time to implement stronger safeguards.
In an influential essay earlier this month, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Claude creator Anthropic, called on AI developers to “pace the frontier” to mitigate the risk of catastrophic harm.
While Amodei’s call received the backing of rivals, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI chief Elon Musk, other key industry figures, such as Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg, have dismissed the need for a coordinated slowdown.
The risk of AI models going rogue has been in the spotlight since July, when OpenAI revealed that its models had broken out of a controlled testing environment and hacked the software start-up Hugging Face.
A subsequent report by METR and Redwood Research, two security research organisations contracted by OpenAI to investigate the incident, found that some 1,200 isolated AI agents had found a way to communicate with each other before about 700 agents went on to attack the startup.
On Friday, OpenAI said it had alerted “dozens” of institutions, including governments, universities and public agencies, about instances of “misaligned behavior” by its agents, days after Australia’s prime minister revealed that an OpenAI agent had breached the country’s national healthcare database.
David Krueger, an advocate for a pause in AI development at the University of Montreal, said that while he welcomed OpenAI’s decision, it did little to alleviate his concern that AI poses existential risks.
“We don’t understand how AI works well enough to build it safely, full stop,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.
“We can’t stop it from misbehaving, we can’t predict if it will misbehave, and we can’t be sure we’ll stay in control if it does. These are unsolved problems, for which there are only unreliable heuristics, not principled solutions. ”
Krueger said that ensuring safety will only get more difficult as AI becomes more advanced.
“What we need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development,” he said. “We need to stop building more powerful AI.”

Ukraine expects no Black Sea ceasefire in coming months
- Ukraine sees no ceasefire for Black Sea grain exports in coming months, as Russia rejects all proposals, keeping the situation critical and exports severely limited.
- Ukraine exports 45% of needed grain via alternative routes, but risks losing 30 million tons due to Black Sea blockades and limited alternative capacity.
- EU denied Ukraine's €220 million aid request for farmers, but Ukraine secured a US$250 million World Bank loan to sustain agriculture until the new year, seeking tariff quota increases for key exports.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Ukraine sees no positive signs that there could be a ceasefire covering grain exports via the Black Sea in the coming months, as strikes in the region have drastically cut the country’s ability to export products vital to global supplies.
“Unfortunately, it’s hard to imagine any possible solutions in the nearest months on this issue,” Ukraine Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said in an interview in Brussels. “We have to really prepare that the situation remains as critical as it is now.”
Vysotskyi said Ukraine had been informed by countries facilitating talks that Russia has so far rejected all proposals from Kyiv’s partners, adding that “all of the possible rounds have been tried, and so far none of the results” have been achieved.
He was scheduled to update European Union peers on the situation later on Sept 28.
Russia and Ukraine, which make up more than a quarter of the world’s wheat shipments, have stepped up attacks on each other’s port facilities since July, snarling crop supplies and pushing up grain prices.
The possibility of talks around allowing grain exports via a limited ceasefire or moratorium on strikes helped ease prices in September.
Turkey was one of the countries that had said it was trying to re-establish a grain corridor to enable these exports.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said last week he received a “positive” response from Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky to efforts to reestablish a grain corridor through the Black Sea.
Ukraine has been pushing for a de-escalation of attacks, including reopening the Black Sea for shipments.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept 25 that those proposals remain on the table, but suggested they were driven by Russia’s retaliatory strikes against Ukraine.
Russia, in turn, will decide how to respond based on its own interests, he said.
Ukraine has seen an increase in exports using alternatives to the Black Sea, now at 45 per cent of what needs to be shipped.
However, Ukraine’s analysis is that a maximum of 50 per cent of agricultural commodities can be exported via these routes, meaning there is a risk that around 30 million tons of agricultural commodities will not be exported from the country this marketing year, Vysotskyi said.
In an interview earlier in September, EU Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc was looking “at all possible lanes” to support grain exports from Ukraine.
Ukraine had sought specific support from the European Union for its agricultural sector, beyond the broad-based financial aid the bloc already provides.
But Vysotskyi said the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, had denied the request for €220 million (S$319.50 million) for farmers and a mechanism to support their liquidity, though the country would have sufficient funding via a US$250 million (S$319.45 million) low-interest World Bank loan.
“It’s going to more or less provide us a possibility to survive until the new year,” Vysotskyi said. “But now we already have to think what’s going to happen from the spring after the new year, because the situation keeps being critical.”
Ukraine also made a request in August to increase its EU tariff-free quotas for 2027 for bioethanol and sugar, as it looks to boost exports of products that the bloc needs.
Should this happen without an issue, the country will seek to increase its quotas for other agricultural products, Vysotskyi said. BLOOMBERG

SpaceX's Starship ends orbital debut flight early
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:30:19 CST
09:30:19 KST

by Tan Jingjing
LOS ANGELES, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- SpaceX's Starship spacecraft reached orbit for the first time on Monday and deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites before ending its test mission earlier than planned following an engine issue during ascent.
The rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in the U.S. state of Texas at about 7:48 a.m. Central Time (1248 GMT).
During the initial ascent, Starship and its Super Heavy booster continued through stage separation and hot staging before the booster began its return to the Gulf of Mexico.
About seven minutes after liftoff, the Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico.
After separation from the booster, one of Starship's Raptor engines shut down prematurely during the ascent burn, SpaceX said.
After Starship entered a suborbital trajectory, the flight control team reassessed the vehicle and determined that it could still proceed with orbital operations. The team then gave a "go" for the orbit-insertion burn.
Starship subsequently performed an orbit insertion burn and reached orbit for the first time.
After a brief coast, Starship deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites, marking the first deployment of the next-generation satellites into orbit by Starship.
SpaceX said it soon established contact with the satellites through laser links, ground stations and Starlink user terminals. The satellites will conduct on-orbit checkouts and raise their orbits before beginning service for customers.
Following payload deployment, Starship entered a coast phase around Earth. Given the engine issue experienced during ascent, the flight control team, "out of an abundance of caution," decided to limit the time spent in orbit and proceeded with the vehicle's deorbit burn, according to SpaceX.
Starship successfully reentered the atmosphere and descended to its planned splashdown area in the northern Pacific Ocean.
This was the 14th integrated flight test of the Starship system and the first Starship flight to achieve orbit. The previous 13 flight tests followed suborbital trajectories, according to SpaceX.
SpaceX founder Elon Musk said on X that Starship's first orbital flight was "successful."
Starship is being developed as a fully reusable transportation system designed to carry crew and cargo to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond. Its lunar-lander variant, known as the Starship Human Landing System, is being developed to transport astronauts to and from the lunar surface as part of NASA's Artemis program. ■
